“I won’t lie to you, it was hard at first. It was a challenge for me,” she said. “But I think I’ve learned to see their sensitive side and to bring out what is pure within them. I’ve come to understand that ‘Godot’ means something different to everyone … I am truly glad to have met these wonderful people.”
Since 2009, the festival has taken place every year except 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, and hundreds of inmates have performed in scores of plays penned by both professionals and prisoners.

While participation doesn’t guarantee a shorter sentence or other privileges, it can earn inmates selected for the performances bonus points, which they can apply toward extra visitors or faster access to parole.
Tuesday wasn’t the first time stepping onto the stage for 32-year-old inmate Pavel Alexandru Cristian, who appeared in “Locked Within Myself.”

“I was selected three years ago. This year, we will be performing a piece — a monologue-based performance — centered on our inner fears,” he said. “I will play the role of a police officer, tasked with drawing certain conclusions by the end.”

Maria Caramalau, a prison police inspector at Vaslui Prison in eastern Romania, said the productions give inmates opportunities to show a side of themselves that even they might struggle to see beyond.
“When you are someone deprived of your liberty you tend to see yourself as having only flaws,” she said.

“But in the moment you receive applause on stage, when a person’s positive side is revealed, it becomes clear that … whether free or behind bars, art has the power to help us escape, in a sense, from our own fears.”
McGrath reported from Leamington Spa, England.

title: Heavy fighting erupts in Haiti as armed forces fight gangs to regain control of key corridor
summary: Armed forces in Haiti have launched an aggressive operation to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions
story: Armed forces in Haiti have launched an aggressive operation to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Armed forces in Haiti launched an aggressive operation on Thursday to remove powerful gangs long entrenched in a key corridor that connects the country’s capital to its western and southern regions.
It is the first significant operation in the five years since violent gangs seized control of Martissant, located in the western tip of Port-au-Prince.

Haiti’s National Police posted a video on X stating that at least 34 suspected gang members were killed in Martissant during a fight with police officers working with a task force composed of members from Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince.
Local media reported heavy gunfire and explosive drones in the area as Haiti’s police posted a video of armored vehicles rumbling through the community.

Martissant is located along Route 2, the main road that leads out of Port-au-Prince to important western and southern cities. Thousands of people would travel through Martissant every day before gangs seized control of the area more than five years ago, disrupting the country’s economy as they prevented goods from entering or leaving the capital. Gangs have since charged tolls or randomly opened fire on cars or buses that dare cross through.
Ever since gangs seized absolute control of Martissant, aid workers and Haitian civilians have been forced to take alternative transportation or use rural back roads.

The fight to control Martissant began in June 2021, when gangs from Grand-Ravine and Village-de-Dieu attacked the Ti-Bois gang. Armed men set fire to homes, killed families, destroyed businesses and seized control of Martissant’s police station.
The clashes forced at least 19,000 people to flee their homes and affected some 800,000 people overall, according to a July 2022 United Nations report.
Several years ago, gangs operating between Tabarre and Carrefour would demand some $380 from those transiting through Martissant, according to a 2023 U.N. report.

Last year, Haiti’s Center for Analysis and Research in Human Rights noted that ever since Martissant fell, hundreds of public and private institutions were relocated and more than one million people were forced to flee their homes.
As the fight in Martissant continues, a U.N.-backed gang suppression force also has made recent inroads against gangs in a push to not only displace them but prevent their return.
“Operations are entering a new phase: increasing pressure on gang networks, dismantling more strongholds, and extending control over strategic areas,” the force wrote Thursday on X.
The gang suppression force said it’s working in places including Tabarre in Port-au-Prince and in Haiti’s central Artibonite region, which has come under repeated violent attacks by armed men.
The force said it has come under fire as it advances along Route 5, “removing obstacles established by gangs to isolate communities and control key routes.”
The force said it also cleared and secured a church and school that gangs had been controlling north of Gros-Morne.

“It is about restoring freedom of movement, reopening access to public institutions, and re-establishing State presence for communities that have endured years of gang control,” the force wrote Sunday on X.
Also fighting gangs are some 2,500 troops deployed by El Salvador last month when four of their own went missing after an Oct. 18 attack in Haiti’s capital.

Following orders by Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, the troops have attacked the main homes of two of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders, Jeff and Lanmò San Jou, this month. Neither one was killed.

Thousands of Haitians poured into the streets of Port-au-Prince and beyond this week in support of Bukele, but experts have criticized the unilateral operations of Salvadoran troops and noted that the use of explosive drones has claimed a growing number of innocent victims.
A small group of Salvadorans are separately working with the gang suppression force.

In late September, El Salvador’s legislature passed a law authorizing the participation of that group in Haiti for another 12 months until October 2027. The law was championed by Bukele and overwhelmingly approved by the country’s congress, controlled by Bukele’s party.
The ongoing clashes with gangs continue as Haiti prepares for its first elections in more than a decade. The country hasn't had a president since Jovenel Moïse was killed in July 2021.

title: Wife of Italian fugitive convicted of terrorism arrested in Argentina over his escape
summary: Argentine authorities have arrested the wife of an Italian fugitive convicted of terrorism-related crimes
story: Argentine authorities have arrested the wife of an Italian fugitive convicted of terrorism-related crimes

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- Argentine authorities have arrested the wife of an Italian fugitive convicted of terrorism-related crimes on suspicion of helping him escape house arrest by rappelling from a fifth-floor apartment in Buenos Aires last week.

Betina Erika Köpcke, 77, remained in custody Thursday after being arrested in the same neighborhood where her husband, Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, had been confined, Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva said.

Bertulazzi, a former member of Italy’s left-wing Red Brigades militant group, was awaiting extradition to serve a 27-year prison sentence for aggravated kidnapping and possession of explosives, among other crimes. The group was responsible for kidnappings and killings of judges, police officers, business executives and politicians in Italy during the 1970s and 1980s.

On Nov. 10, Bertulazzi used ropes and a harness to descend from his fifth-floor apartment to a neighboring house before reaching a vacant lot. Security camera footage showed him climbing over a gate and jumping onto the street.

Monteoliva said evidence recovered from a cellphone Bertulazzi left behind suggested his wife helped plan the escape. The phone contained photographs taken in October 2025 showing Köpcke near the gate through which he fled, the Security Ministry said.
Argentina’s Security Ministry offered a reward of 20 million pesos (about $12,000) for information leading to Bertulazzi’s capture.
Authorities did not immediately detect the escape because Bertulazzi had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor.

A person familiar with the investigation told The Associated Press that Bertulazzi placed the device inside a container lined with a thermal blanket and filled with animal fat to simulate human body temperature and pressure. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the investigation publicly.
After escaping, Bertulazzi traveled by bus through several towns north of Buenos Aires, where surveillance cameras recorded him entering a store to buy a hat, the person said.

Bertulazzi was granted refugee status in Argentina in 2004, but authorities revoked it in August 2024, clearing the way for his arrest. Following a series of appeals, Argentine courts authorized his extradition to Italy in 2026.
Monteoliva vowed to pursue anyone who helped him flee.
“We will investigate every last detail,” she said. “It doesn’t matter who they are or what role they played.”

title: Newborn dies after suspected female genital mutilation in Senegal; relatives arrested
summary: Three people have been arrested in eastern Senegal after a newborn baby girl died following alleged female genital mutilation
story: Three people have been arrested in eastern Senegal after a newborn baby girl died following alleged female genital mutilation

DAKAR, Senegal -- Three people, including the father and grandmother of a newborn baby girl who bled to death after allegedly undergoing female genital mutilation in eastern Senegal, have been arrested, a local official said Thursday.

The baby was allegedly subjected to the procedure on Nov. 12, just a day after she was born in the eastern Tambacounda region, Ndiaye Bousso, the regional director of family affairs, told The Associated Press.
The father was arrested Wednesday on suspicion of arranging the procedure, Bousso said. His mother and another woman suspected of carrying it out had been detained days earlier.

According to Bousso, the baby's paternal grandmother offered to bathe the newborn with the help of the other woman, but allegedly performed the mutilation without the mother’s knowledge. The mother later discovered that her daughter was in pain and bleeding.
The baby haemorrhaged severely and was referred to a regional hospital in Tambacounda on Friday, but died on the way, Bousso said.
Female genital mutilation, or FGM, has been illegal in Senegal since 1999 and is punishable by up to five years in prison, or life imprisonment if the procedure results in death.

Around 20% of women and girls ages 15-49 in Senegal are believed to have undergone FGM, according to the latest data from UNICEF. Its supporters claim the practice is rooted in traditions, but authorities have stepped up awareness campaigns in recent years to discourage it.
“We raise awareness and advocate,” said Bousso, adding that tradition cannot justify such a harmful practice.
“The law is clear and must be applied to its fullest extent,” she said, calling for justice for the baby.
AP’s Africa coverage at: https://apnews.com/hub/africa

title: Myanmar is the first state found responsible for genocide. How did the UN court rule in other cases?
summary: The United Nations’ top court has for the first time ruled that a nation committed what legal scholars call the crime of crimes, finding that Myanmar committed genocide in a brutal 2017 military crackdown against the Rohingya minority
story: The United Nations’ top court has for the first time ruled that a nation committed what legal scholars call the crime of crimes, finding that Myanmar committed genocide in a brutal 2017 military crackdown against the Rohingya minority

THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- The United Nations' top court has for the first time ruled that a nation committed what legal scholars call the crime of crimes, finding that Myanmar committed genocide in a brutal 2017 military crackdown against the Rohingya minority.

The International Court of Justice has been asked to reach that conclusion before, but never found enough evidence to make the determination of a state-sponsored genocide like the one targeting the Rohingya.
The World Court has more cases on its docket dealing with alleged breaches of the 1948 Genocide Convention, including a politically charged case about Israel’s actions in Gaza.

What happened: The Srebrenica massacre was a peak in the violence of Bosnia’s 1992-95 war, which came after the breakup of Yugoslavia unleashed nationalist passions and territorial ambitions across the region.

On July 11, 1995, Serbs overran Srebrenica, at the time a U.N.-protected safe area. They separated at least 8,000 Bosniak men and boys from their wives, mothers and sisters and slaughtered them. Those who tried to escape were chased through the woods and over the mountains around town.

How the court ruled: The court, basing itself in part on verdicts at a United Nations war crimes tribunal, said in a 2007 ruling that the Srebrenica killings amounted to genocide. However, it did not find Serbia responsible. It did find Serbia had violated its obligation to prevent genocide. That obligation is enshrined in the 1948 Genocide Convention.

What happened: In another war that erupted out of the messy breakup of Yugoslavia, Serb forces attacked several regions of neighboring Croatia, killing and wounding Croat citizens. Croatia accused Serbia of controlling forces responsible for attacks from 1991-95 that Zagreb said amounted to genocide.

How the court ruled: In a 2015 decision, the court said that it found genocidal acts, but it said it did not establish genocidal intent. Under the Genocide Convention, intent to destroy a group, in whole or in part, is necessary for a finding of genocide.

What happened: Israel launched a devastating military campaign in Gaza following Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack, when militants stormed through Israeli communities, killing some 1,200 people and taking around 250 people hostage.
The Israeli campaign has laid waste to much of the Gaza Strip and killed more than 74,000 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and militants.

South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive, a claim Israel vehemently denies. At public hearings, Israel insisted that its war in Gaza was a legitimate defense of its people and that it was Hamas militants who were guilty of genocide.

How the court ruled: In a 2024 interim ruling, the court ordered Israel to do all it can to prevent death, destruction and any acts of genocide in Gaza. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the fact that the court was willing to discuss the genocide charges was a “mark of shame that will not be erased for generations.”

There has been no ruling yet on the merits of the case and won't be for years. Israel has until May 2029 to file written arguments and only then can the court schedule public hearings. A final ruling could only come months or years after hearings.

Professor Janina Dill, an Oxford University expert on international law and the use of force, said in a statement that the Myanmar ruling “is very instructive of how the Court approaches some of the crucial questions that it faces in other pending genocide cases, including the polarising case of South Africa versus Israel.”
She said the 9-6 majority in the Myanmar genocide and a number of separate and dissenting opinions from judges “highlight the lingering doctrinal complexities.”
What happened: Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, after earlier illegally annexing the Crimea peninsula.

Shortly after the invasion, Ukraine filed a case accusing Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack. Kyiv argues that those claims amount to a breach of the Genocide Convention.

How the court ruled: The court has already thrown out much of the case. Judges said they have jurisdiction to rule on a request by Ukraine for a declaration that Kyiv is not responsible for genocide, but not on other aspects of the case. Like the South Africa-Israel case, this is at an early stage of proceedings and no final decision on the merits is expected for years.

title: 4 men found guilty of sex crimes against British woman in a case that recalls Gisèle Pelicot's
summary: Four British men have been found guilty of multiple sexual crimes against a woman whose ex-husband drugged and advertised her for sex online
story: Four British men have been found guilty of multiple sexual crimes against a woman whose ex-husband drugged and advertised her for sex online

LONDON -- Four British men were found guilty Thursday of multiple sexual crimes, including rape, against a woman whose then-husband drugged and advertised her for sex online, in a case that raised widespread comparisons to that of Gisèle Pelicot in France.

Joanne Young, who waived her right to anonymity as Pelicot had, spoke of her “relief” at the jury verdict and urged other women who have experienced anything similar to go to authorities in the knowledge that they “can be believed and understood.”

“Knowing what has happened to me without my knowledge or consent has been incredibly difficult to process, and this abuse has cost me my life as I knew it,” she said outside Winchester Crown Court in southern England. “The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way."
The 49-year-old mother of three spoke after the jury found the four men, whose ages range from 32 to 62, guilty of abusing her at her home in Swindon after being recruited on the internet.
Her ex-husband, Philip Young, had previously pleaded guilty to dozens of offenses including 11 counts of rape and 11 of administering a substance with intent.

Norman Macksoni, 48, was found guilty of one charge of rape. Richard Wilkins, 62, was found guilty of one count of rape and one of assault by penetration. Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, was convicted of sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching while Mohammed Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual touching.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.
Justice Pushpinder Saini said the four men faced “significant” prison sentences and praised Joanne Young for her "amazing bravery throughout these proceedings.”

The court heard that over a 13-year period, Philip Young, who served as a locally-elected official for the Conservative Party in Swindon between 2007 and 2010, drugged and raped his wife and invited other men on websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.
Joanne Young said her case raised “serious questions" over how the law deals with consent and urged the government to look into the issue to better protect women.

“Consent has to come from the person themselves, no one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no one should be able to rely on someone else’s word that you agreed,” she said. “At no point did anyone ask me for my consent."

James Foster, specialist prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service, said the men found guilty “chose to commit unspeakable acts of abuse against Joanne Young without bothering to check if she was consenting.”
Domestic abuse charity Refuge said the guilty verdicts represented "long overdue justice” but “cannot undo the devastating abuse inflicted upon” Joanne Young.

“Echoing the case of Gisèle Pelicot in 2024, the atrocities committed against Joanne by Philip Young and multiple other men are a clear reminder that, in the powerful words of Gisèle, shame must change sides," it said.

In December 2024, Pelicot’s ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, and 50 other men were convicted of sexually assaulting her between 2011 and 2020 while she was under chemical submission. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison, while the other defendants received sentences ranging from three to 15 years.
The shocking case of Pelicot and her decision to waive her anonymity and speak publicly prompted a reckoning over rape culture in France and beyond.

Philip Young’s abuse came to light in July 2024, when the local Wiltshire Police force received information that an account on the free mobile messaging and livestreaming app Kik linked to him had uploaded three extreme bestiality images to the platform. Full searches of his devices then identified five videos showing Joanne incapacitated and tied to the bed at their shared home address as well as chat threads which showed that Young had shared intimate images of Joanne online without her knowledge.

“It is hard to put into words the depth of Young’s exploitation and abuse of Jo," said senior investigating officer detective superintendent Geoff Smith. “Young put her health at risk through deliberately drugging her without her knowledge and inviting strangers to rape her, depriving her of autonomy over her own body.”
Joanne Young said she now never feels completely safe, but said that with the support of her loved ones she is "working hard to rebuild my life.”

title: Japan, India agree to enhance military and defense industry cooperation
summary: Japan and India have agreed to enhance their military and arms industry cooperation, including allowing Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges in future joint drills
story: Japan and India have agreed to enhance their military and arms industry cooperation, including allowing Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges in future joint drills

TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japan and India agreed to enhance their military and arms industry cooperation, including allowing Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges in future joint drills, as their defense and foreign ministers met Thursday in Tokyo.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi joined their Indian counterparts, Rajnath Singh and S. Jaishankar, at the “two-plus-two" meeting in Tokyo.

The two Asian powers have been rapidly deepening security, defense and economic ties in recent years amid growing tension and uncertainty in the region. India and Japan also are part of the Quad grouping with the United States and Australia that aims to counter China’s influence.
“Through our cooperation, we hope to serve as the anchor for the Indo-Pacific region,” Motegi told a joint news conference after the talks.
This defense industrial cooperation will proceed under the framework of “design with Japan, make in India,” Singh said.

As an island nation with limited space to safely conduct missile tests and training, Japan needs defense partners that can provide facilities for its military to practice live-fire drills essential to improving missile capability. Japan struck a similar arrangement with Australia this year.

Japan has been fortifying defenses in its southwestern region to deter China's growing military activity and started deploying long-range missiles this year, including Type-12 surface-to-ship missiles mobilized in Kumamoto on the southern main island.
Japan has also significantly relaxed its postwar pacifist principles in recent years and lifted a ban on lethal weapons exports as part of its security, defense and economic growth strategies.

On Thursday, the four ministers agreed to promote cooperation in defense equipment and technology and to accelerate negotiations toward achieving the transfer of Japanese naval radio antenna UNICORN to India.

They reaffirmed deepening cooperation in a range of areas including air and maritime security, information sharing, search and rescue operations, naval shipbuilding and artificial intelligence, according to a ministers' joint statement after the talks.

title: Somalia orders the UAE ambassador to leave as a diplomatic dispute escalates
summary: Somalia’s government has ordered the United Arab Emirates ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours
story: Somalia’s government has ordered the United Arab Emirates ambassador to leave the country within 72 hours

MOGADISHU, Somalua -- Somalia’s government on Thursday ordered the ambassador from the United Arab Emirates to leave the country within 72 hours, accusing the UAE of failing to respect the sovereignty of the Horn of Africa nation.

Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud this week accused the UAE of supporting armed forces outside federal control and weakening Somalia's unity. The UAE has ties with three Somali regions: Somaliland, Puntland and Jubbaland.

The decision to expel the Emirati ambassador and to recall his Somali counterpart for consultations was announced by Information Minister Abdifatah Kasim Mohamud at a news conference in the Somali capital, Mogadishu, after a Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre.
Authorities in Mogadishu urged Somalis and community leaders to unite against perceived “Emirati aggression,” saying appropriate measures would be taken against anyone not complying.
In a post on X Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the UAE president, accused Mohamud of putting personal calculations ahead of Somalia’s national interests.

The decision to expel the Emirati ambassador deepens a dispute that escalated in January, when Somalia annulled agreements with the UAE covering ports, government institutions, security and defense cooperation.
But authorities in Somaliland, Puntland and Jubbaland rejected the federal government's authority to cancel agreements involving their territories.

The quarrel with the UAE comes at a difficult time for Somalia. After more than three decades of operation, the United Nations recently closed its political mission that had helped rival leaders negotiate. No replacement mediator has been agreed amid an ongoing election dispute that sparked armed clashes in Mogadishu earlier this year.
Somalia's Supreme Court earlier this month ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term has expired and ordered elections within 90 days.

title: Migrant boat capsizes off Senegal's coast, leaving 1 person dead and several missing
summary: A migrant boat capsized off Senegal's coast, resulting in one death and several missing people, according to local officials
story: A migrant boat capsized off Senegal's coast, resulting in one death and several missing people, according to local officials
DAKAR, Senegal -- One person died and several others remain missing after a migrant boat capsized off Senegal's coast early Wednesday morning, local officials told The Associated Press Thursday.
The boat, which was headed to Spain, sank off the coast of Yenne, a coastal town south of the Senegalese capital, Dakar, Ousmane Sène, secretary general of the Yenne mayor's office, said.
“The accident happened around 3 a.m.," said Sène. “When we went to the scene, we saw the boat on the shore.”
He said firefighters recovered one body and police arrested one survivor. According to survivors' testimonies, the boat was carrying around 100 people, Sène said.
Two other bodies were also recovered in nearby villages but, according to Sène, it was unclear if they were people who drowned in this particular capsize.

Senegalese coastal areas have become major departure points for migrants attempting the dangerous sea journey to Europe, notably Spain's Canary Islands, an archipelago off West Africa and more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) south of the European mainland.

More than 11,000 migrants reached the Canaries in the first half of November, according to Spanish government figures. The number of people reaching the islands in just those two weeks was more than half the total for 2025, according to Spain's Interior Ministry.
Earlier this month, at least 39 people died after a migrant boat sank near the town of Kébémer in northern Senegal.
Senegalese authorities have stepped up efforts to crack down on people attempting the irregular migration route and have made dozens of arrests.
Senegal's navy said Wednesday it “rescued” over 1,400 migrants at sea in just 48 hours.

During a Council of Ministers meeting on Wednesday, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye deplored the resurgence of migrant departures toward Europe, calling for strengthened controls along Senegal's coasts, according to a government press release.

“The acceleration and complexity of irregular migration demonstrate the urgency for the government to intensify ... the diligent and efficient implementation of public policies concerning youth, education, vocational training, youth employment and entrepreneurship, as well as the economic empowerment of women,” said Faye.

title: University lecturer from Serbia's student-led movement is elected Parliament speaker
summary: A university lecturer from Serbia's student-led movement has become Parliament speaker
story: A university lecturer from Serbia's student-led movement has become Parliament speaker

BELGRADE, Serbia -- A university lecturer from Serbia's student-led movement on Thursday became Parliament speaker as last month's election winners moved to govern after toppling long-ruling strongman Aleksandar Vucic and his party.

Lawmakers backed Aleksandar Cupic with 140 votes in the 250-member assembly, while Vucic's party candidate received 97. The vote reflected the Students’ List group comfortable majority over the Serbian Progressive Party, which had ruled virtually unchallenged for 14 years.

The new student-backed lawmakers, including Cupic, are mostly teachers, professors and experts with established careers but little or no political experience. Their entry into Parliament marks the first time in Serbia that a grassroots protest movement has won the majority needed to form a government.

“I have been given a huge honor, obligation and responsibility,” Cupic said. He promised to restore Parliament's dignity and “dialogue and tolerance” among the lawmakers. “I pledge to be strict and just in this position, as I always have been in life."

The Oct. 25 parliamentary election marked a major shift for Serbia, where Vucic and his party had controlled all levels of power and were accused of stifling democratic freedoms while allowing crime and corruption to flourish. Vucic has denied the accusations.

The students' election victory came after they led anti-corruption protests for two years in response to a canopy collapse at a train station in northern Serbia that killed 16 people in November 2024. Many blamed the disaster on rampant corruption in construction projects.

Cupic's election as Parliament speaker followed more than two days of heated debate dominated by Vucic's accusations that his opponents were attacking and pressuring him and his party, though they still control the government administration and other state institutions. A new government must be voted into office within 90 days after the new Parliament's first session.

As speaker, Cupic will also serve as Serbia's acting president. Vucic resigned in September when he decided to run for prime minister. Cupic is expected to schedule soon an early presidential election, which must be held by the end of the year.

Vucic has accused the students of “revolutionary terror” in his daily appearances in loyal media outlets and social networks, following a surge in postelection arrests that included officials, police officers and a private bank owner who allegedly attempted to siphon off money.
Serbia is a candidate for European Union membership, but its bid stalled under Vucic because of democratic backsliding and close ties with Russia.

title: A van Gogh with a complex past sells for a record $190 million at auction
summary: A vibrant landscape painted by Vincent van Gogh weeks before his death has sold for $190.4 million at auction
story: A vibrant landscape painted by Vincent van Gogh weeks before his death has sold for $190.4 million at auction
LONDON -- A vibrant landscape painted by Vincent van Gogh weeks before his death has sold for $190.4 million at auction, a record for a work by the artist.

“Châtaigniers en fleurs” (Chestnut Trees in Flower) exceeded its $180 million estimate at a Sotheby’s auction in New York on Wednesday. The sale went ahead after an agreement between its current owners and the heirs of a Jewish family that sold it in Nazi-era Germany.

A day before the auction, Sotheby’s announced an agreement between the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which has owned the painting since 1975, and the descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, who sold it in 1936.
A lawyer for the Fischer heirs had asked for the sale to be postponed until Sotheby’s showed the painting had not been sold under duress.

The auction house said that “in recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution.” It did not disclose details of the agreement.

The Fischer heirs said they were “grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era.”
Van Gogh painted “Châtaigniers en fleurs” in a burst of creativity after his release from a psychiatric asylum in May 1890. He took his own life two months later.
The previous record for a van Gogh was $117.2 million paid for “Verger avec cyprès” (Orchard with Cypresses) at a Christie’s auction in 2022.

Paul Cézanne’s portrait “Arlequin” sold for $111 million in Wednesday’s sale of a dozen Impressionist and post-Impressionist works amassed by the late Argentine art collector Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her sugar magnate husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier.
The 12 works sold for a total of $412 million.

title: A cyberattack using artificial intelligence targeted the EU in October, official says
summary: An official in Brussels says a cyberattack using software powered by artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October
story: An official in Brussels says a cyberattack using software powered by artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October

BRUSSELS -- A cyberattack carried out with artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October, an official in Brussels said on Thursday, and some of the bloc's digital tools remain offline.
The official did not elaborate on the cyberattack, or say who could have been behind it. It was the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack using an AI tool.
“AI-assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities," said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive body of the 27-nation EU.
"Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools," he added. "We have seen many global cyberattacks recently, and of course no one is immune to this.”
Regnier said the EU first detected the incident on Oct. 22 and that authorities launched an investigation while also imposing “preventative measures."

Politico first reported the incidents. The news site said the attack lasted at least 10 days and affected translation and reimbursement tools as well as databases used for salaries and timesheets. Regnier declined to confirm that report.

“We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. So far, however, Regnier said that “we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole.”
The EU agency CERT-EU oversees the digital security of the bloc’s various institutions, which all together employ about 40,000 people just in Brussels.

title: Bus crashes into fuel truck in Pakistan and at least 10 people are killed
summary: A bus has rammed into a fuel truck carrying liquefied petroleum gas in southwestern Pakistan, igniting a fire that killed at least 10 people and left several injured
story: A bus has rammed into a fuel truck carrying liquefied petroleum gas in southwestern Pakistan, igniting a fire that killed at least 10 people and left several injured

QUETTA, Pakistan -- A bus rammed into a fuel truck carrying liquefied petroleum gas in southwestern Pakistan on Thursday, igniting a fire that killed at least 10 people and left several injured, police said.
The crash took place on the Makran coastal highway in Balochistan province, senior police officer Muhammad Aslam Bangulzai said.
The victims were taken to a nearby hospital, where some of the injured were listed in critical condition, he said, providing no further details. An investigation was underway.

Deadly traffic accidents are common in Pakistan due to poor road infrastructure and disregard for traffic laws. In August 2022, a passenger bus rammed into a fuel truck in eastern Pakistan, killing 20 people.

title: Mongolia's lawmakers accept president's resignation following corruption accusations
summary: Mongolia’s parliament has accepted President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa's resignation after he was accused of benefiting from a government railway project seven years ago, when he served as prime minister
story: Mongolia’s parliament has accepted President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa's resignation after he was accused of benefiting from a government railway project seven years ago, when he served as prime minister

ULAANBAATAR, Mongolia -- Mongolia’s parliament on Thursday approved the resignation of President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa after recent accusations by another politician in the ruling Mongolian People’s Party that he had benefited financially from a government railway project seven years ago, when he served as prime minister.
The president's resignation highlights infighting underway between the factions of the ruling party and is seen as a political power play by experts.
The accusation came from Nyambaatar Khishgee, the former mayor of the country's capital, Ulaanbaatar, who is from a different faction of the party. He lives in self-imposed exile in Canada.
Khurelsukh's resignation took immediate effect after 96 out of 104 members of parliament — known as the State Great Khural — voted in favor of it.
According to Mongolian law, an election for his replacement must be held within four months, with the parliament speaker serving as interim president during this period.
Khurelsukh, who was in parliament on Thursday, had a warning for Nyambaatar.

“That individual who has flown away like a ‘bird’ must be brought back and made to answer before the law. I hear he is seeking asylum abroad," Khurelsukh said and accused Nyambaatar of taking bribes related to a different development project.
On Tuesday, Khurelsukh had announced he was resigning and said he would cooperate with any investigation, though he denied corruption allegations.
“I have never stolen from my people or my state,” he said. “I will hand over my duties as president and become an ordinary citizen.”
While Khurelsukh is formally not part of the party, he is still active in its politics and a powerful figure in the country, analysts have said.

Marissa Smith, who served as an elections monitor in Mongolia in 2024, said an early election could be an advantage for both the ruling party and Khurelsukh. His term was originally due to end in June 2027.
Khurelsukh's previous resignations had served to boost his political career, said Julian Dierkes, a Mongolia expert at the University of Mannheim in Germany.

Khurelsukh resigned in January 2021 when he served as prime minister so that he could run for president. He won six months later and his Mongolian People’s Party won a majority in the legislature at the same time.

“I see strong parallels to his resignation as prime minister in early 2021, ostensibly responding to protests the way he is claiming to be responding to corruption allegations, but then turning around merely months later to run for office," Dierkes said.
Associated Press writer Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed to this report.

title: Denmark approves security deal with US and Greenland, seeking to finally ease tensions with Trump
summary: Denmark’s parliament has approved an agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic
story: Denmark’s parliament has approved an agreement with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic

COPENHAGEN, Denmark -- Denmark’s parliament on Thursday approved a hard-wrought deal with Greenland and the United States to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, a final step aimed to defuse months of tensions over the Trump administration's pressure about a possible U.S. takeover of the vast, mineral-rich island.

The trilateral deal — between U.S. President Donald Trump and Danish and Greenlandic leaders — paves the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of NATO ally Denmark. It also eases tensions in the Atlantic alliance and with the European Union over Trump’s repeated calls for the vast island to become part of the U.S.

The 109-0 vote in the Folketing amounts to a final step: The deal enters into force once the parliaments of Denmark and Greenland have signed on, followed by formal notification of the United States in a diplomatic note.
Greenland’s parliament approved the deal earlier this month, also with no opposition.
“Today is a big day,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen wrote on Facebook. “It hasn’t been an easy process.”
She said the agreement respects Denmark's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and the right of Greenlanders to self-determination.

Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen wrote on Facebook that Thursday's vote proved that Greenlanders can stand firm in their rights while also finding solutions through dialogue and cooperation.

“We have been through a difficult time, during which many people here at home have been concerned about our country and our future,” he said. “I hope that today’s decision will help bring greater calm and a sense of security.”
The U.S. ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the "strong support" in the Danish parliament for ratification of the deal “paving the way for it to enter into force.”

"The agreement is a tremendous accomplishment, one that modernizes our partnership for the security challenges of the future and bolsters the security of the United States, the Kingdom of Denmark, including Greenland, and all of NATO," he wrote on X.
The aim is to bolster the U.S. military presence on Greenland but keep the self-governing island under Danish control. It would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.

Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark signed the deal in September in New York, after months of quiet, behind-the-scenes negotiations to address his security concerns and Danish and Greenlandic fears of a possible U.S. takeover.

Under the deal, which builds on a defense agreement dating to 1951, the United States can expand its military presence on the island and “modernize and expand” its activities at the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest.

The U.S. can also set up “defense areas” at Narsarsuaq in the south and Mestersvig in the east of Greenland, and can establish additional defense areas in the territory and strengthen its military operations or sites.

The three sides expressed support for a stronger NATO engagement in the Arctic, and for allowing the U.S. military access to Greenland to defend the NATO area — including through the “ Golden Dome ” defense system.

After repeated U.S. warnings about the threat in the region from geostrategic rivals Russia and China, the agreement says only NATO members can establish manned or unmanned military installations on Greenland.

title: A third Ukrainian strike in 4 days halts rail traffic on Russia's Kerch Bridge to Crimea
summary: Ukraine has launched a third aerial attack in four days on the Kerch Bridge, a crucial link between Russia and Crimea
story: Ukraine has launched a third aerial attack in four days on the Kerch Bridge, a crucial link between Russia and Crimea

KYIV, Ukraine -- A third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia to illegally annexed Crimea halted rail traffic across the span, a Russian official said Thursday, after earlier strikes shut down the road section of the landmark that is a symbol of Moscow's invasion.

Train traffic across the bridge stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it was to be restored starting from around 4 p.m. (1300 GMT) on Thursday, the Moscow-appointed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said.

The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump, as well as to demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.

The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine’s war effort and fear being sidelined by Trump’s direct talks with Putin.
“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin told reporters in Shenzhen, China.
He insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered the bridge closed to the transport of military hardware or ammunition.
Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” but vowed to rebuild it.
The rail section is believed to be stronger than the road side, to bear the greater weight of cargo wagons.

The 19-kilometer (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops. It is a potent reminder of Russia’s illegal annexation and has been a prime target for Ukraine.

A large section of the road deck and an arch collapsed in the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, according to Zelenskyy, and the train track was damaged by domestically produced Neptune missiles, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said.
Now Russia will need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where “our drones are waiting for the cargo,” the ministry said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions during the night.

Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations. At least 10 people were reported wounded as Russian strikes caused damage in 12 regions, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.

Russia’s bigger army hopes to exhaust Ukraine on the front line through sheer weight of numbers in terms of soldiers, armor and weapons. But Kyiv’s defenses are largely holding the Russians back, sapping Russian momentum with the help of drones that quickly choke off troop advances.

Russia has resorted to strategic bombing to wear down Ukraine’s resistance, placing special emphasis on knocking out power ahead of winter, while Kyiv’s domestically developed long-range drones and missiles have struck deep inside Russia, often targeting its oil refineries.
In China, Trump called Putin “my friend.” The American president’s relationship with Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has soured.
European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy.
Ukrainian officials fear their country’s fate could be determined by agreements between Trump and Putin, while European governments are alarmed by Moscow’s aggression.
The question of U.S. support for Ukraine, severely curtailed under Trump, could be raised by Democrats in Congress after their wins in the midterm elections.

Britain’s Prince Harry offered a veiled criticism of the U.S. government’s policy toward Ukraine, saying in an interview released late Wednesday that he believes there is a “big separation” between the Trump administration’s stance and that of the American people.

Kushner and Witkoff have led Trump administration efforts to end nearly five years of war following Russia’s all-out invasion of its neighbor and recently have mediated new discussions, though the talks have yielded no major breakthrough.

Kushner said Thursday on X that Washington’s priority at Thursday's meeting in Berlin is to “further strengthen our close coordination with Ukraine and Europe, work toward a unified position on the key elements of a lasting peace, and to jointly prepare the agenda and proposed format for the next round of multilateral negotiations.”

The meeting will also explore how Ukraine’s European backers can fit into postwar security arrangements. Kyiv wants to ensure that Russia doesn’t invade again, while Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders.

Putin said in Shenzhen that the Kremlin is not against European participation in talks, but “we need to understand with what Europe will come to these negotiations.” The Kremlin has proposed to European officials through diplomatic channels to come to Moscow “to determine their position,” Putin said, without elaborating.
No date has been set for the next round of talks, he said.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was due to welcome French President Emmanuel Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham as well as other leaders to the meeting.
Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: South Korea’s top court overturns charges against ex-PM for his role in martial law
summary: South Korea’s Supreme Court has overturned the conviction of former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo
story: South Korea’s Supreme Court has overturned the conviction of former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo

SEOUL, South Korea -- SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korea’s Supreme Court on Thursday overturned the conviction of former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo for aiding ousted President Yoon Suk Yeol’s brief imposition of martial law in December 2024.

Han had been convicted of trying to legitimize the decree by securing its endorsement at a formal Cabinet meeting, a constitutionally required step in imposing martial law. But the Supreme Court ruled 9-3 that prosecutors had not sufficiently proven he intended to help Yoon carry out the unlawful power grab.

The new ruling sends Han’s case back to the Seoul High Court, which sentenced him to 15 years in prison in May. He will remain in detention for now. The Supreme Court extended his detention by two months, and further extensions are possible.
South Korea’s ruling liberal Democratic Party criticized the decision, accusing Chief Justice Jo Hee-de of committing a “judicial insurrection.” Some party leaders threatened to seek his impeachment.

The Supreme Court rejected the Seoul High Court’s finding that Han tried to lend legitimacy to Yoon’s illegal martial law decree by summoning ministers to a Cabinet meeting with the intent of rubber-stamping the decision.

It said prosecutors had failed to prove Han’s intent or whether he knew of Yoon’s martial law plans beforehand. It also noted that Han testified that he tried to dissuade the president from going ahead with the move.

But it did not challenge the appeals court’s finding that Han was guilty of discussing plans with other officials to cut off water and electricity to media outlets critical of Yoon after the martial law declaration, falsifying and destroying the martial law proclamation and lying under oath.

Yoon’s martial law decree, announced late at night on Dec. 3, 2024, followed a standoff with liberal opponents controlling the legislature, whom the conservative leader branded as “anti-state” forces obstructing his agenda and paralyzing state affairs.

The power grab collapsed within hours. Lawmakers broke through heavily armed soldiers and police surrounding the National Assembly and gathered enough votes to overturn the decree, forcing Yoon’s Cabinet to lift it.

Yoon’s powers were suspended on Dec. 14, 2024, when lawmakers voted to impeach him, and the Constitutional Court formally removed him from office in April 2025. After an earlier arrest and release, Yoon was re-arrested in July 2025 and has faced multiple trials over the martial law declaration and other charges. He received a life sentence for rebellion which he has appealed.

In July, the Supreme Court upheld an 8-year prison sentence against Yoon for infringing on Cabinet members’ right to deliberate before declaring martial law; falsifying the official proclamation to cover up the lapse before later destroying the document; and deploying presidential security forces to illegally resist law enforcement efforts to arrest him weeks after his impeachment.
It was the first of several criminal trials related to his martial law decree to reach the highest court.

While Yoon called 11 Cabinet members to his office shortly before declaring martial law, several participants, including Han, have testified that Yoon unilaterally informed them of his decision rather than inviting deliberation. Yoon was also found guilty of violating the rights of nine other Cabinet members by failing to call them to the meeting or notifying them too late.

In a separate ruling Thursday, the Supreme Court upheld a four-year prison term for Yoon’s wife, Kim Keon Hee, on corruption charges including stock price manipulation and bribery, the latest development in Yoon’s sprawling saga.
Han and Kim, both currently imprisoned, did not attend the rulings.

The Seoul High Court sentenced her in April for accepting gifts from a Unification Church official seeking favors and profiting from a stock manipulation scheme. Kim’s lawyers criticized the Supreme Court’s decision, saying in a statement Thursday that the charges against her had not been proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

Shortly after taking office in June 2025, liberal President Lee Jae Myung approved multiple special prosecutor investigations into Yoon’s martial law declaration and other allegations involving his administration and wife.

title: Fire set at home of former Bangladesh interim leader as political tensions rise
summary: Authorities in Bangladesh say a fire at the ancestral home of a former Bangladesh interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate appears to have been intentionally set
story: Authorities in Bangladesh say a fire at the ancestral home of a former Bangladesh interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate appears to have been intentionally set
DHAKA, Bangladesh -- A late-night fire at the ancestral home of a former Bangladesh interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate appeared to have been intentionally set, police said.
The fire occurred as growing waves of violence and damage have followed a declaration by the ousted former prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, that she plans to return to the country soon from exile.

The fire occurred before midnight Wednesday at the home of Muhammad Yunus, who served as interim leader of the country for 18 months following a mass uprising that led to the ouster of Hasina, who was flown out of the country by the military on Aug. 5, 2024.

The fire in an abandoned, ground-floor room of Yunus' house in Chattogram was spotted by a police patrol that immediately doused the flames, Police Inspector Mozammel Haque told local media Thursday. Police are investigating and additional details were not immediately available.

The possible arson comes during ongoing political tensions following an announcement by Hasina she intends to end her exile in India in December. In an interview with The Associated Press earlier this month, Hasina said even death cannot prevent her from returning to Bangladesh.

Hasina has requested a passport and national identity card to facilitate her return, but the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman insists she will not receive the documents and must be handed over by India under an extradition treaty.

Police and BNP leaders blamed Hasina’s supporters for attempting to create anarchy ahead of her intended return. Explosions of crude bombs, arson and roadblocks have taken place in the capital Dhaka and other locations throughout Bangladesh in recent weeks.

Yunus governed until February, when his interim administration handed over power to an elected government under Rahman. He was given the temporary leadership role following a student-led mass uprising that ended Hasina's 15-year rule.

Hasina was sentenced to death on charges of crimes against humanity involving the deaths of hundreds of protesters in the uprising. Her political party, the Bangladesh Awami League, was banned by the Yunus administration.
The Yunus administration and Rahman’s government requested her extradition from India, which did not respond to the requests.
Rahman on Wednesday urged “democratic forces” to remain united to prevent Hasina’s party from returning to Bangladesh politics.

Protests by Hasina's supporters and violence were reported in at least 22 districts nationwide in recent weeks. On Wednesday, at least two BNP supporters died in a clash with Hasina supporters in the southwestern district of Narail, police and media reports said.

Grameen Bank, a small-credit agency founded by Yunus that shared in the Nobel Prize award, also has come under attack. According to the bank, at least 72 branches in the country's 40 districts were targeted by arson attacks and vandalism between Nov. 10 and Nov. 19.

At Hasina's ancestral home in Gopalganj district, protesters have regularly blocked highways leading to the country’s longest bridge connecting Dhaka with southwestern and southern regions. Protesters recently torched a police station and repeatedly clashed with security officials. Hundreds of paramilitary border forces remained deployed in the district to maintain order.

Police in Dhaka on Tuesday arrested former Mayor Mohammad Sayeed Khokon, a Hasina supporter, and on Wednesday arrested former Hasina Cabinet minister and ally Nurul Islam Nahid and Joytika Joti, an actress.

On Thursday evening, the Dhaka Metropolitan Police in a statement said that they arrested 107 people, all involved with Hasina's party and other associate bodies, in the capital city in the last 24 hours. Nahid and Joti were among them, it said.
Police said they arrested them for their alleged involvement with sabotage.
The country’s leading English-language newspaper, Daily Star, reported that the homes of former Hasina administration and party officials Dipu Moni and Sujit Roy Nandy were set on fire Wednesday.

title: Pakistan military says it killed 22 militants in raids on hideouts in northwest
summary: Pakistan's military says security forces have raided militant hideouts in the northwest near the Afghan border, setting off gunbattles that killed 22 militants
story: Pakistan's military says security forces have raided militant hideouts in the northwest near the Afghan border, setting off gunbattles that killed 22 militants

ISLAMABAD -- Pakistani security forces acting on intelligence raided militant hideouts in the northwest near the Afghan border, setting off gunbattles that killed 22 militants, the military said Thursday.

It alleged that the militants killed were backed by neighboring India. There was no immediate comment from New Delhi, but Pakistan often accuses Afghanistan and India of supporting the Pakistani Taliban and other militant groups, allegations both countries deny.
The raids took place over the past 48 hours in the South Waziristan, Bannu and Tank districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the military said in a statement.
The military reported last week that security forces had killed 74 militants over several days in raids on hideouts in the northwest and in southwestern Balochistan province.
The military said troops were searching the areas for any remaining militants and pledged to continue operations against what it described as foreign-backed terrorism.

President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in separate statements praised the security forces for eliminating “Indian-supported” militants and vowed to continue the fight against militancy. Sharif said militants and their supporters would not be allowed to spread unrest in Pakistan and that the nation stood behind the forces fighting them.

Militant attacks targeting Pakistan’s police and security forces have surged in recent years. Authorities have blamed the Pakistani Taliban, who are known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan or TTP, and allied militant groups for most of the violence.

The Pakistani Taliban are a separate group from but allied with Afghanistan’s Taliban, who took power in Kabul in 2021. Many TTP leaders and fighters are believed to operate from sanctuaries across the Afghan border, straining relations between Islamabad and Kabul.

title: For the first time, UN's highest court finds a country responsible for genocide: Myanmar
summary: The United Nations' top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority during a 2017 military operation
story: The United Nations' top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority during a 2017 military operation

THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- In a landmark judgment, the United Nations’ top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation and ordered the Southeast Asian nation to allow people who fled the violence to return home.

International Court of Justice President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention.”

The 15-judge panel of the World Court, which included Navi Pillay, the respected international jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize last month, rejected Myanmar’s defense that the 2017 campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents.

Iwasawa said that “the court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers.”

The decision marks the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide and comes as the World Court also is handling genocide allegations linked to the Gaza conflict and the war in Ukraine.
The atmosphere following the hearing was electric, with lawyers and members of the Rohingya, some of whom had traveled thousands of miles (kilometers) to attend the reading, hugging and crying.

“I’m beyond ecstatic today, hearing the judgment, being read out in detail. A lot of those moments and instances that the judges really went into detail, it really validates the kind of experience that Rohingya have,” said Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the court’s ornate, wood-paneled Great Hall of Justice for the nearly three-hour reading of the ruling.
There was no immediate reaction from the Myanmar delegation in The Hague or from the government in Myanmar.

The court also ordered Myanmar to commit to reparations including allowing Rohingya “safe, voluntary and dignified return to their place of residence.” It ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish people found to have committed genocidal acts and to pay compensation to Rohingya. The amount will be decided in later court proceedings.

An umbrella organization of Myanmar opposition groups said in a statement that “the struggle for justice will continue, and this judgment must now be enforced,” calling on the international community to ensure it is fully implemented.
The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand.”

Shortly after the ruling was read, U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said his government was expelling Myanmar’s defense attache from the U.K. and “calling urgently for a U.N. Security Council session to discuss the judgment.”

In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.
The court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part.”

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

In a 2007 judgment, the court said that Serbia “violated the obligation to prevent genocide” in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian town.
Judges at The Hague-based court have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

“The International Court of Justice’s landmark ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar’s military. The ruling also provides a significant precedent for victims of genocide, and other grave crimes, across the world in their own quest for justice,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch.

The Muslim-majority nation of Gambia launched the proceedings in 2019, two years after it peacefully ousted a longtime military dictator, Yahya Jammeh, who committed widespread abuses against civilians. Since then, there has been a big push for accountability for the crimes committed by Jammeh’s regime.
The Rohingya genocide case was widely covered by the Gambian media, capturing the attention of many Gambians.
Outside the courtroom, Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow paid tribute to the Rohingya.

“The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived, they testified, and today they were believed. Many of them are here with our delegation from across the world and from the refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar. Their courage made this judgment possible,” he said.
Associated Press writers Grant Peck and David Rising in Bangkok and Monika Pronczuk in Dakar, Senegal, contributed to this report.

title: Wreck of Australia's first warship built at home found 128 years after sinking
summary: The wreck of Australia’s first Australian-built warship, HMCS Spitfire, has been found 128 years to the day after it sank off the country’s north coast
story: The wreck of Australia’s first Australian-built warship, HMCS Spitfire, has been found 128 years to the day after it sank off the country’s north coast

MELBOURNE, Australia -- The wreck of the first Australian warship built in the country, HMCS Spitfire, was found 128 years to the day after it sank off the north coast of what is now Queensland state, officials said Thursday.

The 19-meter (62-foot) schooner was launched in Sydney in 1855 to fight a potential Russian invasion. But Spitfire had been operating as a fishing boat four decades later when it sprung a leak and foundered on Aug. 21, 1898, off Piper Island, documents show.

A Royal Australian Navy mine hunter vessel found and exposed 16 meters (52 feet) of the wreck nearly three months ago, also on Aug. 21, after a monthlong search using a dive team and remotely operated vehicles, a joint statement from multiple agencies said.
“It is remarkable luck that Spitfire was discovered on the 128th anniversary of its sinking,” Queensland heritage officer Celeste Jordan said in the statement.
The discovery was not announced sooner because of reporting processes between government agencies required under laws designed to protect shipwrecks, the Defense Department explained Thursday.

Bearing the designation of HMCS, meaning Her Majesty’s Colonial Schooner, Spitfire was commissioned in 1855 during the Crimean War when the British colonial government of New South Wales in Sydney feared the Russian Pacific Fleet would invade, Australian National Maritime Museum archaeologist James Hunter said.

Britain was at war with Russia in a conflict centered on Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula. Gold had recently been discovered in New South Wales and the neighboring colony of Victoria, making them lucrative targets for conquest.
The Australian colonies then relied on Britain’s navy for defense and British warships were rare in the most distant reaches of the empire.

The Crimean War ended in 1856 without the Australian two-mast sailing vessel ever being used in battle. Spitfire became a pilot vessel in 1857 at Moreton Bay in what would soon become the Colony of Queensland, but was then still part of New South Wales, documents show.
The Queensland government sold Spitfire in 1885 into private ownership for use as a fishing boat.
Shipbuilder John Cuthbert delivered Spitfire two months after winning the contract. The speed suggested the warship’s construction already had been underway for a different purpose, Hunter said.
It was built from native timbers including an ironbark keel, blackbutt frames and kauri planking. The ship had copper sheathing below the waterline.
Russia’s Pacific Fleet at the time was mostly iron-hulled, steam-powered and “armed to the teeth warships,” Hunter told Australian Broadcasting Corp.
Spitfire was armed with a single cannon that fired 32-pound (14.5-kilogram) iron cannonballs.
“Would that have bounced off the side of one of those larger, Russian iron-hulled warships? Probably,” Hunter said.

There are no plans to salvage the wreck, which is largely buried in seabed sand. Authorities have not revealed Spitfire's exact location because it lies at a depth that can be reached by scuba divers. The ship is protected by federal and state law.
Vice Admiral Matthew Buckley, chief of the Australian navy, said Spitfire represents the beginning of the service's continuing story.
“Spitfire occupies a unique place in Australia’s naval history as the first warship built in Australia for Australian service,” Buckley said.

title: Walmart raises its outlook for the year for the 3rd time after a solid quarter
summary: Walmart reported solid sales for the fiscal quarter as the discounter continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices
story: Walmart reported solid sales for the fiscal quarter as the discounter continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices

NEW YORK -- Walmart reported solid third quarter sales gains as the retailer continues to attract a growing number of customers across the economic spectrum that are seeking to cut costs in the face of rising prices.

The company topped Wall Street’s profit and sales projections, and it raised its annual guidance for the third time this year, but the outlook released Thursday was more conservative than industry analysts had expected.

Comparable sales, which include digital channels and stores, rose 2.9%. That is better than last quarter's 2.6% increase, when Walmart reported its weakest comparable sales growth in six years. But it's still a slowdown from the 4.5% growth registered during the same period last year.

Still, slowing comparable sales, particularly in Walmart stores, also reflect a strategic shift toward e-commerce, Walmart+ memberships and advertising. Global e-commerce sales rose 17%, while U.S. e-commerce sales increased 23% during the latest quarter, the company said.

Walmart said that more than 80% of U.S. e-commerce orders are being fulfilled from stores, including its third party marketplace orders. Stores enabled faster delivery speeds on a wide range of assortments, the retailer said.
Shares rose nearly 1% before the opening bell Thursday.

“We delivered strong results, growing our core business and gaining market share,” Walmart's CEO John Furner said in prepared remarks. “The strength of our omnichannel model gives us room to do even more.”

Walmart is considered a barometer of consumer spending given its vast customer base. More than 150 million customers use its website or visit its stores every week, according to Walmart. Analysts look to the massive retailer for clues about what to expect from the industry as a whole during the critical holiday shopping season.

Consumers in the U.S. have remained resilient in the face of painful inflation, but they have also grown more selective about what they buy. Many rely on retailers like Walmart as a one-stop shop for low-priced household goods, groceries and pharmaceuticals.

The latest U.S. retail sales data revealed that shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as Americans pulled back on a variety of purchases, from cars, clothing and furniture and even their own hobbies.
Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to Commerce Department data released this week.
Walmart has been hammering its low price message while refining its store label fashion brands like Scoop and Free Assembly.

Walmart is also trying to increase subscriptions to its shipping programs. During the third quarter, Walmart launched a combined Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus annual membership bundle for $120 per year. The package saves shoppers nearly $100 compared to buying both plans separately, it said.

Walmart, based in Bentonville, Arkansas, has begun to capture a larger share of wealthier consumers. The biggest gains in market share for Walmart have been coming from households with annual incomes over $100,000, the retailer has said.

Walmart’s quarterly net income was $4.94 billion, or 62 cents per share, in the three-month period ended Oct. 31. Adjusted per-share results were 65 cents, higher than the 64 cents Wall Street had expected, according to FactSet. In the year-ago quarter, the company earned $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share.
Sales rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion in the latest quarter. Analysts were predicting $187.38 billion, according to FactSet.

The company said that comparable sales were driven by groceries and general merchandise categories like furniture and toys. But the figure was once again hit by federal legislation that requires pharmacies to dispense some high-cost Medicare drugs at capped prices, the retailer said.

For the full year, Walmart now projects earnings per share to be in the range of $2.84 to $2.89, up from the prior guidance of $2.80 to $2.87. Sales should be up anywhere from 4.9% to 5.2%, up from the prior forecast of 4% to 5%. That would mean a forecast for sales in the range of $748.12 billion to $750.25 billion, according to FactSet.
Analysts expected $2.89 per share and sales of $752.68 billion for the year, according to FactSet.

title: (Not) up in the air: Travelers' trepidations spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups abound
summary: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses
story: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses

NEW YORK -- At this point, it's practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.

And for 2026's busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there's another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.

The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She's pretty sure she's not the only one.

“For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having ... I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.
It's an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days' tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it's a familiar one, too.

Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it's one they're likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.
But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.

“For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.”

In some ways, the country's aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.

“Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy ... and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.

“You've got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There's nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.”
