title: China bars Bloomberg reporter from trilateral meeting after she shouted question at earlier event
summary: Chinese officials have blocked a Bloomberg TV journalist from a key event for shouting out a question to President Donald Trump
story: Chinese officials have blocked a Bloomberg TV journalist from a key event for shouting out a question to President Donald Trump

NEW YORK -- It's a scenario seen every day: A reporter shouts a question out to a leader at an event. The leader either answers or ignores it. In China, though, Bloomberg TV journalist Annmarie Hordern was blocked from a key event by Chinese officials Thursday, apparently as retribution for having shouted a question in a way that the government considered rude.

Hordern was barred from Thursday's trilateral meeting among President Donald Trump, Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, after having called out a question during an Trump meeting with Xi. She had asked Trump if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States.

A White House official said the Chinese insisted the reporter not be allowed in despite the White House having pushed for admission. The official insisted on speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity around the issue.

The White House did not immediately respond to a query about what steps it took to advocate for the reporter. Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents' Association, said on X that it was “commendable that the WH is advocating for press access.”
A pool report from the incident said the Chinese “have passed along a message that yelling questions is considered extremely rude and we will be pulled from the room if we do so.”
China’s Foreign Ministry did not respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press, and an email to Bloomberg seeking comment was not immediately returned.

The incident, which reflected the way China typically seeks to tightly control news events, recalled a previous one in 2022, in which a White House pool reporter said she was knocked off balance after being yanked by her backpack when she tried to shout a question to President Joe Biden. The question was about human rights ahead of a meeting between Biden and Xi in Bali, Indonesia.
The reporter lost balance without falling and was pushed toward the door, a pool report said at the time. Two White House staff members intervened and said the producer should be left alone.

China's approach to journalists, particularly foreign media, has long been chilly and uneven. In recent decades, international reporters have been expelled both for their coverage and for perceived misbehavior during news events. Resident correspondents are occasionally detained and questioned — and in some cases in past years, compelled to sign “self-criticism” reports — for showing up where the government doesn't want them to be.
Chinese journalists who stray from the party line can face even more stringent measures, including censorship, dismissal and at times even imprisonment.
Associated Press reporter Michelle L. Price contributed from Shenzhen, China.

title: Christie’s halts Frida Kahlo painting from auction at Mexico’s request
summary: Christie’s has withdrawn a Frida Kahlo painting from an auction in New York after Mexican authorities requested more information about its provenance
story: Christie’s has withdrawn a Frida Kahlo painting from an auction in New York after Mexican authorities requested more information about its provenance

MEXICO CITY -- Christie’s withdrew a Frida Kahlo painting from an auction in New York this week after Mexican authorities requested additional information about its provenance, the auction house confirmed Thursday.

The painting, “Congreso de los pueblos por la paz,” or “Congress of the Peoples for Peace,” had been scheduled for auction on Tuesday. It depicts a white dove on a tree bearing fruit alongside a smiling sun, the moon, and two slices of watermelon.
Mexican authorities asked Christie’s to hold the sale until the painting's provenance could be clarified, citing a declaration that recognizes Frida Kahlo’s work as an artistic monument of Mexico.

“In collaboration with the seller, we decided to withdraw the lot at this time for further research,” a Christie’s spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press. “We look forward to selling this work at a later date."
The same painting was auctioned in 2020 by Sotheby’s without any objections.
Kahlo’s works in Mexico are considered artistic monuments and are protected under the country's federal law on monuments and archaeological, artistic, and historical sites.
Mexican authorities said they were working with the Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo Museums Trust, administered by the Bank of Mexico.
Kahlo painted “Congreso de los pueblos por la paz” in October 1952 and donated it to the World Peace Council's peace congress held in Vienna that year.

The painting left Mexico more than three decades before the 1984 decree declaring Kahlo’s work an artistic monument. The decree prohibits the permanent export of her works that were in Mexico when it was published.
Kahlo, whose health was seriously deteriorating, sent the painting to the congress through her husband, the painter Diego Rivera. She died in Mexico City two years after creating it.
The trip to Vienna was recorded in the memoirs of Emma Hurtado, Rivera’s last wife, and has also been mentioned by historians such as Raquel Tibol.
Last year, Kahlo’s 1940 self-portrait “El sueño (La cama)," or The Dream (The Bed), sold for $54.7 million, setting an auction record for a work by a female artist.

title: Average US 30-year mortgage rate rises to 7.28% this week, ending a four-week slide
summary: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate rose this week for the first time since early October, reflecting a ramp-up in U.S. government bond yields amid signs that inflation is heating up
story: The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate rose this week for the first time since early October, reflecting a ramp-up in U.S. government bond yields amid signs that inflation is heating up
The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate rose this week for the first time since early October, reflecting a ramp-up in U.S. government bond yields amid signs that inflation is heating up.
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage in the U.S. rose to 7.28% from 7.11% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.26%.
The average rate eased in the four weeks heading into this week and hadn't increased since Oct. 8, when it hit 7.40%, its highest level in nearly three years.

Higher mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, limiting homebuyers’ purchasing power at a time when affordability challenges continue to sideline many aspiring homeowners.

Borrowing costs on 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, often sought by borrowers refinancing a home loan, also rose this week. That average rate climbed to 6.66% from 6.45% last week. A year ago, it was at 5.54%.

Rates on home loans are influenced by inflation, Federal Reserve policy and bond-market investors’ expectations for the economy, among other factors. They generally follow the trajectory of the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans.

That yield had been mostly trending lower since early October, after climbing to its highest level since 2002, but it has been rising again following new data showing hotter inflation. The 10-year Treasury yield was at 5.05% at midday on the bond market Thursday.

The signs pointing to accelerating inflation have raised the odds that the Federal Reserve will hike its key interest rate at its next meeting in December. The central bank kept rates unchanged late last month, after raising them in September.
While the Fed doesn’t set mortgage rates, its decisions to raise or lower its short-term rate are watched closely by bond investors and can ultimately influence rates on home loans.

“The debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves,” said Anthony Smith, a senior economist at Realtor.com. “That is a tough backdrop for mortgage rates heading into what is already a seasonally slow stretch for the housing market.”
Mortgage rates have been marching higher overall since late February, when the U.S. war with Iran began, pushing up the price of oil and driving inflation higher.

In late February, the average rate on a 30-year mortgage briefly dipped to 5.98%, its lowest level going back to late 2022. Going by the latest average rate, a home shopper financing a $400,000 home loan is now paying roughly $343 more a month than when the rate was just below 6%.

Elevated home loan borrowing costs have weighed on home sales this year, deepening a national housing slump that dates back to 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. They declined last month to their slowest annual pace in more than 16 years as mortgage rates surged.
And the latest monthly tally of home purchase transactions that have yet to be finalized points to potentially more sluggish home sales in coming months.

Pending U.S. home sales fell 4.7% last month from September and sank 16.7% from October last year, the National Association of Realtors said Wednesday. There’s usually a month or two lag between a contract signing and when the sale is finalized, which makes pending home sales a near-term bellwether for the housing market.

title: Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs
summary: The Senate has approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower...
story: The Senate has approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower...

WASHINGTON -- The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.

The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.

Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.
Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.
A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.

Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.

“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said.

Majority Republicans stymied Merkley's effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.”
The bill's sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process," he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.
“I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.

“In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government.
“Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.
The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.
“We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said.

Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations,” adding that he hopes “to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.
But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered.

Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation’s bodies of water, land and wildlife.

“Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process” to debate and amend the bill, she said. “Don’t sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.”

Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe's ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. “Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation,” he said.

Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.
“A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill,” Granholm wrote in a social media post. “But it would still need this president’s signature.”
Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure.

But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would “irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home.” He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California’s environment.
Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.

title: US stock futures jump on enthusiasm for Anthropic's blockbuster IPO
summary: U.S. stock futures are popping on enthusiasm for the market debut of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic later Thursday
story: U.S. stock futures are popping on enthusiasm for the market debut of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic later Thursday
NEW YORK -- U.S. stock futures are popping on enthusiasm for the market debut of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic later Thursday.

The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool raised a record $81 billion after pricing its initial public offering at $83 per share, higher than its earlier pricing range. Its trading debut is widely watched by investors looking for signs of where the AI boom may be going, and whether growth in adoption of the technology and massive AI spending can translate into sustained profitability for AI companies.
Futures for the S&P 500 rose 1.3%, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.7%. Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq advanced 2.2%.

Anthropic’s decision to go public also came at a time of market volatility and rising concerns over an AI slowdown, particularly following the Nvidia fallout and an expectation that the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the U.S. midterms could lead to greater regulation of the industry.

Investors on Thursday set aside some of that anxiety and bid up AI-related stocks. Micron Technology rose 5%, Marvell Technology gained 4.6% and Nvidia rose 1.7%. The company's stock has fallen for five straight days after former CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang was ousted following his extramarital affair that raised U.S. national security concerns, even as the company logged stronger-than-expected revenue and profit.
In European trading, Britain's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%. France's CAC 40 was flat, while Germany's DAX was lower by 0.1%.
In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.7%. SoftBank Group, which invests heavily in AI, added 4.6%. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron climbed 2.8%, while memory maker Kioxia Holdings added 3.1%.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index gained 1.4%. Memory chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 3.4%, while Samsung Electronics was 1.1% higher.
Taiwan’s Taiex dropped 4.4%, with its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., falling 3.5%.
In the U.S., all eyes are on Anthropic. OpenAI, its main rival, is also expected to go public but said earlier this year it wasn't planning to do so before 2027.

Significant growth is expected from growing AI adoption and from Anthropic’s “position at the frontier of model development, particularly in areas such as coding and cybersecurity,” Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar, said in a commentary.

However, Anthropic “will need to sustain rapid growth while managing the enormous cost of developing and running its models, and there is still considerable uncertainty around how the competitive landscape and economics of generative AI will evolve,” he added.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in September issued a warning over the risks that rapid AI developments could pose to humanity and called for an AI slowdown over safety needs. His call was echoed by AI leaders including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

In commodities trading, oil prices were mostly stable. A recovery in global oil supply has eased some supply concerns surrounding the situation in the Middle East. But the U.S. and Iran have not yet reached a deal and Iran on Wednesday widened its attacks on Gulf neighbors, underscoring risks to the region's energy shipments.
Brent crude, the international standard, rose 0.8% to $92.67 per barrel. It was trading at roughly $72 a barrel before the war began in late February.
Benchmark U.S. crude added 1% to $83.38 per barrel.
AP Business Writer Chan Ho-him contributed.

title: Kenya picks US consortium for critical minerals project as residents seek answers
summary: Kenya’s government has selected a consortium of U.S. companies to develop niobium and rare earths deposits on its coast
story: Kenya’s government has selected a consortium of U.S. companies to develop niobium and rare earths deposits on its coast

NAIROBI, Kenya -- Kenya’s government said Thursday that it had selected a consortium of U.S. companies as the preferred bidder to develop niobium and rare earths deposits on its coast, while residents said they were still waiting for information on the project.

The mining ministry said it had issued a notice of its intention to award the Mrima Hill project in Kwale County to the Frontier Minerals Consortium, which comprises Frontier Minerals LLC, Bunker Hill Mining Corp., ReElement Technologies and American Resources Corp.

The ministry stressed that the notice is not a license. It said the consortium must now “go to the ground,” engage communities and obtain “all requisite consents” before applying for a prospecting license.

Residents and farmers have told The Associated Press that they fear losing their land. Elders from the local Digo community worry about damage to a sacred forest where they say their ancestors are buried.

“Until now, we have received no information from the government on the content of the project,” said Justus Mwero, chairman of the Mrima Farm Owners Community-Based Organization. “It will be hard for us to express our consent or opinion to the company with no information.”
Countries including the U.S. are racing to secure the rare earth minerals used in electric vehicle motors, wind turbines and defense technologies, seeking alternatives to China’s dominance.
The ministry said it had “deliberately” chosen investors before starting formal consent processes. Mining Minister Hassan Joho told the AP on Nov. 2 the community was consulted before seeking bids.

“The government should make the proposal public, so that the company can be held accountable. The government should not distance themselves from their responsibilities and leave it to the investor,” said Fakii Omar of the Kwale Mining Alliance.
The Mrima Hill Sacred Grove was designated a national monument in 1992.
“The notice does not mention if the protected status of the forest has been revoked," Omar added. "Can the proposed mine coexist with the protected status under current laws?”

A previous attempt to mine the site ended in arbitration. In 2013, Kenya’s environment regulator rejected an environmental assessment for a license held by Cortec Mining Kenya, citing the site’s protected status, according to Extractives Daily. An arbitration tribunal of the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes later ruled that the license should not have been issued without environmental approval, and Kenya won the case.

The Centre for Litigation Trust, a Kenyan civil society group, has asked the High Court in Kwale County to suspend a proposed Kenya-U.S. agreement on Mrima Hill’s minerals until residents are consulted. The attorney general has challenged the court’s jurisdiction.

title: Trump wants Supreme Court to let EPA cancel billions in Biden-era climate grants
summary: The Trump administration is appealing to the Supreme Court in its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program
story: The Trump administration is appealing to the Supreme Court in its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program

WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration is appealing to the Supreme Court in its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program, the largest grant cancellation case ever and one that could affect Republican President Donald Trump's push to defund the priorities of prior administrations.
The justices have not said whether they will take the case.

If they do, it could resolve a fight over grants that the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded in 2025. Democratic President Joe Biden's administration awarded the money under a 2022 law to finance clean energy projects and accelerate the transition from fossil fuels. Trump has targeted other grants, such as those considered to be supporting diversity, equity and inclusion. A favorable outcome at the high court could help his administration defeat other grant lawsuits, according to the government's filing this month.

At issue is the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, commonly referred to as a “green bank." Climate United Fund and other nonprofits were picked to operate the program authorized by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. If the justices decline to take the case, the groups could regain access to their money because a federal appeals court already ruled in their favor.
The EPA canceled the nonprofits' grants soon after the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025, with EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin accusing the groups of mismanagement and potential fraud.

The nonprofits' lawsuit argues that the EPA broke the law and violated the Constitution. It demands access to their grant money so they can run the program. The administration says it is immune from legal and constitutional claims and contends the groups filed their case in the wrong court.

If the justices eventually side with the EPA, it could "have far-reaching implications for the government’s ability to reshape grant programs and to terminate grants that do not advance a particular administration’s policy priorities,” said Romany Webb, deputy director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University who has supported Climate United’s arguments.
The EPA says the $16 billion at stake is the largest grant cancellation case ever and is another reason it warrants Supreme Court review.
The courts have so far tried to thwart the administration's priorities, the EPA wrote in its petition to the Supreme Court.
The EPA and Climate United declined to comment.

In August, a divided federal appeals court in Washington sided with the nonprofits and said the administration improperly terminated the grants. The release of any money was paused to give the Supreme Court a chance to weigh in.
The justices ruled for the administration recently in decisions over canceled National Institutes of Health grants and teacher training grants.

The administration has built its arguments around the Tucker Act, which gives the Court of Federal Claims exclusive authority over contract disputes. The claims court can award money, but not direct the government to take certain actions in the way federal courts can.

The nonprofits argued the way the EPA canceled the grants did not upend a contract with the federal government, but was done illegally and undercut spending on entire programs Congress had required, a constitutional violation. The government argues the matter is a contract dispute.

The administration’s broad use of contract cancellations to enact policies is a novel approach, according to Bob Wagman, president of the Court of Federal Claims Bar Association and a partner at the firm White & Case.

“I would hate to think that the only programs that could be supported have a four-year life,” he said, mentioning cancer research as an example of a grant program that would need longer than a single administration to pay off. “It is just not good for the country.”
Zeldin last year told Fox News that he suspected the green bank “was a clear-cut case of waste and abuse.”

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan said that when the government was asked for evidence of fraud, the EPA did not provide it and shifted its position to more general concerns about the level of oversight over the program. Chutkan said the government cannot terminate the contracts in violation of the law and that the groups should have access to some of their frozen money, which is held in an account at Citibank.
The administration has been adamant that nothing requires them to make these grants to these groups.

Passage of the Inflation Reduction Act created the green bank. Trump’s tax and spending bill passed last year rescinded part of the law that established the bank and the money that had not already been obligated to its recipients. The EPA has said that those changes mean it should not have to release any money to the groups.
Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott in Providence, R.I., contributed to this report.

The Associated Press receives support from the Walton Family Foundation for coverage of water and environmental policy. The AP is solely responsible for all content. For all of AP’s environmental coverage, visit https://apnews.com/hub/climate-and-environment

title: Turkish authorities carry out a raid on another opposition TV station and appoint trustees
summary: Turkish authorities have raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations, Sozcu TV
story: Turkish authorities have raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations, Sozcu TV

ANKARA, Turkey -- ANKARA, Turkey (AP) — Turkish authorities raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations on Tuesday, detaining several executives and appointing trustees to manage operations in a move critics described as the latest step in a crackdown on independent media.

The predawn raid against Sozcu TV came just weeks after trustees similarly took control of another opposition-leaning news channel, Halk TV, in an alleged corruption investigation that critics said was politically motivated.

Press freedoms in Turkey have steadily eroded during the more than two decades that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has been in power, and a majority of media outlets are either under government control or aligned with it. The country ranks 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders’ world press freedom index.

A statement from the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s office said the move against Sozcu TV was part of an investigation into the channel’s alleged violation of Turkey’s anti-terror financing laws and suspected links to a network that was led by the late U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen.

The cleric, who died in 2024, was accused by Turkey of orchestrating a failed military coup in 2016 and his network of supporters has been branded a terrorist organization. Gulen had denied the accusations.
The prosecutors' office cited suspicion that Sozcu TV and other media outlets linked to its owner, Burak Akbay, were being financed by overseas accounts.

Tuesday's raid follows a widening crackdown on the opposition, with dozens of mayors from the main opposition party arrested on corruption charges since 2024, including former Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu. The popular politician was widely regarded as a possible challenger to Erdogan.
The government denies any involvement in legal moves against the opposition, insisting that Turkey’s courts operate independently.

The action against Sozcu TV drew condemnation from opposition parties and media groups. Some critics linked the decision to impose a trusteeship to the channel devoting extensive coverage to an investment fund scandal that led to the resignation and subsequent arrest of a senior member of Erdogan’s ruling party.
Main opposition New Party leader Ozgur Ozel accused Erdogan’s government of intolerance toward “even the smallest criticism or a single inconvenient truth being heard.”
He vowed not to “surrender to these would-be dictators.”

Musavat Dervisoglu, the leader of the center-right opposition Good Party, described the move as “an overt assault on democracy, the rule of law, the sense of justice, and the public’s right to be informed.”
“Turkey will speak, and the voice of the truth cannot be silenced!” he wrote on X.
In a joint statement, Turkish journalism associations expressed solidarity with Sozcu TV journalists and called for the decision to appoint trustees to be reversed.
“Following Halk TV, the appointment of trustees to Sozcu shows that the media climate in Turkey has entered a dark winter,” the statement read.
On Tuesday, Sozcu TV’s regular early morning news program was replaced by a recorded discussion about longevity.
Other television stations, including HaberTurk and Tele1, have similarly been placed under trusteeship.

title: Federal Reserve's Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing
summary: Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome
story: Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome

WASHINGTON -- Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome.

The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook's lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov. 6. Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed's board of governors, a charge she denies.

President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president's efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed's independence and reflect Trump's desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs.

“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook's lawyer, wrote in a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.”

In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that "the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.”

Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a Nov. 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating.

The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Labor Secretary.

The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire her if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry is an effort to meet those conditions.

Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor “for cause,” but the Supreme Court didn’t address whether Cook’s actions met that standard. The committee will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, the White House has said.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was asked at a press conference Oct. 28 if he or the Fed would be involved in the hearing against Cook, and he said, “not to my knowledge.”

title: After a 13-year wait, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations
summary: The global rollout of "Grand Theft Auto VI" is underway, taking players back to Vice City
story: The global rollout of "Grand Theft Auto VI" is underway, taking players back to Vice City
LOS ANGELES -- After a 13-year wait, “Grand Theft Auto VI” has begun its global rollout, sending players back to Vice City and kicking off one of the most anticipated entertainment launches in years.
Players in New Zealand were among the first to enter Rockstar Games’ sprawling Florida-inspired world as midnight Thursday arrived, hours before the game becomes available across the United States.

Internet providers there had prepared for a massive surge in downloads. Chorus New Zealand expected about 35 petabytes — 35 million gigabytes — of additional traffic across its network as players downloaded the massive game.

“The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, the company’s network strategy manager. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.”
In Wellington, Adam Simmons launched the game from his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low so he wouldn’t wake his wife and daughters.
“The gameplay dynamics are just amazing and the graphics are great and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep,” he said after about half an hour of play.
Shares of Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, rose more than 8% Wednesday as the rollout continued.

In the Dallas area, Bryan Banuelos, a mobile auto detailer, told customers he wouldn't be taking calls Thursday so he could focus on “GTA VI.” His social media post actually drove some business beforehand, with customers trying to get their cars detailed before he disappeared into Vice City.
“Tomorrow will be the beginning of a new era for the gamers that like GTA,” Banuelos said.

The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.

Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released.

At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.

Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.
The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.

Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.

Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture.

Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity.

Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release.

The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity.
Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight.
In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack.
Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.

The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.
The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.

“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.

The long wait is partly a product of the extraordinary staying power of its predecessor. “Grand Theft Auto Online,” the multiplayer component of “GTA V,” has kept players engaged for years through updates, activities and in-game purchases.
Music has long been woven into the “Grand Theft Auto” experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.
“Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album,” a 34-track collection of original songs tied to the game, is scheduled for release Friday.

A separate 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” by Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice is scheduled for release Dec. 11. The adaptive score is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.

The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.
Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.
Associated Press journalists Charlotte Graham-McLay in Wellington, New Zealand, and Tong-hyung Kim in Seoul contributed to this report.

title: Anthropic forges ahead with its IPO even as AI fears mount and markets wobble
summary: Anthropic is preparing to sell stock to the public in a shaky moment for artificial intelligence companies
story: Anthropic is preparing to sell stock to the public in a shaky moment for artificial intelligence companies
NEW YORK -- Investors fearing an AI bubble are getting jittery. Financing costs are rising. Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry.
It's not an ideal time for an artificial intelligence company to sell stock, but Anthropic is pressing ahead with its blockbuster initial public offering anyway.
No ordinary sale, the Claude chatbot maker's IPO could raise more than $60 billion on Thursday, a massive haul that, depending on the ultimate pricing and other issues, could rival SpaceX's in June.
But Anthropic is facing headwinds as it prepares for its coming-out party.
Tech stocks have done well so far this year, but the path higher has been rocky, especially for AI-related companies. That's not a reassuring setup for the IPO.

One particularly volatile AI stock, CoreWeave, plunged 15.5% on Oct. 14 over fears it wouldn't be able to borrow enough, cheaply enough to fund its growth. The stock then swung wildly. On Wednesday, the company, which buys chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, surged 25% after an encouraging earnings report, only to plunge 7% the next day.
Most stocks move no more than 2% on the average trading day.

Adding to the sector volatility recently has been the abrupt departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang, a high-profile AI booster, built Nvidia into a linchpin of the industry and a major financial backer of other AI companies. Stock in the AI chip designer dropped 4% Monday, dragging the broader S&P 500 down for a third day in a row.
Nvidia has agreed to buy an estimated $10 billion of Anthropic stock after the IPO. It also sells chips to Anthropic but the latter also buys from AMD and others.

As to whether the gyration in AI-tied stocks argues for an IPO delay, note that volatility can cut both ways: It might be signaling the much debated AI bubble could burst soon so it's better to sell stock now, fast. And history shows demand for IPOs can disappear quickly.
In 2021, nearly 400 companies went public in the U.S., but then investors got scared of a possible recession the next year and demand dried up with only 71 making market debuts.

Another reason to sell stock now is that the other way to raise money — borrowing — has gotten more expensive. That's partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability.

Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial." Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting its resources are limited to pay interest and principal.

On the plus side, it has ample cash, although it will likely run through it quickly if it can't raise more soon given its outsized spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion in computing and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.
Higher interest rates are not the only problem. Politics threatens to slow growth, too.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democrat governors vowing to stop new construction.
It wouldn't be unprecedented for Anthropic to postpone its IPO at the last minute.

After a bout of volatility following President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025, several companies postponed their initial offerings, including the online ticket marketplace StubHub and Klarna, a buy now, pay later business. And an Australian data center company, Firmus, called off its IPO last month because of jitters in the market.
But newly elected Democrats don't take office until January. Anthropic could be betting that selling now is best before the feared crackdown begins in earnest.

If the company does go ahead as expected, it will beat rival OpenAI to the market. That's an important advantage should investors suddenly fear they have too much exposure to the sector and decide they don't want to buy stock in the next public AI company.
And despite the jitters, companies on public markets are still fetching top prices. One measure of investor enthusiasm shows they are paying nearly as much as ever to buy stocks.

The measure championed by the famed American economist Robert Shiller comparing share prices to corporate profits over the previous decade shows shares have been more expensive only once before — the 2000 dot-com crash — and are higher now than on the eve of the 2008-09 Financial Crisis.
Stocks currently trade at 40 times their long term earnings, according to Shiller's measure. That is a third higher — meaning more expensive — than the average going back before 1900.
That's good news for Anthropic, meaning it may be able to fetch top dollars for its shares this week, though maybe not so good for its IPO investors.

title: Should court filings related to the search of Ilhan Omar's home be released? A judge will decide
summary: It's been more than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar
story: It's been more than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar

WASHINGTON -- More than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, a federal judge heard arguments Tuesday on a request by media organizations to unseal court records related to the search — and to an immigration-fraud investigation that the Minnesota Democrat claims is politically motivated.

Over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, maintain that the public has a First Amendment right to access the search warrant and other court filings that led to the Oct. 12 search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents.

During a hearing on the request, Chief Judge James Boasberg said he agrees with Justice Department attorneys that it's premature to unseal a search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government's investigation. But the judge said he will privately review other sealed court filings for possible public release as soon as next week.

Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. Omar, who has denied wrongdoing, said in a social media post that the search was an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”

Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the investigation told The AP last month on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election.
Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift.

Boasberg gave the government until Friday to provide him with proposed redactions to sealed court filings that could shed light on some of the underlying legal arguments involved in the Omar investigation. The judge said redacted versions of those documents could be released as soon as next Monday.

The 67-page search warrant affidavit, which contains information about witnesses and other details of the investigation, will remain under wraps for now. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made.

The news organizations' attorneys argue that the government's privacy concerns are outweighed by the “enormous public interest in and historic significance of a search warrant executed at the home of a sitting member of Congress.”
Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano said the government isn't trying to keep the affidavit under seal permanently.
“It's not our position. It's never been our position,” she told the judge.

Boasberg noted that Vice President JD Vance and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin already have publicly commented on the contours of the Omar investigation. Serano said she can't control what others in the Trump administration say about the case.
“It seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg replied.

Boasberg, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama, is himself a frequent target of Trump's ire. Trump called for Boasberg's impeachment last year after the judge blocked the president's administration from deporting planeloads of Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act.
___ Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report.

title: Target will take momentum from strong third quarter into the holiday shopping season
summary: Target is reporting its strong quarterly sales gains in roughly five years, fueled by a revitalized product lineup, expanded same-day deliveries and price cuts that brought in customers battered by inflation
story: Target is reporting its strong quarterly sales gains in roughly five years, fueled by a revitalized product lineup, expanded same-day deliveries and price cuts that brought in customers battered by inflation

NEW YORK -- Target delivered its strong quarterly sales gains in roughly five years, fueled by a revitalized product lineup, expanded same-day deliveries and price cuts that brought in customers battered by inflation.
The company raised its annual earnings and sales outlook again on Wednesday after an encouraging third quarter.

Target reported a better-than-expected 7.1% increase in net sales, the best performance since the fourth quarter of 2021. The company also posted its third straight quarter of quarterly comparable sales, which include sales from online and its physical stores.

Sales made through digital channels operating for at least 12 months increased 9.8% from the same quarter last year, while comparable sales at established stores rose 4.6%. The three-month period that ended Oct. 31 overlapped with back-to-school shopping season.
Shares were essentially flat before the opening bell.

The Minneapolis retailer reported growth in a majority of its six core merchandise categories, led by electronics, gaming equipment, sporting goods, toys, trading cards and collectibles, a category Target refers to as "Fun 101.” It also cited higher sales of beauty products, food and beverages.

But Target CEO Michael Fiddelke, a 20-year company veteran who became chief executive in February, told reporters this week that the sales momentum was not limited to certain categories or based on any one initiative. He said Target has seen business pick up across its markets among shoppers of all incomes.
“It’s the cumulative impact of changes across our business that is driving this guest preference for Target,” Fiddelke said.
The company said November net sales so far are in line with the full-year outlook.

Together, comparable store and digital sales in August, September and October increased 5.6% though that figure is being compared to a 2.7% drop in the year-ago period. The retailer also reported a 5.6% gain in the first quarter and a 3.8% uptick in the second quarter of this year.

In March, Fiddelke unveiled a multibillion dollar investment plan aimed at reversing a post-pandemic sales slump. The overhaul included a focus on stocking products and brands that would help restore Target's reputation as a place to go for affordable yet stylish items.

Target launched a new Target Beauty Studio concept in more than 600 locations in September. The new area, which features upscale beauty products and staff trained to offer advice, partly replaced the Ulta shops that were in some stores before Target and Ulta Beauty ended their partnership in August.
Company executives said work to improve the offerings in Target's clothing and home goods departments was ongoing.

With U.S. consumers expressing concerns about the U.S. economy and their own finances, Target also has promoted price reductions this year, including cuts on nearly 2,000 additional items during the third quarter.
The company said most of the new items it has for the holiday shopping season cost $20 or less, including thousands priced at $5 and under.

Target is one of the first big retailers to report third-quarter earnings. The results could give industry analysts and economists another read on how U.S. consumers responded to ongoing inflation pressure before the end-of-year holidays.

Target said it earned $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, including a 50-cent benefit from a government tariff refund. In the third quarter of 2025, the company reported $689 million, or $1.51 per share.
Net sales rose 7.1% to $27.07 billion compared to $25.27 billion in the year-ago period.
Analysts were expecting $2.08 per share on net sales of $26.5 billion, according to FactSet.
Target now expects net sales for the full year to be up roughly 6%, one percentage point higher than the guidance it gave in August.
The company projected full-year earnings per share of $10.65 to $11.40. That includes a $2.14 tariff refund benefit. In August, the company expected earnings of $9.90 to $10.90 per share.
Analysts were projecting profits of $10.25 per share on sales of $110.27 billion.

title: Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting found in Manhattan closet sells for $4.8M
summary: A painting dug out of a New York City closet this year after being stashed away since the 1980s has sold at auction for $4.8 million
story: A painting dug out of a New York City closet this year after being stashed away since the 1980s has sold at auction for $4.8 million
NEW YORK -- A long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting that had been buried in the closet of a Manhattan apartment for decades sold at auction Tuesday for $4.8 million.

The 1930 landscape painting “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” is likely the first in a series of three works depicting Lobo Peak in northern New Mexico, according to Christie’s auction house. Its existence was known from a 1931 photograph, but its whereabouts had been kept secret until recently.

A Manhattan woman in her 90s nonchalantly told her niece one day in 2022, “Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.” Her family believes she received the painting as a graduation gift from her mother, who had purchased it in 1963 from a New York gallery for $3,800.

The woman, who died recently, displayed it in her East Village apartment for many years until the mid-’80s when she noticed a guest looking at it a little too closely. From then on she kept it in her closet, safely hidden behind coats and boxes.

When the family finally unboxed it this year, they discovered it has all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work, including her signature marking on the back: a star with her initials scrawled in the middle.

The 10-x-24-inch (25.4-x-61-centimeter) oil painting is among O’Keeffe's early love letters to New Mexico, where she settled and lived for decades. The identity of the winning bidder was not disclosed; it sold for $4,878,000.

Known as the “mother of American modernism,” O’Keeffe maintained a home and studio in Abiquiu and a nearby summer residence tucked between the red-rock cliffs of Ghost Ranch. She died in 1986 at age 98 and is best known for her paintings of flowers and American Southwest landscapes.
The second piece in the “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico” collection is at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the other, for many years, was in the collection of the Rockefeller family.

title: How three leaders donated the $20 million Melinda French Gates gave them with no strings attached
summary: Philanthropist Melinda French Gates launched a $240 million Global Leaders program in 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries without warning or requirements other than donating the money b...
story: Philanthropist Melinda French Gates launched a $240 million Global Leaders program in 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries without warning or requirements other than donating the money b...
Dr. Alfiee Breland-Noble says she was shocked when philanthropist Melinda French Gates picked her to receive $20 million to donate however she wanted.

The psychologist, author and founder of The AAKOMA Project, a nonprofit supporting the mental health of young people of color, has long admired French Gates’ work, especially in the diversity of her support initiatives. Breland-Noble just never expected to be the focus of one of those initiatives.

“It really was shock and awe,” she said. “My mom just had a knack and a penchant for finding people that nobody else was helping and she would help them. And so for me, the excitement was I get to honor my mother’s legacy by doing the same thing.”

In 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, French Gates launched the $240 million Global Leaders program, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries, including Breland-Noble, without warning or requirements other than donating the money by the end of 2026. It was part of her plan to donate $1 billion to support women and girls at a time when nonprofits focusing on their issues receive only about 2% of all U.S. philanthropic funding.

Now, with nearly all the money donated, Pivotal has seen enough to call the trust-based philanthropy initiative a “huge success” and is looking for ways to replicate it and encourage other donors to do the same.

“There are so many great ideas out there that might never cross my path but might cross someone else’s,” French Gates said in a statement to The Associated Press. “That’s one reason I started the Global Leaders program: to partner with experts whose firsthand knowledge could broaden Pivotal’s perspective and deepen our impact.”
According to Pivotal, the average grant the Global Leaders handed out was approximately $240,000, with 91% of the donations going to organizations that had not received funding from Pivotal before.

Haven Ley, Pivotal’s chief strategy officer, said a final report on the Global Leaders program will come next year, but that the organization is already looking for ways to build on it. “We did this not just for the impact," Ley said, “but because it was a model that was intriguing to us.”
French Gates said the different vantage points on the world’s challenges have made Pivotal more responsive and helped the Global Leaders be more impactful.
“For me, this is as much about expanding who gets to make decisions about funding as it is about where funding goes,” she said.
For Breland-Noble, being able to donate to others on a grand scale was a meaningful new experience.

Though she has been working in the mental health field for decades, she is relatively new to running her own nonprofit. Breland-Noble established The AAKOMA Project, which stands for African American Knowledge Optimized for Mindfully Healthy Adolescents, in 1999 as an academic research lab, only turning it into a nonprofit in 2018 so that it could put its research findings into action.

To donate the $20 million that French Gates had given her, Breland-Noble created The MATTIE Fund – short for Mindful Advocacy for Totally Transformative Inclusion and Equity, but also named for, and inspired by, her mother Mattie McLeod Breland.

The MATTIE Fund donated to well-established groups like Asian Mental Health Collective. But Breland-Noble made a point of expanding her donations to groups outside her network, searching Google and LinkedIn to find ideas. She asked her Instagram community for recommendations, as well as audiences at her speaking engagements.

Those searches led to her support of BackSpinz Music Academy in North Carolina, which trains young people to use their creativity, and Daddy Stroller Social Club, which helps new fathers deal with postpartum depression.
Breland-Noble said she was thankful to French Gates for the opportunity to give.
“She saw me and supported me and pulled me out – like a needle in a haystack,” said Breland-Noble. “I then had the ability to do that for somebody else.”

Former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern said she is also grateful for the opportunity to make $20 million in donations. And she knows she took the decidedly tougher route by not making large gifts to established organizations.
“I wanted to use this funding to achieve things that otherwise may not have existed were it not for this opportunity,” she said. “That took time.”

She began working with the International Rescue Committee on a program to prevent postpartum hemorrhaging for women in areas affected by war and other humanitarian crises, where 58% of maternal mortality occurs. The resulting Safer Births in Crises Consortium now focuses on preventing the deaths of mothers in South Sudan, Burkina Faso and Papua New Guinea.

What Ardern did not anticipate was that her donations through The Matariki Fund for Women would coincide with funding cuts for international aid. As a former prime minister who previously dispatched such aid, she said she had two distinct reactions to seeing life-saving programs cut.

“One is we’ve just got to get on with it. What do we do? How can we help?” Ardern said. “And then I think about how I can advocate for the restoration. How we can lift the profile of this collective approach to voters? Because ultimately, they’re the ones that demand from their leaders that we keep having this impact.”
Ardern said she has no plans to become a full-time philanthropist. She prefers her new job at the University of Sydney as a professor, announced last month.

“I’ll be working on empathetic leadership, but I’m also attached to the School of Public Health," she said, adding that she intends to continue working on global health issues. “My view is there is absolutely a role for political leadership to rebuild trust, reduce insularity, and reduce the grievance that people feel. Actually, what’s interesting is that the public think that it’s their job too.”
Gary Barker, on the other hand, not only used the $20 million he received from French Gates to expand his philanthropic work, he used it to convince other funders to also support his nonprofit.

Barker is the founder and CEO of the Equimundo Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, which engages men and boys in promoting gender equality, and launched the Caring Masculinity Fund to distribute French Gates’ donation.

“The Minderoo Foundation in Australia looked at what Melinda funded us to do and said, ‘Would you come do the same at the country level in Australia?’,” said Barker. “Her voice saying, ‘This is worth investing in and that this is not taking funds or attention away from women and girls’ is a political boost in addition to boosting our credibility as an organization.”
Barker said the experience has made him seek similar relationships with funders.
“We don’t want to go back to piecemeal fundraising,” he said. “We’re not gonna wanna do it any differently from here on out.”
