title: Skydance to combine Warner Bros. TV Group and Paramount Television Studios
summary: Skydance is combining Warner Bros
story: Skydance is combining Warner Bros

NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Skydance will combine two of its key TV production units, Warner Bros. Television Group and Paramount Television Studios, bringing such shows as "The Pitt,” “Ted Lasso,” “Reacher” and “Landman” under the same roof.

The combined entity will be known as Warner Bros. Television Studios, with Channing Dungey and Matt Thunell serving as presidents. The merger of the studios will be completed in early 2027, according to a memo released Wednesday.

“Bringing together two of the industry’s most prolific television studios creates a formidable creative engine, uniting extraordinary talent, resources, acclaimed programming and iconic franchises with the global scale to compete at the highest level," George Cheeks, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV, said in the memo.
It’s the latest move since Skydance-owned Paramount last month closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, ushering in a new Hollywood giant under the leadership of David Ellison.
The new Warner Bros. Television Studios will house more than 120 TV series, including HBO's “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone,” Netflix's “Emily in Paris” and CBS' “Marshals.”
CBS Studios — another studio that produces shows such as the “NCIS” and “Fire Country” franchises — will continue to operate as a standalone entity under David Stapf.

title: Xi and Carney call for deeper ties as Canada looks beyond US for trade
summary: The leaders of China and Canada have called for deeper ties as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing
story: The leaders of China and Canada have called for deeper ties as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing
SHENZHEN, China -- The leaders of China and Canada  called for deeper ties Tuesday as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties.
The meeting came a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to maintain an integrated North American auto industry.

“Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the people of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace, stability, development and prosperity,” said Xi. “This is the right choice.”
Carney said that the exchanges between Canada and China have increased in the past months and praised that now there is “greater predictability and stability” in their relationship.
“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” he said.
Xi and Carney reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

title: Why France is sending soldiers into Ukraine and how Russia is responding
summary: Russia is responding forcefully to France's confirmation that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine for training and maintenance help with supplied weaponry
story: Russia is responding forcefully to France's confirmation that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine for training and maintenance help with supplied weaponry

PARIS -- Russia is responding forcefully to confirmation from France that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine to provide training and maintenance help with some of the weaponry it has supplied for the war.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said: “This is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,' but direct participation in the war.”
France says the soldiers and weapons specialists are noncombatants.
“Since we are not at war with Russia, these, in fact, are not combat units,” French Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo said.
Here's a closer look:
Speaking on Wednesday to French broadcaster RMC, Rufo said French personnel are “a very long way from the front line. They come to carry out occasional missions.”

She didn't specify their numbers, but said that they are “a few soldiers, specialists, including armaments engineers, who work — or can come to work — on an occasional basis to maintain complex equipment, such as Mirage aircraft or Caesar howitzers, and provide targeted training on certain equipment.”

France first delivered Mirage 2000-5 fighters last year to Ukraine and trained pilots and mechanics for them. The French Defense Ministry says the aircraft have helped fend off missile and drone attacks.
It also says that with donations from allies and purchases, Ukraine's force of high-precision French-made Caesar howitzers has grown to become the largest in the world.
France has also supplied precision bombs, cruise missiles, air defense systems, light tanks and other equipment.

Rufo told French lawmakers on Tuesday that France is “accelerating” its support in light of Russia's air campaign against Ukrainian targets. She spoke of a “complete absence of any intention to engage in combat” and described as “absurd” Lavrov's accusation that France is directly participating in the war.
Only a “very limited" number of French personnel are engaged in “the extremely limited” missions, Rufo said.

Her comments came after French media, including broadcaster RFI and Le Monde newspaper, reported that small contingents of French military officers stay in Ukraine for short rotations as part of the so-called Operation Volia, since at least this summer.

French military personnel have been operating in Ukraine for more than six months and France isn't alone in providing such support, Lavrov said Tuesday at a news conference in Manila, Philippines, where he was attending a summit of Southeast Asian nations.

“We have conveyed our concern through the available channels, warning the relevant countries that this is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,’ but direct participation in the war,” he said, without naming the countries.
“This is just like the assistance with target designation, the provision of satellite data and much else,” he said.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that Moscow will regard any foreign troops in Ukraine as legitimate targets and it will be up to the Russian military to determine a response.

The United Kingdom has soldiers in Ukraine, but officials haven't disclosed how many or what their role is. The U.K. Defense Ministry confirmed two deaths of British soldiers in Ukraine in the past year, in both cases in accidents.

Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, dozens of countries have trained more than 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers, at locations outside the country — in France, the U.K., the United States, Poland, Germany and elsewhere — including on Patriot missile batteries, F-16 combat jets and other equipment. They have also trained recruits, officers, medics and other specialists for combat.
Jill Lawless in London, Sylvie Corbet and Catherine Gaschka in Paris, and Lorne Cook in Brussels, contributed to this report.

title: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
summary: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week
story: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week

TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.

Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.

Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.

One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.

“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.

The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.

The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.

“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.

Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.

Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.

But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.

Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.

Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.

Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.

“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.

These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.

Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”
Wu reported from Bangkok.

title: Pete Rose posthumously pardoned by Trump after career hits leader reinstated by MLB
summary: President Donald Trump says he has posthumously pardoned Pete Rose more than two years after the baseball star’s death and a year after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred
story: President Donald Trump says he has posthumously pardoned Pete Rose more than two years after the baseball star’s death and a year after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump on Thursday said he had posthumously pardoned Pete Rose more than two years after the baseball star’s death and a year after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred.
“I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND,” Trump posted on social media.

Rose, baseball's career hits leader at 4,256, entered guilty pleas on April 20, 1990, to two counts of filing false tax returns, admitting he failed to report $354,968 during a four-year period. That was about eight months after Rose agreed to a permanent ban from baseball.

″I know I’m not a bad person, but I did make some mistakes and it’s in the eyes of the judge,″ Rose said that night during his weekly talk show on WCKY-AM in Cincinnati. ″All you can say is it’s up to the judge.″

The pardon comes after Manfred issued a sweeping decision last May that opened a pathway for Rose to be considered for baseball's Hall of Fame. Manfred declared that individuals on MLB's permanently ineligible list would have their statuses restored at death, a ruling that impacted 17 people, most notably Rose and Shoeless Joe Jackson.

Under a rule adopted by the Hall’s board of directors in 1991, anyone on the permanently ineligible list can’t be considered for election to the Hall. The earliest Rose or Jackson could now be inducted would be in 2028.

Rose agreed to his permanent ban in August 1989 after Major League Baseball investigator John M. Dowd concluded he bet numerous times on the Cincinnati Reds while playing on and managing his hometown team from 1985-87.

Facing a sentence of up to six years in prison and $500,000 in fines, Rose was sentenced on July 19, 1990, by U.S. District Judge S. Arthur Spiegel in Cincinnati to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform 1,000 hours of community service as a gym teacher’s assistant with inner-city youths in Cincinnati as part of a one-year probation period. The first three months of the probation were to be spent at the halfway house.
Rose repaid the Internal Revenue Service $366,042.

“History and the tincture of time will decide his place among the all-time greats of baseball,” Spiegel said. “With regard to Pete Rose, the individual, he has broken the law, admitted his guilt, and stands ready to pay the penalty. Under our system of law and sense of fairness, when he has completed his sentence, he will have paid his debt to society and should be accepted by society as rehabilitated. Only time will tell whether he is to be restored to his position of honor for his accomplishment on the ball fields of America.”

Rose reported that Aug. 10 to the U.S. Penitentiary Marion Camp in Illinois, a minimum security facility, and was released Jan. 7, 1991. He entered Talbert House to start serving his probation and departed on April 5.

A 17-time All-Star during a playing career from 1963-86, Rose was the 1963 National League Rookie of the Year, 1973 MVP and 1975 World Series MVP. A three-time NL batting champion, he broke the prior hits record of 4,191 set by Ty Cobb from 1905-28.
AP Baseball Writer Jay Cohen contributed to this report.

title: Drone operator films Pochettino’s first Man United training session, footage posted online
summary: Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session as Manchester United coach came under closer scrutiny than expected when a drone operator filmed it
story: Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session as Manchester United coach came under closer scrutiny than expected when a drone operator filmed it

MANCHESTER, England -- MANCHESTER, England (AP) — Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session as Manchester United coach came under closer scrutiny than expected when a drone operator filmed it on Thursday.

About 12 minutes of the session was uploaded onto a YouTube account called CC OVERVIEW with a man, who also appeared to be controlling the drone hovering around the Carrington training ground, providing his own live commentary.
“Let’s get closer,” he said before zooming in on the Argentine coach Pochettino talking to several players formed in a huddle.
“I can definitely see Harry Maguire," he added. “That there is Bruno (Fernandes), definitely, (I can) tell by the gestures.”
The account justified the filming in a pinned post that said it's legal.

“It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it. The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn’t fly over anyone or even near anyone,” the post said. “The drone is correctly labelled and I hold all the relevant licenses, public liability and insurance required.”
The post said no sensitive information had been revealed with regard to how struggling United would line up at fourth-place Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.
“As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the manager's first training session,” he wrote. “There are many media there so certainly won’t be the only footage of training released.”
Pochettino replaced Michael Carrick, who was fired last week with United in 18th — the relegation zone — after its worst start in 40 years.

title: Trail Blazers' Damian Lillard facing Bucks for the first time since they waived him
summary: Portland Trail Blazers guard Damian Lillard wasn’t expecting anything too out of the ordinary as he prepared to play at Milwaukee for the first time since the Bucks waived him in the summer of 2025
story: Portland Trail Blazers guard Damian Lillard wasn’t expecting anything too out of the ordinary as he prepared to play at Milwaukee for the first time since the Bucks waived him in the summer of 2025

MILWAUKEE -- Portland Trail Blazers guard Damian Lillard wasn’t expecting anything too out of the ordinary as he prepared to play at Milwaukee for the first time since the Bucks waived him in the summer of 2025.

Lillard already accompanied the Trail Blazers to Milwaukee last season while he was recovering from a torn Achilles tendon. Even though Lillard didn’t play in the Trail Blazers’ 115-103 victory that night, the Bucks aired a tribute video to him before the game.

“I think the fact that I was here last year when we played, that takes away the first-time-coming-back type of feel,” Lillard said during the Trail Blazers’ shootaround before their Thursday night game with the Bucks.

This will mark the second straight night that the Bucks have played against one of their former superstars. Milwaukee lost 137-130 at Miami on Wednesday as two-time MVP Giannis Antetokounmpo had 27 points, 14 rebounds and nine assists while facing the Bucks for the first time since getting traded to the Heat last summer.

The Bucks acquired Lillard in September 2023 after the seven-time all-NBA guard requested a trade from Portland that summer. The Bucks believed that pairing Antetokounmpo and Lillard would enable them to contend for multiple titles.
It didn’t work out that way.

Milwaukee lost to Indiana in the first round of the playoffs each of Lillard’s two seasons with the Bucks as injuries prevented the two superstars from playing together for an extended postseason run.

“I thought it was a necessary experience,” Lillard said. “I made some really good friends, crossed paths with some good people. It was an experience that I needed. We won a lot of games. We just didn’t have a healthy run.”

Antetokounmpo missed Milwaukee’s 2023 postseason while recovering from a calf strain. Lillard sat out the Bucks’ final 14 regular-season games in 2023-24 due to deep vein thrombosis in his right calf, returned for Game 2 of the playoffs and then tore the Achilles tendon in his left leg in Game 4.
Lillard says he has no regrets about coming back for the postseason that year.
“I view myself like a warrior,” Lillard said. “If I’m good enough to go, I’m going to go. If my mind is in it, I’m going to be in it. That’s what I did. It ended how it ended, and that’s OK.”

Lillard’s Achilles tear meant he wouldn’t play at all in the 2024-25 season. Rather than keeping Lillard on their roster, the Bucks made the surprising move to waive him, even though he had $112.6 million remaining on his contract. The Bucks agreed to stretch out those payments over the next five years.
Lillard says he understands the reason behind the Bucks’ decision. The move gave the Bucks the payroll flexibility to sign former Indiana Pacers center Myles Turner.

“It was pretty simple,” said Lillard, who returned to Portland in the summer of 2025 on a three-year, $42 million deal. “I was injured. I wasn’t going to be available to play last season. The team was focused on bringing somebody in here that they could pair with Giannis so they could still be a competitive team, which is the business side of it.”

The Bucks have suffered this season without the star power that Lillard and Antetokounmpo brought to the roster. Milwaukee entered Thursday’s game with a 1-14 record that represented the worst start in franchise history. The only remaining Bucks from Lillard's Milwaukee tenure are AJ Green, Kyle Kuzma, Ryan Rollins, Jericho Sims, Gary Trent Jr. and two-way player Pete Nance.

In the meantime, Lillard has come back from his injury to score 20.1 points per game at the age of 36 while helping Portland win nine of its first 14 games. He’s part of a backcourt that also includes Jrue Holiday, who played on the Bucks’ 2021 championship team before getting included in the trade that brought Lillard to Milwaukee.

“I think the thing I’m most happy with or most excited about is I know that I’m not completely back all the way connected,” Lillard said. “I’ve been able to be as productive as I have without fully getting all the way back in form. I know there’s more to come.”

title: Five players reach double figures as No. 5 Duke routs Fordham 111-44
summary: Toby Fournier and Emilee Skinner each scored 18 points to lead No. 5 Duke to a 111-44 rout of Fordham, marking the Blue Devils’ second victory by more than a 60-point margin in eight days
story: Toby Fournier and Emilee Skinner each scored 18 points to lead No. 5 Duke to a 111-44 rout of Fordham, marking the Blue Devils’ second victory by more than a 60-point margin in eight days

DURHAM, N.C. -- Toby Fournier and Emilee Skinner each scored 18 points to lead No. 5 Duke to a 111-44 rout of Fordham on Thursday, marking the Blue Devils’ second victory by more than a 60-point margin in eight days.
Riley Nelson had 14 points, Aaliyah Crump provided 13 and Autumn Fleary posted 11 for the Blue Devils (5-0), who shot 60.1% from the field.

Ugne Sirtautaite scored 11 points, and Anastasija Veljovic and Precious Omoshola each finished with 10 for Fordham (5-2), which played its fourth consecutive road game. The Rams, who weren’t credited with an assist, missed all 11 of their 3-point attempts.

Duke is 5-0 for the third time in coach Kara Lawson’s seven seasons, but for the first time since 2022-23. The Blue Devils won 85-23 last Thursday at Norfolk State for what had been their most lopsided result of the season.

Fournier, who led the Blue Devils in scoring for the third game in a row despite logging only 20 minutes, shot 8 for 11 from the field but only 2 for 7 on free throws. Skinner, who delivered a game-high seven assists, made seven of 10 shots from the field.

Duke outscored the Rams 15-2 in the first five minutes of the second quarter to boost the margin to 36-10. Ten Blue Devils scored in the first half, which ended at 52-20 with Duke shooting 64.7% from the field. The third quarter began with Duke going on a 15-2 run.
Fordham had been off to its best six-game mark in 14 years and had four starters averaging double-digit points.

title: Ravens to deactivate CB Humphrey for Carolina game after "criminals" comment about Baltimore
summary: The Ravens are deactivating cornerback Marlon Humphrey for this weekend’s game at Carolina after the veteran said on a podcast that “criminals” are among the things Baltimore is best at making
story: The Ravens are deactivating cornerback Marlon Humphrey for this weekend’s game at Carolina after the veteran said on a podcast that “criminals” are among the things Baltimore is best at making

OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- The Ravens are deactivating cornerback Marlon Humphrey for this weekend's game at Carolina after the veteran said on a podcast that “criminals” are among the things Baltimore is best at making.
Coach Jesse Minter announced the move Thursday and said Humphrey was sent home and would not practice.

“I would say this: He's very remorseful. I think he really understands that words mean a lot, especially to people in this city," Minter said. “When you say something like that, it's not a reflection of our team and our organization and how we want to operate.”
Humphrey apologized for the comments Wednesday, and Baltimore mayor Brandon Scott said a verbal apology was “not enough.”
“They’re best at making criminals,” Humphrey said on the podcast. “Yeah no, that’s obviously going to get cut out.”
Minter said Wednesday he loved the city. A day later, he made the announcement that Humphrey was being removed for the rest of the week. He said it would be a one-game deactivation.

“Having to be a leader when the team needs you the most is my job. This is a team thing in my opinion,” Minter said. "He’s going to deal with a lot of stuff from this. This is about the team and putting us in the best position to be successful — going down there for one reason, to play well and win the football game.”

title: Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft advanced in election process for the Pro Football Hall of Fame
summary: Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft have advanced to the final step in the election process for the Pro Football Hall of Fame
story: Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft have advanced to the final step in the election process for the Pro Football Hall of Fame
Bill Belichick and Robert Kraft have advanced to the final step in the election process for the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Belichick and Kraft, who won six Super Bowls together with the New England Patriots, will be among a group of 15 candidates that will include 13 players who will be considered in the same pool at the Hall of Fame’s annual selection meeting ahead of the Super Bowl.

A 25-person selection panel will reduce the list of candidates from 15 to 10 to seven. Selectors then may vote for six of the seven. Any candidate receiving 80% approval would be elected to the Class of 2027.
Belichick was chosen from a group that included Tom Coughlin, Mike Holmgren, Dan Reeves and Mike Shanahan.

Kraft was picked from a group that included Doug Williams, late Bears owner Virginia McCaskey, longtime NFL player, scout and personnel executive John Wooten and former Canton Bulldogs owner Ralph Hay.
Belichick was not elected in his first year of eligibility last year. His snub was criticized intensely around the NFL.

“If he’s not a first-ballot Hall of Famer, there’s really no coach that should ever be a first-ballot Hall of Famer, which is completely ridiculous because people deserve it. He’s incredible,” Tom Brady said.
Brady was Belichick's quarterback for all six Super Bowl titles with the Patriots. Belichick also won two as a defensive assistant coach with the New York Giants.

Belichick’s career included a sign-stealing scandal dubbed “Spygate” in the 2007 season. He was fined $500,000 after the team was caught filming defensive signals from the New York Jets during a game in Week 1. The Patriots went 16-0 that season before losing to the Giants in the Super Bowl.
Belichick’s final season in New England was 2023. He’s in his second season coaching in college at North Carolina. The Tar Heels are 5-5.

Kraft has owned the Patriots since 1994. His teams have won six Super Bowls and played in five others. Under Kraft, the Patriots have won more division titles (20), conference crowns (11) and playoff games (36) than any other NFL team.
The Hall's Class of 2027 will be announced at “NFL Honors” in Los Angeles in February and enshrined next August in Canton.

title: Shelton beats Jodar and now needs help from Zverev to advance at the ATP Finals
summary: U.S. Open finalist Ben Shelton has done his part and now needs some help from top-ranked Alexander Zverev to advance at the ATP Finals in Turin
story: U.S. Open finalist Ben Shelton has done his part and now needs some help from top-ranked Alexander Zverev to advance at the ATP Finals in Turin
TURIN, Italy -- TURIN, Italy (AP) — U.S. Open finalist Ben Shelton did his part. Now he needs some help from top-ranked Alexander Zverev to advance at the ATP Finals.
Shelton twice aced his way out of trouble in the first-set tiebreaker and beat Rafael Jodar 7-6 (8), 7-5 on Thursday.
If Zverev wins a set against Arthur Fils later in the final match of the group, Shelton will reach the semifinals of the elite event for the season’s top eight players.
Zverev has already advanced with two wins, while Fils is 1-1.
Fils’ only chance of advancing is by beating Zverev in straight sets.
Jodar was eliminated after losing all three of his matches.
Carlos Alcaraz has already advanced from the other group.
No matter if Shelton advances or not, having won two of his three group matches is quite an improvement compared to when he lost all three during his debut at the Finals last year.
Shelton served aces to save two set points in the tiebreaker.

Also late in the first set, a shot from Shelton clipped the net and hit Jodar in the back at the net. Jodar ended up on the ground and grasped his back when he got up but didn’t appear bothered as the match wore on. Shelton asked Jodar if he was OK and the players slapped hands.
In the final game of the match, Shelton slipped and fell over backward. But he got right back up and served three straight aces to finish it off.

title: This marathoner ran 7 races this year. Doing them pregnant was not part of the plan
summary: Deirdre Keane, a 38-year-old nurse practitioner and management consultant, achieved her goal of completing all seven World Marathon Majors
story: Deirdre Keane, a 38-year-old nurse practitioner and management consultant, achieved her goal of completing all seven World Marathon Majors
Deirdre Keane had already run more than 60 marathons when she decided to take on a new challenge of completing the World Marathon Majors. She just didn’t expect to be running them while pregnant.

Earlier this month, the 38-year-old nurse practitioner and management consultant ran the New York City Marathon – her hometown race – in her third trimester. It was the seventh marathon she had finished while pregnant and was the final race she needed to achieve her goal of running all the World Marathon Majors in the same year.

“I knew how bizarre it was to be running a marathon at 34 weeks, but I also knew how fit I was and self-aware of my body at this point,” Keane said. “And while it is very unusual, I wasn’t the first woman to have ever done this.”
After getting married last year, Keane and her husband Brian began talking about starting a family. Expecting pregnancy to take a while, Keane made other plans for herself in the interim.
“In my mind, 2026 was going to be my year of bucket list items,” Keane recalled. “I was like, this is going to be my last hurrah before settling down and becoming pregnant, becoming a mother.”
She signed up for 11 races: the seven World Marathon Majors, a trail marathon in Ireland, two ultramarathons and an Ironman race.

Keane kicked off her quest by running the Tokyo Marathon in March. But when the Boston and London Marathons rolled around in April, she noticed she was running a bit slower than usual and wasn’t quite feeling like herself. So, she took a pregnancy test.
It was positive, but she wasn’t going to let that get in the way of her goals.

She promised her husband she would take the next marathon in Ireland slowly. She also agreed to forgo the Ironman and the second ultramarathon – she had already completed the first before finding out she was pregnant.

“Brian was understandably skeptical and worried at first. Neither of us fully understood the physical limitations of pregnancy and why. The research we found was surprisingly limited and frustrating,” Keane said. “So, we decided to take it one marathon at a time, with me not pushing the pace and keeping walking in my back pocket.”
Keane was initially nervous to tell her OB-GYN about her marathon plans but was relieved when she got the go-ahead.

“I don’t think she thought I would do them towards the end, especially being so pregnant at New York. But I am very stubborn and determined,” Keane said. “Plus I got lucky, I was feeling good. So I was able to do it.”

Exercise is generally considered safe and beneficial during most healthy pregnancies. Experts recommend that pregnant women who were physically active before pregnancy or regularly engaged in vigorous aerobic exercise can continue those activities with approval from their doctor. There is limited research on intensive exercise beyond the recommended amount.

With the approval of her doctor, Keane flew to Australia in August to compete in the Sydney Marathon at 25 weeks pregnant, followed by Berlin at 29 weeks. She then completed the Chicago Marathon at 31 weeks in just under 4 hours and finished with the New York City Marathon at 34 weeks in 4:06.55.

Keane was more worried about the race in New York “because I was starting to look heavily pregnant and feel it too." But she had friends along the course while her husband appeared at multiple spots with water to keep her hydrated.

“The marathon passed a block away from Weill Cornell at mile 16, where I’m delivering, so there were plenty of jokes about just pulling off there to have the baby or testing the medical volunteers’ training on the course with an unusual medical intervention of a delivery,” she said.
Keane’s determination was modeled for her at an early age by her father, John, an Irish immigrant who ran marathons in the 1980s and 1990s.
He died of cancer when she was 13, but continued to run in his final months, completing his final New York City Marathon one day before undergoing surgery to have a tumor removed, Keane said.
Years later, when Keane went to college, she was inspired to run a marathon in her dad’s honor. That’s when she caught the bug.

“I loved marathons from the beginning, because it really shows me what the human body is capable of, not only from a physical standpoint, but from a mental standpoint,” she said. “I realized how much grit I have and how capable I am to overcome hard things.”

Since then, running has become a constant in Keane’s life. She says it helped her cope with the emotional toll of working as a nurse practitioner at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York during the COVID-19 pandemic.

During the pandemic, feeling isolated and needing something to look forward to, Keane signed up for the World Marathon Challenge: Running 7 marathons on 7 different continents in just 7 days. She completed the challenge in 2023 and was the fastest woman to do so that year.

Now, with the World Majors in her rearview, Keane says she’s taking time to reflect on the past 8 months. Just as she learned from her father’s example, she hopes to pass the lessons running has taught her on to her son.

“I want to teach my son resilience and that he can do hard things,” she said. “And that when life inevitably gets tough and throws challenges at him, he will push through them and see the other side of them, whether we elect to do them like a marathon or some things that are way beyond our control.”

title: South Africa beats Bangladesh on Day 5 of first cricket test after Harmer shines again
summary: Simon Harmer has run through Bangladesh’s tail and South Africa has knocked off the 12 runs required to win the first test in Johannesburg
story: Simon Harmer has run through Bangladesh’s tail and South Africa has knocked off the 12 runs required to win the first test in Johannesburg

JOHANNESBURG -- Simon Harmer ran through Bangladesh's tail and South Africa knocked off the 12 runs required to win the first test by nine wickets on Thursday, taking a 1-0 lead in the teams' two-match cricket test series.

Resuming on 100-5 at the Wanderers, Bangladesh's lower-order batters couldn't handle the off-spin of Harmer, who took four of the remaining five wickets to help dismiss the tourists for 168 and have figures of 6-51.
It revived memories of Harmer taking 6-16 on Day 5 of the series-clinching victory over Australia last month.

The Proteas lost first-innings century-maker Marques Ackerman — for a second-ball duck — on the way to reaching their target before lunch, at 12-1. Soon after getting bowled off a no-ball, Aiden Markram (8 not out) scored the winning run.
South Africa dethroned Australia for the top spot in the ICC test team rankings with that series win last month and is the reigning world test champion.

In Harmer it has a 37-year-old player enjoying a renaissance in a test career that was drifting until a year ago, when he returned after a two-and-a-half-year absence and is now a reliable match-winner.

Having already removed Najmul Hossain Shanto and Mahfijul Islam late in Day 4, Harmer took the final four wickets of the match in his brilliant four-over burst that came after overnight batter Litton Das got an inside edge and played onto his own stumps off Kagiso Rabada (3-46).
Mushfiqur Rahim added 34 runs to his overnight 5 before gloving Harmer to a close fielder, for a dismissal that was only given after the Proteas reviewed a not-out call.
In his next over, Harmer had Mehidy Hasan Miraz stumped for 4, before removing Hasan Mahmud (4) and Ebadot Hossain (0) in consecutive balls to wrap up the innings.
Despite making 400 in the first innings after winning the toss, Bangladesh barely avoided an innings defeat.
The second test is at Centurion starting on Monday, and South Africa will head into it atop the points table in the World Test Championship for 2025-27.

title: NFL Mexico: Vikings-49ers marks return to Mexico City, though the league never truly left
summary: The NFL's presence in Mexico continues to grow, even though the last regular-season game there was in 2022
story: The NFL's presence in Mexico continues to grow, even though the last regular-season game there was in 2022
MEXICO CITY -- Many fans will no doubt view Sunday's matchup between the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings as marking the NFL’s return to Mexico.
The reality is, the league never truly left.

Although Mexico last hosted a regular-season game in 2022, the league’s growth in the country has been steady, according to Arturo Olivé, managing director of NFL Mexico. Over the past 18 years, the league’s domestic fan base has surged from roughly 10 million to 40 million, according to the NFL.

"We have grown significantly over these years thanks to the constant, continuous, daily work of our team,” Olivé said. “Eighteen years ago, we chose our battles and focused our attention on the specific areas we needed to improve in order to expand our fan base.”

In Mexico, the NFL trails only soccer — the national sport — in total fans. The game's popularity is no coincidence; American football is as much a part of Mexican sports tradition as soccer, boxing, and lucha libre.
The Mexico game will be the last of the nine international NFL games played this season, a league record.
To expand its reach, NFL Mexico invested heavily in flag football, which has steadily gained traction and now boasts roughly 4 million players nationwide.

While impressive, Olivé acknowledges that in a nation of more than 130 million people, there is still vast room for growth. To accelerate adoption, the league signed an agreement with the National Commission of Physical Culture and Sport (CONADE) to expand the sport across public schools.
“With 4 million children in the program, we are barely scratching the surface. Forty million fans in Mexico is a lot, but there are still another 80 or 90 million people we could reach,” Olivé said.

CONADE, the agency that oversees Mexico’s federal sports budget, is eager to promote flag football ahead of its debut as an Olympic sport at the 2028 Los Angeles Games. Mexico’s women’s national team has already secured an Olympic berth.

"We believe this alliance turns schools into spaces for participation, well-being and talent development,” said Rommel Pacheco, general director of CONADE. “We want more girls, boys, and young people to play an accessible and inclusive sport.”
Olivé noted that initiatives such as flag football and Play 60 have been particularly effective at drawing women to the game. Today, women account for 47% of Mexico’s 40 million NFL fans.
NFL Mexico focused on grassroots programs knowing the country already possessed a deep-rooted football culture dating back more than a century.
“We have been an important market for the league long before the NFL Mexico office was established,” Olivé said. “American football has been broadcast in Mexico for 61 years.”

In a nation steeped in soccer culture — and one that has hosted three FIFA World Cups — this passion for gridiron football might come as a surprise. Yet Mexico supports a major college football league with 32 participating teams, alongside a seven-team professional league that recently celebrated its 10th anniversary.

Football was first introduced to Mexico in 1896 by Mexican students returning home from U.S. universities. The first official game took place that year in Xalapa, in the Gulf state of Veracruz, where the students and their friends faced a squad of American sailors from a U.S. ship anchored at a nearby port.
Soon after, several clubs formed in Veracruz, and the sport eventually spread to Mexico City and local universities.

The National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), which today enrolls more than 400,000 students, began fielding teams in the 1920s. By the 1950s, most Mexican universities had football programs, and the sport rivaled soccer in popularity.
Even after soccer reclaimed its undisputed spot at the top, football remained hugely popular — a fact that did not go unnoticed by the NFL.

On Aug. 5, 1978, the Philadelphia Eagles faced the New Orleans Saints in a preseason matchup in Mexico City. Roughly 30,000 fans packed Estadio Ciudad de los Deportes to watch the Saints’ 14–7 victory in the first NFL game played south of the border.

The league returned 16 years later when the Houston Oilers met the Dallas Cowboys at Estadio Azteca in the first of six preseason American Bowls hosted in Mexico. The final exhibition in that series took place in 2001, when the Raiders played the Cowboys.

Mexico hosted its first regular-season NFL game in 2005, when the Arizona Cardinals defeated the San Francisco 49ers before 103,467 spectators at Estadio Azteca, setting what was then an NFL attendance record.
The league returned in 2016 for a matchup between Oakland and Houston, followed by four additional regular-season games through 2022, when the 49ers once again faced the Cardinals.

"I fell in love with the 49ers in the mid-80s because of Joe Montana. I’ve attended every game held in Mexico, and it’s great that they’re back,” said Octavio Zúñiga, a 50-year-old fan. “Last time (in 2022), they came out carrying the Mexican flag as they entered the stadium. That commitment to the Mexican fan base is truly appreciated.”
Mexico currently holds a contract guaranteeing an annual NFL game through 2028, and Olivé believes the groundwork is in place to extend that partnership even further.

“Right now, our priority is to consolidate our regular presence with one game per year. We have a three-year contract that we hope will serve as a springboard to keep building from 2029 onward,” Olivé said. “That will give the league the confidence to say, whenever Mexico is ready, we are bringing back what never truly left.”

title: Why top-ranked women's basketball teams are playing at Columbia in rare mid-major scheduling coup
summary: Columbia is pulling off a rare scheduling coup for a mid-major women’s basketball program: the Lions are hosting teams ranked in the top five of the AP Top 25 poll
story: Columbia is pulling off a rare scheduling coup for a mid-major women’s basketball program: the Lions are hosting teams ranked in the top five of the AP Top 25 poll
NEW YORK -- Columbia is pulling off a rare scheduling coup for a mid-major women's basketball program: the Lions are hosting teams ranked in the top five of the AP Top 25 poll.
They open their doors for No. 5 Duke on Saturday and had second-ranked Michigan visit on Nov. 12.

Kudos to Columbia for getting the heavyweights to agree to play them at its intimate Francis S. Levien Gymnasium, which seats 2,700. There are various reasons the Blue Devils and Wolverines agreed to the games — scheduling challenges and NIL are among them.

For Duke coach Kara Lawson, playing the game made sense. The two teams had a competitive home-and-home series a few years ago and Lawson is always trying to build a strong schedule for her Blue Devils. So Duke reached out to see if Columbia would do another home-and-home set over the next two seasons.

“When you look at the Ivy League, there’s a lot of strong teams there. Columbia being one of the contenders every year,” she said. “It’s a great opportunity for us to get a quality opponent on the road, and then obviously they’ll come to Cameron next year.”

The Lions are indeed a good team, but welcoming two of the five best teams in the country would have been unthinkable years ago. Ivy League rival Princeton had been the only ranked team to ever play at Columbia and that’s because the two schools are in the same conference.
Sandwiched between the Duke and Michigan home games, Columbia headed to College Park on Sunday and took on No. 19 Maryland.

It’s been 12 years since a mid-major program has played three consecutive regular-season games against ranked teams, including two top-five opponents, according to STATS Perform. New Mexico did it in 2014, although two of those games were on neutral courts.

Many of the smaller schools need to play those “buy” games to help pay for their team’s budgets. Columbia opted to play a home-and-home with Michigan and Duke, although the Lions will still get some money from them for the road games. Their contest against Maryland last Sunday was a guarantee game, with the Terrapins paying Columbia to come.

Women’s teams can make usually between $20,000 to $50,000 for those games, depending on how far they have to travel and how much schools want to offer. Men’s programs pay sometimes three or four times as much for guarantee games.
“It’s becoming more of a factor with NIL,” Fairfield coach Carly Thibault-Dudonis said of playing guarantee games. “We’ve taken what we can get.”
Thibault-Dudonis has built Fairfield into one of the top mid-major programs over the last few years. Fewer teams want to play the Stags and even fewer want to make the trip to Connecticut.
“Each year it’s gotten harder and harder,” she said. “Constantly trying to find home games, period. You try to get top-three teams in conferences to play you.”
One option will be more neutral-site games.

While men’s basketball has a lot of games at neutral sites where both teams get paid to play, women’s basketball is still catching up. There are a few tournaments now such as the Players Era, Champions Classic and Coretta Scott King that will pay teams to participate.
There are also some one-off games that do as well. Still, women’s basketball has a way to go to reach the level the men are at.
Louisville coach Jeff Walz said scheduling is a constant challenge coaches face every season.

With the Atlantic Coast Conference playing 18 leagues games now, he has fewer nonconference games to schedule. Walz schedules a few guarantee games to go along with a couple of competitive contests with schools like UConn or Kentucky. He'll also go on the road sometimes to play against teams led by some of his former assistant coaches or programs he has relationships with.
“You are going to find out a lot about your team when you go on the road and play a really good mid-major program,” he said. “If we get beat at Ball State, I don’t think it’s a terrible loss.
"It tells us and our players that we've got a lot of work to do so that if we are going to win at Duke and Notre Dame, we'd have to get better.”
LSU coach Kim Mulkey has no qualms about her nonconference schedule that isn't usually the most challenging. She believes she's helping smaller schools fund teams when they travel to Baton Rouge.
The Tigers have won their first three games this season over Southeastern Louisiana, Texas Southern and McNeese State by an average of 87 points.

“It’s very easy because people want money. People want money. We help their budget," Mulkey said. "A lot of them that come here in nonconference and you know what? I feel for them. Maybe that’s why I do play a lot of them. We have what we need but I know how hard it is at our level.
"These programs, they still need to go get players, and if we can give them some money to come here and play, we’re growing the game. We’re helping them maintain a program.”
This phenomenon isn't unique to LSU or women's basketball.

“You always had buy games. This just didn’t start. You’ve got it in football. You’ve got it in men’s and women’s basketball and I’m sure in other sports," Mulkey said. "I don’t know if it’s as much money, but this just didn’t start with the NIL era. You’ve always helped people that want to come play you and give them money, some of them more than others. That’s negotiated ahead of time. It just didn’t start.”
Columbia has earned the right to host top teams with its play.
The Lions have gotten better the last few years, reaching the NCAA Tournament twice as an at-large team and winning the WBIT last season. Now more schools are willing to play them on the road.

“It’s a gauntlet. I love a challenge” Columbia coach Megan Griffith said of playing three Top 25 teams in a nine-day stretch. “We have to prove a resume for March. Not that March hinges on (these games), but it gives you another chance, right?
"So very intentionally, we always look for a couple of these Quad 1 games.”
Columbia also happens to be located in New York City, another draw for opponents like Michigan and Duke as both have strong alumni fan bases in the Big Apple.

title: Sri Lanka ekes out 82-run lead as Pakistan pacers toil to stay in control of 2nd test
summary: Pakistan’s depleted pace attack has toiled to limit Sri Lanka’s second innings to 309-9 and a lead of 82 runs after three days of the second cricket test in Rawalpindi
story: Pakistan’s depleted pace attack has toiled to limit Sri Lanka’s second innings to 309-9 and a lead of 82 runs after three days of the second cricket test in Rawalpindi
RAWALPINDI, Pakistan -- Pakistan's depleted pace attack toiled to limit Sri Lanka's second innings to 309-9 and a lead of 82 runs after three days of the second cricket test on Thursday.
Half-centuries from Sunal Dinusha (54), captain Kusal Mendis (53) and Milan Rathnayake (60) denied Pakistan's bid to win inside three days.

"I am really happy how our boys fought back after struggling in the first innings,” Dinusha said. “Milan is still at the wicket and if he can get more runs for us it will be very good. It’s still game on, we have a good lead of 80 runs.”

Pakistan confirmed early Thursday that fast bowler Saqib Khan would miss the remainder of the test due to the left hamstring strain he sustained late on day two soon after taking the wicket of opener Lahiru Udara and bowling only 1.2 overs.

In the absence of Saqib, the series' leading wicket-taker, his fellow pacers rose to the occasion. Mohammad Abbas has bowled 33 overs for 2-54, Aamer Jamal has done 24 overs for 3-67, and Razaullah has 24.4 overs for 2-110.
"Unfortunately (Saqib) got injured but credit goes to the three other seamers for putting in a good effort,” Pakistan wicketkeeper Ghazi Ghori said.

"(Sri Lanka's) senior players showed lot of responsibility, Mendis played and missed a lot, but stayed in … (and) we have to put up a disciplined performance to chase whatever runs we require because there’s still a lot for the bowlers on this wicket.”
The stamina was no doubt helped by rolling Sri Lanka for 98 on the seamer-friendly pitch on day one.
Overnight batters Pasindu Sooriyabandara (38) and Dhananjaya de Silva (37) were removed in the morning session.

Jamal trapped de Silva plumb lbw off an inswinger and the batter burnt a review, then Sooriyabandara, dropped on 31, couldn't capitalize and was caught down the leg side by wicketkeeper Ghazi Ghori off Razaullah.

Mendis and Dinusha dug in against the ultra accurate seam bowling of Abbas, the pace of Razaullah and deceptive bowling of Jamal as they brought Sri Lanka within 12 runs of the huge first-innings deficit of 227 runs.
Their 81-run stand look destined to deny Pakistan a wicket in the middle session until Mendis went for a needless sweep against Salman Ali Agha close to the tea interval and was bowled.

Dinusha raised his half-century after tea with a reverse sweep against part-time spinner Mohammad Taha and nudged Sri Lanka ahead with a 53-run stand with Rathnayake, who showed plenty of aggression with his crisp drives. It was Dinusha's third half-century to go along with three centuries in seven test matches.

Jamal broke through for Pakistan in the first over with the new ball when Dinusha couldn’t control a pull shot off a short ball and was brilliantly snapped at midwicket by Tayyab Arif. Dinusha walked off in disbelief.

Rathnayake guarded the tailenders by keeping the strike to himself for the last half an hour, but Abbas was rewarded for his impeccable bowling when Prabath Jayasuriya chipped a catch to the covers and Lahiru Kumara offered a return catch to the seamer.

Rathnayake raised his aggressive second test half-century just before the close and stood valiantly against the second new ball with an unbeaten fifty off 82 balls with 11 fours. He had No. 11 Asitha Fernando for company when bad light forced early stumps.

title: Luka Doncic calls his play 'unacceptable' as Lakers' 9-game winning streak ends
summary: Luka Doncic wants the blame placed on him after the Los Angeles Lakers’ nine-game winning streak ended with a shocking loss to the previously struggling Utah Jazz
story: Luka Doncic wants the blame placed on him after the Los Angeles Lakers’ nine-game winning streak ended with a shocking loss to the previously struggling Utah Jazz
LOS ANGELES -- Luka Doncic wants the blame placed on him after the Los Angeles Lakers' nine-game winning streak ended with a shocking loss to the previously struggling Utah Jazz on Wednesday night.
Doncic wasn't great despite his 29 points in the Lakers' 109-97 defeat, missing 10 of his 12 3-point attempts and committing nine turnovers. His streak of 11 straight 30-point games also ended.

Although the ugly game was the culmination of a punishing stretch played mostly at less than full strength by Los Angeles, the Slovenian superstar still feels a personal responsibility when he can't will the Lakers to victory.

“Honestly, I've just got to do way better than this,” Doncic said. “This is unacceptable for my part. I've got to lead the team in better ways. Got to look at this game, got to move on and learn from this.”
The Lakers are still 13-3 and atop the Western Conference after their first loss of November was handed to them by a two-win opponent that only ended a 12-game losing streak one night earlier.

Playing without injured second-leading scorer Austin Reaves, the Lakers made only 38.2% of their shots and 27.3% of their 3-point attempts against the Jazz, both season lows. LA managed only nine 3-pointers, tying its season low.
Doncic claimed the blame, but his teammates and coaches weren’t having it.

“Of course he’s going to say that,” Jake LaRavia said. “It’s obviously not on him. It’s a team game. He’s been carrying the offensive load, so if there’s ever bad shooting nights, it’s on the rest of the team to help be better.”
All of the Lakers had an off night, but they rely heavily on Doncic, the league's top scorer during one of the best starts to a season in NBA history.

Doncic's usage rate — a statistic that estimates a player's involvement on offense — is at 40.6%, the highest in the league and the highest of his career. Doncic took 28 shots against the Jazz, and that was only tied for his fourth-highest total this season.
Lakers coach JJ Redick says he's confident Doncic's current preeminence to the Lakers' offense won't prove to be unsustainable.
“The shot creation that is required from him, I think it takes its toll,” Redick said. “That's part of it when Austin is out, for sure.”
Fatigue isn’t allowed to be a factor, Doncic said.

“All NBA teams play 82 games, so that can’t be an excuse,” Doncic said. “I’ve got to do way better, I know that. I feel like we had some open shots we didn’t make. But it’s one game. We’ve got to move on.”
Yet the culprit in this stinker against Utah was most likely the game accumulation that drags down every NBA team at times.

The loss came on the back half of a back-to-back set after the Lakers had to rally from an 18-point deficit late in the third quarter to beat Charlotte on Tuesday night. Doncic scored 37 points, but Quentin Grimes dramatically stepped up with a career-high 47, even forcing overtime with his 10th 3-pointer.

The loss to Utah was the Lakers' third game in four days without the high-scoring Reaves, who has a bruised heel, and it was their 10th game already in November. No team has played more games this season than the Lakers' 16 in the first 29 days, and their top three scorers have all missed games due to injury already.

“Frankly, if you’re playing 82 games, you’re going to have some horrible shooting nights,” Redick said. “My belief in the group and who we are, I’m not going to overreact to a bad offensive night for us.”
The Lakers host Sacramento (1-13) on Friday.

title: San Diego State beats Texas Southern 97-51
summary: Led by Latrell Davis' 20 points, the San Diego State Aztecs defeated the Texas Southern Tigers 97-51 on Wednesday
story: Led by Latrell Davis' 20 points, the San Diego State Aztecs defeated the Texas Southern Tigers 97-51 on Wednesday
SAN DIEGO -- Latrell Davis scored 20 points as San Diego State beat Texas Southern 97-51 on Wednesday.

Davis shot 6 for 12 (5 for 9 from 3-point range) and 3 of 4 from the free-throw line for the Aztecs (5-0). Jeremiah Cherry scored 13 points while shooting 6 of 6 from the field. Tae Simmons and Chance Gladden added 12 points apiece.
Karris Bilal led the Tigers (1-5) in scoring, finishing with 22 points. Texas Southern also got 12 points and 11 rebounds from Bencao Vungo. Xander Wedlow finished with 10 points.

Cherry scored 13 points in the first half to help put the Aztecs up 57-23 at the break. San Diego State extended its lead to 83-36 during the second half, fueled by an 11-2 run. Davis scored a team-high nine points in the second half.
Up next
San Diego State's next game is Tuesday against Iowa State. Texas Southern hosts New Orleans on Saturday.

title: NASA's Voyager 1 phones home from an awe-inspiring one light-day away
summary: NASA’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away
story: NASA’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- NASA’s Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity’s first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space.

Flight controllers received the spacecraft’s call Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That’s how long it took for the radio signals to traverse the more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) at the speed of light.
“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” the Jet Propulsion Laboratory’s director, Dave Gallagher, said in a statement.

It’s another day in the history books for Voyager 1, which launched in 1977. It swept past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, snapped the most distant photo ever taken of our “Pale Blue Dot” in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998, and crossed from the sun’s sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012.
NASA could not confirm this newest distance record until Thursday. But that didn’t stop the space agency from wishing everyone a “Happy Voyager light-day … day!” via social media the day before.
Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are NASA’s longest-operating space missions, still churning out data despite powering down most of their instruments to keep exploring.

Voyager 2 actually beat its twin into space by two weeks. But its route to Jupiter and Saturn plus Uranus and Neptune was slower and longer, and it did not reach interstellar space until 2018. It won’t reach the one-light-day mark until 2035.

Both spacecraft are doing well for their 49 years of age, plowing through space at 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) with plutonium for power. Picture-taking ended long ago, but they send back bits of precious data almost every day on their never-before-explored environment.

Each carries a so-called Golden Record brimming with the sounds of Earth. The project was led by the late Cornell University astronomer Carl Sagan, who also coined the phrase “Pale Blue Dot” for Voyager 1’s farewell glimpse of Earth.
NASA expects the gold-plated phonographic records — time capsules for anyone or anything that might encounter them — to last more than 1 billion years.
“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler,” NASA’s Joe Westlake, the heliophysics division director, said in a statement. “

title: (Not) up in the air: Travelers' trepidations spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups abound
summary: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses
story: At this point, it’s practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing— crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses

NEW YORK -- At this point, it's practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses.

And for 2026's busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there's another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a nationwide ground stop last week — the first since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation.

The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She's pretty sure she's not the only one.

“For a lot of people, especially as they’re paying attention and because it’s in the news where they’re tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we’re having ... I think more and more people are now getting anxious,” said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel.
It's an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days' tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it's a familiar one, too.

Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it's one they're likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic.
But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few.

“For the most part, air travel still remains strong,” said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People “might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it.”

In some ways, the country's aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute.

“Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy ... and frankly, it is taken for granted,” said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum.

“You've got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places,” he said. “But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It’s a commodity. There's nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that’s a clear sign of its success — that you’re in a bus.”

At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she's used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she's not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she's not rattled by it.
“I literally haven’t had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I’m like, just, okay, here’s another thing,” said Jolene, who lives in Miami.
She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, “the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday.”

And instead of flying this year, they’ll drive to "Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something," she said. “But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there’s just not much choice. What are you going to do?”
If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can't just be stuffed into the overhead compartment.

Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade.
Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index.
It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter's flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper.

She saw a promotion on American Airlines’ online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college.
The upfront cost was worth it, she said, because it’s a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn’t go bad. She's keeping the rolls in her garage
“The funny part," she said, “is we have to buy toilet paper anyway.”
AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story.

title: Chinese tech firms fear AI hits from US curbs after Nvidia fallout
summary: Chinese tech firms are facing challenges as the U.S. tightens restrictions on access to advanced chips
story: Chinese tech firms are facing challenges as the U.S. tightens restrictions on access to advanced chips
HONG KONG -- Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the U.S. tightens restrictions on China's access to the world's cutting-edge chips.

Chinese tech giant Alibaba, which on Thursday announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new U.S. rules could affect some of its global data center expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions.

The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centers in third countries, the latest U.S. move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models.
As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing U.S. export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips.
But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the U.S. to close what some policymakers called a loophole.

As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data center investment plans in China and abroad.

Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies.

For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53% year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan ($9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10% from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan ($41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected.
While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60% during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan ($7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout.
Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new U.S. rule on chip access “sets everyone back in China.”

“Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said.

“Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new U.S. rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute.

A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centers could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027.

Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster.

Analysts expect the U.S. will step up its chip export control policies against China after Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, raised U.S. national security concerns. Earlier reporting by The New York Times suggested that U.S. officials suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited in part to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available to Chinese companies.
Beijing has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and has called the new U.S. rules blocking Chinese companies' remote access to computing power overseas “economic coercion.”
Analysts and industry leaders in China say the U.S.’s tightening of chip export control measures would ultimately accelerate China’s push to make its domestic chip industry self-sufficient.

“Over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we actually see the industry is actually progressing very fast,” said Tencent's Lau.

title: Mullin, appearing before Congress, defends his flight to LSU-Texas game after nationwide ground stop
summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is defending his flight to a football game during a nationwide flight grounding
story: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is defending his flight to a football game during a nationwide flight grounding

WASHINGTON -- Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended before a House committee Wednesday his flight to a weekend LSU-Texas football game as travelers across the U.S. were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights, saying canceling it could have caused confusion.

Mullin spoke at a congressional hearing about threats facing the country at a time of looming questions over cyber infrastructure, the future of immigration enforcement and his decision to fly to the college football game.

The hearing in front of the House Homeland Security Committee is a standard yearly opportunity for members of Congress to grill top administration officials over national security threats. But it comes as the U.S. has faced a series of cyber and technology problems that have left Americans feeling vulnerable.

The hearing is also the first opportunity for Democrats after their midterm drubbing of Republicans to grill the Cabinet official who is key to President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda. Two others facing questioning are FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton.
The secretary has faced scrutiny over his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday to watch the LSU-Texas game.

Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.
On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.
Mullin said the trip had been planned for weeks so that he could take his nieces to the game and that there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.

“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.
Mullin had said Tuesday and reiterated Wednesday that he is required to fly on government planes and that he personally paid for the trip.

Mullin, whose department includes the agency tasked with protecting the country's cyber infrastructure, was front and center in the Republican administration's response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.

The Trump administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.
At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn't giving the American public clear answers.

“We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn’t have one single incident. That in itself is a great success," Mullin said.

During a news conference Friday with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy at the White House, he pushed for more funding for the aging air traffic control system while also assuring the public that the government was not seeing any signs of a deliberate cyberattack.

The Trump administration has been attempting to offer reassurances about a spate of outages over the last week that have affected everything from Microsoft and the Federal Aviation Administration to the banking industry, United Airlines and a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration national security officials have said there was no indication that the events are related or attributable to a cyberattack or hostile activity.

Clayton told the committee Wednesday that the outages are “not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.” Instead, they appear to be “separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes.”

Mullin's sprawling Department of Homeland Security also includes an agency designed to play a central role in the federal government's response to cyber incidents. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.
