title: Anthropic promises to pursue humanity's benefit. Its IPO filing gives it wiggle room
summary: When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence
story: When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence

When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity's benefit as it develops artificial intelligence.

The San Francisco startup, which plans an initial public offering this month, has sketched out a governance structure that it says will protect the company’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests. But the mechanisms it describes give the company wide leeway to decide how to measure whether it's benefiting society, experts say.

Like its rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory.

“I think then the real test emerges if and when the question of public benefit becomes costly” — or when the public benefit comes into conflict with making a profit, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute.

In its regulatory filings, Anthropic pledges to pursue long-term benefits of humanity through the responsible development of advanced AI. “We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings,” the company said. Anthropic also has pledged at least 5% of its stock to a “public benefit” fund and its founders have committed to donate 80% of their wealth.

Other tech companies have pledged to do good including Google, which prominently featured its then-motto, “Don’t Be Evil,” in its investor prospectus when it went public in 2004. But the words were not legally binding, and critics have accused the tech giant of leaving them behind.
Elon Musk's takeover of Twitter in 2021 shows how the conflict between profit and public good might play out in real life, said Stavros Gadinis, a law professor at UC Berkeley School of Law.

“Let’s say that Twitter’s directors felt that Elon was the wrong guy to police the public square because they didn’t trust him, they didn’t like him, they didn’t think he’d be fair, whatever it was,” Gadinis said. “But he made them an offer that was so high compared to what their advisors told them the company was really worth that it would be against their fiduciary duties to not sell to Elon. This is the situation that the public benefit charter is trying to avoid.”
Had Twitter been a public benefit corporation, it could have been required to consider factors beyond maximizing shareholder value when selling the company.

There aren't many public benefit corporations whose shares are publicly traded and they are all much smaller than Anthropic and OpenAI. They include the eyewear company Warby Parker, the insurance company Lemonade and software developer Veeva Systems, which had a conventional corporate structure when it went public in 2013 and converted to a public benefit corporation in 2021.
Anthropic's idealistic ambitions for how it develops AI could run up against competitive pressure, such as from China, Kreps said.

Anthropic and OpenAI’s models have gone from answering almost any question, even if it was dangerous, to becoming much more circumspect. But as they face more competition, including from open-source Chinese models that likely will tell you whatever you want, she said, "will they start to rethink some of those guardrails? And what happens then?”
The setup generally is not preferred by shareholders because it gives more power to the company’s board than it does to shareholders.

Whatever a company decides as its public benefit mission, it will likely be much more difficult to measure than profits. That's particularly true for AI companies, whose leaders have exalted AI as the solution to many of humanity's problems — from curing cancer to creating economic prosperity.

“There are these echo chambers, the Silicon Valley bubble where they really think that what they’re doing is for the good of humanity,” Kreps said. And someone immersed in that environment, she added, might not even ask the right questions or understand how “public benefit” should be measured.
A Long-Term Benefit Trust created by Anthropic is intended to operate as an independent body of trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.

Through a special Class T common stock, the trust “generally has the authority to elect and remove” Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of Anthropic's board of directors, according to the IPO filing. The Class T common stock is a single share that allows the five trustees to vote as a unit. It has no economic rights — meaning they get to vote but they don't see any financial benefit or losses from the share and can't sell it.

“The LTBT’s arrangements are designed to minimize the LTBT’s and the Trustees’ exposure to our financial performance and grant the Trustees sufficient independence to ensure we are striking this balance appropriately,” the filing said.

Three of the company's board directors are elected by the trust directly, and another three are elected by other shareholders, which include the company founders with a 50.1% voting majority. A seventh director, with a potentially tie-breaking vote, is nominated by the trust and the holders of the Class T shares, but cannot be appointed or removed without consent from the board’s nominating committee, which is expected to be controlled by the founders.
Effectively, the trust can only hold Anthropic accountable on issues such as AI safety and the company's broader mission up to a point, Gadinis said.

The trust “cannot determine the everyday decisions of these directors or the management of the company," he said. "If they disagree, they will have to go through the effort of removing directors, and they may not be able to remove a majority.”

As a public company, Anthropic also will be required to report finances and generally be more transparent than a privately held one. Many public companies dealing with AI, including Google and Microsoft, regularly update the public on efforts to develop AI responsibly.
The incentive for transparency could be as powerful as other mechanisms set up in Anthropic's corporate structure, Gadinis said.

“I do think that by being public, we are going to get a lot more information, because a lot of people are going to be asking questions, and companies will be responding to these questions. not only because they’re required by security laws, but also because they want to build this kind of trust with the investing community," he said.

title: Fans cheer as popular online platform for spinoff stories nears full return after security incident
summary: The Archive of Our Own, a popular global fandom site, is making a limited return after a security incident led to a shutdown on Oct. 29
story: The Archive of Our Own, a popular global fandom site, is making a limited return after a security incident led to a shutdown on Oct. 29

In a comeback tale like one from Harry Potter battling back his nemesis or a “Heated Rivalry” hockey hero rebounding from injury, a top global fandom site that was sidelined by a security incident is now on the mend.

The activist group behind the popular Archive of Our Own, or AO3, platform, a collaborative online space which serves up fans’ spinoff narratives derived from well-known published stories, says it’s undergoing a limited return after a shutdown on Oct. 29.
“AO3 is now up!” said a status page for the Organization for Transformative Works, an activist group behind the platform, on Sunday.

The outage sent fans of the platform — readers and authors alike — into a desperate void for the past two weeks with a “Bad Gateway” message stirring frustration. The return drew many expressions of joy Sunday.

The organization, in a summary it posted on Instagram of its 2025 results, said nearly 2.6 million AO3 works were created, with nearly 40 billion page views. Nearly 2 million accounts have been created, it said.
AO3 hasn't been without its critics, who have warned about sexual content that could be available to minors and fandom racism through the platform.

The group said some features like user icons have been disabled and importing of external work isn’t available, while downloads are currently only possible in the web-language HTML format. It promised those features will ultimately return.

The team predicted that the security incident would take up to four weeks for AO3 to get back up, while floating the prospect of a partial revival “in a degraded state” — which appears to be what was taking place on Sunday.

The organization said contributors’ “works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are still safe” and that no drafts were deleted during the outage — but it couldn’t rule out that the user database might have been compromised.
“We understand that the wait and uncertainty surrounding AO3’s return have been difficult, and we apologize for the inconvenience,” the status update said.

AO3 is a hub of content from fans who have produced content that riffs off fiction, art and other culture and entertainment: Imagine a repository of sequels, prequels and derivatives dreamt up by adoring aficionados of some of the world’s best-known titles.
The result is catchy products like “fanfic” — fiction from fans — and similar fanart, as well as “podfics,” readings of narratives shared in audio form.

A recent listing of “ship stats” — or the number of references to relationships of stars from literature — shows that pairings of characters featured in the Harry Potter, Heated Rivalry and anime fandoms were the most prominent this summer.
The reaction from fans of the fandom platform was swift and exuberant.
“So, we've all agreed we don't need to sleep tonight, now that AO3 is finally back, right? Right!?” quipped yet.another.loon on the Threads social media site.
User Verkielos gushed: “Just got email from AO3 about a fic update. The world is healing!”
Associated Press writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.

title: AI cheating fears spook South Korea ahead of high-stakes college entrance exam
summary: South Korean officials are scrambling to prevent cheating on a national college entrance exam using technology
story: South Korean officials are scrambling to prevent cheating on a national college entrance exam using technology

SEOUL, South Korea -- Days before South Korea comes to a standstill for its all-important college entrance exam, the nation is reeling after the top scorer on its tax accountant test was found to have cheated with a hidden camera and artificial intelligence.

The scandal has left authorities scrambling to prevent cheating on the exam, which will be taken Thursday by more than 500,000 students, as concerns grow that AI and smart devices are making fraud harder to detect.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin on Monday rejected calls by some lawmakers to postpone the exam until stronger anti-cheating measures are in place, telling a legislative hearing that a delay would cause “even a larger disruption” to students.

Choi said that he was confident that proctors could spot AI-powered smart glasses, which typically have thick, horn-rimmed frames. Education authorities are also offering guidance on detecting devices such as microcameras, Education Ministry officials said.

Worries about cheating deepened over the weekend after a 34-year-old man who scored the highest on a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a hidden microcamera and smartphone to get answers from AI.

Han Won-seok’s unusually high scores had drawn suspicion after he discussed them during recent media interviews. The case follows other incidents involving AI-assisted cheating in the past several months, including test-takers caught using AI-powered smart glasses on an English standardized test in June and on some university essay exams in October.

In a video posted Sunday on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, Han said that he used a concealed camera to capture the questions, fed the images to a generative AI tool and received answers on a smartphone. He said that he would cooperate with police, who are investigating the case.

Han had previously said that he scored 397.5 out of a possible 400 points on the first-stage, multiple-choice test in April, and 663 out of 800 on the second-stage essay exam in July, unusually high marks that one Korean newspaper likened to “running a 100-meter sprint in under five seconds.”

The national college entrance exam, known as “Suneung,” or the College Scholastic Ability Test, is a high-stakes annual event in a country notorious for intense academic competition, where prospects for jobs, social standing and even marriage can depend on which university a person attends.

South Korea goes to great lengths each year to create an ideal testing environment, effectively bringing the country to a standstill by delaying the start of the workday and stock market trading to ease traffic for test-takers and pausing flights during the English listening section of the exam. Police officers often use cars and motorcycles to escort test-takers who are running late, while the military sometimes suspends training in areas near testing sites.

But it’s difficult for authorities to come up with equally sweeping measures to prevent cheating with AI devices, which the Seoul-based Hankyoreh newspaper warned in an editorial Monday could threaten “the very foundations of the examination system.”

Education authorities had focused for months on preventing the use of AI-powered glasses, but Han’s case has raised doubts about whether they are prepared for cheating involving other, less conspicuous devices.

Education authorities will deploy at least one specially trained supervisor at each of the 1,300 test sites nationwide to identify such glasses. Officials also are considering requiring test takers to hand over their smart devices and shutting down public Wi-Fi connections at test sites, according to Prime Minister Han Seongsook's office.

Song Geun-hyeon, another senior Education Ministry official, said that the ministry has provided proctors with new guidance on detecting test-takers using hidden cameras and other devices, including watching for suspicious movements involving “their sleeves, collars or buttons, and certain gestures.”
The ministry was working with the Ministry of Science and Information and Communication Technology on anti-cheating measures for the college entrance exam, which are due to be announced on Tuesday.

Vice Education Minister Choi Eun-ok said that the discussions with the science ministry also include temporarily restricting telecommunications at test sites. It wasn't immediately clear whether that's feasible, considering laws prohibiting electronic signal jamming, or concerns that it could interfere with communication in surrounding areas.

Song said that metal detectors and radio detectors would be limited, while deploying thermal cameras would be highly unlikely because of privacy concerns. Supervisors can't search belongings without the consent of the test-takers.

“At the government-wide level, we would also need to give further consideration to measures that will make it easier to identify (AI) smart devices,” said Song, adding that officials are debating whether to require manufacturers to design the devices to emit “flashing lights or sounds” while in use.

title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025, company conducts probe over Nvidia fallout
summary: Singapore-based company has been at the center of the claims involving Nvidia.
story: Singapore-based company has been at the center of the claims involving Nvidia.

Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.
Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

The company told The Associated Press that it runs a “legitimate and lawful business” and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations “that are not supported by verifiable evidence.” It did not address specific allegations.
“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said in an emailed statement.
Alice Huang “left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” the statement said. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters.”

A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was “no evidence” of illicit chip transfers.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that “it doesn't matter to me” whether Alice Huang is a spy. He said his concern is “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions” or not.

“Jensen’s foibles are his foibles. Obviously, it’s a problem if in fact he was having relationships with subordinates,” Bessent said in an appearance on Fox News Channel's “Sunday Morning Futures.” “I want to keep coming back to: ‘What was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?’”
Bessent said the Nvidia board of directors should look outside the company for a new CEO because “they need a dramatic shake-up.”
Singapore’s government said Thursday that it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible “false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers.”
Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed’s then-CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers.

Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided “inaccurate” information to downplay her role at the company.
An earlier New York Times report suggested U.S. officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China.
As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced Thursday that he was stepping down as CEO.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”
Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated.
The Associated Press has been unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.
By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.

Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was “actually still our boss” and remained involved in daily operations.
The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3 billion.
In a separate statement Thursday issued under James Tan’s name, Megaspeed said it takes its obligations under U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously.”
The company said it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to cooperate fully with other relevant U.S. authorities.

title: DOJ dropping Alaska midterms Senate certification lawsuit, saying case is 'moot'
summary: The Justice Department is giving up on its controversial lawsuit that sought to potentially block the certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate race.
story: Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to win the Alaska Senate race.

The Justice Department is giving up on its controversial lawsuit that sought to potentially block the certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate race, telling an appeals court Thursday evening that the issue is now "moot" in an apparent acknowledgment of Democratic Senator-elect Mary Peltola's current lead in the electoral tally.
The Associated Press projected Tuesday that Peltola will win the race for the Senate, the ninth Senate pickup for Democrats in the next Congress.

Ahead of the election, President Donald Trump had directed the Justice Department to preemptively file a lawsuit to try to block the certification of the crucial Alaska Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan lost, citing name confusion among the candidates.

Republicans have alleged that candidate Dan J. Sullivan was running a sham campaign to purposefully confuse voters and draw votes away from incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan based on their names being similar.
A federal judge in Alaska dismissed the lawsuit on Nov. 1, saying there was "no workable plan" to investigate the claims in relation to the votes submitted.

In a Thursday filing from DOJ's third-ranked official Stanley Woodward, the department requested the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals vacate the order entered by a district judge in Alaska that dismissed DOJ's lawsuit -- but still acknowledged the dispute is now not worth any further litigation.

"This Court should deny the motion to summarily affirm the district court’s judgment," Woodward said. "Instead, this Court should vacate the district court’s order dismissing this lawsuit, because the case has become moot."

Later in the filing, Woodward opines on what he describes as an unfair hand given to the Trump administration in being unable to dispute ballots that may have been accidentally cast for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan instead of incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

"The United States therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means of “determin[ing] whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan” and vindicating the United States’ asserted injury," Woodward writes.

The filing comes after days of President Donald Trump repeatedly calling for the Alaska election results to be ruled in favor of Sen. Sullivan by combining the votes of Dan J. Sullivan as well as another Republican candidate he alleges was unlawfully recruited by Democrats as a spoiler in the race.

title: Army postpones plan to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azide until Monday
summary: Two rapid controlled detonations scheduled to take place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Friday have been postponed by three days.
story: The detonation is planned at an Army ammunition plant in Iowa.

The controlled detonation of nearly 10,000 pounds of lead azine at a U.S. Army plant in Iowa has been postponed until early next week, Army officials announced Thursday, a day before the planned blast.

"Public safety is the Army’s top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow’s controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23," Army Secretary Adam Telle said in a post on social media.
Two rapid, controlled detonations were scheduled to take place at the Middletown plant midday Friday to safely dispose of degraded lead azide, according to the U.S. Army.
Telle said Monday is the "latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material."

His announcement comes hours after two environmental groups asked a federal court to halt the plan -- alleging that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency approved a permit for the detonations without adequately considering the potential health and environmental consequences or fully evaluating alternatives -- as some officials also expressed concerns about the Army's plan, how it was communicated to the public and risk of potential lead exposure.

"Public communication is essential to public trust. Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information," Telle said Thursday.

Republican Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley said on social media that he raised concerns and questions about the controlled detonation with the Army and "emphasized the need for increased communication," and that the delay is "to further educate the public."
Here's what to know about the operation.
Sixty-eight barrels -- approximately 9,700 pounds -- of the explosive material are set to be detonated, according to Army Sustainment Command spokesperson Justine Barati.
The detonation was initially scheduled to occur at approximately noon CT Friday, the Army said in a public advisory on Wednesday. A time for Monday's detonation has not yet been announced.
The barrels will be detonated "inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete: and surrounded by two-story-high sand barriers, the advisory said.

"Before and during the detonation, the soil above the earth-covered magazines will be thoroughly saturated with water, and water misters will be spraying," the advisory said. "These measures should reduce the amount of lead that migrates from the detonation through the air off the installation."

The blast is expected to result in loud noises and ground vibrations, as well as a dust plume "that will contain some lead" and is expected to linger for up to one hour, depending on wind speed, the Army said.

The Army will be updating plume maps up until and after the detonation, Barati said. Ahead of the operation, the Army released maps on potential airborne exposure to toxic lead dust via the air and on surfaces, which it said are being updated before and after the detonation.

"The U.S. Army has taken extraordinary measures to mitigate the plume by following strict permit requirements set by the EPA such as earthworks, soil wetting, and air sampling," the Army said in a public advisory earlier this week.

The blast could also break windows. Due to that risk, the Army said it had asked residents near Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park to temporarily evacuate the area for several hours before and after the scheduled detonation "out of an abundance of caution." Updated guidance in light of the postponement has not yet been released.
Middletown, which is located near the Iowa-Illinois border in southeastern Iowa, has a population of nearly 400 people, according to U.S. Census data.

Residents who need a place to stay were invited to the Armed Forces Reserve Center. Those who couldn't evacuate were advised to stay indoors and keep all windows and doors closed during the possible exposure period.
People were also being advised to clean play surfaces for children and windowsills once the U.S. Army determines the air exposure period has ended.
In addition to air monitoring during the blast, sampling will occur afterward to "identify material that may need to be cleaned up," the Army said.

"A large 'safe zone' area has been identified and extends well beyond the area that the blast can reach," the Army said. "Fire and emergency responders will be staged and on standby to respond to an emergency if needed."

Lead exposure is a particular concern for young children. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there is no safe blood lead level for children. Even low blood lead levels "are associated with developmental delays, difficulty learning, and behavioral issues," the CDC said. Many children with lead in their blood will not show symptoms immediately after an exposure. Parents concerned about lead exposure should speak with their child's primary care provider about lead level testing.

Due to the controlled detonation, multiple school districts in the area planned to close their doors on Friday out of an abundance of caution. They included the Burlington Community School District, which serves Middletown, as well as Mediapolis, Columbus, Danville and Winfield Mt. Union. The schools have yet to issue updated plans in the wake of the detonation's postponement.

The controlled detonation is to dispose of the degraded lead azide, which is highly sensitive and extremely unstable, the Army said. Due to the risks of accidental detonation in packing and transporting it, "safely destroying it in place is the only responsible option," the Army said.
Lead azide is the primary explosive used to initiate munitions.

According to the EPA, which permitted the detonation, the "recrystallization of the stored lead azide has increased the material's sensitivity to friction and shock, and disturbing the containers of lead azide could create an unacceptable risk of unintentional detonation."
The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant makes medium- and large-caliber munitions for the Department of Defense.
The day before the planned detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club filed an emergency motion, seeking a stay of the EPA-issued permit authorizing the detonation.

The filing argues that the detonation could spread lead dust across a large area, potentially reaching communities more than 100 miles from the plant. The Army's latest modeling projects that lead dust could settle across an area approximately 25 miles long and 5 miles wide, including homes and waterways, according to the filing. The groups further argue that people, livestock and wildlife could also continue to face exposures to lead once it settles into the ground.
The filing also questions the Army and EPA's handling of public notification, alleging that some of the potentially impacted communities were not given direct or timely notice.
The groups asked the federal appeals court to rule by 10 a.m. CT Friday, right before the detonation was initially scheduled to occur.

Prior to the detonation's postponement, Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek and Gov.-elect Rob Sand, both Democrats, also criticized the communication from the Army while calling for Friday's detonation to be paused.

"An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation," Sand said in a statement on Thursday. "The public deserves to know, if this is the safest option, why other options were worse. If it isn't as safe as possible to do this tomorrow, it shouldn't happen tomorrow."
ABC News has reached out to the Army and EPA for comment on the emergency motion and has not yet received a response.

title: Trump pardons late baseball great Pete Rose after historic China trip
summary: On the way back from his Asia trip, President Donald Trump said Thursday he issued a "complete and total pardon" to baseball legend Pete Rose, who died in 2024.
story: Once banned from baseball, Rose was convicted on federal tax charges in 1990.
President Donald Trump said Thursday he issued a "complete and total pardon" to baseball legend Pete Rose, who died in 2024.

Trump posted the announcement to his social media platform as he was returning from his trip to Asia where he met with other world leaders, notably the first-ever trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia.
Rose, who holds the Major League Baseball record for most career hits, was sentenced to five months in prison after being convicted of tax charges in 1990.

Rose was also permanently banned from baseball in 1989 following an investigation into his betting on baseball games while managing the Cincinnati Reds. Rose also pleaded guilty to federal income tax charges in 1990.

He and 16 other former players were removed from baseball's permanent list of banned players last year, making him eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame posthumously. The decision applied only to dead players who had been placed on the ineligible list.

"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND, whose record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken," Trump, then rattled off a number of Rose's other baseball accomplishments.
Rose had 4,256 hits over his career, not in a single season as Trump wrote.
"And, just like the Great Roger Clemens, who won 354 games, was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess!" Trump wrote.

Clemens, who is third on baseball's all-time career strikeout list with 4,672, was a seven-time Cy Young Award winner with a career record of 354-184 and a career earned run average of 3.12. He came up short in Hall of Fame balloting in the 10 years he was eligible because of allegations he used performance-enhancing drugs, which he denied.

MLB removed Rose from its permanently ineligible list in May 2025, making him eligible for future Hall of Fame consideration. Trump has previously said he wanted Rose to be pardoned and up for reconsideration for the Hall of Fame.
Rose is expected to be on the ballot next year for the Hall of Fame's Classic Era Committee, which considers those who played before 1980 but weren't elected to the Hall.
Just last week during a surprise briefing at the White House today with Ultimate Fighting Championship President Dana White, Trump said he would pardon Rose.

"I think Pete Rose was very mistreated. He was, you know, 4200 and some odd hits, way ahead of anybody else. A record can never be broken," Trump said then. "And he was caught gambling. Now it's illegal, right? But he was gambling on his own team."
"He shouldn't have done it. But he went through 40 years of hell, and they never -- and they should have given him a pardon," Trump said.

"They should have given him into the Baseball Hall of Fame a long time ago. And I spoke to the commissioner about it, and he agreed to do it. And then he waited, though, and Pete Rose died. So it didn't help him too much. But, I would give Pete Rose a pardon. I would do that," Trump added.

title: Iran live updates: Republicans block war powers resolution
summary: President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.
story: The resolution failed by a vote of 48-51.

Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.

Republicans block Iran war powers resolution again, in 1st since midterms
Republicans thwarted another effort by Democrats to pass a House-approved Iran War powers resolution on Thursday.
The resolution failed by a vote of 48-51. It would have needed 51 votes to pass. This was a non-binding resolution and would not have required President Donald Trump's signature to be approved.
Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski and Sen. Rand Paul were the only Republicans to vote in favor of the resolution. Sen. John Fetterman was the only Democrat to vote against it.
Thursday's vote was the first war powers vote taken in the Senate since before the midterm elections.

Many Democrats have framed their election victory as a rebuke of the Iran war, and hoped that this vote -- one of more than a dozen votes Democrats have forced on the matter -- would win over more Republicans.

Sen. Tim Kaine has led a number of Iran War powers resolutions in the Senate. In remarks on the Senate floor just before Thursday's vote, he said the war had been "deeply unpopular from its very first days."

"Its unpopularity was made absolutely manifestly clear by the election and its results from Nov. 3," Kaine said. "A historic repudiation of the party holding on to the White House with much of that energy-driven by American's deep dissatisfaction with a war waged unilaterally by a president ... causing costs to dramatically rise on every American family when the president said he would try to bring down costs."
-ABC News' Allison Pecorin
Tower in Riyadh damaged by Houthi strike, no injuries reported
A tower in Riyadh's Financial Center was damaged after it was hit by a Houthi projectile Thursday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense announced.
No injuries were reported, but damage was visible on the exterior of the building in an image posted by the Civil Defense directorate on X.
The Saudi Press Agency reported damage to several floors and neighboring buildings.
Houthis target Riyadh with missile, Saudi spokesperson says

Saudi Arabian military spokesperson Col. Turki al-Maliki said in a post to X on Thursday morning that Saudi forces "dealt with" a missile attack targeting the capital Riyadh launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.
"Debris fell and material damage is being assessed," Maliki wrote.
Trump says Iran 'looking at gases' and 'biological weapons' amid dirty bomb report
President Donald Trump said on Thursday in Shenzhen, China, that Iran was looking at "gases" and "biological weapons" amid reports of a potential Iranian dirty bomb threat against Washington, D.C.

During an interview with Fox News on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China, Trump said, "Well, there is indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear. Nuclear is much harder. And they're looking at gas and they're looking at the bio, you know, the biological weapons, not nice, and other things.”

The president's comments come as sources told ABC News that while U.S. intelligence has picked up some chatter about the possibility of targeting U.S. officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb in Washington, the sources cautioned that the credibility of the underlying intelligence has not been verified. CNN was first to report the news.
In the interview, Trump said, "We'll see what happens" after Jan. 1, without providing additional context.
Pressed further about whether D.C. residents should be “panicked” about a possible attack, Trump said, “I don’t think so,” and added that if an attack occurs, the U.S. will “wipe them out.”
-ABC News' Nicholas Kerr

title: What Obama said to newly elected Democrats after midterm gains
summary: Former President Barack Obama told Democratic U.S. House members-elect on Wednesday that they should value their ideological diversity even if they have disagreements.
story: The event was after Hakeem Jeffries was nominated as first Black House speaker.

Former President Barack Obama told Democratic House members-elect that they should value their ideological diversity even if they have disagreements, and that they should not forget about the constituents they serve, according to excerpts of his remarks that his office provided to ABC News.

The meeting, held at the Folger Shakespeare Library near the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday afternoon, was held just hours after New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries was nominated to become the first Black Speaker of the House.

"There is generational change coming to the Democratic Party, which is vital, in part because what that means is you are attuned to today's circumstances ... But the values that you represent stay the same, the values of that this is a country that has to include everybody and not just some," Obama said during the closed-door meeting, according to the excerpt.

He also said that "the diversity of this class is its power. And I don't just mean ethnic diversity or racial diversity or religious diversity. It's also regional diversity and ideological diversity," as he encouraged members-elect to listen to each other even when they disagree.
The incoming House members feature many new members of color as well as candidates from a wide range of economic and professional backgrounds.

"And the key, though, is to recognize that in that diversity, if you listen and you are extending grace to those inside your caucus that you don't agree with 100% of the time, you're going to agree on core values and you're going to agree on a basic direction," Obama said.
The meeting, which was announced abruptly on Wednesday, was not open to reporters.

Jeffries shared a video on Instagram where he introduced Obama at the event. After walking out to applause, Obama was greeted by chants of "four more years," to which he said, "I believe in the Constitution, people."
Obama also emphasized to members-elect, according to the excerpts, that they should not forget about the people they serve.

"There is a danger, though, that you get caught up in national politics and national debates and your national communications and showing up on cable shows and Instagramming to death and all that," he said. "... There is the danger sometimes that you forget that this really is about individual lives, regular folks, day to day, counting on you to help them in ways that you can."
But, he told attendees, they can be there for their constituents and avoid making them feel unseen.

"I think a lot of people's cynicism about politics is not just politics, but business and media, and everything, people feel as if they have no agency, that they're not seen, not listened to, and are disempowered from the major forces that control their lives," Obama said. "At the very least, if their congressman knows they're there and cares about them, that can help generate the kind of hope that we're going to need."
Obama's office did not share excerpts from a question-and-answer session the former president held with attendees.

Ohio Rep.-elect Don Leonard, who flipped a GOP-held seat in a shock result and who has said he did not vote for Jeffries in leadership elections, wrote on X on Wednesday that someone had asked Obama about Elon Musk, who spent heavily in the midterms and said Wednesday that he feels "pretty foolish about having spent so much money" without seeing much of a result.

According to Leonard, Obama had said it was time for a constitutional amendment on campaign finance. Obama has previously said he would support amending the Constitution for campaign finance reform and to regulate campaign spending.

title: Xi tells Trump US must do 'the right thing' over Taiwan to avoid 'great turbulence'
summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping used his meeting with President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday to warn against the creation of "turbulence" over the issue of Taiwan.
story: He warned in May that the U.S. and China could "come into conflict" over Taiwan.

LONDON and HONG KONG -- Chinese President Xi Jinping used his meeting with President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday to urge bilateral cooperation on issues including AI, but also warned against the creation of "turbulence" over the issue of Taiwan.

Xi and Trump met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in southwestern China, first privately and then as part of a trilateral sit down with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

According to a readout of the meeting between Xi and Trump, the state-run Xinhua News Agency said the Chinese leader suggested areas of cooperation including AI, while cautioning that divergence over the fate of Taiwan could undermine bilateral relations.
"On the Taiwan issue, the United States must keep doing the right thing to avoid the emergence of great turbulence in the China-U.S. relationship," Xi said, as quoted by Xinhua.
During their meeting in May, Xi warned Trump that China and the U.S. could "come into conflict" if the issue of Taiwan is handled "improperly."

Taiwan is an independent island nation that Beijing considers a wayward Chinese province. During the Chinese Civil War -- which took place intermittently between 1927 and 1949 -- nationalist forces retreated to the island while the Chinese Communist Party took control of the Chinese mainland.
Ever since, Chinese leaders -- with Xi among them since his rise to power -- have vowed to take control of Taiwan, whether through diplomatic or military means.

American backing for Taiwan is a longtime grievance for Beijing. Though Washington does not officially recognize Taiwan as an independent state, U.S. administrations have traditionally backed the maintenance of the status quo and provided significant military, diplomatic and economic backing for Taipei.
Xi has been pushing for the U.S. to curtail its arms sales to Taiwan, including a proposed $14 billion deal that would include American missiles, anti-drone weapons and air-defense systems.

The arms package for Taiwan was approved by the US Congress in January but has been held up by the White House, awaiting final approval from the president. Trump has previously said the deal could serve as a "negotiating chip" in talks with Beijing.

Speaking to media in Taipei, Taiwanese Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Chen Ming-chi highlighted U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's comments, reported by The Hill in September, that military sales to anyone require the same careful consideration.

"Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan Strait. Even though China's economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under this context, the U.S. very much understands our defense needs," he said. "We do continuously communicate with them, and we believe the U.S. understands the situation we face and our determination on defense investment completely."
China regularly conducts large-scale military drills around Taiwan, with daily air and naval patrols around the island maintaining pressure on Taipei.
From Wednesday into Thursday, Taiwan's Defense Ministry reported one sortie of Chinese military aircraft plus the presence of seven Chinese naval vessels and two other "official ships" around Taiwan.
The ministry also reported that two Russian Tu-95 bombers flew into the island's air defense identification zone on Thursday.

The joint China-U.S.-Russia statement released by the Xinhua also endorses "the principle of state consent," which holds that countries cannot be bound by international courts without their agreement, the New York Times reported. China has invoked this principle to reject a 2016 international tribunal ruling against its South China Sea claims, according to the Times.

title: Trump China trip: Iran and Ukraine not in 'peace declaration' and more takeaways
summary: Trump heads back to Washington after meeting with Xi and Putin -- the first sitdown between the three superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
story: Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.

President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.

Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."

The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.

Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.

"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
"It's not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up," Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.

"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.

In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The "peace declaration" released after the meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.

"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.

"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.

The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.

The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world's oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.

Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.

"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.

As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.
