title: Illinois man pleads not guilty over thwarted mass shooting at Hindu temple
summary: A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Chicago-area Hindu temple has pleaded not guilty to all charges
story: A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Chicago-area Hindu temple has pleaded not guilty to all charges
CHICAGO -- A 19-year-old man accused of planning a mass shooting at a Chicago-area Hindu temple that officials say was only thwarted when his gun jammed pleaded not guilty to all charges Thursday.

Alexandros Paporakis was indicted by a grand jury earlier this month on nine charges, including terrorism and armed violence, both felonies. Paporakis also faces weapons-related charges, including possessing a firearm without a serial number.
Those charges could carry a maximum sentence of life in prison, his attorney, Fedor Kozlov, told reporters. Kozlov said he filed a demand for a jury trial.

Authorities say Paporakis planned to attack a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, on Oct. 11, the first day of the Hindu holiday of Navaratri. Paporakis drove to the temple’s parking lot and tried to fire at a person outside, court documents show. Police say the gun jammed.
Police say Paporakis, who was arrested later that day, told a co-worker that he would try again.

Prosecutors say Paporakis wrote in a document that he was a neo-Nazi and white supremacist who fantasized about killing non-white people. The indictment alleges he wrote that he intended the shooting to terrorize Indian immigrants.
Police say they recovered a rifle, ammunition, a tactical vest and a patch “displaying imagery associated with white supremacist extremism” from his house.
Paporakis has not been charged with a hate crime, despite calls from local and national South Asian leaders for state and federal authorities to do so.
Paporakis briefly appeared in court Thursday in a tan jumpsuit alongside Kozlov, who announced his not guilty plea. He is due back in court on Jan. 7.
He remains in detention after a judge ruled his release would pose a threat to the community. Kozlov said Paporakis is being held in a medical facility in the Cook County jail.
He is aware of the gravity of what he is accused of, and is “taking it day by day,” Kozlov said.
“He sees the world as a 19-year-old, in my mind, child," Kozlov added. “It’s hard to describe and understand how he feels and how he processes it.”
Prosecutors declined to comment following Thursday's hearing.

Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Senate approves bill to speed up permitting reviews, force data centers to pay for energy costs
summary: The Senate has approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower...
story: The Senate has approved bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower...

WASHINGTON -- The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.

The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.

Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.
Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.
A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.

Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.

“Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said.

Majority Republicans stymied Merkley's effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.”
The bill's sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process," he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.
“I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.

“In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government.
“Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.
The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.
“We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said.

Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations,” adding that he hopes “to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years.
But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered.

Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation’s bodies of water, land and wildlife.

“Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process” to debate and amend the bill, she said. “Don’t sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.”

Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe's ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. “Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation,” he said.

Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.
“A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill,” Granholm wrote in a social media post. “But it would still need this president’s signature.”
Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure.

But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would “irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home.” He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California’s environment.
Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.

title: Maine parents sue town over autistic daughter's metal rooster statues
summary: A fight over whether giant metal roosters in Maine are illegal advertising or artwork that comforts an autistic child has landed in federal court
story: A fight over whether giant metal roosters in Maine are illegal advertising or artwork that comforts an autistic child has landed in federal court
A fight over whether giant metal roosters in Maine are illegal advertising or artwork that comforts an autistic child has landed in federal court.

David and Sara LeBlanc sued the town of Ogunquit this week, alleging that enforcement of its sign code violates their First Amendment rights. They want to display the roughly 6-foot-tall (1.8 meters) ornaments for their daughter, Pyper, but the town considers them advertising for the couple's adjacent restaurant, the Omelette Factory.
“The roosters are a symbol of one thing: How much we love our daughter,” David LeBlanc said in a statement. “But the town made up an entirely different meaning for them.”

After issuing multiple fines, the town granted the couple a disability variance that allows them to keep two roosters but specifies that they must be attached to a railing. More fines followed when the couple declined to build a railing and chained them to two posts instead. They have since removed all of the tin statues, according to the lawsuit, which points out that other local businesses display lobster buoys, antique farm equipment and large tiki statues without incurring fines.

"This is governmental discrimination based on the content of speech and the identity of the speaker," the lawsuit states. “Such discrimination is presumptively unconstitutional, and the Town cannot justify it.”

The LeBlancs are represented by the Institute for Justice, which won a similar case in New Hampshire in 2025 when a judge sided with a bakery owner in a dispute over a large mural high school students painted on his building. The town of Conway had argued the mural featuring doughnuts and other baked treats was a regulated sign, but the judge found the town infringed on the bakery owner's free speech rights.

Ogunquit's town clerk, Christine Murphy, did not respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday. Meanwhile, many of the LeBlancs' original roosters have been adopted by local residents and businesses, and their supporters around the world have been buying their own to display.
“Every time Pyper spots another rooster in someone's yard, her face lights up,” Sara LeBlanc said in a statement. “This town has embraced her. We wish the town government would, too.”
____ Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

title: Federal review faults leadership failures in Grand Canyon fire that destroyed lodge
summary: Leadership failures along with a lack of preparedness and poor communication were the driving factors of a wildfire that destroyed a historic lodge and dozens of structures at Grand Canyon National Park
story: Leadership failures along with a lack of preparedness and poor communication were the driving factors of a wildfire that destroyed a historic lodge and dozens of structures at Grand Canyon National Park

Leadership failures along with a lack of preparedness and poor communication were the driving factors of a wildfire that destroyed a historic lodge and dozens of structures along the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park.

A federal review of the Dragon Bravo Fire recently made public noted that while drought conditions and extreme fire behavior contributed, systemic weaknesses in the National Park Service related to authority and qualifications hindered decision-making at critical moments.
The 2025 fire should be considered a warning, according to the multiagency team of experts that reviewed the handling of the fire.

“The findings indicated many of the challenges observed during the fire were foreseeable, preventable, and reflective of broader institutional issues that extend beyond a single park, region, or agency,” the report stated.

The Dragon Bravo Fire was sparked by lightning in July 2025. The park service allowed it to burn for days before it exploded into a fast-moving conflagration that forced evacuations and consumed the Grand Canyon Lodge, historic cabins, employee housing and other critical infrastructure. Suppression costs topped $141 million over three months.
The park service initially defended its handling of the fire, saying a sudden and extreme shift in the wind far exceeded forecasts.

Grand Canyon officials referred questions about the findings to the U.S. Interior Department, which oversees the park service. The Interior Department did not immediately answer emails sent by The Associated Press.

The review, ordered by the Interior Department's deputy secretary, provides a timeline that starts with the day the fire ignited. It details weather conditions and includes photos of the towering plume that could be seen from the South Rim, the lodge awash in flames and the charred remains of the historic building.

The review noted that it was known by park officials that the region was experiencing persistent drought and had dense fuels in close proximity to nationally significant historic structures. Fire planning and policy documents existed, but the review stated those plans “were not fully translated into effective preseason preparedness actions or operational readiness.”

The recommendations include requiring agency administrators to undergo the needed training to handle complex incidents and ensuring that communication flows through proper channels so that decision-makers get firsthand, accurate and timely information.

The review highlighted a breakdown in communication that resulted in a multiday delay in fire retardant being used as the flames intensified. The decision to use retardant came only after several structures, including the lodge, already had been lost, according to the findings.

The review also stated that the park service's continued authorization of the confine and contain strategy did not reflect awareness of changing conditions or escalating risk. The recommendations also call for fire leadership to reevaluate their strategies regularly and to reconsider weather conditions, fire behavior and the availability of resources.
The review team described the Dragon Bravo Fire as a defining event for Grand Canyon National Park and a consequential case study for the Interior Department and the U.S. Wildland Fire Service.

The experts stated in the review that the resulting loss of historic structures, the displacement of employees, the risks to firefighters and the significant suppression costs underscore the stakes associated with managing wildfires in complex landscapes.

“What began as a small, naturally ignited fire rapidly evolved into a high-consequence, cross-boundary incident that tested leadership, governance, preparedness, decision quality, and execution across multiple programs and agencies,” the team stated.
Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico.

title: Divided appeals court blocks Pentagon from expelling several transgender troops from US military
summary: A federal appeals court has blocked the Pentagon from forcing several transgender troops out of the military, after finding President Donald Trump’s ban was unlawfully imposed
story: A federal appeals court has blocked the Pentagon from forcing several transgender troops out of the military, after finding President Donald Trump’s ban was unlawfully imposed

WASHINGTON -- A federal appeals court on Tuesday blocked the Pentagon from forcing more than two dozen transgender troops out of the military, several months after it found that President Donald Trump’s administration unlawfully imposed the ban.

The decision — implementing an earlier ruling by the same appeals court panel — could set the stage for the issue to return to the Supreme Court, which previously allowed the ban to go forward for now in a different case.

Trump's administration had asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to delay the June 1 ruling's implementation while it petitions the Supreme Court to take up the case. A three-judge panel voted 2-1 on Tuesday to reject the administration's request for a stay of the circuit's decision.
The Supreme Court had ruled in the administration’s favor last year, allowing the Pentagon to start enforcing the ban while the litigation proceeded.

Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins, partially joined by Judge Judith Rogers, ruled in June that the Pentagon's policy was designed to exclude people from the military based on their gender identity. Their majority decision would bar the military from kicking out current service members named in the lawsuit, but it wouldn't allow new transgender recruits to join.

Plaintiffs’ attorneys challenging the Pentagon ban say 27 service members are covered by Tuesday’s order. Shannon Minter, legal director of the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, said the plaintiffs are all “decorated troops who have met every standard the military sets.”

“The Trump administration asked the court to let it keep pushing these service members toward the door while it tries to get a different answer from the Supreme Court. Today, the D.C. Circuit said no,” Minter said in a statement.

On Tuesday, Wilkins said the administration hasn’t shown how retaining the plaintiffs currently serving in the military would cause any irreparable harm to the government or endanger national security. Wilkins also noted that the scope of the June 1 majority opinion was narrower than the injunction that the Supreme Court stayed last year.
“To the extent the government suggests that any injunction against the Executive Branch imposes irreparable harm, I am also unpersuaded,” Wilkins wrote.

The panel's June 1 majority opinion partially upheld a March 2025 ruling by U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, who concluded that Trump’s executive order to exclude transgender troops from military service likely violates their constitutional rights.

In January 2025, Trump signed an executive order that claims the sexual identity of transgender service members “conflicts with a soldier’s commitment to an honorable, truthful, and disciplined lifestyle, even in one’s personal life” and is harmful to military readiness.

In response, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a policy that presumptively disqualifies people with gender dysphoria from military service. Gender dysphoria is the distress that a person feels because their assigned gender and gender identity don’t match. The medical condition has been linked to depression and suicidal thoughts.
Wilkins was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama. Rogers was nominated by President Bill Clinton, also a Democrat.

Circuit Judge Justin Walker, who was nominated by Trump, a Republican, wrote a dissenting opinion in June that said judges lack the power to second-guess the decision to exclude transgender troops. Walker also voted to grant the government's request to suspend the decision.

title: Fed minutes: Higher interest rates needed in December as inflation worries mount
summary: Nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect the central bank will lift its key interest rate by a quarter point in December, minutes from a meeting last month showed, while some supported a hike in October and two floated the possibility of a half-poin...
story: Nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect the central bank will lift its key interest rate by a quarter point in December, minutes from a meeting last month showed, while some supported a hike in October and two floated the possibility of a half-poin...

WASHINGTON -- Nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect the central bank will lift its key interest rate by a quarter point in December, minutes from a meeting last month showed, while some supported a hike in October and two floated the possibility of a half-point increase next month.

The minutes, released three weeks after the Oct. 27-28 meeting of the Fed's rate-setting committee, also said a “vast majority” of the 19 members of the Fed's policymaking committee worried that inflation could persist even if gas prices kept declining and the impact of tariffs and the buildout of AI infrastructure faded.

The minutes will solidify expectations for a rate hike not only in December but likely early next year as well. Wall Street investors already see the odds of a December rate hike at nearly 95%, according to CME Fedwatch. When the Fed lifts its key rate, over time it can also raise borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and credit cards. Home sales have withered as mortgage rates have topped 7% in recent months.

The Fed kept its key rate unchanged at 3.9% in October after raising it for the first time in three years in September. Chairman Kevin Warsh at a news conference Oct. 28 gave little guidance on the central bank's next moves, but the statement issued after the Fed's meeting acknowledged that “inflation remains elevated.”

The minutes said “some" policymakers supported lifting rates in October. Two of them, Fed governor Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, formally dissented in favor of higher rates. President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook, but the Supreme Court ruled in June she could keep her position while the case is litigated.

Inflation has accelerated this fall and is showing signs of broadening beyond industries directly affected by higher oil and gas prices or tariffs, a trend that has raised alarm among many policymakers. Several have spoken out in favor of more rate hikes in the past week.

Fed governor Christopher Waller said in an interview on CNBC early Wednesday that inflation is “headed in the wrong direction and it’s spreading out ″ into more goods and services. Waller is one of the Fed's seven governors and a member of its rate-setting committee.

“If you really want to get it down, you’ve got to start taking more aggressive actions,” Waller said. He reiterated his support for a half-point rate increase at the Fed’s December meeting, double the usual hike. He also said that several more hikes — not just the two that many economists forecast — might be needed to tame inflation.

The minutes suggested that one other official also agreed that a half-point increase should be considered in December, though it’s not clear that the official is a voting member. Twelve of the 19 members of the committee vote on rate decisions, though all participate in the debates. The minutes don’t identify which officials took which positions.

Waller noted that in the past three months, core inflation, which excludes the volatile food and energy categories, has run at about a 3.5% annual rate, far above the Fed’s target of 2%. Businesses increasingly appear willing to pass on their own rising costs and also believe their customers can handle price increases of about 3%, he added.
“That’s the kind of psychology I think we need to start breaking,” Waller said.

Waller also took a shot at Warsh by arguing that one reason he supported a half-point hike is that without greater communication, financial markets won’t know whether a quarter-point increase in December will be followed by a similar move in January. If investors do have a sense of further hikes in the pipeline, they’ll push up market rates in anticipation and help the Fed cool inflation, Waller said.
Yet Warsh has steadily refrained from providing such guidance, which he has said locks the Fed to a predetermined path.

Separately, John Williams, president of the New York Fed and vice chair of the Fed's rate-setting committee, has pushed back against the potential for a half-point increase. He told Axios Tuesday, “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action.”

Other Fed officials have suggested many more hikes are likely necessary. Alberto Musalem, president of the St. Louis Fed, said Tuesday in a speech in Buenos Aires that “the economy will likely require several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027” to bring inflation down.

The economy is expanding at a healthy pace, he added, and interest rates aren’t high enough to restrain borrowing and spending sufficiently to cool inflation. Musalem does not have a vote on rates this year.

Mary Daly, president of the San Francisco Fed, said last week that she is leaning toward supporting further rate hikes, and added that she also worries that companies are increasingly willing to pass on higher costs to consumers.
“That’s the inflationary impulse that we want to avoid,” Daly said.

title: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo can't undergo surgery after swallowing a hat
summary: The Cincinnati Zoo says staff members are doing everything they can to help its beloved hippo Fiona after she swallowed a knit hat
story: The Cincinnati Zoo says staff members are doing everything they can to help its beloved hippo Fiona after she swallowed a knit hat

Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's famed hippo, underwent a colonoscopy this week, and now veterinarians are trying a new way to help her pass a knit cap that she swallowed after it slipped into her enclosure.
The zoo's animal care team borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, hoping the shaking will help move things along through her digestive tract, the zoo said Wednesday.
Video released by the zoo Wednesday shows Fiona snorting and moving about her indoor enclosure.
Veterinarians sedated her Tuesday for a second time to evaluate her condition, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo’s director of animal health.
An ultrasound showed some bunching of her intestines, indicating she is still trying to pass the obstruction, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy, using a 9-foot scope, he said.
Specialists have told the zoo that surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos, he said.

Fiona, who became a global sensation as a tiny newborn after her premature birth in 2017, has inspired books, a line of beer and a bobblehead. During her first year, the zoo recorded her progress while fans worldwide followed her growth online.
She initially couldn’t stand on her own and weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms) at birth, 25 pounds (11.3 kilograms) less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

The beloved hippo swallowed the hat just over a week ago. A visitor tossed it into the air, and a ceiling fan caught and catapulted it through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.
Zoo staff are now monitoring her around the clock, trying to keep her hydrated and giving Fiona her favorite foods to help her pass the knit cap, the zoo said.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked,” Curley said Wednesday. “And they were happy to see her respond.”

title: Trump administration signals plan for seawall work at Washington golf course as legal fight drags on
summary: The Interior Department intends to seek bids for a contractor to work on the seawall at a Washington, D.C., park where President Donald Trump plans to redevelop a historic public golf course into a world-class venue
story: The Interior Department intends to seek bids for a contractor to work on the seawall at a Washington, D.C., park where President Donald Trump plans to redevelop a historic public golf course into a world-class venue

WASHINGTON -- The Interior Department has issued a notice that it intends to seek bids for a contractor to begin work on the seawall at a Washington park where President Donald Trump plans to redevelop a historic public golf course into a world-class venue.

Those plans were put on hold by a judge over the weekend. The Interior Department's notice, announced Friday before the judge's action, said the formal solicitation will go out on Nov. 30. The notice said it was not a solicitation but “pre-notice of an upcoming solicitation ONLY.”

The seawall has recently become a central reason in the Trump administration’s argument over why East Potomac Park, which includes the East Potomac Golf Links, is in need of a renovation. Trump, a Republican, has targeted the golf course as one of his projects to remake the District of Columbia in his image.
The Trump administration sought to close the park, citing safety factors including the seawall, which it argued was in precarious condition.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes rejected that argument during a hearing on Friday in a lawsuit challenging Trump’s plans to renovate the historic public course.
Reyes issued a temporary restraining order the following day to stop work related to the construction of the golf course.
Reyes was nominated by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, in 2023.

title: Los Angeles homelessness agency reaches settlement with feds in dispute over spending
summary: A Los Angeles government agency that oversaw hundreds of millions of dollars in homelessness spending has reached a settlement with federal housing authorities in a dispute over claims that the agency misused funding
story: A Los Angeles government agency that oversaw hundreds of millions of dollars in homelessness spending has reached a settlement with federal housing authorities in a dispute over claims that the agency misused funding

LOS ANGELES -- A Los Angeles government agency that oversaw hundreds of millions of dollars in homelessness spending has reached a settlement with federal housing authorities in a dispute over claims that the local agency misused funding.

Under the deal announced Tuesday, the LA Homeless Services Authority will return $150 million and be “permanently severed” from federal funding by the end of 2027, according to a statement by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.

California accounts for nearly a third of the homeless population in the United States. A 2025 survey found that more than 72,000 people were homeless on any given night across Los Angeles County, a slight decrease from the year before.

Last year, HUD moved to cut off the money going to LAHSA after audits found reckless spending and a lack of transparency at the authority, which was responsible for doling out money to provide shelter and services for homeless residents. LAHSA sued to overturn the suspension.
The settlement stipulates that Los Angeles County will take over LAHSA's portfolio of projects and responsibilities for homeless services, subject to oversight by HUD.

“From the outset, we have maintained that LAHSA did not engage in wrongdoing and that HUD’s suspension lacked a legal foundation," Gita O’Neill, LAHSA's interim CEO, said in a statement. “Our focus now is on working closely with our local partners to ensure continuity of services, support an orderly transition, and remain true to our mission of connecting our unhoused neighbors with the services, resources, and pathways to housing they need.”

LAHSA, which was jointly funded by the city and county, was formed in 1993 as a result of a lawsuit settlement. It coordinated and managed money for shelter, food programs and a wide range of services, but it had long been dogged by accusations of misspending.

In April 2025, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors voted to shift more than $300 million in annual taxpayer money out of LAHSA to create a new department on homelessness. The city of Los Angeles also began exploring how it could sidestep LAHSA and directly contract with homeless service providers.

The region’s homelessness crisis is especially visible in downtown Los Angeles, where hundreds of people live in makeshift shanties that line entire blocks in the notorious neighborhood known as Skid Row. Encampments are increasingly found in suburban areas under freeway overpasses.

title: A Somali American Uber driver was strangled and run over by a passenger, authorities say
summary: A Somali American man is in critical condition after authorities say he was attacked by an Uber passenger
story: A Somali American man is in critical condition after authorities say he was attacked by an Uber passenger

MINNEAPOLIS -- An Uber passenger was charged Tuesday with attempted murder in a weekend attack near Minneapolis on a Somali American driver who was strangled with a seatbelt, run over by his own car and left in a ditch, authorities said.

Mohamed Yusuf, 51, is fighting for his life, has broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding from the attack, which occurred after the passenger allegedly told Yusuf he didn’t like the name Mohamed, according to court documents.

Samit Apurva Patel, 25, was charged with attempted second-degree murder and carjacking, but there wasn’t enough evidence to prove the attack was motivated by bias, said Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty. She said that decision “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community is feeling right now.”
An attorney representing Patel at his first court appearance Tuesday declined comment. A person who answered a phone number associated with Patel’s address said, “No comment,” before hanging up.

Dave Risk, a defense attorney in Minneapolis not connected to the case, said that to prove bias, prosecutors would have had to show that Patel intentionally targeted Yusuf because of a protected characteristic like race or religion.
In this situation, the pair likely met randomly, and Risk said that would make it tough for prosecutors to show Patel was motivated by bias.

Yusuf’s son Mustafa Osman said his father has been through five surgeries and is not doing well. He said Yusuf has driven taxis and Ubers for years and is known for his empathy and skill at de-escalating tense situations, making the attack especially shocking.
“We don’t have words to describe how bad it’s been. We haven’t really processed everything yet. It’s an emotional roller coaster," he told The Associated Press.

The violence early Saturday in the Minneapolis suburb of Hopkins has increased fear among the Somali community after years of targeted rhetoric, including from President Donald Trump. Minnesota has the largest Somali population in the U.S., with many concentrated in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. The overwhelming majority are American citizens.

According to court documents, Yusuf was on the phone with his brother, who is also an Uber driver, when Yusuf picked up the passenger near a Minneapolis bar just before 1 a.m. Saturday. The drop-off location was in the nearby suburb of Hopkins.

Yusuf's brother says he heard the passenger tell Yusuf he didn’t like the name Mohamed, the court documents say. He later heard Yusuf screaming in Somali that he was being choked with a belt and run over by the car, according to the filings.
Moriarty said the motive remains unknown but said, “There were some serious issues going on with this gentleman at the time he went home that so alarmed his parents that they called 911.”
She said she did not believe there was a recording of the call between Yusuf and his brother, and there was a camera in Yusuf’s car but it was not on.

Patel's parents called for a wellness check after Patel arrived home appearing intoxicated and “exhibiting signs of emotional distress and belligerent behavior,” according to the court filings. When officers arrived, they found Yusuf's car in the driveway with the exterior and driver's seatbelt damaged, according to the filings. Dirt, burs and a shoe were found in the driver's side interior, and the phone call with Yusuf's brother was still active through the car's system, court records show.
Officers said Patel told them he had been drinking and “admitted he took an Uber home, but he claimed not to know where his Uber driver was," the filing says.
Officers found Yusuf in a patch of burs in a ditch off the side of the road using location data from his smartwatch and a drone with thermal imaging.
Osman, 27, said he was shocked when he got a frantic call from his uncle saying something had happened to his dad.

Osman, the oldest of Yusuf’s five children, described his father as empathetic and good at de-escalation. He said his father has delt with aggravated or aggressive passengers during his many years driving.
“Anytime he’s in trouble, he’s the one that will calm things down, whether it’s between the family or if it’s while he’s at work," he said.
Yusuf came to the U.S. in 1993 and spent some time working as a taxi driver in Chicago, said Osman. The family lived in Minnesota, which was where Osman was raised, and had moved back in 2018.
Uber said in a statement that it was horrified by the attack, has been in touch with the driver’s family and has banned the rider from the platform.

Jaylani Hussein, executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, said dozens of community members have been stopping by the hospital to show support for Yusuf.

“We feel as a community we’re under threat, constantly,” Hussein said. “Our community has, unfortunately, been feeling the brunt end of a disinformation and demonization campaign that has been going on now, and it’s coming from every corner.”

The Trump administration's largest immigration enforcement effort, Operation Metro Surge, targeted the Twin Cities. Leading up to that operation, Trump said immigrants from the war-torn East African country have “caused a lot of trouble,” and he wants them to leave. He also referred to Somali immigrants in the U.S. as “garbage.”

Muhiyadin Yusuf, who knows Mohamed Yusuf but is not related to him, has been driving for ride-hailing apps in the Twin Cities for more than a decade. He said he's felt unsafe in general because of comments from Trump and other politicians targeting Somalis. But since Saturday, he's reduced his nighttime driving hours and added a third camera to his car. Some friends of his have stopped driving altogether.
“As a Muslim, as an immigrant, as a driver and as a Somali community, it affects me,” he said. “I'm scared now, more than before.”
Fingerhut reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press/Report for America reporter Laura Turbay contributed from Little Rock, Arkansas.

title: From pop stars to poets to politicians, hundreds gathering for joyful tribute to Gloria Steinem
summary: Luminaries from political figures to pop stars were gathering in Manhattan for a joyful tribute to the trailblazing activist and feminist Gloria Steinem
story: Luminaries from political figures to pop stars were gathering in Manhattan for a joyful tribute to the trailblazing activist and feminist Gloria Steinem

NEW YORK -- Luminaries from political figures to pop stars to poets were gathering Wednesday in Manhattan for a joyful and music-filled tribute to Gloria Steinem, the trailblazing activist, prolific author and most visible symbol of American feminism.
“It’s Steinemite!” declared the invitation received by about 1,000 guests, an indication of the buoyant mood that organizers say Steinem, who died in September at 92, had wanted for her memorial.

In a way, the late afternoon celebration promised to mirror the spirit of Steinem's famed talking circles, which she hosted at her Upper East Side home for more than 50 years: a vibrant mix of people from near and far, reflecting Steinem’s extensive travels and eclectic tastes in art and music.

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton was expected to be one of the main speakers. There were performances planned from pop star Cyndi Lauper and actor-singer Cynthia Erivo, as well as poetry and choral presentations. Organizers requested that the location not be disclosed ahead of time for security reasons.

“Gloria wanted a true celebration filled with laughter and friends across generations,” said Jill Heller, director of programs at Gloria's Foundation, which is working to preserve Steinem's home as a center to further her work. The presenters “reflect how expansive a life Gloria lived but also just the spirit of community, celebration and hopefulness that she wanted for this moment,” Heller said.
Close friend Amy Richards, a chief organizer of the event, said Steinem “definitely wanted people to have a good time. She hoped that new people will meet each other, and there will be laughter.”

Steinem became an activist after an early career as a journalist. She has said she might have remained a journalist had editors been willing to let her write about social issues of importance, like the nascent women’s movement — but they weren’t interested. It was at a meeting where women spoke out about illegal abortions that she decided to change paths.

“That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me,” Steinem told The Associated Press in 2022. “Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we’re not living in a democracy.”

Steinem went on to co-found Ms. Magazine and the National Women’s Political Caucus. She traveled constantly, to campuses and rallies and protests, despite an early fear of public speaking. And when she was at home in New York, her living room was a constant gathering place, where groups and movements were born as women gathered from across the country and around the globe.
Steinem, a prolific author, died just weeks before the release of her final memoir, “An Unexpected Life.”

“As I write this, I’m both older than I ever imagined I would become and happier than I ever imagined I could be,” she wrote in the introduction. “I’ve been rewarded with friends who are my chosen family. I have trusted friends in other countries, and we strive to be safe and free, and share hopes for a peaceful democracy in the world.”
Steinem added that she planned to live to 100.

title: US Catholic bishops meet after Democrats' big wins help reshape abortion debates
summary: U.S. Catholic bishops are meeting in Baltimore this week following the Democrats’ midterm victories
story: U.S. Catholic bishops are meeting in Baltimore this week following the Democrats’ midterm victories

U.S. Catholic bishops are holding their annual fall meeting in Baltimore this week. The gathering comes just after Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories reset the political dynamics around some of the bishops’ priorities, including immigration, abortion and artificial intelligence.
The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops is now facing a divided government as it seeks to influence both the faithful and public policy.

“Midterm elections are the opportunity for people to assess where we are as a country and where we hope to go,” said Bishop Michael Burbidge of Arlington, Virginia. “I think what the citizens are asking — and we’re certainly praying for — is that those who are elected will be devoted to doing all that is right and just and true and somehow find a way to begin working together and addressing the issues that impact individuals and families.”

Catholics overall are politically mixed. Catholic voters split roughly evenly between Republican and Democratic candidates for the U.S. House, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.

There was a split between white Catholics and Latino Catholics: Just over half of white Catholics supported the Republican House candidate in their area, while about two-thirds of Latino Catholics supported the Democratic House candidate in their area.

Nationally, just over half of Catholics said the Trump administration’s actions on immigration enforcement had “gone too far,” according to The AP Voter Poll. A similar share disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement was doing its job.

During the first half of Republican President Donald Trump’s second term, Catholic leaders emerged as strong critics of the administration’s immigration crackdown. Last fall, U.S. bishops issued a rare “special message” on immigration, decrying “the vilification of immigrants” and “indiscriminate mass deportation.”

Bishops are expected to hear updates Wednesday from their committees that deal with migration and abortion. They will also hear from a new task force on “preserving human dignity in the age of artificial intelligence.”

Catholic theology does not fit neatly into American political categories. While Catholic leaders have criticized current Republican immigration policies, they have also taken Democratic leaders to task over support for abortion rights. Targets of criticism included former Democratic President Joe Biden, who is Catholic.

“I think we're still trying to wrap our minds around what actually just happened,” said Bishop Robert Boxie III, an auxiliary bishop of the Archdiocese of Washington, while speaking about the midterms at a Georgetown University forum. He added the elections showed the power of “collective action” over money, including in “communities that had been sort of written off.”
Ahead of the midterms, U.S. bishops led a campaign urging Catholics to exercise their right to vote while putting faith before politics.

“The Church’s contribution to the public life of a nation is not a political or partisan program; rather, it reflects our commitment to the dignity of every person, who is created in the image and likeness of God,” Archbishop Paul Coakley, the conference's president, said in a statement.

That message became muddled in late October, when the White House released images and a video of a group of Catholic bishops praying over Trump in the Oval Office. At least two bishops expressed regret during the ensuing backlash.

“I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purpose,” Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, wrote in a statement. “I pray I am more prudent and wise going forward, even as I remain resolute in my openness to engaging and praying for political leaders at all levels.”
Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP’s collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. The AP is solely responsible for this content.

title: Ex-boxer Goran Gogic pleads guilty to drug charge, faces at least 10 years in prison
summary: Former heavyweight boxer Goran Gogic has pleaded guilty to a drug charge and likely faces 10-20 years in prison
story: Former heavyweight boxer Goran Gogic has pleaded guilty to a drug charge and likely faces 10-20 years in prison

NEW YORK -- Former heavyweight boxer Goran Gogic pleaded guilty to a drug charge Wednesday, a year after his trial was upended when it was revealed that a juror had been offered a $100,000 bribe to return a not guilty verdict.

Shackled at the ankles, Gogic, 47, spoke through an interpreter as he admitted conspiring to smuggle 20 tons (18.1 metric tons) of cocaine to Europe from Colombia through U.S. ports using commercial cargo ships.

He pleaded guilty in Brooklyn federal court to conspiracy to violate the Maritime Drug Law Enforcement Act, a charge that carries a mandatory minimum penalty of 10 years in prison and a maximum of life.
Under the plea agreement Gogic signed with prosecutors, the boxer agreed to forfeit $1 million associated with his crimes.

Prosecutors said they plan to ask at a sentencing scheduled for Feb. 16 that Gogic be ordered to serve 23 years in prison. His lawyer said the former athlete, who is from Montenegro, is likely to be deported when he is released from prison.
Gogic has been described by law enforcement officials as a “major drug trafficker” who operated on a “mammoth scale.”

He fought professionally in Germany from 2001 to 2012, compiling a 21-4-2 record, according to boxing website Sport & Note. He was listed as 6-foot-5 (1.96 meters) and weighed in at anywhere from 227 pounds (103 kilograms) to 250 pounds (113 kilograms).
“Gogic stepped outside the ring and into the drug trade, and today justice delivered a knockout blow,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said in a news release.
Alan Futerfas, Gogic's lawyer, said he had no comment Wednesday.

A year ago, law enforcement authorities arrested three people in a jury tampering plot and alleged one of them called a juror in Gogic's trial multiple times on his cellphone before the juror agreed to meet him on Staten Island.
During the meeting, the man told the juror that associates in the Bronx were willing to pay him to return a not guilty verdict, according to a criminal complaint.
When word of the bribery attempt was reported to court officials, a federal judge abruptly dismissed the jury just as it was about to hear opening statements.

title: Fishermen from Ecuador sue Trump administration over boat strike
summary: A group of Ecuadorian fishermen has sued the Trump administration over allegations that the U.S. military attacked their fishing vessel and kidnapped them after mistakenly identifying them as drug smugglers
story: A group of Ecuadorian fishermen has sued the Trump administration over allegations that the U.S. military attacked their fishing vessel and kidnapped them after mistakenly identifying them as drug smugglers

WASHINGTON -- A group of Ecuadorian fishermen has sued the Trump administration over allegations that the U.S. military attacked their fishing vessel and kidnapped them after mistakenly identifying them as drug smugglers.

The fishermen allege American drones struck their boat, the La Negra Francesca Duarte II, in the eastern Pacific Ocean off the coast of Ecuador on March 17, according to a federal lawsuit filed Monday.

The vessel was engulfed in flames, with two of the men suffering serious burns, the lawsuit says. The men allege they were held against their will by the U.S. for around 24 hours and treated in cruel and inhumane ways.

“The foregoing attack, kidnapping and torture took place despite the fact that the government of Ecuador, after a three-hour inspection, had just cleared the ship and its crew of any illicit activity,” according to the lawsuit, which was filed in U.S. District Court in Pittsburgh and reported earlier by The New York Times.

The lawsuit is the second against the Trump administration over U.S. military attacks on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America. At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls “narco-terrorists” in September 2025.

U.S. officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims that the vessels have been carrying drugs. Democratic lawmakers and some legal experts also say the attacks amount to extrajudicial killings on the high seas.

The Pentagon and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit. The Trump administration has justified the strikes in general by declaring drug cartels to be “ unlawful combatants ” and said the U.S. is now in an “armed conflict” with them.

The lawsuit was filed under a U.S. admiralty law that allows for claims against severe injuries inflicted on the high seas as well as unlawful attacks, kidnapping and torture. The fishermen's U.S. attorney, Daniel Kovalik, said he sued in Pittsburgh because of the maritime law expertise in the court's jurisdiction in western Pennsylvania, which includes the three rivers that flow through the city and a port on Lake Erie.

After their ship was attacked, the men jumped into the ocean before using small emergency boats that were on the larger vessel, the lawsuit says. They approached a ship marked with U.S. flags where men in uniforms spoke English.

The lawsuit alleges that the fishermen's hands were tied, hoods were placed on their heads and they were given little water and no food. One of them, Jordy Alexander Flores Lucas, was told through a translator that the men on the boat were the ones who launched the attack.
“They laughed about what they had done and about how they had destroyed the fishing vessel — a vessel which provided the livelihood of all of the plaintiffs," the lawsuit alleges.

The fishermen spent seven days on a Salvadoran ship that took them to El Salvador, the lawsuit says. Most were held in a comprehensive care center for migrants, while two injured men were brought to a hospital. All of the men were eventually flown back to Ecuador by the end of March.

title: Here are the GTA 6 songs you'll hear cruising around Vice City
summary: Grand Theft Auto 6 players carry out missions to songs by artists such as Cardi B, Lana Del Rey and Travis Scott.
story: Grand Theft Auto 6 relies on a murderer's row of musical hitmakers to provide the backbeat for cruising around Vice City.

The latest installment in the video game franchise, which officially launched on Thursday, features 34 original songs from a range of artists, including Cardi B, Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen. The game's official album was created in partnership with Atlantic Records, and will be available on music platforms such as Spotify and Apple Music beginning on Nov. 20.
Rockstar Games, the company behind the GTA series, is also offering fans limited-edition vinyl and CDs featuring the original tracks.
Music is an essential part of the GTA experience for players like 34-year-old Kansas City resident Cameron Logan Cox, who credits the game's music over the years with helping springboard his career.
"I went on to become a filmmaker and director for a hip-hop label," he told CBS News. "I really don't think I would have had that musical affinity if not for GTA."

In addition to the official GTA 6 soundtrack, gamers will be exposed to countless other tracks through "in-game radio," a feature in GTA 6 that allows players to listen to songs from fictional radio stations while they carry out their missions. They can turn on a station while they drive through Vice City, or via their phone.
"My favorite thing in GTA has never been a mission," Cox told CBS News. "It's the car, the radio and nowhere I have to be."

GTA 6 offers 22 stations, according to industry media outlet GameStop. Some have DJ personas, such as the Cocoteo FM station, which is hosted by characters voiced by Puerto Rican singers Bad Bunny and RaiNao, according to Rolling Stone.

title: Gamers, start your engines. Grand Theft Auto 6 is ready to roll.
summary: The latest, long-awaited version of the hit video game franchise launches at midnight local time on Nov. 19 in countries worldwide. Here's what to know about GTA 6.
story: In the immortal words of Carl "CJ" Johnson from an earlier edition of Grand Theft Auto, "Ah s***, here we go again." After 13 years and two delayed launches, video game fans are finally getting their hands on Grand Theft Auto 6.

GTA, as it's widely known, has evolved since its launch in 1997 into one of the biggest franchises in entertainment and one of the few sure hits in the ferociously competitive video game world. Tens of millions of people globally are expected to pick up their joysticks as Rockstar Games, the company behind the series, rolls out GTA 6 on Nov. 19 in countries around the world.

As fans eagerly await the latest GTA installment, Rockstar has whipped up interest with a series of trailers and even an extended look on Netflix. In typical fashion, however, the company has kept the hype simmering by withholding key information about the game ahead of its official launch this week.

"Having been over a decade since the last full release of a Grand Theft Auto game, all that energy just keeps getting bottled up and bottled up, and people are reading into every tweet and every little piece of news that's coming out of Rockstar to try and glean all the details of this game," Andrew Marok, director of equity research for digital media at financial firm Raymond James, told CBS News.
Here's what to know about the long-awaited release of GTA 6.
What is GTA 6 about?

The latest GTA installment centers on the stories of Lucia Caminos, the game's first-ever female protagonist, and Jason Duval. Jason, who has been working for drug runners, craves a quieter life but keeps getting dragged back into crime, according to Rockstar's synopsis of GTA 6. Lucia, meanwhile, has recently left Leonida Penitentiary, where she landed after "fighting for her family."

When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair becomes entangled in a wider conspiracy. The series is based in Vice City, inspired by Miami, in the fictional state of Leonida. Rockstar has touted the location as the most detailed version of the game yet, with architecture, beaches, roads and bars all inspired by South Florida.
There's "this concept of GTA 6 being just bigger than the game," Marok said.  "It's also about the immersion in the world of Vice City."
What equipment do I need to play the game?

Players will need a PlayStation 5 or an Xbox Series X/S console to play GTA 6. Rockstar told players who are preloading the game to plan ahead, as they may need up to 212 GB of storage space, depending on their device.
When can people start playing?

The game officially debuts worldwide on Thursday, Nov. 19. Rather than a single launch time, GTA 6 is rolling out at midnight local time in countries around the world, giving some users access before others. This website shows the countdown time by country.

Pre-orders for the game began back in June. But users weren't allowed to start pre-downloading on their PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles until Nov. 10, according to Rockstar. Gamers were also able to purchase a "code-in-box" version, a physical case that contains a code users can input to download the game from the PlayStation Store or Xbox.
How much does it cost?
Grand Theft Auto 6 costs $79.99 for the "standard edition" and $99.99 for the "ultimate edition." The latter contains an exclusive collection of cars, weapons and apparel.
What are players saying?

New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game. One 25-year-old told CBS News he set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — rather than his home in the United Kingdom, to access it as soon as possible.
"It's definitely more immersive than previous entries," he told CBS News, requesting anonymity because he is taking a day off from work to play GTA 6. "Visually, it's incredible."
Other gamers were also quick to praise GTA 6's visual quality and action-packed plot.

"The gameplay dynamics are just amazing, and the graphics are great, and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive," Adam Simmons, a 50-year-old in Wellington, New Zealand, where the game has already rolled out, told The Associated Press.

On Metacritic, a review aggregator website, players gave GTA 6 a score of 99 out of 100. "Grand Theft Auto VI, against all odds, has somehow managed to not only meet but surpass all my expectations," one user wrote.
How long does it take to play?
Insider Gaming, a website focused on the video game industry, said it takes an average of roughly 50 hours to complete all of the missions in GTA 6.
When will online play launch?

The online, multiplayer version of the game introduces new missions and allows players to stay immersed in the world of GTA after completing the more linear single-player version. It's free with the option of in-game purchases, according to Marok of Raymond James.
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, hasn't confirmed GTA Online's availability, though it seems likely given its enormous revenue potential.
"That's where GTA 5 made so much of its money," Marok said.
Will there be a PC version?

Rockstar Games did not respond to a request for comment about whether it will release a desktop version of the game. Historically, a PC version has been released about 12 to 18 months after the console version, according to Marok. However, the company could decide to launch it sooner.

"I think that there are reasons why Rockstar and Take-Two would want the PC version of the game out sooner than usual, and a lot of that has to do with the Grand Theft Auto Online component of the game, which is the multiplayer, ongoing monetization piece of it," he told CBS News.
Who plays GTA?
Male millennials and Gen Zers represent the key demographic playing GTA 6, according to a recent report from Sensor Tower. The company estimates 72% of players are male, while 57% are under 35.
What music is featured in the game?

GTA 6 features an original adaptive score from Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo featuring Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay. The music is "dynamically tuned to the different ways players engage with the world of Vice City and Leonida throughout Jason and Lucia's story," Rockstar Games said on its website.
The 30-track "Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score" is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations with Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
Who are the voice actors?

Rockstar has not disclosed the full voice cast. However, actress Manni Perez was nominated for her voice acting in the "Best Performance" category at The Game Awards, an annual ceremony that celebrates the video game industry. Actor Stephen Root has also confirmed to the AP that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly disclosed his participation.
How many GTA 6 units have already been sold?

The company had sold 19 million units, including pre-order copies, and generated $1.84 billion in revenue by Thursday, according to Sensor Tower. The market intelligence and digital analytics platform said earlier this month that GTA 6 is the "most pre-ordered game in history."
Raymond James projects that Rockstar will sell 50 million units of the game from launch through the end of Take-Two's fiscal year 2027, which runs until March 31.
"That would be by some distance the biggest launch in video gaming history," Marok said.

GTA 5, released in 2013, has sold nearly 235 million copies, according to Take-Two. The game has generated more than $10 billion in revenue over the last 13 years, according to Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross who studies sports and major events.
How much did GTA 6 cost to make?
Rockstar hasn't disclosed the exact figure, but analysts estimate GTA 6 cost upward of $1 billion to produce, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
"I would be shocked if it was under a billion dollars because they've been working on this for the better part of a decade," Marok said.
Asked about the price tag during a recent Wall Street Journal event, Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick didn't offer an exact figure, saying only, "It was expensive, and it took a long time."

title: CBS to air Kennedy Center Honors in December
summary: CBS has reached a one-year deal to air the awards ceremony next month, sources said.
story: The Kennedy Center Honors may have left the Kennedy Center itself, but the annual awards gala isn't leaving its longtime broadcast home. CBS has reached a one-year deal to air the awards ceremony next month, according to sources familiar with the arrangement.

This year's event, scheduled to be taped on Sunday, Dec. 7, and aired on Dec. 27, will be held at Capital One Arena in downtown Washington. Honorees include musicians Paul Anka and Barbara Mandrell, composer David Foster, actor Andy Garcia and playwright David Mamet.

In September, the Kennedy Center board voted to close the performing arts center amid a legal dispute over building upgrades and attempts to add President Trump's name to the facade. Mr. Trump said he would only help fundraise for renovations if his name was added to the facade. A federal judge in Washington, D.C., however, ruled that only Congress had the authority to change the building's name.

While modest maintenance projects continue, planning for the major renovations are underway and a construction schedule cannot be set until an ongoing federal court case halting construction is resolved. A court hearing is set for Thursday.

CBS has broadcast the Kennedy Center Honors each year since 1978. The multiyear contract lapsed after the 2025 show, but the arts center and the network reached a short-term deal for this year's show last week. The program will also stream on Paramount+.

President Trump co-hosted the show in 2025, punctuating artistic performances with several speeches throughout the evening. The White House did not respond to a CBS News inquiry on whether the president would attend this year.

title: Bezos says he was "heavily involved" in casting Pattinson as 007
summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says "it was obvious" to him and others that Robert Pattinson should be the next James Bond.
story: Amazon founder and executive chairman Jeff Bezos said Tuesday that he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

Speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley and The World forum in California, the head of the retail and entertainment giant that now owns the rights to the 007 franchise spoke about what he called the "real old-fashioned screen tests" for five Bond finalists, complete with "full costume, real sets."

On Friday, the team of selectors spent several hours going over the screen tests of each actor, Bezos said in remarks reported by Semafor, adding that while they were all "extraordinarily talented … there was something special about Rob."
Bezos said the group was initially biased against Pattinson, "because he's already so famous," and they had been inclined to choose someone "a little more unknown."
The role of the iconic British spy has historically gone to lesser-known actors, who have then made their name doing the Bond movies.
"But in the screening tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond," Bezos said of Pattinson, who shot to fame with his starring role in the "Twilight" vampire movies.

Amazon bought MGM, which co-owns the rights to the Bond franchise, in 2022. Pattinson will be the first Bond not forged under the creative stewardship of the Broccoli family, who had run the franchise since 1962, when the first movie featuring 007, "Dr. No," was released.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement after he was unveiled as the seventh actor to take on the role. "To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

He will step into the shoes of Hollywood leading men Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig to star in the 26th Bond movie, which will be directed by Denis Villeneuve. It is expected to hit screens in 2028.

title: New James Bond is announced after rampant speculation
summary: After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced who the new 007 will be.
story: Robert Pattinson is the new 007. After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced Monday that Pattinson will be the next James Bond.
He will be the seventh actor to play the role since the first Bond film, "Dr. No," was released in 1962.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "... To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The naming of Pattinson comes five years after the beloved franchise's last film, 2021's "No Time to Die," which marked the first time in Bond's 64-year history on the silver screen to end with the character's death.
But 007 will be reborn in the 26th Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve. It will be the first since Amazon MGM took over the franchise.
For months, fans had been debating the merits of other potential 007s, including names like Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult.
Pattinson only entered the rumor mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role, the Associated Press reported, along with a few other finalists.

"Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey," Villeneuve said in a statement. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."
Pattinson is already associated with three mega-franchises: "The Batman," "Twilight" and "Harry Potter."

Since his breakthrough in "Twilight," Pattinson has also worked in more independent films such as "Good Time," "The Lighthouse" and "Mickey 17." Earlier this year, he drew rave reviews for his villainous performance in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey."
The British royal family responded to the news on social media, saying: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."
Now in the Bond role, Pattinson follows in the footsteps of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig.

title: Raye leads the 2027 Grammy nominations. See the list.
summary: English singer-songwriter Raye is up for 11 awards at the 2027 Grammys, followed by Spanish singer Rosalía​ with nine nominations.
story: English singer-songwriter Raye leads the 2027 Grammy Award nominations, the Recording Academy announced Monday.

Raye is up for 11 awards at February's ceremony: record, song and album of the year — the first time she's been nominated in those big categories — as well as songwriter of the year non-classical, a variety of pop categories and music video.
Her 11 nods also mean she has tied Beyoncé's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist.
Speaking of Bey: She continues her reign as the most-nominated artist in Grammy history, scoring her 100th nod for "Morning Dew (Donk)" in the R&B solo performance category.

Raye, who is riding the success of her critically acclaimed album "This Music May Contain Hope," has 15 Grammy nominations across her career. She's never won one, though she was previously recognized by the Recording Academy with the noncompetitive Harry Belafonte best song for social change award.

Spanish singer Rosalía, fresh off her album of the year win at the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards on Thursday for her avant-garde "Lux," follows Raye with nine nominations. She's a first-time nominee in all the categories she's up for: record, song and album of the year as well as pop solo performance, alternative music performance, alternative music album, Latin song, global music performance and music video.

Following her are Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers and first-time nominee Ella Langley, who are tied with seven nods each. Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026's best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each.
Taylor Swift's nomination is her fifth consecutive studio album to be nominated for album of the year, something only one other artist has ever done: Kendrick Lamar.

Only recordings commercially released in the U.S. between Aug. 31, 2025, and Aug. 28, 2026, were eligible for nominations. The final round of Grammy voting, which determines the winners, will take place between Dec. 10 and Jan. 7.
The 2027 Grammy Awards will air Feb. 7 at 7 p.m. Eastern, live on ABC for the first time since 1972, from the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. It will also stream on Disney+ and Hulu.

title: 4 NFL officials work 2 games each due to ground stop, a rarity
summary: Four NFL officials worked two games Sunday — a rarity stemming from Friday's nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA that threw airlines' schedules into complete disarray.
story: Cincinnati — Don Willard did something on Sunday that the NFL hopes doesn't ever have to be duplicated — refereeing two games in one day.

Willard was the referee Sunday afternoon for the Miami Dolphins' game against the Indianapolis Colts in Indianapolis before he and three other members of the crew made the 114-mile trip to work the prime-time contest between the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals.

The reshuffling happened after the Federal Aviation Administration called for a nationwide ground stop Friday. The stop caused consternation and chaos for professional and college teams throughout the country and even resulted in moving at least one college football game from Saturday to Sunday.

NFL officials audibled by reassigning game officials for this week's matchups to stadiums closer to cities where they reside so they could drive, and Willard was asked to take over as the lead ref for the two games.

Willard usually works NFL games as a side judge. About an hour before kickoff in Indianapolis, he did the traditional microphone check and then he handled the coin toss duties typically reserved for referees.
Willard wasn't the only one doing double duty Sunday.

Umpire Terry Killens, field judge Jabir Walker and side judge Justin Larrew also jumped in a minibus and made the two-hour drive down I-74 to work the game in Cincinnati. It's the first time this officiating crew has worked together.
The four officials arrived in Cincinnati at 6:39 p.m., giving them some time to prepare before the 8:20 p.m. kickoff.

There were two instant replay reversals during the first half. A 23-yard completion to Pittsburgh's Germie Bernard was overturned when replay saw Bernard's toe was just out of bounds. An interception by Cincinnati's Jordan Battle was also reversed when a second look showed the ball hit the ground.
However, the crew called only 12 penalties in a game that usually sees a lot of flags because of the intensity of the Steelers-Bengals rivalry.

"I thought they did a great job managing a very difficult game, very testy game, obviously by both sides. So hats off to those guys for what they pulled off today. I know it was a long day for them," Bengals coach Zac Taylor said.
League officials didn't make any of the four officials who did double duty available to the media for either of Sunday's games.
NBC Sports rules analyst Terry McAulay, who worked three Super Bowls, said during Sunday night's "Football Night in America" pregame show that what the crew did was extraordinarily challenging.

"At a high level, it's a brand-new crew working together to work this game tonight that did not have at all the normal preparation - studying tendencies, studying formation style of play, and especially for this game, studying matchups on both sides of the ball. AFC North divisional games are brutal to officiate," he said. "Just working one NFL football game for three hours is incredibly mentally exhausting. When it's done, you're mentally drained. These guys have to do it now twice in one day. They don't have the normal recovery time. I know when I did it, my recovery time was never less than four hours."
The Dolphins didn't have any travel issues, a team spokesman said.
