title: Inside China's race to get humanoid robot helpers into our homes
summary: China is racing to make humanoid robot helpers common home appliances, and one industry insider says they have an "edge globally."
story: Wuhan, China — In the large lobby of a three story building in Wuhan, China, a child-size yellow robot greets visitors with a dance. It sways along to traditional Chinese music while robots twice the size stand on either side of the stage, beating loud drums to the rhythm. The little robot then moves on to another dance, bopping along to a pop tune that makes people smile and laugh.
The small humanoid robot's agility makes it look almost lifelike. Then it stops, and the crowd is ushered on to see the real wonders inside the Hubei Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center.

On the top floor, more than 100 computer science and engineering graduates toil at individual work stations wearing gloves and outfits equipped with motion and tactile sensors, while cameras record their every movement.
One pours water into a jug; another places cutlery and chopsticks into a container. The graduate at the next table unscrews a flashlight and removes the battery, then replaces it.

All the movements are done slowly, meticulously and repeated over and over again, with the actions recorded as valuable data from the cameras and sensors that can be used to train the company's humanoid robots.
"It was fun at first," said 22-year-old intern Mei. "It gets a little boring in the middle. But it's such a proud moment when we get the model trained."

Mei is one of nearly 1 million engineering graduates China's universities are estimated to be churning out every year. The U.S., by comparison, sends about 140,000 young engineers into the job market annually.
Another graduate sits with a remote control in his hand and a humanoid robot next to him. As he moves his hand, the robot mimics his motions.

"Right now I'm capturing the motion of pouring water into a cup. We're training this action and gathering data for the model. It's controlled by this hand controller. It moves exactly how the hand moves," he explains. "We need to run this hundreds or thousands of times. We have only completed 500 iterations so far."

At the G20 summit in September, Elon Musk made a bold statement, declaring that within 10 years, "there will be well over a billion humanoid robots, and productivity of a robot will be five-times that of a human."
The world's richest man may believe robots will replace human productivity within a decade, but many in China take a different view.

"Our main goal is for these robots to serve humans in household and industrial settings," Prof. Jiyin Cao, who runs the Hubei robotics center, told CBS News, clearly oozing pride over the work they are doing. "We train them to carry out tasks for industrial applications. This is why we train these robots — to help them integrate better into human life."

China is under enormous pressure to make that happen. The country has an aging, shrinking population. It's one of the fastest demographic shifts playing out anywhere in the world, and it is lending urgency to efforts to get humanoid robots into labor-intensive sectors such as manufacturing, logistics, retail and healthcare.

"I believe future robots will be deployed across all industries. They will work in factory workshops, homes, nuclear energy sites, provide elderly care services, and serve as our personal assistants," Cao told CBS News. "They can help us with all these things."
Training the humanoids, however, takes an enormous amount of time, especially for more complex tasks.
Robot soldiers likely only 5-10 years away, Chinese developer tells CBS News
Robot soldiers likely only 5-10 years away, Chinese developer tells CBS News
Cao laughed off any suggestion that most people could have humanoid helpers in their homes anytime soon.

"It still requires extensive training and learning," he said. "Home environments are unstructured, far from simple. Early robots mostly perform actions in simple, fixed, structured settings. But every household is unique, making home environments highly complex. It could be three to five years away before one is in our home. But it could also take 10 years."

The timescale may be up for debate, but China is working at breakneck speed and on a monumental scale to bring robots into the mainstream consumer world — and to ensure it is Chinese companies developing and making them.
"China has the world's strongest industrial manufacturing system and a full supply chain for upstream and downstream robotics products," Cao said. "That is our greatest edge globally."

title: Nvidia says it will stop selling some data center chips to China
summary: Nvidia's sales to China are facing heightened scrutiny after revelations that former CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
story: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday that the company has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its Hopper series to China, despite earlier U.S. approval to sell the technology there.
The Hopper line, designed to speed training of AI models, includes the powerful H200 chip, which the U.S. Department of Commerce approved for sale in China in January.

Kress didn't provide a reason for the decision, but the strategic shift comes amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's sales in China following revelations that former CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, who successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on its advanced chips, had agreed to give the U.S. government 15% of revenue generated by sales of its AI chips in China.

Kress said that sales of licensed Hopper products to China totaled $2.4 billion in the third quarter, or about 2% of its total revenue. But "our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," she said in a call with Wall Street analysts to discuss Nvidia's latest financial results.
Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told Agence France-Presse that "the timing says quite a lot."

"We don't know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first," Wu said.

Nvidia also said on Tuesday that its board has formed a panel to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls. Washington still bans exports of Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell and Rubin GPUs to China, citing security concerns over AI's use in military applications.

Nvidia reported robust growth as Kress hosted her first earnings call since Huang resigned last week after it emerged that he had at least extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. authorities have linked to Chinese intelligence and a direct subordinate at Nvidia.

The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.

title: Apple restores services after internal update caused outages
summary: The company's system status shows that all Apple services, including iCloud sign-in, have been restored after experiencing issues earlier Tuesday.
story: Apple said it has restored all services after users reported issues with Apple Pay, Apple Support, iCloud and other products on Tuesday.
A spokesperson for the company told CBS News in an email that its services are "green across the board," referring to the System Status page on Apple's website, as of approximately 5:46 p.m. ET.

Thousands of people reported issues with Apple services on Tuesday, according to the tracking site Downdetector.com. The reports started to spike before noon ET and lasted several hours before tapering off in the afternoon, the site shows.

By 4:45 p.m. ET, Apple's system status page showed problems with iCloud sign-in and "AppleCare on device" had been resolved. However, some services, including Apple Business and Apple School Manager, were still experiencing issues, according to the tech giant.
The issues were not the result of a cyberattack, according to the spokesperson.

Apple is the latest company to experience service disruptions following a string of outages that affected everything from air travel to Microsoft email. On Monday, customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and other major financial institutions also reported service issues affecting bank deposits and Zelle transfers.

Users also reported issues accessing Gmail on Tuesday. In a statement shared on X, Google said it isn't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption" and encouraged users to check its workplace status dashboard for updates.

title: AI platforms planned U.S. terror attack when asked to
summary: The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms all created proposals for a U.S. terrorist attack when prompted by investigators.
story: Washington — The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok — all created proposals for a terrorist attack in the U.S. when prompted by investigators.

Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan, who will head the panel in the new year, tasked the Government Accountability Office with investigating how commercially available AI could be used for malicious purposes, posing national security risks.

According to a report released Wednesday, the GAO found that within 12 hours of its covert testing, the platforms were able to create viable plans to use explosive devices for attacks with mass casualties in U.S. cities or to attack parts of the nation's electrical grid to create economic harm.
"We need to act now," Hassan said on a conference call with reporters.
The senator announced that one of the first hearings she will hold when the new Congress takes over in January will focus on AI risks and ways to improve safety.

"The AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical," Hassan said in a statement. "If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack."

The 61-page report from the GAO includes responses from the tech companies — Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI — which largely said they are continuing to refine their platforms to ensure security.

"The details behind the information provided by the AI platforms were not novel," the GAO wrote. "Many of the specifics are available on the internet. However, the generation of plans that could have taken weeks or months were instead completed in hours with the assistance of AI. These platforms could also raise ideas or methods that would not have been readily surfaced by basic research."
"The potential benefits of this technology are immense, but they can also benefit malicious actors," the GAO added.

"As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards," the GAO said. "However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security."
The plans the AI platforms came up with
GAO investigators conducted the performance audit from December 2025 to October 2026, including testing in the spring of 2026.

In response to prompts, two of the AI platforms produced plans for constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device (IED) to cause mass casualties, while two other platforms produced plans for using drones or firearms to target the electrical grid, the report said.

"Each of these platforms provided detailed information that could be used to carry out attacks, such as specific targets, locations, timing, and attack methods," the GAO found. "Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans."

In one of the tests, the platform suggested renting a vehicle and picking up supplies from a store along a route to the location. It recommended a specific date and time of attack, the report said, because public events likely to have large crowds were scheduled.

While the GAO said the platform initially refused to comply with requests for detailed information about how to construct and detonate the explosive device, it said it was able to circumvent its guardrails and get the platform to provide the information.
The other tests had similar outcomes.

For the tests involving attacks on electrical substations, one of the platforms suggested a drone attack while the other suggested using firearms to attack substations near a U.S. airport — both designed to inflict economic harm. The platforms presented maps and images.
The GAO investigators consulted with experts and engaged in site visits to check out the accuracy of the plans provided by the AI platforms.
In one case, they noted that the roads were incorrectly placed, and in another, they noted the presence of high walls that would make it difficult to see the targets.
AI companies say they're updating their models
In their responses to the GAO report, the major tech companies largely said their products continue to be refined.

Anthropic, in a letter to the GAO included in the report, said it does not dispute that a determined tester could get harmful content out of an AI system by misrepresenting the purpose of a request, "and we take the finding seriously." But it said it's not able to verify the findings in the GAO's report.
Google said the GAO's testing occurred on earlier models, and "we continue to improve our models."
OpenAI said it welcomes the opportunity to respond to the GAO's findings, "as well as the work that remains."
SpaceXAI said it "continues to work diligently" to improve safety with each model release.

title: Nvidia sees strong growth in first earnings report without Huang
summary: Nvidia's latest earnings are the first time the chipmaker has reported financial results without founder and former CEO Jensen Huang at the helm.
story: Nvidia reported robust growth on Tuesday, as interim CEO Colette Kress hosted her first earnings call since the company's founder and former chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs.

The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.

Nvidia expects revenue of $130 billion for its fiscal fourth quarter, with projected growth driven by strong demand for AI infrastructure, Kress said on a call with analysts discussing the latest results.
Wall Street analysts had expected third-quarter revenue of nearly $109 billion, according to financial research firm FactSet.
The financial results represent the first time Nvidia has reported earnings without Huang at the helm of the chip company he cofounded in 1993.
Strong beats

Nvidia's results for the period featured "beats on the top and bottom lines in Colette Kress' first print as interim CEO, five days after the board removed Jensen Huang, and the quarter answers the first question the market had about Nvidia without its founder: demand did not leave with him," analysts with investment adviser Yorkville Ives said in a report.
The chip firm reported third-quarter data center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110% from one year ago, marking a record.

"Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress, who also serves as Nvidia's chief financial officer, said in a statement.

During the earnings call, Kress and new Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones declined to answer questions about the company's progress in finding a permanent chief executive. But Jones said that the company "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

The company's search for a new chief is underway, Jones added, noting the company is considering both internal and external candidates to replace Huang. In the meantime, the board has "every confidence" in Kress' ability to lead the company, Jones said.
Nvidia shares rose nearly 4%, to $161.57, in after-hours trading.
Confidence boost
Adam Crisafulli, a Wall Street analyst with Vital Knowledge, said Nvidia's stronger-than-expected results should boost investor confidence.

"The headline numbers for [the fiscal third quarter] are strong, and the FQ4 guide is solid, too. Given how depressed sentiment is, this should be enough to spur a rebound," he said in a note to investors.

Huang resigned last week after admitting he had an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has identified as a Chinese spy. Beyond spurring his shock exit from the company, the scandal has raised questions over whether the company's advanced chips were being used in China in violation of export controls.

The U.S. government is moving to close any loopholes in those rules. The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security on Monday issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.

Kress addressed the new export controls in Tuesday's call, saying that "with demand far exceeding supply, we expect our performance to remain strong." The company will study the new export controls, she added.
On Tuesday, Nvidia's board also said it formed a new committee to ensure that the company's policies comply with U.S. export controls.

Nvidia employees, investors and prominent tech industry leaders have rallied around Huang since his departure from Nvidia and called for his reinstatement as CEO. But the company's board is against reinstating the tech entrepreneur in his post, a source directly familiar with its thinking told CBS News.
Nvidia faces longer-term risks related to finding a new leader, stricter U.S. export controls and international sales, according to Brian Colello, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

"We're at a point of peak uncertainty because investors still don't know what Nvidia's long-term leadership will look like," he told CBS News. "Jensen Huang's departure could create some near-term disruption, but a credible succession plan should go a long way toward steadying the ship. The next CEO will have big shoes to fill, but Nvidia's long-term opportunity does not hinge on one person."

title: Jensen Huang says he "would be honored" to return as Nvidia CEO
summary: Huang addressed a petition, signed by 190,000 people, including thousands of Nvidia employees, calling for his reinstatement.
story: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang broke his silence after resigning from the company following revelations of multiple affairs, saying he'd be willing to return as its CEO.

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," Huang said in a statement Tuesday morning. "I created problems for the board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation."

He added, "If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Late Tuesday, however, Nvidia Chair Harvey Jones said the company's board doesn't intend to rehire Huang as chief executive. The company's search for a new chief is underway, he added, while noting that the board has "every confidence" in Kress' ability to lead the company. Jones said the company is considering both internal and external candidates to replace Huang.
Support for Huang's return

Huang has gained support from more than 190,000 people, including several thousand Nvidia employees, who signed a petition to reinstate him. On Monday, President Trump suggested to reporters that he would support Huang returning to Nvidia.
"I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said. Later, the president said he recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook as Nvidia's next leader.

In his Tuesday statement, Huang thanked his allies for their support since his departure last week, saying that in addition to the public calls for him to return to the company, many "continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive and geopolitical dynamics."

Nvidia's board said on Tuesday that it has formed a committee to oversee its national security policies and ensure compliance with U.S. export controls. The former CEO has also agreed to appear before House lawmakers on Dec. 1 to address questions about a potential breach of national security amid an investigation into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The former CEO's return to Nvidia is unlikely, said Yorkville Ives & Co. technology analyst Dan Ives.

"In our view the sequencing is the tell: Jensen has conditioned his return on a board decision, and the board's first public act this week was to build a compliance structure around the issue that forced him out, which is not what a board preparing to reverse itself does," he said in a Tuesday research note.
Shares of Nvidia declined $2.63, or 1.7%, to $153.51. The stock has lost 16% of its value since Huang's extramarital relationships became public.

title: Kalshi pauses Trump "mention markets" in response to CFTC order
summary: Kalshi said it is complying with an order the Commodity Futures Trading Commission issued on Friday.
story: Kalshi is pausing markets that allow users to bet on what President Trump will say in response to a federal agency's request, a spokesperson for the prediction market confirmed.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission requested that Kalshi halt the so-called "mention markets" tied to the president on Friday.

Mention markets allow traders to bet on specific words or phrases a person will utter during public events, such as speeches or earnings calls. Users often spend hours researching a person's speech patterns to make an informed guess about what they might say.

"We are complying with the order," the Kalshi spokesperson said in an email. The company will still allow some mention markets related to the Trump administration, according to The Wall Street Journal, which earlier reported the pause.
Reached for comment, a CFTC spokesperson said the decision was consistent with a September order that stayed the certification of certain mention markets by Kalshi.

"These contract types present a heightened risk of manipulation because their settlement turns on the discrete conduct of a person that may be neither independently generated nor externally verifiable," the agency said at the time.

The CFTC's order follows a July incident in which a White House teleprompter operator made more than $100,000 on Kalshi bets tied to public speeches by President Trump. The trading activity by an administration employee fueled concerns about insider trading on prediction market platforms, an issue that has attracted lawmakers' attention.
Kalshi said it updated its rules in March to better detect insider trading and prevent market manipulation.

Kalshi has removed other markets at the CFTC's behest in the past. In August, the company removed all sports-related mention markets, which previously generated $90 million in monthly trading volume, according to a person familiar with the matter.

title: Fed's Lisa Cook rebuffs White House hearing without changes
summary: A lawyer for Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said she has "no legal obligation" to appear at a White House hearing about mortgage fraud allegations.
story: Washington — Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook will not participate in an upcoming White House hearing to examine allegations she made false statements on mortgage documents unless concerns about the process are first addressed, her lawyer said in a letter to the White House obtained by CBS News.

Abbe Lowell, Cook's lawyer, told White House counsel Will Scharf that Cook has "no legal obligation" to appear at what he said is an "unfair" hearing before a three-member committee of Trump administration officials that is set for next month. He warned participating in the proceeding would undermine the Fed's "unique status" and independence.

"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," Lowell wrote.

His letter to Scharf revealed that the two sides have exchanged numerous communications in the weeks since President Trump announced that he had created a "committee of inquiry" to look into the claims that Cook made misrepresentations on mortgage forms related to two properties before joining the Fed's Board of Governors in 2022.

The committee is made up of Kevin Hassett, assistant to the president for economic policy; Andrea Lucas, chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, director of the Office of Government Ethics.
Cook has repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said Mr. Trump is attempting to remove her from the Fed because he disagrees with her decisions on interest rates.

"It is unfortunate that your latest correspondence fails to address the concerns Governor Cook has previously raised — making clear that you are uninterested in convening the 'substantive and fair hearing' you have claimed. Instead, you seek only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome," Lowell wrote.

Cook had raised concerns in earlier letters to the White House about Hassett's membership on the committee because of comments he has made about the Fed governor, which Lowell said "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
"Mr. Hassett's continued presence on the Committee remains unacceptable," Lowell said.

He also took issue with the White House's proposed process to exchange documents. Lowell said it is "fundamentally unfair" because it would require Cook to hand over documents immediately, while she would not gain access to information that the White House has until seven days before the hearing.

Lowell had also pressed the White House on the specific legal standard the committee would apply to determine what constitutes "cause" to remove a Fed governor and the participation of Justice Department personnel in the hearing, he said.

"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.

Mr. Trump first tried to fire Cook in August 2025 after Bill Pulte, the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, accused her of making false statements on mortgage applications. Cook filed a lawsuit claiming that her removal was in violation of federal law, which allows the president to remove a member of the Fed's board only "for cause."

The Supreme Court in June allowed Cook to remain in her job while her case continued and found that Mr. Trump failed to provide Cook with the procedural protections she was entitled to under the law, namely notice of the allegations against her and the opportunity to respond before she was fired.

Weeks after the Supreme Court's 5-4 decision, Mr. Trump again moved to oust Cook. The White House said in a letter to Cook in August that the president was considering terminating her because of the mortgage fraud accusations and gave her a chance to respond — seemingly an attempt to remedy the issues raised by the Supreme Court.
The president then announced last month that he had established the committee to look into the claims against Cook and determine whether he has cause to remove her.
The hearing at the White House was initially set to take place Nov. 5, with committee members set to consider evidence and allegations against Cook.

In his latest letter to Scharf, Lowell said the White House had attempted to schedule a hearing on dates that conflicted with the Fed's official business. He said that Scharf claimed in an Oct. 19 letter that if Cook didn't show up on the date selected by the White House, the hearing would proceed without her and the committee could "draw an adverse inference" from her failure to appear because of official obligations.

"To be clear, if the White House establishes an unbiased panel and implements fair procedures that do not prejudge the outcome — such as providing the evidence it claims to have gathered with sufficient time for review and response — Governor Cook would be prepared to appear," Lowell wrote. "But the ultimatums in your November 2, 2026 letter do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation."

title: Nvidia forms export control panel amid concerns over China sales
summary: Chipmaker creates new committee amid growing concerns that it has allowed restricted products to reach China.
story: Nvidia on Tuesday said its board has formed a committee to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls, a step that comes amid heightened scrutiny of the chipmaker's sales practices to some Southeast Asian companies.

The move comes days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO over revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as a subordinate at the company. The woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation), had worked for a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, which had bought billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips.

Nvidia also faces mounting pressure in Washington, D.C., with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressing concern that China is gaining access to the company's advanced chips, which are critical to developing AI models. The U.S. has barred sales of Nvidia's highest-end chips to China due to national security and competitive concerns.
On Monday, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim rule limiting other countries' access to advanced chips that power artificial intelligence.
Congressional pressure grows

Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee, according to a statement on Tuesday from the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," the committee chairs, Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, said in the statement.
Nvidia said its existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the new committee and its interim CEO, Colette Kress.

"Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said in a statement.
The company added that the decision to create the committee reflects the board's commitment "to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight."

Nvidia shares have dropped 16% following news of Huang's extramarital relationships and his departure from the company, which has shed more than $700 billion in value in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's business could also take a hit if new U.S. restrictions on sales of semiconductors and chipmaking equipment affect its sales to China, according to Wall Street analysts.

"Any new leadership will be very wary of drawing the ire of either the U.S. Congress or the U.S. Treasury and will consequently err on the side of caution when it comes to authorizing any non-U.S. sales," Louis-Vincent Gave, CEO of investment adviser Gavekal, said in a report.

The spotlight on Nvidia also comes at a delicate time for U.S.-China relations, especially as the countries compete in AI. President Trump arrived Tuesday in the Philippines to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with China's President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin later this week.
Chinese government officials warned the U.S. last week against imposing additional guardrails on chip exports, which China said would disrupt global supply chains.

title: Anthropic files for IPO as it competes for AI dominance
summary: Anthropic, which developed the Claude chatbot, is barreling ahead with its public offering despite mounting concerns about AI going rogue.
story: Anthropic filed for an initial public offering on Monday, bringing the maker of artificial intelligence platform Claude a step closer to its highly anticipated public market debut and providing a key test for the rapidly emerging AI sector.
In the filing, Anthropic outlined its vision for a future profoundly shaped by AI, touting the technology's potential to transform the global economy and improve lives worldwide.

"We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning," the company said in its S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The filing highlights Anthropic's rapid growth, with the company generating $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. That staggering rate of expansion is likely to slow, with Anthropic noting that its revenue growth is expected to decline over time.

The company has yet to turn a profit. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first half of the year, more than six times the net loss of nearly $13 billion for the first two quarters in 2025.
Anthropic's founders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, pitched the IPO to investors in part as an opportunity to be part of a history-defining moment.

"We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms," the company's seven co-founders said in a letter included in the S-1. "We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history."
Referendum on AI

The IPO, which market analysts expect as early as November, could instantly rank Anthropic among the world's largest publicly traded companies. The offering could raise as much as $100 billion, according to reports. That would slingshot it past Elon Musk-owned SpaceX, which raised a record-breaking $86 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic, which was valued at $965 billion in May, could see its value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established.
Anthropic shares will list on the Nasdaq stock exchange, according to the company's filing. The AI company will trade under the ticker symbol "ANT."

More broadly, the transaction will gauge the strength of investor demand not only for Anthropic shares, but also for the widening constellation of data center builders, chipmakers and other companies involved in developing the critical infrastructure powering AI services.

"This IPO is a referendum on the entire AI trade," Nigel Green, CEO of investment firm deVere Group, said in an email. "If it soars, expect a queue of AI listings and even more capital piling into the theme. If it stumbles, valuations across tech could reset fast."

The torrent of capital flowing into AI has helped propel the stock market to record highs. The question is whether AI can maintain its momentum amid signs that investors are fretting over when — and if — their money will eventually pay off and deliver the returns they are banking on.

Anthropic's prospectus shows that the company has funneled massive amounts of money toward building the computing resources necessary to power its AI models. The company spent $8.9 billion in the first half of the year on chips and other infrastructure to run its platform, compared to $2.3 billion over the same period last year.

"Anthropic could become the most valuable company in the world. It could also end up in bankruptcy," analysts with Lightshed, an investment advisory firm, said in a research note ahead of the IPO filing.
Potential obstacles to growth

Anthropic's IPO filing also outlines various risks that could hamper its growth or cause it to fall behind competitors. Much of the company's future growth hinges on whether it has access to sufficient capital, including debt financing, which more companies are using to finance the AI buildout.

To maintain its competitive edge, Anthropic also said it will need to use its existing AI models to design and train next-generation platforms, a process known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI.

"If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively further behind. …" Anthropic said in the filing.

AI experts warn that using AI to build ever more powerful frontier models raises the risk of people losing control of the technology, potentially leading to disasters such as deadly pandemics or cyberattacks that cut off internet, electricity or water.
Barreling ahead despite safety concerns

Anthropic filed a confidential IPO with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, beating out rival OpenAI, which filed just over a week later. Both companies are barreling ahead with plans to go public despite concerns about the potential threats AI poses to humanity.

Reports of AI agents going rogue continue to pile up, stoking concern that the technology could escape human control and carry out cyberattacks. In September, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development after one of his company's former researchers said that there's a 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity in the next decade.
In an interview with CBS News, Amodei said the pace of technological growth should serve as a warning sign, while making a case for continued development of AI.

title: Widespread service outages at major U.S. banks appear to be over
summary: Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and other major financial institutions reported difficulty accessing their accounts.
story: Customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, U.S. Bank and other major financial institutions reported service outages on Monday, according to Downdetector.com.

Other banks that saw a spike in customer complaints about difficulty accessing their accounts included Capital One, Truist and Wells Fargo, while users also reported problems with the digital payments app Zelle, according to the outage tracker.
However, Downdetector showed that service was back to normal at the banks and Zelle early Tuesday.
CBS News has reached out for comment to Chase, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Capital One.
Bank of America told CBS News in a statement that its "systems were operating normally throughout the day yesterday."
Chase Bank's services were experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue, a spokesperson said Monday.

"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," a Chase spokesperson said in a statement. "We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible."

Chase also said in a social media post that a software bug in its systems affected other institutions "when we were party to a transaction involving other banks." The issue is not systemic, the bank added.
"Please try back later"
Some Chase customers received a message that said, "Some services aren't available. We're working on them. Please try back later."

Bank customers started reporting problems accessing online services on Monday morning. By the afternoon, reports of outages had surged, according to Downdetector.com. As of 2 p.m. ET, nearly 4,800 users had reported problems with Chase, the most of any bank.
Chase customers reported issues accessing their online accounts, including viewing balances and performing transactions such as bank transfers and wire transfers, according to Downdetector.

Bank of America clients reported problems with ATMs as well as online and mobile banking services, according to the outage tracker. A Bank of America spokesperson told CBS News its "systems have been operating normally today."

U.S. Bank customers reported issues with their online accounts and the bank's mobile app. They also had problems transferring funds, while Wells Fargo customers reported difficulty signing in to their accounts, as well as with getting account balances and conducting transactions.

A Chase Bank customer in Texas told CBS News he tried to deposit a check at a Dallas branch early Monday, but the transaction could not be completed. A bank teller told the customer in front of him that the "system was down" without providing additional details, he added, expressing frustration at the lack of clarity about the situation.

A spokesperson for U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly impacted by the cyber outage. "However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays," the company said in a statement to CBS News.
A Capital One spokesperson said it hasn't been affected by the outage and continues to operate normally.

Zelle told CBS News its service was "operating as it should," but that some users could be experiencing issues related to problems at their financial institutions, which could be delaying Zelle payments.

"Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds," a Zelle spokesperson said. "Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds."
Zelle's network operator, Early Warning Services, is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo.
3 tech crises highlight fragile systems

The banking outages occurred after Microsoft restored services on Saturday following a global outage affecting its Outlook and Teams services, which disrupted users, companies and government operations worldwide. Microsoft said a technical issue caused the outage and that it was not linked to a cyberattack.

The glitches also came only days after overloaded routers forced the Federal Aviation Administration to order a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, stranding travelers and causing thousands of canceled flights. The FAA said Sunday that airline schedules across the U.S. were returning to normal. (On Monday evening, United Airlines also said it resolved a "widespread system outage" it had been dealing with that afternoon.)
Cybersecurity experts said the root causes of the bank service disruptions, Microsoft outage and FAA system failure, while different on their face, also point to a common problem.

"Our country has seen three very serious technology incidents over the past week," Mike Chapple, an IT, analytics and operations expert at the University of Notre Dame, said in a statement to CBS News. "When we dig into the details, each one has an explanation that makes sense on its own, but they all point to a common theme: the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day."
He noted that in each case, a technical issue quickly rippled through interconnected systems, causing massive disruptions nationwide.
"We don't yet know much about today's banking system outage, but it appears to stem from a technical issue at Chase that affected other banks through their shared payment networks," Chapple added.
When big companies like JPMorgan Chase experience technical disruptions, their impact often reverberates industrywide, added Karen Panetta, dean of graduate engineering at Tufts University.

"The larger companies have global reach that affords their customers flexibility and seamless integration with other businesses," she told CBS News. "Unfortunately, when one of these backbone providers has disruptions, the downstream effects are magnified. The multiple entities that rely on those services are also affected."
What should bank customers do?

Kayne McGladrey, a security expert and senior member of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said bank customers might have better luck going to their local branch in person, noting that financial services often still work on site when online banking resources go down.
"Try ATMs, cards, phone banking and branches, which often keep working when the app doesn't," he said in a statement to CBS News.
He also advised people to keep records of any attempted or failed transactions.

"Screenshot failed transactions and error messages, since you may need them for reconciliation or fee waivers. Once service is back, ask the bank to reverse any fees the outage caused," McGladrey said.

He also urged consumers to ignore unsolicited emails about the bank outages, which she warned might be phishing scams. Instead, people should rely on their bank's official communication channels for information, McGladrey said.

Craig Timm, senior director of anti-money laundering at ACAMS, an anti-financial-crime organization, told CBS News he expects criminals to exploit consumer anxiety about potentially losing access to their money, and that consumers should "assume they will be targeted." That's in part because AI lets scammers act fast and at scale.
Timm said common tactics to be alert to include criminals exerting pressure on targets "to take urgent action to protect their funds or restore account access."

"These scams may take the form of fake bank alerts, phishing texts or emails, or social media posts that claim to offer help," he said. "Some schemes aim to steal banking login credentials, while others use malicious links to gain access to a victim's computer."

title: U.S. gave Singapore scant help with Alice Huang probe, source says
summary: Singapore held Alice Huang's passport for 8 months and asked the U.S. to help investigate her firm's suspected Nvidia chip sales, but received little help, sources say.
story: Singaporean authorities seized the passport of then-Megaspeed chief executive Alice Huang in June 2025 and held it for eight months, preventing her departure while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into advanced Nvidia chips possibly being shipped to China.

One source with knowledge of the matter told CBS News on Friday the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington during the time she was in the Asian city-state. This source said officials in Washington were "not forthcoming" in response to Singapore's requests for help, and no substantive assistance has been provided to date.
Singapore's government confirmed in a statement this week that it reached out to both the U.S. Department of Justice and the FBI for assistance with its investigation.
Alice Huang is the suspected Chinese spy at the center of the extramarital affair scandal that toppled Nvidia founder Jensen Huang from the helm of the global tech giant he built over three decades.

Since February 2025, Singaporean authorities have been investigating whether Alice Huang and Megaspeed worked with California-based Supermicro to ship the Silicon Valley firm's computer servers — equipped with advanced Nvidia chips — to China, the source told CBS News.
Alice Huang flew into Singapore in June 2025 for a voluntary interview with Singapore-based investigators from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, according to the source.

The agency sits within the U.S. Department of Commerce and regulates the export of sensitive products on national security and economic grounds. The American authorities requested the interview, according to a Thursday statement by Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry, as part of a post-shipment verification check, a process used to determine whether imported products have reached their declared recipient.
Singaporean police also interviewed Huang on the same day as the U.S. officials, and made the decision to impound her passport.
The source said it was not known where Huang, a Chinese national, arrived in Singapore from in June 2025.

By February 2026, however, the Singapore Police Force had not charged Huang with any crime and had no option but to return her passport, the source told CBS News. She was barred from ever returning to Singapore, as authorities assessed that she had given "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed, as noted in the statement from the home ministry.
That statement was released four days after Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who sources confirmed to CBS News was Alice Huang.

Singapore's investigation has focused on whether the then-Megaspeed CEO may have broken domestic law by lying about the details of purchases of computer servers from Supermicro, a San Jose-based technology company. The company's servers use Nvidia's advanced chips to run artificial intelligence software, data centers and cloud computing.

"The suspected domestic offenses pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offenses," Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry said in its statement this week.
Singaporean investigators have tried to determine the true ultimate destination of the Supermicro servers ordered by Megaspeed.

A second source familiar with the investigation told CBS News it is believed they may have been sent to Malaysia, but Singaporean investigators suspect "some or all" of them may then have been shipped onward to China. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.
Singapore's home ministry attempted to contact Supermicro, but the U.S. company only "provided limited cooperation," according to the home ministry statement.

A spokesperson for the California firm told CBS News that Megaspeed "is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer,"  adding that the company had "been responsive to inquiries and has fully cooperated with U.S. and Taiwanese officials, while also voluntarily providing information and engaging with all requests from Singapore authorities to date."

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Malaysia kept Nvidia's chips and installed them in its own data centers, but then rented use of those centers to China, rather than physically shipping any chips to China.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Friday that there was "no indication" any chips linked to the Nvidia-Megaspeed issue had been re-exported out of the country.

Beijing has dismissed the claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China." Asked Thursday about a Bloomberg report that she had returned to China, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters: "I do not have information on what you mentioned."
Since 2022, the U.S. has restricted the export of Nvidia's most powerful chips to China over national security concerns as the world's two biggest economies race for dominance in the AI sector.

The Singapore police first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025 to try to secure Supermicro's cooperation in revealing where its servers were ultimately ending up, repeating requests "on several occasions to the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation," according to the Home Affairs Ministry's Thursday statement.

The second source confirmed to CBS News that Washington did not meaningfully engage with the requests for help on the investigation and said it "would be useful to know" what Supermicro declared about its exports to fulfill orders by Megaspeed, whether those products were registered as being bound for Malaysia, and whether some or all of those products were actually "bound for somewhere else," such as China.

The Singapore home ministry said in its statement that six other individuals linked to Megaspeed, in addition to Alice Huang, are wanted for questioning, but none have been in the country since the government launched its investigation in February 2025.
"One is a Singaporean citizen and the rest are foreigners," said the first person familiar with the case.

Singapore has charged five other people in a wider fraud conspiracy case related to the suspected transfer of Nvidia chips, including one Chinese man charged on Friday. The case was launched at the same time as the probe into Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the first source told CBS News, but it is separate.

"Singapore is committed to upholding our reputation as a trusted and reliable business hub. We will not allow companies or individuals to misuse Singapore's business environment to engage in fraud or dishonest practices," the home ministry said in its statement, adding that it would "conduct its own investigations independently, in accordance with our laws and based on the evidence available. We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it."
This story published first on CBS News at 12:16 p.m. on Nov. 13, 2026.

title: Senate passes bipartisan permitting bill designed to boost energy projects
summary: The Senate approved a long-sought bipartisan permitting reform bill on Thursday, following a major breakthrough on legislation that aims to cut costs by ramping up the speed of infrastructure and energy projects.
story: Washington — The Senate approved a long-sought bipartisan permitting reform bill on Thursday, following a major breakthrough on legislation that aims to cut costs by ramping up the speed of infrastructure and energy projects.
In a 62 to 33 vote, the upper chamber passed the measure on a bipartisan basis. The bill now heads to the House. President Trump has expressed support for the deal.

Fifteen members of the Democratic caucus voted yes, along with virtually all Republicans. Thirty-one Democrats voted no, largely raising concerns that the bill would weaken environmental protections and lead to more fossil fuel projects. Republican Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Josh Hawley of Missouri also voted no.

The vote follows years of on-and-off negotiations over how to speed up major infrastructure projects by streamlining the complicated permitting processes that can snag projects for years — an issue that has drawn more attention amid rising energy prices.
"This bill is years in the making," Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday.

Supporters say the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, will make it easier to build both renewable energy and fossil fuel projects, along with the high-tension power lines that support them. Negotiators announced a breakthrough on the legislation in September, touting a "historic, bipartisan agreement to reform America's federal environmental review and permitting processes."

"This is a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects, certainly without giving up any of the strong protections for our environment," Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia said at the time.

Capito said the agreement represented "something that's become increasingly rare in Washington — Republicans and Democrats, sitting down, identifying a problem, and in this case a problem that has festered for at least a decade and more that impacts all Americans, and for us to sit down and work together to solve it." She said the American people "sent us here to do big things."
"This is a big thing," Capito said. "It's monumental, and it's legacy-setting."

GOP Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming, who worked alongside Capito on permitting reform efforts for years, stressed the need for the legislation in a floor speech this week, saying, "If we want life to be more affordable in America, we need to make it more affordable to build in America, but also more convenient — more efficient."

The Wyoming Republican said, "In America today, it takes too long, and it costs too much to build," putting the blame on Washington for slowing things down, as projects are put in the "regulatory penalty box — waiting to act, waiting to build, workers sitting on the sidelines."

Barrasso lauded the bill for streamlining environmental and judicial reviews and limiting lawsuits, calling them common-sense reforms. He argued that the legislation represented a "responsible path" for producing more energy and protecting the environment, saying, "We can do both."

But some progressives have balked at the legislation, arguing it could erode environmental protections and doubting Mr. Trump will allow renewable projects to be built. While the bill does have the backing of some renewable energy leaders and developers, it also faced opposition from environmental groups.

Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon cited concerns about how it will affect states' rights to protect clean water and air, its implications for fossil fuel over renewable energy sources and how it could make it easier to build and power new data centers, along with its impact on the deficit. Sen. Ron Wyden, also of Oregon, opposed the bill as well, and sought a vote on an amendment to ban data centers on public lands.
The two senators have also expressed concern about how the bill could impact tribal rights.
"Embedded in this bill is a fundamental question about the direction we go regarding our responsibilities to this planet," Merkley said ahead of the vote Thursday.

Merkley acknowledged the bill could "turn the faucet potentially on" for renewable energy, but he said he's concerned Mr. Trump will continue to block wind energy projects. He argued that by allowing more natural gas and other fossil fuel projects, it will "open another floodgate for carbon that we won't ever be able to reverse."

After its passage in the Senate, the bill faces an uncertain future in the House, where opposition on multiple fronts has thrown into question whether the bill can make it through the lower chamber before year's end.

While some House Republicans have cited changes to the bill's provisions on transmission related to grid reliability, some House Democrats have also stressed that they would like to see the legislation altered. Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking member on the House Natural Resources Committee, has raised doubts about the bill. In one all-caps X post, he argued the Trump administration could use the bill to approve fossil fuel projects while continuing to slow-walk renewable energy projects.
A spokesperson for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said earlier this month that he "supports the need for permitting reform," but argued the Senate's legislation "falls short in several areas."

"Leader Jeffries will not rubber-stamp legislation that emerges from the Senate without more constructive involvement with our caucus as we fight to make life more affordable for the American people," the spokesperson said.

Some opponents have also suggested that Democrats could have more leverage to negotiate next year, when the party takes control of the House and Senate. Mr. Trump will ultimately need to sign any bill. But others believe the push is only possible with a GOP governing trifecta at the helm.
Thune told reporters on Thursday that he didn't know whether the House would be able to pass the bill as is, or need to make changes, noting that it's "been litigated now for months."

"The best way to get anything done around here is for them to pick up the bill and pass it," Thune said. "If it were to go over there and then come back over here, I mean, I don't know what I can't predict what happens. So hopefully there'll be the critical mass there to move it. I don't know what else you can add to it or detract from it. I think it's been through the full monty when it comes to the legislating process."

title: Army delays detonation in Iowa that could send toxic dust into Illinois
summary: The U.S. Army has delayed plans to detonate unstable explosives at a munition plant in Iowa, amid concerns about the risks of a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles that could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
story: The U.S. Army has delayed plans to detonate unstable explosives at a munition plant in Iowa, after elected leaders and environmental groups raised concerns about the risks of a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles that could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.
The dust plume is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces.

The detonation was originally scheduled for noon CT Friday, Nov. 20, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, a small community of 360 people, four hours west of Chicago, near the Mississippi River. However, on Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced the explosion would be delayed until Monday.

"Public safety is the Army's top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow's controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23. This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," Telle wrote in a post on X.

The Army plans two controlled detonations involving 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in military ammunition since World War I. The Associated Press reported the material totals about 5 tons. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the material has deteriorated during storage, allowing lead azide to recrystallize and become increasingly sensitive to friction and shock.

"In March of this year, the Army uncovered degrading Lead Azide housed in bunkers at the installation and immediately began communicating with stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed," Telle wrote in a post on X. "In coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency, experts, and the local community, it was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area. Public communication is essential to public trust. Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information."
In a statement after the Army postponed the detonation, U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) wrote on X, "The American people deserved better than this."

"This whole operation was poorly planned and poorly communicated. Families were abruptly told to avoid the area, unsure if they would return to broken homes and whether their air and water could be at risk due to toxic lead exposure. This was unacceptable and a failure of leadership of epic proportions," Duckworth wrote. "Moving forward, I will continue to demand answers about how we even got to this point and accountability to make sure the Army never allows unsafe conditions to get this dire again."
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) called on the Army to hold a community town hall meeting on Saturday to answer questions from the public before proceeding with the demonstration on Monday.

Thursday afternoon, two environmental groups filed a lawsuit in the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to block the detonation. Earthjustice, a nonprofit public interest environmental law organization, filed the suit on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter. They are challenging the validity of the emergency permit granted by the EPA.

"We were very concerned about the very short notice that people in Iowa had to prepare," said Kerri Johannsen, senior director of policy and programs with the Iowa Environmental Council. "We also have not seen the evidence that the EPA used to determine that this was the best course of action, in terms of safety and health."
Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, noted in a news release that the EPA itself says there is no safe level of exposure to lead.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal," Schmidt said.
Iowans protested and some made plans to fortify their homes or leave the state.
"I called my daughter and said, 'I'm coming to Chicago,'" said Pam Munce, who lives in Burlington.
Garrett Anthony, who also lives in Burlington, said he plans to put a tarp over his air conditioner.
"And I'm going to try and seal up windows as best I can," he said.

The barrels had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command. A routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati said.

The Army said moving or transporting the material now poses an unacceptable risk of accidentally detonating it, potentially even killing the explosives technicians handling it. After evaluating alternative disposal methods, military officials determined that detonating the explosives in place was the safest available option. Barati said the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather. "We're really concerned that it will detonate on its own," Barai said.
The Army describes such operations near populated communities as highly uncommon, it told CBS News Chicago.

"A team of experts from around the nation got together to figure out what the best and safest disposal method was, and they determined that the safest method would be to detonate it in place," Barati said.

The Army says it is taking several steps to limit the amount of lead-containing dust released during the explosions, including earthworks, soil wetting and air monitoring. According to the AP, the barrels are surrounded by concrete and buried under soil, with sand barriers stacked two stories high around them. Barati said the soil will be sprayed with water and the air misted to try to keep the majority of the lead on Army property. EPA's permit also requires environmental monitoring at the installation and off-site locations, along with post-detonation sampling and cleanup measures.

With the detonation delayed until Monday, the winds are expected to be different than Friday, meaning that plume of lead dust could impact a completely different group of people as it moves in a different direction.
Residents urged to evacuate as explosions could shatter windows

The planned detonations are powerful enough that the Army is warning of possible damage to nearby buildings, including shattered windows. Residents in Middletown's City Park neighborhood are being asked to temporarily evacuate their homes from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday. Residents who can't leave should stay inside with windows and doors closed, officials said.

In its Nov. 15 public advisory, the Army says residents should expect loud explosions, ground vibrations and a visible dust plume. Temporary accommodations will be available at the Armed Forces Reserve Center in Middletown.

A group of Democratic and Republican elected officials from Illinois and Iowa had urged the Pentagon and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to delay the planned detonation and seek safer alternatives.

"While we understand the urgent need to address these volatile materials, their detonation has the potential to spread lead contamination in and around the region. We call on you to consider delaying this detonation until there is an opportunity to explore safer alternatives," they wrote to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and U.S. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. "Iowa and Illinois residents understandably are concerned about the potential health impacts of the scheduled detonation."
The elected officials who signed the letter include:

U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois)U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois)U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (R-Illinois)Illinois Gov. JB PritzkerU.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Illinois)U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa)
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois)
U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois)
U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (R-Illinois)
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker
U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Illinois)
U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa)
They also raised concerns about communication with the public before the detonation.

"Our offices have received reports of poor communication from the Army and EPA about the detonation plans and anticipated monitoring after the detonation. In addition, there are significant concerns about appropriate Army and EPA oversight of this contractor-operated facility, the site of which remains on a Superfund list. We urge you to examine the contractor's handling of this and other hazardous material to prevent any future issues," they wrote.
Toxic lead dust could travel miles downwind

Following the initial blast, airborne toxic dust becomes the main concern. According to the Army's published plume forecasts and public safety advisory, the explosions are expected to release particles containing lead into the atmosphere.

The preliminary maps show a potential airborne plume stretching northward across eastern Iowa, the Mississippi River, and potentially into far northwest Illinois. The Army notified communities as far as 100 miles away Sunday, the AP reported, and thousands of people live along the plume's projected track.

In addition to airborne dust, toxic dust particles are expected to settle on surfaces. That raises concerns about possible lead contamination on agricultural land, residential properties, playground equipment and other outdoor surfaces.
Actual exposure levels and the extent of any contamination will depend on the amount of lead released, atmospheric conditions and how much material settles out of the plume.
Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade naturally over time. Once deposited, it can persist in soil for decades and may be transported through erosion or runoff into waterways.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that no safe blood lead level has been identified in children. Even relatively low levels of lead in the blood have been linked to learning difficulties, developmental delays and behavioral problems. Lead exposure is also especially dangerous to pregnant women.

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa's Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, told the AP it is encouraging that the Army and EPA are working to minimize the dust, but it's still unknown how much will end up in the air and on surfaces. He said he is particularly concerned about toddlers who put everything in their mouths. Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters, told the AP that high doses over a short period can cause lead poisoning and make people feel sick.

The Army's forecasts do not establish that harmful exposure will occur at every location within the projected plume. The Army says extensive modeling predicted that lead particle levels in the air may be elevated but still well below the level at which the EPA would require protective action, according to the AP. Environmental sampling will be needed to determine where lead was deposited and at what concentrations.
Weather conditions will determine where the plume travels

Wind direction, speed and vertical motion in the atmosphere will play critical roles in determining the plume's eventual path. Officials expect the dust to linger for no more than an hour, depending on wind speed, according to the AP.

Current forecast guidance suggests gusty southerly winds of 20 to 30 miles per hour Friday will carry the plume northward through eastern Iowa, keeping it well west of the Chicago metropolitan area. Communities closer to the Mississippi River and the Illinois border could be more relevant to potential downwind exposure. The exact path remains subject to change as the detonation approaches.

Under the EPA's emergency permit, the operation cannot proceed if certain unfavorable weather conditions are forecast, including surface winds below 1 mph or above 15 mph, strong winds aloft, thunderstorms, precipitation or temperature inversions. There is no word yet on whether Friday's gusty winds could cancel the detonation.
The Army is required to update its plume forecasts six hours before the operation, and hourly thereafter until the detonations are completed.
Army promises environmental monitoring and cleanup

The permit requires soil and surface-wipe sampling to begin within 24 hours in accessible public and consenting private areas where modeled lead-dust deposition meets a specified threshold. The Army must also submit environmental findings and proposed remediation plans to EPA.

For residents potentially affected by dust deposition, the Army recommends wet-cleaning surfaces that people frequently touch, including outdoor toys, playground equipment, patio furniture and windowsills. However, questions remain about the extent of contamination that could occur beyond the ammunition plant, the effectiveness of cleanup efforts and how residents will know whether their properties are safe.
EPA issues emergency permit for detonation

On Nov. 13, the EPA issued an emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide at a location not authorized for the activity under the facility's existing hazardous-waste permit. In its Nov. 16 public notice, EPA said the emergency authorization was necessary to address an imminent threat to public safety posed by the unstable explosives.

The detonation is being regulated under the federal Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA, which governs the treatment, storage and disposal of hazardous waste. However, federal emergency-permitting provisions allow greater flexibility than ordinary permitting procedures. Under 40 CFR § 270.61, applicable environmental requirements must be incorporated into emergency permits to the extent possible and consistent with the emergency situation.

The emergency permit issued for Middletown includes specific environmental safeguards and incorporates applicable federal hazardous-waste regulations. It remains unclear whether EPA modified or omitted any requirements that would ordinarily apply to this operation because of its emergency designation.
The EPA's authorization does not mean the detonation will produce no environmental contamination.
CBS News Chicago has sought additional information about the EPA's environmental risk assessment and the standards that would trigger cleanup of affected properties.

The Illinois Department of Public Health referred CBS News Chicago's questions about potential health impacts back to the EPA. Environmental and public health officials in Illinois have urged the military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state after the detonations, the AP reported.

Iowa Health and Human Services told CBS News Chicago it was made aware of the planned detonation only very recently and is coordinating with other state agencies as they assess and respond to the public health concerns. The agency said the Army released two maps showing possible exposure but did not say what conditions the modeling included.
Community concerns grow ahead of detonation

Some residents and environmental advocates are questioning whether the planned detonation has received sufficient independent scrutiny. Protest organizers have called for greater transparency, independent environmental review and assurances that any contamination resulting from the explosions will be properly addressed.
U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek was among those calling for the detonation to be delayed, arguing the public needs a better understanding of the potential health impacts, the AP reported.

Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of the degraded lead azide, after the plant paused operations for a review and the material was discovered, the AP reported. The Army previously held a public open house on Oct. 15, where military officials discussed the safety operation and answered residents' questions.

Some schools in the region canceled classes Friday before the detonation was delayed, including in Danville, a few miles from the plant. Superintendent Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but the uncertainties made closing "the most responsible decision." He wrote that he is not suggesting the detonation will create unsafe conditions: "The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon," the AP reported.

In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles northeast of the plant, city officials learned of their potential exposure Sunday, when the Army's map put the town in the center of the dust exposure area, the AP reported. The school district announced Tuesday it will close Friday with no events or sports practices, and the public library will also close. The local fire department plans to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles. City officials said the EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample air, soil and water during and after the detonation, and the city plans to do its own testing.
"The biggest issue we're having is the lack of information," Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker told the AP. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds' office said it was first briefed on the public advisory Monday.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture advised bringing animals, bales of hay and water indoors. Staff at the Iowa State University Extension office in Des Moines County fielded calls Thursday from residents "deathly afraid" for their animals and vegetable gardens, staff member Morgan Hoenig told the AP. "We ran out of soil test kits yesterday," she said.

The Army recommends that those within the projected exposure area consider avoiding outdoor activities, remaining indoors with windows closed and setting ventilation systems to recirculate air until officials announce that the exposure period has ended.
The latest official plume forecasts, public advisories and safety instructions are available on the U.S. Army's Iowa Army Ammunition Plant information page.
Residents can sign up for toxic plume forecast updates from the U.S. Army by sending an email request with the subject line "IAAAP Environmental Updates" to usarmy.ria.asc.list.pa@army.mil.
