title: DOJ moves to dismiss lawsuit over Alaska Senate race
summary: The Trump administration is moving to effectively drop its legal challenge to Democrat Mary Peltola's win in Alaska's Senate race.
story: The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, ending a much-criticized gambit by the president to prevent one of his political rivals from taking office.

The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that the second Sullivan's candidacy is legal and that he could be on the ballot. Earlier this month, a federal judge in Alaska threw out the Trump administration's lawsuit.

Attorneys for the state, which is currently controlled by Republicans, also objected to the administration's move, calling it legally "meritless" and filing papers to help get the initial case dismissed. The administration moved Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.

In their filing, Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court's dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway. They said the court "should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground."

"The United States therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means of 'determin[ing] whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan,'" Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward wrote in the filing.

That decision comes after Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats' 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in its midterm blowout. Peltola won by more votes than were taken by the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan.

In a statement responding to the filing, Peltola said it was time to move on: "Now that the election is over and the voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in, I'm eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans."
Messages from The Associated Press seeking comment were also left with Sen. Sullivan's campaign and the Alaska Department of Law.

The Department of Justice filed the lawsuit at President Trump's direction, saying that a Peltola win should not be certified until an investigation can determine if voters were confused. The administration never explained how such an investigation could take place given the secrecy of the ballot.

The case was filed before The New York Times reported on texts and other documents that appeared to show Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting the retired schoolteacher from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg. He was listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot, with no party preference, to distinguish him from the senator, who was identified as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan has long insisted he ran on his own and Peltola has denied any involvement, saying she was "not interested in tricking voters."

Mr. Trump also has demanded that Peltola be prosecuted for the scheme, and federal investigators swarmed into Alaska before Election Day. Tricks involving decoy candidates such as the second Sullivan have been a staple of U.S. politics for decades, and Mr. Trump's allies have also used them, though occasionally the schemes do lead to criminal charges.

Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy also ordered an investigation into Peltola's campaign after The Times report came out and, prior to Election Day, the DOJ's top prosecutor in Alaska called the reporting "troubling."
It was at least the second time since the Nov. 3 election that the Department of Justice has acted to dismiss one of its high-profile lawsuits interfering in states' handling of their elections.

Just days after the election that saw Democrats flip control of Congress and peel off big wins in races for governor and state legislatures, the Justice Department moved to drop a lawsuit seeking to prevent California officials from counting roughly 20,000 ballots. The Trump administration alleged the ballots belonged to suspected noncitizens, but election officials questioned the validity of the data and said the government's list contained many U.S. citizens.

title: White House national cyber director leaving his post
summary: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his position, a White House official told CBS News.
story: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his position, a White House official told CBS News.
Cairncross was fired, multiple sources told CBS News.

White House chief of staff Stephen Miller — who took over for Susie Wiles earlier this month — had long wanted Cairncross out of the job, sources said, telling people he didn't think Cairncross had the expertise needed to be national cyber director.
Miller immediately teed up a search process for a replacement. Cairncross will be replaced by Kirsten Davies, who serves as the Pentagon's chief information officer, the sources said.
Axios was first to report that Cairncross will leave.

Cairncross' departure comes as the U.S. reels from a series of technological outages over the last week that have hit Microsoft services, air traffic control systems, banks and the National Security Agency's internal network.

Authorities investigating the outages have "seen nothing that would indicate that they are related," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told lawmakers this week. He said he is "98% confident" the outages are not the result of malicious foreign activity, though he acknowledged that he had "absolutely not" seen so many outages in a short period of time.

The national cyber director, a Senate-confirmed post, advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates cyber strategy across the federal government. An attorney, Cairncross has served in the role since August 2025.
The job was created in 2021. In recent years, the U.S. has faced a series of cyberattacks linked to actors in Iran, Russia, China and other U.S. adversaries.

The Trump administration released its cyber strategy in March, which Cairncross' office oversaw. The seven-page document vowed to "detect, confront, and defeat cyber adversaries before they breach our networks and systems," harden critical infrastructure, maintain a U.S. edge in artificial intelligence and modernize federal tech systems.
In a November 2025 appearance at the Aspen Cyber Summit, Cairncross said one of the administration's primary goals is "introducing costs and consequences" on adversaries.

"I think, as a country, we have not done a terrific job of sending a signal to our adversaries that this behavior is not consequence-free," he said. "And we need to do that because it is scaling and it is becoming more aggressive every passing day."
If the Trump administration intends to nominate another permanent national cyber director, it only has a narrow window before the Senate changes to Democratic control in January.
In a statement, Cairncross called the role "the honor of a lifetime."

"I leave my role as Director of Cyber incredibly proud of our work to strengthen America's cybersecurity, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in Super Intelligence. None of it would have been possible without President Trump's extraordinary leadership," he said.

title: Marine Corps hero under federal investigation
summary: Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, whose bloodied visage was depicted in an iconic Iraq War photo, is under investigation stemming from his tenure as a high school JROTC instructor.
story: Henderson, Nevada — One of the most celebrated Marine Corps veterans, whose heroism during the Iraq War earned him the nation's second-highest award for combat valor and a place in military history, is the subject of a criminal investigation over allegations stemming from his tenure as a high school instructor for a Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps, CBS News has learned.

Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, who served in the Marine Corps for 34 years, is under investigation by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service, the primary federal law enforcement agency for matters involving the Navy and Marine Corps.

The allegations against the highly decorated Marine veteran have not been disclosed by the law enforcement agency. However, federal agencies told CBS News that the investigation concerns the period of time when he worked as a JROTC instructor at the Basic Academy of International Studies. The academy is a public high school in Henderson, Nevada, operated by the Clark County School District.

The federal investigation marks a dramatic turn for a Marine whose actions on the battlefield made him a symbol of military courage. Kasal's heroism was captured in a 2004 photograph showing him in the Second Battle of Fallujah. His uniform was soaked in blood, and he was being helped out of a building by two Marines. His right leg was shattered, and his body riddled with gunshot wounds and grenade fragments, but he still gripped a pistol and combat knife. The scene was later immortalized in statues installed at two Marine bases. He retired after 34 years of service and was the recipient of two Purple Hearts and the Navy Cross, the second-highest decoration for combat valor, behind the Medal of Honor.

On Wednesday, the Marine Corps told CBS News that the service is "aware of the allegations against a retired Marine Sergeant Major which occurred while he was employed as a civilian JROTC instructor by the Basic Academy of International Studies."
The Marine Corps also said that the Naval Criminal Investigative Service "is actively investigating the allegations, as the Department of the Navy's lead for felony-level criminal investigations."
Separately, Denise Caskey of NCIS confirmed that its field office at Camp Pendleton in California is conducting the investigation.

NCIS does not typically confirm active investigations, making this an unusual case. The agency commonly investigates matters of homicide, sexual assault, fraud and even terrorism and espionage cases. The agency also conducts counterintelligence investigations, working with other federal agencies to identify threats to national security.
Kasal did not reply to CBS News' multiple attempts to contact him.

CBS News traveled to Henderson, Nevada, and over the course of the last two weeks spoke to nearly 40 people, including former students, school district employees, city officials, parents, U.S. military service members and Marine veterans who served with Kasal. Some asked for anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly or feared reprisal.

The cadets CBS News spoke to alleged Kasal often gave rides home to a select group of female cadets. He would take them to Starbucks and spend time with certain students outside of school-sponsored functions. Some also described instances when he was alone with a cadet in a room.

A former school district employee told CBS News that Kasal was advised on several occasions about the perceptions surrounding his relationships with students and was warned against putting himself in potentially compromising situations, including being alone in a room with a cadet.

One former female cadet described developing an unusually close relationship with Kasal after meeting him in 2020, when she was 14. She said she confided in him about difficulties at home and personal matters, including her relationships with boys. After knowing her for barely a year, Kasal offered to adopt her, saying in a text message, "I'm not asking as charity. I'm asking because your [sic] wanted."

When her family members learned of Kasal's offer, she said, they made it clear that adoption was not an option. She said that her relationship with Kasal continued, and she remained comfortable confiding in him about deeply personal matters. The cadet alleged some of their conversations involved sexual rumors that had been spread about her and why Kasal believed some of the problems she was experiencing stemmed from her relationship with her father. In retrospect, she said she realizes that those conversations were inappropriate for an instructor to have with a teenage student.

She now says she thinks Kasal crossed other boundaries, alleging that Kasal invited certain cadets to spend time at his home and at his cabin, she said, including for at least one birthday celebration. He did not extend invitations to everyone in the program. She also claimed that Kasal drove one student home nearly every day.

The Clark County School District told CBS News Kasal was hired by the school district three months after he retired from the Marine Corps, in August 2018. He resigned in August 2025, the school district said.
Enrollment in Basic Academy's JROTC program fluctuates from year to year, averaging roughly 135 students. The program is overseen by a senior Marine instructor and a senior enlisted leader.
When Kasal transitioned from the Marine Corps to the high school JROTC program, he sought to restructure it to more closely resemble the military service.

Some former cadets described him as professional and organized, crediting him with establishing strict standards and bringing a sense of discipline to the program. They also praised the time, energy and personal resources he devoted to his students.

Samantha Francisco, 22, who was in the program from 2018 to 2022, said, "I can't say enough about how amazing he was," and that "he genuinely cared about everybody and taught us incredible lessons." She added that she and her husband, who was also in the JROTC program, still talk weekly about Kasal or something he taught them.

Ashley Vazquez Romo, 22, another cadet from that period, said Kasal "poured his heart and soul into the program." She recalled that he sometimes helped pay for program outings and purchased equipment, including a CPR training mannequin, so students could practice.

Damien Greenwell, 22, who participated in the JROTC program from 2018 to 2022, told CBS News that he deeply respects Kasal for his military service and mentorship, especially to cadets with a troubled home life. But Greenwell also said that over the years he questioned Kasal's conduct on several occasions, adding that even if the decorated Marine's intentions were innocent, his actions could appear inappropriate to an outside observer.

"He would mentor us on how to be a proper leader — which is his job — but he would go a bit beyond this. Sergeant Major [Kasal] helps people in a time of need and that's very honorable," Greenwell said.

"If someone couldn't eat, he would pay for their food. If someone didn't have a ride home, he would help them out. It's awesome, it's great and very commendable," Greenwell said. "But if you're regularly getting Starbucks for a girl … it looks kind of weird … and with driving people home on a consistent basis, it looks bad. You need to have a certain kind of boundary between you and students."
Greenwell told CBS News he remembers a night that still "shocks him a little." It happened in 2024, two years after Greenwell graduated.

Greenwell claimed he went to Lowe's home improvement store around 9 p.m. and saw Kasal's truck in the parking lot. In the store, he observed Kasal walking with a student who he believes was a senior at the high school or a newly minted graduate.

"It was just really weird to me," Greenwell said, recalling that he briefly exchanged greetings with Kasal and the student before the two continued down the aisle. CBS News is withholding the student's name for privacy reasons.

Greenwell said over the years of observing Kasal, he developed doubts about him. He believed the optics could be interpreted as inappropriate, but at the same time wonders if Kasal could just be trying to help students navigate the difficulties of life. But even if he found a relationship between Kasal and a student odd, he was "not gonna say anything. Like, who am I to tell [a] sergeant major?"
Daniel Gillian, who participated in the program from 2018 to 2022 and later enlisted in the Marine Corps, said JROTC was good for him and that Kasal was part of the reason he ended up joining.

The program "gave me a lot of structure and discipline," Gillian said, adding that Kasal helped him "become a better person overall, and once you become a better person, things will fall into place for you."

Gillian said he never witnessed Kasal engage in inappropriate behavior. He sees Kasal as having made an effort to create memorable experiences for students by organizing group hikes, camping trips and other activities outside the classroom. He said Kasal recognized that some students did not have a good home life, and he wanted to make the JROTC program enjoyable and inclusive, emphasizing that all cadets were invited to participate.

Still, he acknowledged that Kasal appeared to favor certain cadets, sometimes buying them coffee, for instance. Gillian said Kasal had also bought coffee for him, but he didn't think it was inappropriate, describing him as a "nice guy."

Gillian also alleged Kasal would take cadets on hikes without seeking permission from the school, but he said this was more a matter of convenience. The hiking trail was only a few minutes away from Basic Academy.
"It was about a 10-minute drive from Basic, and [about] 20 cadets would go. Whoever wanted to go, they would go. We would all carpool," Gillian said, and the hikes were just about an hour.

"Legally, you gotta get [trips] ran through the school, and they gotta approve of it, … but [Kasal is] not gonna wait for [the school] to take two weeks to [approve] an event that takes one day to get back."
One former male cadet, who joined the program in 2019 and now serves in the U.S. military, alleged that Kasal invited him to visit his cabin in Iowa over the summer.

The trip was not school-sponsored, he said, and "it was just going to be the two of us." He says he declined the invitation because he was playing a sport that summer. At the time, he said, he did not consider the invitation to be inappropriate, believing Kasal had extended it because they shared an interest in the sport.

Greenwell said that at one point, he heard a rumor that Kasal was trying to adopt a fellow cadet but that he didn't believe it was true. When CBS News told him that Kasal had offered to adopt a former female cadet, Greenwell said he was "very surprised, shocked and disappointed."
"Even if you have the best intentions in the world, it still looks bad, no matter how you put it, because she's a minor," said Greenwell.

The Defense Department and local school districts share responsibility for overseeing JROTC programs because they are federally sponsored and operate in high schools nationwide. Although instructors are employed by school districts, they must also be certified by their respective military branches, which are responsible for monitoring their professional conduct and ensuring compliance with military standards.
The military services certify and oversee instructors, while school districts handle employment decisions, classroom supervision and compliance with local education policies.

JROTC instructors must acknowledge in writing that they will not engage in prohibited activities between JROTC instructors and students. The rules ban instructors from developing personal, intimate or sexual relationships with cadets, engaging in inappropriate communications and attending social gatherings with students on a personal basis. The restrictions apply from an instructor's first contact with a cadet until six months after the student leaves the JROTC program.

Under the rules, instructors are generally not allowed to give students rides in their personal vehicles, including rides home from school. Exceptions may be made when a student's safety or welfare is at risk or for official school functions involving multiple students. The rules specifically prohibit an instructor from transporting a single student in their personal vehicles.

Instructors are also not allowed to have cadets or other students in their homes. Other interactions, such as purchasing coffee or refreshments for students, are not explicitly prohibited. But such interactions could raise questions about compliance with the rules.
Instructors must sign the acknowledgment before beginning their duties as JROTC instructors and recertify it annually.
When CBS News received the initial news tip regarding Kasal, the Marine Corps said it was aware of allegations and of an investigation, but made no mention of NCIS' involvement.

The Henderson Police Department initially said it had no record of a complaint about Kasal. The Clark County Detention Center and the Clark County District Attorney's Office also did not have any complaints about Kasal on file when contacted some two weeks ago.

Later, during that same period, a spokesperson for the Henderson Police Department said the Clark County School District Police Department was handling the matter. Multiple calls and emails to the Clark County School District and the school district's police department went unanswered. Lt. Bryan Zink of the Clark County School District police department referred inquiries to the school district.
Last week, when CBS News emailed to check in on its inquiry, an email sent in error to CBS News asked a human resources manager to "disregard the request."
When CBS News asked why the request for information was being disregarded, Bryan Callahan, the district's public information officer, emailed for the first time: "We are looking into your request."

When questioned by a CBS News reporter in Henderson earlier this week, Callahan said he was not aware of an investigation of Kasal by the Clark County School District or the school district's police department.

Before he retired from active duty, Kasal reflected on his time in Iraq. The Second Battle of Fallujah in November 2004 was the bloodiest battle involving U.S. Marines since the Vietnam War, marked by brutal house-to-house fighting against Iraqi insurgents.

In 2018, Kasal told CBS News' David Martin that he had entered the building to rescue fellow Marines trapped by insurgent gunfire during one of the war's bloodiest battles. By the time he emerged, Kasal had been shot seven times, shielded a wounded Marine from an exploding grenade and refused medical treatment until others received care.
His actions earned him his second Purple Heart and the Navy Cross.
The photograph of Kasal became an iconic symbol of Marine resilience and sacrifice. The Marine Corps Heritage Foundation named a photojournalism award for Kasal.

The photograph inspired a bronze statue called the "No Man Left Behind" monument, which is installed at both Camp Pendleton in California and Camp Lejeune in North Carolina, according to the Marine Times. The sculpture was the work of John Phelps, a Navy Vietnam veteran whose son Chance was killed in Iraq in 2004, the newspaper reported.

When CBS News first learned about the criminal investigation into Kasal earlier this month, the retired sergeant major was in New York as the guest of honor at an event hosted by the NYPD Marine Corps Association to commemorate 251 years since the founding of the U.S. Marine Corps and honor Marines who also serve as New York City police officers. The New York Post reported that Kasal was presented a framed retirement shadowbox by NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch at police headquarters in Manhattan.
James LaPorta reported from Henderson, Nevada. Julia Kimani Burnham and Eleanor Watson reported from Washington, D.C.

Editor's note: For the past three years, James LaPorta has served as a judge for the Marine Corps Heritage Foundation annual awards program. He has never judged the award category named for retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal.
This story published first on CBS News at 9:28 p.m. on Nov. 19, 2026.

title: Musk says he's "not MAGA," feels "foolish" about midterm spending
summary: After opening his wallet to assist GOP candidates in the 2026 midterms, billionaire Elon Musk said Wednesday he feels "pretty foolish" about spending hundreds of millions of dollars in the race.
story: After opening his wallet to assist Republican candidates in the 2026 midterms, billionaire Elon Musk said Wednesday he feels "pretty foolish" about spending hundreds of millions of dollars.

The world's richest man — who served in President Trump's administration in 2025 — also argued he is "not MAGA" and described his political beliefs as "quite moderate" during an interview at The New York Times' DealBook Summit.

Musk donated vast sums of money to super PACs backing House and Senate Republicans. One of his largest investments was in Texas, where over $150 million of his fortune was transferred to a group supporting Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

Those bets largely did not pay off. Democrats won large majorities in the House and Senate, with Paxton losing to Democratic candidate James Talarico, who made Musk's support of his GOP opponent part of his pitch to voters. Democrats also won the Texas governor's office, a notable shift for the state where Musk has based many of SpaceX and Tesla's operations.

Musk told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin his objective in the midterms was to help Republicans hold on to their Senate majority in order to prevent either party from controlling the presidency and both houses of Congress in 2029 — a goal he said "failed."

"Obviously, the Republicans were routed in this election, and … I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it. Or maybe it would have been much worse without that," the billionaire said, adding that "probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money."
Musk later said his goal was to preserve some "checks and balances," calling himself "ideologically quite moderate" and saying he doesn't have any "extreme political views."
Sorkin noted that Musk has made controversial statements on immigration and "MAGA stuff."

Musk responded: "I'm not MAGA. ... I'm not sure what MAGA means, but I don't think I'm, like, if it means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties."

It's a change in tone for Musk, who has donned MAGA hats in the past, and joked at one 2024 Trump rally: "I'm not just MAGA, I'm dark MAGA." Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars assisting the Trump campaign and other GOP candidates that year, and later led the Trump administration's cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency. Musk and Mr. Trump had a brief falling-out last year, but Musk has appeared to maintain a close relationship with the president since then.
Musk also traveled to China this week for Mr. Trump's trip to the country.

Musk's alliance with Mr. Trump has drawn scrutiny from Democrats, who have vowed to aggressively investigate the Trump administration when they take the House and Senate next year. Musk is expected to be one focus of their oversight probes.

In Wednesday's interview, Musk said he is not worried that Democratic Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa could pose problems to his businesses, saying, "Based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."
"The new governor, actually, I think, is going to be quite moderate," Musk said. "I don't think she's sort of a far-left governor."
He also said some Democrats' comments accusing him of illegality are "a little over the top," telling The Times, "There are definitely a few people grumpy about ... my funding in this past election."
"Hopefully in this country, you still need to do an actual crime before you go to prison. Aspirationally, that should be how it works," he said.
Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona suggested he was unmoved by Musk's MAGA about-face.
"You are still getting a subpoena," Gallego wrote on X.

title: Trump pardons deceased MLB slugger Pete Rose
summary: President Trump said Thursday he has granted a "Complete and Total Pardon" to Pete Rose, MLB's late all-time hits leader who was banned from the league for gambling.
story: President Trump said Thursday he has granted a "Complete and Total Pardon" to Pete Rose, Major League Baseball's late all-time hits leader who was banned from the league and, until recently, the Baseball Hall of Fame for gambling.

The president announced the move in a post on Truth Social, writing that Rose — who died in 2024 — "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess!"

Mr. Trump did not specify what the pardon of Rose will cover. Rose wasn't charged with gambling, though he did plead guilty in 1990 to filing false income tax returns, serving five months in prison. Asked for more details on the pardon, a White House official pointed to Rose's tax charges.
During his more than 20 years as a player, most of them with the Cincinnati Reds, Rose racked up a record 4,256 hits and won three World Series. He later managed the Reds.

But his career was marred by the revelation that he had placed bets on games, including some Reds games. Rose agreed to a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball in 1989 — a move that prevented him from being inducted into the Hall of Fame.

He asked to be reinstated on four occasions. Twice, in 1997 and 2020, then-MLB Commissioner Bud Selig and current Commissioner Rob Manfred, respectively, did not respond to the petitions. His petitions in 2015 and 2022 were rejected.

He was then posthumously reinstated last year. Manfred met with Mr. Trump less than a month before Rose was reinstated. Manfred said at the time that Rose came up during their conversation, "but I'm not going beyond that." Under Hall of Fame rules, Rose could be inducted as early as 2028.

Mr. Trump has long argued that Rose was mistreated by the league, a view that stretches back to before his first term as president. In late 2015, Mr. Trump wrote on social media: "He's paid the price. So ridiculous - let him in!"

The president has repeatedly floated issuing Rose a pardon. In a White House event earlier this month, Mr. Trump acknowledged that Rose shouldn't have gambled but noted that sports betting is now widely legal, and pointed out that "he was gambling on his own team."
It is unclear what effect the pardon will have. Rose was released from prison in 1991, and pardons do not apply to the Baseball Hall of Fame.

title: Iran war powers measure again falls short in Senate
summary: The Senate rejected a resolution aimed at reining in President Trump's ability to strike Iran, despite GOP frustration with the war following the party's losses in the midterm elections.
story: Washington — The Senate rejected a House-adopted resolution aimed at reining in President Trump's ability to strike Iran, losing Republican support despite frustration with the war following the party's losses in the midterm elections.

In a 48 to 51 vote, three Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky — joined all but one Senate Democrat — Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania — in support of the measure.

Thursday's vote marked the first time either chamber has weighed in on the war since the midterm elections, which dealt Republicans sweeping losses. Voters cited the war in Iran, and its toll on the economy, as among their top concerns.

Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, who has led Democrats' repeated efforts to restrict the president on Iran, urged his GOP colleagues to back the measure ahead of the vote. In a speech on the Senate floor, Kaine said it's become apparent over the course of recent months that the war is unpopular, "but its unpopularity was made absolutely manifestly clear in the election results from Nov. 3."

"A historic repudiation of the party holding onto the White House, with much of that energy driven by Americans' deep dissatisfaction with war, waged unilaterally by a president who said he would not, causing costs to dramatically rise on every American family," Kaine said. "And so it is my hope, that in the aftermath of a clear message from the American public that they want us to stop this illegal, catastrophic war, the Senate will demonstrate that we're listening."

The resolution would have directed the president "to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran," but its impact would have been largely symbolic. Under the War Powers Resolution of 1973, the president must withdraw forces from hostilities "if the Congress so directs by concurrent resolution." But administrations of both parties have argued that the process is unconstitutional. The White House argued against its validity after a similar measure was adopted over the summer.

One Republican who had voted in favor of a previous effort, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, voted against the measure on Thursday. Tillis told CBS News that "this one doesn't go to the president, so it's just a statement from Congress. I've made that statement."

"I'm using other vehicles to try and figure out how to replenish supplies, but hold Hegseth accountable," Tillis said of the defense secretary, citing the funding process. "I think I've been pretty clear that I think he's a failure."

The Senate adopted a resolution aimed at reining in the president on Iran in June, when four Republicans joined the bulk of Democrats in favor. The outcome prompted intense pushback from Mr. Trump, who took aim at the GOP senators who had supported the resolution at a testy lunch meeting with Senate Republicans a day later. After the lunch, a separate effort to restrict the president's war powers fell short when key Senate Republicans shifted their votes.

Since the war began in late February, Democrats have forced more than a dozen war powers votes. Most have fallen short. One advanced in May, helped along by four Republicans and a handful of GOP absences. That effort ultimately stalled after Republicans' meeting with the president.
Ahead of the midterms, the Senate voted on another House-adopted concurrent resolution. It narrowly fell short, despite some GOP members becoming more vocal in their opposition to the war.

title: CBS to air Kennedy Center Honors in December
summary: CBS has reached a one-year deal to air the awards ceremony next month, sources said.
story: The Kennedy Center Honors may have left the Kennedy Center itself, but the annual awards gala isn't leaving its longtime broadcast home. CBS has reached a one-year deal to air the awards ceremony next month, according to sources familiar with the arrangement.

This year's event, scheduled to be taped on Sunday, Dec. 7, and aired on Dec. 27, will be held at Capital One Arena in downtown Washington. Honorees include musicians Paul Anka and Barbara Mandrell, composer David Foster, actor Andy Garcia and playwright David Mamet.

In September, the Kennedy Center board voted to close the performing arts center amid a legal dispute over building upgrades and attempts to add President Trump's name to the facade. Mr. Trump said he would only help fundraise for renovations if his name was added to the facade. A federal judge in Washington, D.C., however, ruled that only Congress had the authority to change the building's name.

While modest maintenance projects continue, planning for the major renovations are underway and a construction schedule cannot be set until an ongoing federal court case halting construction is resolved. A court hearing is set for Thursday.

CBS has broadcast the Kennedy Center Honors each year since 1978. The multiyear contract lapsed after the 2025 show, but the arts center and the network reached a short-term deal for this year's show last week. The program will also stream on Paramount+.

President Trump co-hosted the show in 2025, punctuating artistic performances with several speeches throughout the evening. The White House did not respond to a CBS News inquiry on whether the president would attend this year.

title: Putin says Russia won't negotiate with Ukraine after bridge strike
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin said Russia will not negotiate any limited ceasefire now with Ukraine, citing a Ukrainian strike on a highly symbolic bridge this week.
story: President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia will not negotiate with Ukraine on a limited ceasefire, citing a Ukrainian strike this week on a major bridge connecting Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Putin made the remarks to reporters in Russian after meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. He said he had discussed the possibility of a ceasefire in certain areas of Ukraine, but would not move forward with negotiations after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian state news agencies.

The 12-mile bridge, which Putin ceremonially opened himself in 2018, is hugely symbolic as it links the Russian mainland with Crimea — territory that Russian forces occupied about four years earlier. The missile strike this week wasn't the first time Ukraine had targeted the piece of infrastructure, but it inflicted severe damage. Russia also struck two major bridges in Kyiv the same day.

Putin played down the bridge's strategic importance on Thursday and said he had heard the calls "from all sides" for a naval ceasefire or a suspension of strikes on energy facilities, but he ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing the attack on the bridge.

"Honestly, I discussed the issue with my colleagues at the Security Council, and I asked them to think about it and go back to the issue, so that we could reach some agreements," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency TASS. "However, we will not make agreements after strikes on the Crimean Bridge. We will respond to these strikes."
Putin vowed that Russia's retaliation for the strike on the bridge would be severe, TASS reported.
While Putin claims frequently to want peace, he denies that Russia started the war with his order for a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine have been relentless.

It's not clear how much Ukraine came up in Mr. Trump's one-on-one meeting with Putin on Wednesday, or in the meeting with both Putin and Xi on Thursday. Last week, the White House said Ukraine wouldn't be a topic of discussion, but before he left for Asia, Mr. Trump said the three leaders would be discussing the war. The White House readout of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was sparse on detail, and did not mention Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff have been in Germany to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders of Germany, France, the U.K. and other European nations — a group known as the Coalition of the Willing — about Ukraine and other topics.
Kushner said they discussed the "latest efforts to achieve a just, lasting and durable peace in Ukraine."

"We are grateful for his leadership, constructive engagement, and close partnership as we work together toward our shared goal of ending this terrible war and building a secure and prosperous future for Ukraine and Europe," Kushner posted to X.
Merz, speaking to reporters after the meeting, called the China summit a photo-op and said the trilateral format "will not bring peace" in Ukraine.
As he went to shake Putin's hand before an earlier meeting Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, Mr. Trump referred to the Russian leader as "my friend."
"Who is he?" the president said, pointing at Putin and smiling. "He's my friend."

title: Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for a rare 3-way meeting in China
summary: Russia says Putin, Trump and China's Xi agreed during a rare meeting to boost gas and oil production, and "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war."
story: President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.

The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.

The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.

Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.

The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."

They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the "International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
"A great relationship"

The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.

"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Focus on Ukraine
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.

"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."

Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."

Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."

Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons, with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.

Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program, ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year.

China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi, however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence.
Global trade and AI

The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."

Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed, is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.

Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.
Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence.

"We do not want to do anything to destroy the tremendous potential of this technology," he said. "We have to watch it, we have to be careful, we have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements."

Beyond AI, the U.S. and China have sought to stabilize their economic relationship over the last year, following a tit-for-tat trade war that sent tariffs above 100% in 2025. A tariff truce between the two countries is set to expire on Jan. 10 of next year.

Mr. Trump said in his APEC speech the U.S. is committed to "growth and stability" in the Asia-Pacific region, and argued the American economy is "thriving like it has never thrived before." He also said the U.S. is negotiating "numerous trade agreements" and expects to sign some agreements with APEC members in the near future.

During Xi's remarks earlier in the session, the Chinese leader called on countries in the region to "look out for each other" and "expand our shared interests," including on free trade and economic growth.
Foreign conflicts loomed large during the Trump-Putin-Xi talks. Iran is one contentious area, given China's status as one of the largest customers of Iranian oil, and Russia's ties with Iran.

The White House previously said the war in Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said he expected the issue to come up, calling it "my favorite subject."

Taiwan is another frequent discussion topic between the U.S. and China. During the U.S. president's visit to Beijing in the spring, Xi reportedly delivered a stern warning about the island, which he has long vowed to reintegrate with mainland China, floating potential "clashes and even conflicts" if the issue isn't "handled properly."
And Mr. Trump was expected to press Xi to release two detained Americans during his visit to China, CBS News has reported. Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.

title: Law firm that cut deal with Trump has done $11.8M in pro bono work
summary: A lawyer representing the law firm Kirkland & Ellis said it has provided nearly $12 million in free legal services for the Trump administration.
story: Washington — A major law firm that reached an agreement with President Trump to avoid being targeted by an executive order told Congress it has provided nearly $12 million in free legal services for his administration. The firm disclosed the departments receiving the services, as well as the requests it turned down.

Kirkland & Ellis was one of 10 law firms that cut deals with the White House last year after the president signed directives that punished four other firms that either employed his perceived political enemies or represented clients he disfavors.
As part of the agreement, announced by Mr. Trump on Truth Social in April 2025, Kirkland & Ellis pledged to provide $125 million in pro bono legal services to causes supported by the president.

A trio of top Democrats in Congress, Sens. Adam Schiff and Richard Blumenthal, and Rep. Jamie Raskin, launched an investigation into the deals last year, and earlier this month, a lawyer representing Kirkland & Ellis disclosed details of the free legal work the firm has done.

The lawyer, Beth Wilkinson, said in a Nov. 5 letter to the three Democrats that Kirkland & Ellis has provided more than 6,000 hours of pro bono services valued at $11.8 million representing the Commerce Department, U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, U.S. Postal Service and the Defense Department, as well as for a $550 billion investment pledge between the U.S. and Japan.

As of the end of September, Kirkland & Ellis has devoted 15,469 hours of legal services worth more than $18.7 million on non-government pro bono matters related to causes specified by Mr. Trump in his April 2025 Truth Social post, including in support of veterans and other public servants, a fair justice system and combating anti-Semitism, Wilkinson said.

Kirkland & Ellis has also turned down requests to work on projects for the Trump administration, including "Trump Accounts," the census, the renaming of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, and challenges to the Postal Service's handling of mail ballots, according to Wilkinson's letter.

The firm has also declined administration requests for it to represent third parties on a pro bono basis, including a veterans' group backing construction of Mr. Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch and scientists involved in cases regarding the Trump administration's position on climate change.

"Critical to Kirkland's willingness to enter into the Truth Social agreement was that it retain absolute discretion in deciding which matters to take and could decline to take matters suggested by the Administration," Wilkinson wrote. "In practice, Kirkland has exercised that discretion and declined numerous matters. And it has never faced any repercussions or threats from the Administration for turning down work."

A federal judge has blocked the Kennedy Center from closing its doors for two years during proposed renovations and prohibited its board from adding Mr. Trump's name to the building. Judges have also temporarily blocked the Trump administration from starting construction on the arch and prevented the Postal Service from enforcing new regulations for mail voting ahead of this month's midterm elections.

Blumenthal, Raskin and Schiff have also demanded the other nine law firms that cut deals with the White House provide information about their agreements. The 10 firms collectively agreed to provide roughly $1 billion in free legal services in order to avoid being targeted by the president and his administration.

"The Trump Administration also unsuccessfully tried to involve Kirkland & Ellis in work supporting the President's political vanity projects, such as the renaming of the Kennedy Center or supporting the illegal construction of his triumphal arch in Washington, DC — raising serious questions of whether other firms acceded to these demands," they wrote to each of the law firms in letters Wednesday.

Raskin told reporters on Capitol Hill that the arrangements between the White House and law firms raise legal questions. A federal law called the Antideficiency Act prohibits the executive branch from spending outside of congressional appropriations and says federal employees cannot accept free services.

"It's an extremely problematic thing if you've got law firms that have been shaken down for their service to Donald Trump, and they're out there doing millions of dollars of work for the federal government," he said.

Mr. Trump rolled out a series of executive orders last year that sought to impose sweeping punishments on five firms in all: Perkins Coie; Paul, Weiss; Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr LLP; Jenner & Block; and Susman Godfrey. The orders targeted the firms' clients, access to federal buildings and government officials, and security clearances held by their employees.

The president rescinded his directive against Paul, Weiss after the firm pledged $40 million in pro bono legal services. Kirkland & Ellis said in its letter to the Democrats that Paul, Weiss' agreement was "the first of its kind and set forth a precedent for how firms that wished to avoid immediate irreparable harm and protracted, intrusive litigation could resolve potential disputes with the Administration."

The four other firms — Perkins Coie, WilmerHale, Jenner & Block and Susman Godfrey — each filed lawsuits challenging Mr. Trump's executive order. Four different federal judges all sided with the firms and invalidated the measures as unconstitutional. A federal appeals court has been considering since May the Trump administration's bid to restore them.

In addition to providing information about the amount of work Kirkland & Ellis has done for the Trump administration, Wilkinson's letter detailed the firm's efforts to reach a deal with the president. She said Ballard Partners, a consultant for Kirkland & Ellis, spoke to May Mailman, a White House official, in March 2025, "in which she expressed the Administration's openness to achieving resolutions with law firms."

Mr. Trump's former chief of staff, Susie Wiles, worked at Ballard Partners for nearly a decade before leaving in 2019. The firm made more than $88 million in lobbying revenue last year, CBS News found.

Four people were involved in negotiations with Kirkland & Ellis on behalf of the Trump administration, Wilkinson said, including Mailman, two officials from the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and Boris Epshteyn, an outside adviser to the president. Kirkland & Ellis did not communicate with the president about the deal, she said.

title: Meet the 19 new senators set to be sworn in to Congress
summary: From a former wheelchair basketball Paralympian to a Methodist pastor and one senator returning after defeat, the new class hails from different backgrounds and parts of the country.
story: Washington — Nineteen new senators are preparing to take their seats in the 120th Congress in January — the largest class in almost five decades — after Democrats flipped a slew of seats in the midterm elections, and some incumbents chose to retire.

From a former wheelchair basketball Paralympian to a Methodist pastor and one senator returning after defeat, the new class hails from different backgrounds and parts of the country. But mostly, they're much younger: With several freshmen in their 40s and one in his 30s, the Senate's average age is dropping by a couple of years — to 63.
These are the new senators:
Abdul El-Sayed, D-Michigan

Abdul El-Sayed, 42, is a former Michigan health official who defended an open Senate seat in Michigan after Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek reelection. El-Sayed, a Democrat, defeated former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, running on a leftist platform including "Medicare for All." He won a bruising campaign, despite reservations about his appeal to Jewish and Black voters over his opposition to U.S. support for Israel and his progressive platform. At the same time, top Republicans, including President Trump and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz called him a "jihadist" and sought to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood, and even implied that electing him could be deadly to Americans.
With his victory, El-Sayed will become the first Muslim senator in U.S. history.
Adam Hamilton, D-Kansas

Adam Hamilton, 62, is a fifth-generation Kansan and pastor. He defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, flipping the seat for Democrats for the first time in nearly a century. Formerly a Republican, Hamilton ran on an affordability-focused agenda, while appealing to a cross-party coalition to take on Marshall. As a pastor, Hamilton led the U.S.' largest United Methodist church and is a well-known author and speaker.
Andy Barr, R-Kentucky

Republican Andy Barr, 53, has represented Kentucky in the House since 2013, and won the Senate seat after Sen. Mitch McConnell announced he would retire. Barr, an attorney, had the president's endorsement, and billed his Democratic opponent in the race as too extreme for the Bluegrass State. In the House, Barr served as co-chair of the Congressional Horse Caucus and the Congressional Bourbon Caucus, two of Kentucky's defining interests.
Annie Andrews, D-South Carolina

Democrat Annie Andrews, 46, is a pediatrician who defeated Trump-endorsed incumbent GOP Sen. Darline Graham, who had been appointed to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, after his sudden death in July. Andrews campaigned on healthcare access and affordability, along with fighting corruption in Washington. With her victory, she became the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the Senate, and the first Democrat elected to represent the state in the upper chamber since 1998.
Barry Moore, R-Alabama

Republican Barry Moore, 60, has represented Alabama in the House since 2021. A member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, Moore ran as a staunch supporter of Mr. Trump and touted being the first elected official to endorse the president in 2015. He won the seat after Sen. Tommy Tuberville launched a gubernatorial bid, rather than seeking reelection. Moore and the state's other senator, Katie Britt, both hail from Enterprise, Alabama, and attended the same high school.
Chris Pappas, D-New Hampshire

Democrat Chris Pappas, 46, has represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019 and defended an open Senate seat in the Granite State after Sen. Jeanne Shaheen opted not to seek reelection. Along the campaign trail, Pappas billed himself as an independent voice for the state and ran on his record in the lower chamber, where he's a member of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus. With his victory, Pappas is set to become the first openly gay male senator in the chamber's history.
Harriet Hageman, R-Wyoming

Harriet Hageman, 64, a Republican, has represented Wyoming as the state's at-large representative in the House since 2023. Hageman's Senate victory came after GOP Sen. Cynthia Lummis, a first-term senator, announced she would not run for reelection. Hageman grew up on a ranch and attended college on a livestock judging scholarship. A former litigator and staunch supporter of Mr. Trump, Hageman first came to Congress after defeating former GOP Rep. Liz Cheney.
James Talarico, D-Texas

James Talarico, 37, is a Texas state representative, former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who flipped the Senate seat for Democrats in the Lone Star State. Talarico defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who had bested incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the primary. The Texas Democrat calls himself a progressive Christian, and ran on fighting corruption and lowering costs, overcoming widespread GOP criticism that he was too extreme for the state, as they pointed to comments he's previously made on issues like veganism and gender. Derided as "Tofu Talarico" by Republicans, he toasted Democrats' victory on election night with Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa at a Whataburger.
Josh Turek, D-Iowa

Josh Turek, 47, is a state representative and former wheelchair basketball Paralympian. A Democrat, he flipped Iowa's Senate seat after Sen. Joni Ernst opted not to seek reelection, defeating GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson. On the campaign trail, he touted his background in the state legislature representing the most conservative district held by a Democrat in the state, and he pledged to work — including with Mr. Trump — to deliver for Iowans.
Julia Letlow, R-Louisiana

Julia Letlow, 45, has represented Louisiana in the House since 2021, when she became the first Republican woman to represent the state. She won the Senate seat after defeating incumbent Sen. Bill Cassidy in the primary, following Mr. Trump's endorsement. Letlow, who previously worked in education, initially came to Congress after winning a special election for Louisiana's 5th Congressional District following the death of her husband, who died in 2020 from complications related to COVID-19 before he could be sworn into office.
Juliana Stratton, D-Illinois

Juliana Stratton, 61, is a former state representative and Illinois lieutenant governor who launched a Senate bid after Dick Durbin, the No. 2 Senate Democrat, announced his retirement. Stratton, a fellow Democrat who ran on a progressive platform, is the fifth Black woman ever to be elected to the upper chamber, where she and Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland will make history, with three Black women serving simultaneously for the first time.
Kevin Hern, R-Oklahoma

Republican Kevin Hern, 64, has represented Oklahoma in the House since 2018, and joins the Senate's ranks after Sen. Alan Armstrong was appointed as a placeholder following Markwayne Mullin's departure to become Homeland Security secretary earlier this year. Hern, a former aerospace engineer and businessman, who at one time owned 24 McDonald's franchises, chaired the conservative House Republican Policy Committee in the House. He's set to be sworn in later this month, due to Armstrong's temporary appointment to the position.
Kurt Alme, R-Montana

Kurt Alme, 60, a Republican, is a Harvard-trained former U.S. Attorney for the District of Montana, nominated to the position twice by Mr. Trump. Alme comes to the Senate after GOP Sen. Steve Daines opted not to seek reelection, in a move that sparked controversy when Daines made the announcement just before the filing deadline and endorsed Alme, blocking any major challengers. Alme, who has also served as Montana's budget director, said he plans to target government spending, telling supporters on election night, "My first bill will say, if Congress can't balance a budget, Congress doesn't get paid."
Peggy Flanagan, D-Minnesota

Peggy Flanagan, 47, is Minnesota's lieutenant governor and a former state representative. She held on to an open seat for Democrats after Sen. Tina Smith opted not to seek reelection. Flanagan defeated the GOP candidate, former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya, after winning the Democratic primary in August against a more moderate candidate. Flanagan ran on progressive priorities like Medicare for All and secured endorsements from top progressives. With the victory, Flanagan is set to become the first Native American woman in the U.S. Senate.
Mary Peltola, D-Alaska

Mary Peltola, 53, is a former congresswoman who became the first Democrat to represent the state in the House in 50 years in 2022. She ultimately lost her reelection bid for Alaska's sole House seat in 2024, before going on to defeat incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan this cycle. Peltola, who framed herself as an independent voice for the state, is set to become the first Alaska Native to be elected to the Senate. Republicans accused Democrats of foul play after another candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Dan Sullivan, joined the race and advanced to the ranked-choice November election. But as it turned out, Peltola won by more than 12,000 votes, and the second Dan Sullivan won just about 4,800, far less than the margin of victory.
Roy Cooper, D-North Carolina

Roy Cooper, 69, is a popular former two-term North Carolina governor who flipped the Senate seat for Democrats after Sen. Thom Tillis decided not to seek reelection. Cooper faced off against former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley in the race, making an affordability message central to his campaign, like with his "Make Stuff Cost Less" tour throughout the state. Cooper is also the longest-serving state attorney general in North Carolina's history, where he's become known for his love of diet soda. The self-identified "diet soda sommelier" is fond of Diet Sun Drop and said he dreamed of drinking it from the Stanley Cup if the Hurricanes won (they did win).
Scott Colom, D-Mississippi

Democrat Scott Colom, 43, is a district attorney and seventh-generation Mississippian who defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a major upset that few saw coming this cycle. Colom, who will be the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction, campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues, while pledging to deliver for the Magnolia State in places that he argued Hyde-Smith fell short. Colom may have taken the political world by surprise with his victory, but when he arrives at the Capitol, he's sure to be recognized from what may have been the catchiest ad of the midterms cycle — the "Pick Another Senator" spot that seized on Hyde-Smith's response to rising beef prices.
Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio

Sherrod Brown, 74, is a former three-term Democratic senator who lost his reelection to Ohio GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno in 2024. But he's back, after defeating incumbent Sen. Jon Husted in November. Brown's strong working-class brand in the Buckeye State resonated with voters, as issues like affordability and data centers were the dominant concerns. Husted was appointed to fill Vice President JD Vance's Senate seat last year until this past special election. Now, Brown will take his seat and serve out the remainder of Vance's Senate term, which will end in early 2029.
Troy Jackson, D-Maine

Democrat Troy Jackson, 58, is a fifth-generation logger who was previously president of the Maine state Senate. He ousted GOP Sen. Susan Collins, who had survived several challenges to her reelection in her nearly three decades in the upper chamber. Jackson, who became the Democratic nominee after Graham Platner exited the race, billed himself as a champion of the working class on the campaign trail. And though he first ran for office more than two decades ago as a Republican, his politics have since shifted leftward, with backing from prominent progressives like independent Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts.

title: DOJ taps prosecutor for probes into Mar-a-Lago raid, docs case
summary: The Justice Department has tapped the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles to work on probes into the FBI's raid on Mar-a-Lago and the Trump documents case.
story: Washington — The Justice Department has tapped the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles to work on the ongoing criminal investigation into the FBI's 2022 raid of President Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence and former special counsel Jack Smith's handling of the investigation into classified documents found there, according to multiple sources familiar with the move.

Bill Essayli, currently the first assistant U.S. attorney in the Central District of California, will continue leading his office as he works on the other investigations. The probes are part of a sprawling Justice Department inquiry into an alleged "grand conspiracy" of former law enforcement and Democratic officials of depriving Mr. Trump's rights during his first presidency.

While sources told CBS News that Essayli will only focus on the Mar-a-Lago raid probe and the investigation into the classified documents case, the "grand conspiracy" probe has also centered on whether Obama- and Biden-era officials were part of a long-running conspiracy to keep Mr. Trump out of political office, and whether former CIA Director John Brennan lied to Congress in 2023 about an intelligence assessment on Russian interference in the 2016 election.

Smith was appointed in November of 2022 to take over the Justice Department investigations into Mr. Trump, one related to his conduct after the 2020 presidential election, and another tied to his handling of classified records after he left office. The cases both resulted in criminal charges against Mr. Trump. He pleaded not guilty and denied wrongdoing.

Smith's dual cases against Mr. Trump were ultimately closed in late 2024 after he won the presidential election. Prosecutors wrote that Justice Department regulations forbid the prosecution of a sitting president.

One source familiar with Essayli's assignment said he was designated as a special assistant U.S. attorney to work on the investigation related to Smith's probe of Mr. Trump's retention of classified documents. Such assignments are typically temporary, though they can be extended.
Politico first reported Essayli's new assignment.
It was not immediately clear who may be overseeing other parts of the grand conspiracy investigation that are focused on the intelligence assessment of Russia's actions in 2016.
In recent months, investigators have sought to interview former FBI agents involved in the classified documents case, but their interviews were later postponed, two sources said.

Lawyers for some of the agents previously asked U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, who presided over the classified documents case, for clarification on whether they are permitted to speak about the investigation. They raised concerns that doing so could violate Cannon's standing February court order that barred any public disclosures about the probe.

The grand conspiracy investigation, based out of Fort Pierce, Florida, has been plagued with internal disputes and doubts about its viability, resulting in the departure of multiple officials assigned to work on it in recent weeks. Earlier this month, Jason Reding Quiñones, the top federal prosecutor in South Florida overseeing the probe, abruptly resigned. Two months before that Joe diGenova, who was tapped by Attorney General Todd Blanche to supervise the investigation, also resigned.
Earlier in the year, the career prosecutor overseeing the investigation was also sidelined after she expressed concerns about the strength of the evidence, CBS News previously reported.
Last year, a federal judge ruled that Essayli was serving unlawfully in his role as first assistant in the office in violation of the Federal Vacancies Reform Act.

Essayli — a former California Republican state lawmaker — was named interim U.S. attorney in April 2025, a role that's typically limited to just 120 days. But days before the clock ran out, Essayli resigned and then-Attorney General Pam Bondi named him first assistant U.S. attorney. Under federal law, the person in that role becomes the office's acting head when there's a vacancy.

The Supreme Court is weighing whether to take up appeals on the legality of similar arrangements in U.S. attorneys' offices in Nevada and the Northern District of New York in the coming months, which could imperil Essayli's role.
Spokespeople for the Justice Department and the Central District of California did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Obama gives pep talk to freshman House Democrats in surprise visit
summary: Former President Barack Obama was the surprise guest at a hastily called meeting of Democrats who just won House seats.
story: Washington — Groups of newly elected Democratic members of the House of Representatives rushed to board buses outside the Capitol on Wednesday bound for a meeting with a "special guest."
When they arrived at their destination, they learned the guest was none other than former President Barack Obama.

"I did not know who the special guest was, but I knew it was going to be someone special," Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, of Texas, told CBS News. "And then obviously we get here, and we get to see it's President Obama!"

The meeting was arranged by House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, fresh off his nomination to become the next House speaker. If elected in January, he would make history as the first African American to serve in the role.

"We're excited about the opportunities that are in front of us to deliver big, meaningful bold progress to the American people," Jeffries said as he introduced Obama to cheers and chants of "four more years."
"I believe in the Constitution, people," Obama quipped.

The former president engaged in a broad discussion, moderated by Jeffries, about the challenges and opportunities of the next Congress, urging the House Democrats to "get stuff done." Obama addressed practical matters, like providing robust constituent services to bigger picture policy goals such as lowering costs, making health care more affordable and creating accessible housing, his office said.

"The opportunity for this class to be part of a majority that delivers for the American people and reimagines how both government can work and politics can work — it is a thrilling moment for me to watch," Obama said, according to excerpts obtained by CBS News. "And I want to make sure that everybody here knows I will do everything I can behind the scenes to be helpful."

Rep.-elect Patty Garcia, of Illinois, said the former president answered a "mix of questions" from new members including his advice to them, his message after this month's election victories, what the party can build on and immigration.

Garcia first met Obama when he was a senator and she was a student at the University of Illinois. The incoming congresswoman said the event with the former president was a "full circle" moment as she prepares to represent a Chicago-area district.

"I think being able to see him in different roles, and you know, very encouraging message, of you know, 'You all represent different constituencies, very diverse, and at the end of the day, you need to kind of find a common ground that can help deliver for everyone as much as possible and make an impact,'" Garcia said.
Rep.-elect Katy Padilla Stout, of Texas, worked for the Obama administration as an intern at the Department of Education.
"I think it was just the pep talk everyone needed to come hear and remind us why we're here, who sent us here, and the importance of the work that we have here to do," Padilla Stout said.

Since leaving office, the former president has worked to lift up a new generation of leaders and relishes his role transitioning from player to coach and serving as a sounding board to those in public service, according to a source familiar with his thinking.

He congratulated the freshman class and emphasized the importance of generational change telling them "you are right for this moment," adding that they "know the struggles that the majority of people are going through right now, as opposed to the struggles that folks were going through in my generation."

"He said, you know, he thinks everyone who plays a part in American history, it's like a relay and you're always, you know, passing it off to the next generation," Padilla Stout said. "He did denote that like half the people that came through were like, 'You're the first person I voted for!' ... He was like, 'It just makes me really proud to know that we planted those seeds and they're coming to fruition.'"

Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, of New York, said Obama offered a unifying message even as the party faces divisions over its leadership. The democratic socialist was one of 11 members who voted against Jeffries for speaker but noted "we're in ongoing negotiations and continuing to have meetings with him."

"What is unifying for our freshman class is taking money out of politics, taking on corruption, taking on corporate greed, and really fighting for an economy that works for working people," Valdez told CBS News. "And I think that's something that's really unifying from people who are from, you know, Montana to Tennessee to Texas to New York."
She said the former president shook "every single incoming member's hand," calling it a "beautiful" gesture.
As Michigan's Christina Hines exited the event, she described it in one word.
"Life-changing."
