title: Gamers, start your engines. Grand Theft Auto 6 is ready to roll.
summary: The latest, long-awaited version of the hit video game franchise launches at midnight local time on Nov. 19 in countries worldwide. Here's what to know about GTA 6.
story: In the immortal words of Carl "CJ" Johnson from an earlier edition of Grand Theft Auto, "Ah s***, here we go again." After 13 years and two delayed launches, video game fans are finally getting their hands on Grand Theft Auto 6.

GTA, as it's widely known, has evolved since its launch in 1997 into one of the biggest franchises in entertainment and one of the few sure hits in the ferociously competitive video game world. Tens of millions of people globally are expected to pick up their joysticks as Rockstar Games, the company behind the series, rolls out GTA 6 on Nov. 19 in countries around the world.

As fans eagerly await the latest GTA installment, Rockstar has whipped up interest with a series of trailers and even an extended look on Netflix. In typical fashion, however, the company has kept the hype simmering by withholding key information about the game ahead of its official launch this week.

"Having been over a decade since the last full release of a Grand Theft Auto game, all that energy just keeps getting bottled up and bottled up, and people are reading into every tweet and every little piece of news that's coming out of Rockstar to try and glean all the details of this game," Andrew Marok, director of equity research for digital media at financial firm Raymond James, told CBS News.
Here's what to know about the long-awaited release of GTA 6.
What is GTA 6 about?

The latest GTA installment centers on the stories of Lucia Caminos, the game's first-ever female protagonist, and Jason Duval. Jason, who has been working for drug runners, craves a quieter life but keeps getting dragged back into crime, according to Rockstar's synopsis of GTA 6. Lucia, meanwhile, has recently left Leonida Penitentiary, where she landed after "fighting for her family."

When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair becomes entangled in a wider conspiracy. The series is based in Vice City, inspired by Miami, in the fictional state of Leonida. Rockstar has touted the location as the most detailed version of the game yet, with architecture, beaches, roads and bars all inspired by South Florida.
There's "this concept of GTA 6 being just bigger than the game," Marok said.  "It's also about the immersion in the world of Vice City."
What equipment do I need to play the game?

Players will need a PlayStation 5 or an Xbox Series X/S console to play GTA 6. Rockstar told players who are preloading the game to plan ahead, as they may need up to 212 GB of storage space, depending on their device.
When can people start playing?

The game officially debuts worldwide on Thursday, Nov. 19. Rather than a single launch time, GTA 6 is rolling out at midnight local time in countries around the world, giving some users access before others. This website shows the countdown time by country.

Pre-orders for the game began back in June. But users weren't allowed to start pre-downloading on their PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles until Nov. 10, according to Rockstar. Gamers were also able to purchase a "code-in-box" version, a physical case that contains a code users can input to download the game from the PlayStation Store or Xbox.
How much does it cost?
Grand Theft Auto 6 costs $79.99 for the "standard edition" and $99.99 for the "ultimate edition." The latter contains an exclusive collection of cars, weapons and apparel.
What are players saying?

New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game. One 25-year-old told CBS News he set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — rather than his home in the United Kingdom, to access it as soon as possible.
"It's definitely more immersive than previous entries," he told CBS News, requesting anonymity because he is taking a day off from work to play GTA 6. "Visually, it's incredible."
Other gamers were also quick to praise GTA 6's visual quality and action-packed plot.

"The gameplay dynamics are just amazing, and the graphics are great, and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive," Adam Simmons, a 50-year-old in Wellington, New Zealand, where the game has already rolled out, told The Associated Press.

On Metacritic, a review aggregator website, players gave GTA 6 a score of 99 out of 100. "Grand Theft Auto VI, against all odds, has somehow managed to not only meet but surpass all my expectations," one user wrote.
How long does it take to play?
Insider Gaming, a website focused on the video game industry, said it takes an average of roughly 50 hours to complete all of the missions in GTA 6.
When will online play launch?

The online, multiplayer version of the game introduces new missions and allows players to stay immersed in the world of GTA after completing the more linear single-player version. It's free with the option of in-game purchases, according to Marok of Raymond James.
Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, hasn't confirmed GTA Online's availability, though it seems likely given its enormous revenue potential.
"That's where GTA 5 made so much of its money," Marok said.
Will there be a PC version?

Rockstar Games did not respond to a request for comment about whether it will release a desktop version of the game. Historically, a PC version has been released about 12 to 18 months after the console version, according to Marok. However, the company could decide to launch it sooner.

"I think that there are reasons why Rockstar and Take-Two would want the PC version of the game out sooner than usual, and a lot of that has to do with the Grand Theft Auto Online component of the game, which is the multiplayer, ongoing monetization piece of it," he told CBS News.
Who plays GTA?
Male millennials and Gen Zers represent the key demographic playing GTA 6, according to a recent report from Sensor Tower. The company estimates 72% of players are male, while 57% are under 35.
What music is featured in the game?

GTA 6 features an original adaptive score from Justice, the Grammy-winning French electronic duo featuring Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay. The music is "dynamically tuned to the different ways players engage with the world of Vice City and Leonida throughout Jason and Lucia's story," Rockstar Games said on its website.
The 30-track "Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score" is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations with Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
Who are the voice actors?

Rockstar has not disclosed the full voice cast. However, actress Manni Perez was nominated for her voice acting in the "Best Performance" category at The Game Awards, an annual ceremony that celebrates the video game industry. Actor Stephen Root has also confirmed to the AP that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly disclosed his participation.
How many GTA 6 units have already been sold?

The company had sold 19 million units, including pre-order copies, and generated $1.84 billion in revenue by Thursday, according to Sensor Tower. The market intelligence and digital analytics platform said earlier this month that GTA 6 is the "most pre-ordered game in history."
Raymond James projects that Rockstar will sell 50 million units of the game from launch through the end of Take-Two's fiscal year 2027, which runs until March 31.
"That would be by some distance the biggest launch in video gaming history," Marok said.

GTA 5, released in 2013, has sold nearly 235 million copies, according to Take-Two. The game has generated more than $10 billion in revenue over the last 13 years, according to Victor Matheson, an economist at the College of the Holy Cross who studies sports and major events.
How much did GTA 6 cost to make?
Rockstar hasn't disclosed the exact figure, but analysts estimate GTA 6 cost upward of $1 billion to produce, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
"I would be shocked if it was under a billion dollars because they've been working on this for the better part of a decade," Marok said.
Asked about the price tag during a recent Wall Street Journal event, Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick didn't offer an exact figure, saying only, "It was expensive, and it took a long time."

title: Hardcore GTA fans ditch work so they have time to play
summary: Some employees locked in their time off months ago, so they're free to start playing Grand Theft Auto 6 as soon as it launches on Nov. 19.
story: Cameron Logan Cox was honest with his employer when he recently submitted a request for paid time off.

"I literally just put GTA 6," the 34-year-old filmmaker and creative director at a music label in Kansas City told CBS News. He said his coworkers were already well aware that he'd be out of action when Grand Theft Auto 6 is officially released on Thursday.
"They all know I'm a huge gamer," he said. "We don't have anything too pressing happening, so it worked out nicely."

Cox is hardly alone. Other avid GTA fans told CBS News they've cleared their work schedules so they can dive headlong into Rockstar Games' latest, and long-awaited, installment in the hit franchise. According to data from payroll processor Gusto, PTO requests for the day of GTA 6's commercial release this week are up 9% compared with the two prior weeks.
In short, GTA 6 is as much a cultural happening as a video game. Analysts say the game, which took 13 years to make, is expected to be the largest entertainment release of all time.

"While it's common for people to plan time off around major entertainment releases and cultural events, the anticipation surrounding GTA 6 is on another level," Bart Spiegel, a partner at PwC who leads the consulting firm's global entertainment and media practice, said in an email. "It's the kind of cultural moment that could rival the Olympics in terms of the attention it commands, so there's certainly going to be an impact on workplaces."
Spoiler alert

One 27-year-old woman told CBS News that she submitted her PTO request back in March to be ready for this week's GTA launch. She knew she would want to start playing as soon as the game went live and to avoid online spoilers.

"I genuinely believe that this is one of, if not the biggest, gaming events in a lot of our lifetimes, and spoilers are going to spread so fast," said the Grays Harbor, Washington state, resident. "It's going to be nearly impossible to avoid them."
The woman, who works as a clerk for the U.S. Postal Service, has already pre-downloaded GTA 6 and plans to start playing at 9 p.m. PST on Wednesday.
"I'm probably just going to go throughout the whole night," she said.
Another player based in the U.K. told CBS News he is also trying to avoid spoilers. The 25-year-old is taking a long weekend beginning on Wednesday to "give [GTA 6] the attention it deserves."

The man, who works in tech finance and who requested anonymity because he's not authorized to speak to the media, set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — so he could begin playing as soon as possible.
Gaming time off
Meanwhile, some companies are resigning themselves to the temporary brain drain and preemptively giving employees time off to focus on GTA.
Logitech, a California-based computer and electronics manufacturer, introduced a new perk for employees earlier this month: GTO (Gaming Time Off).

And in August, a U.S. Army unit in Georgia offered active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play GTA 6 in exchange for reenlisting. The Third Infantry Division told CBS News that 43 of the 130 soldiers who were eligible selected this option as part of their reenlistment, along with other standard incentives.

While some U.S. employees may ditch work on Thursday, their absence from the office isn't expected to cause major economic disruptions, according to Victor Matheson, an economics professor at the College of the Holy Cross.
"Even if 5 million workers in the U.S. took the day off, the total U.S. labor force is 170 million people," he said in an email. "That's like 3% of the labor force."

So far, more than 17 million preorder copies of the game have been downloaded worldwide, according to Sensor Tower, a digital market intelligence company. Matheson expects the game to rack up more than 50 million users by year's end.
As for Cox, 27 years have passed since he first played Grand Theft Auto on an original PlayStation console owned by a relative. Yet the excitement is as fresh as ever.
"It feels like I'm a kid again," Cox told CBS News.

He'll be in good company when the game launches, as his son is also planning to stay home from school on Thursday and Friday. Cox agreed to let him take time off to celebrate his birthday, which falls on Friday.
"He has all of his schoolwork turned in. That was the condition," he told CBS News. "I was, like, as long as all your work's done, your grades are good, I'm fine with that."

title: Iran war powers measure again falls short in Senate
summary: The Senate rejected a resolution aimed at reining in President Trump's ability to strike Iran, despite GOP frustration with the war following the party's losses in the midterm elections.
story: Washington — The Senate rejected a House-adopted resolution aimed at reining in President Trump's ability to strike Iran, losing Republican support despite frustration with the war following the party's losses in the midterm elections.

In a 48 to 51 vote, three Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky — joined all but one Senate Democrat — Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania — in support of the measure.

Thursday's vote marked the first time either chamber has weighed in on the war since the midterm elections, which dealt Republicans sweeping losses. Voters cited the war in Iran, and its toll on the economy, as among their top concerns.

Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, who has led Democrats' repeated efforts to restrict the president on Iran, urged his GOP colleagues to back the measure ahead of the vote. In a speech on the Senate floor, Kaine said it's become apparent over the course of recent months that the war is unpopular, "but its unpopularity was made absolutely manifestly clear in the election results from Nov. 3."

"A historic repudiation of the party holding onto the White House, with much of that energy driven by Americans' deep dissatisfaction with war, waged unilaterally by a president who said he would not, causing costs to dramatically rise on every American family," Kaine said. "And so it is my hope, that in the aftermath of a clear message from the American public that they want us to stop this illegal, catastrophic war, the Senate will demonstrate that we're listening."

The resolution would have directed the president "to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran," but its impact would have been largely symbolic. Under the War Powers Resolution of 1973, the president must withdraw forces from hostilities "if the Congress so directs by concurrent resolution." But administrations of both parties have argued that the process is unconstitutional. The White House argued against its validity after a similar measure was adopted over the summer.

One Republican who had voted in favor of a previous effort, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, voted against the measure on Thursday. Tillis told CBS News that "this one doesn't go to the president, so it's just a statement from Congress. I've made that statement."

"I'm using other vehicles to try and figure out how to replenish supplies, but hold Hegseth accountable," Tillis said of the defense secretary, citing the funding process. "I think I've been pretty clear that I think he's a failure."

The Senate adopted a resolution aimed at reining in the president on Iran in June, when four Republicans joined the bulk of Democrats in favor. The outcome prompted intense pushback from Mr. Trump, who took aim at the GOP senators who had supported the resolution at a testy lunch meeting with Senate Republicans a day later. After the lunch, a separate effort to restrict the president's war powers fell short when key Senate Republicans shifted their votes.

Since the war began in late February, Democrats have forced more than a dozen war powers votes. Most have fallen short. One advanced in May, helped along by four Republicans and a handful of GOP absences. That effort ultimately stalled after Republicans' meeting with the president.
Ahead of the midterms, the Senate voted on another House-adopted concurrent resolution. It narrowly fell short, despite some GOP members becoming more vocal in their opposition to the war.

title: Diapers are often cited in child injury reports, but not recalled
summary: Despite hundreds of rash reports and a handful of lawsuits against different brands, the Consumer Product Safety Commission has never announced a diaper recall and does not have dedicated standards for diapers.
story: An average baby goes through about 3,000 diapers in the first year. But in the last 15 years, hundreds of children have suffered from rashes and "chemical burns" allegedly caused by various diaper brands, according to a CBS News analysis of Consumer Product Safety Commission incident reports.
So far, lawsuits and parents' complaints have not resulted in recalls or federal legislation requiring ingredient transparency.
Natalie St. Ward, a mom of three, stumbled upon Millie Moon diapers when her oldest son, who is now 5, was just a few months old.

"Our firstborn, especially, was huge and rolly, and it was the best for big thighs," St. Ward said. "It was also the only diaper that he never blew out in. So, loved Millie Moon to the freaking world."
But this summer, her then-2-and-a-half-year-old daughter developed a rash where her diaper was.
"It was like a switch," St. Ward said. "She was totally fine, no rash at all, and then just, it looked like she was burning. You know, blistering, red, super uncomfortable."

She took her daughter to her pediatrician, who gave her a steroid cream. The cream helped, but she said switching to a different diaper was what appeared to clear up the rash. She tried to rotate between Millie Moon and different brands, since they still had some left over, but "every time that I had a Millie Moon on her, it would flare up like crazy," she said.
Her youngest, at 9 months old, also had a similar reaction to Millie Moon diapers that cleared up after switching to a different brand, she said.

Hundreds of parents have reported similar incidents involving rashes and what appeared to be "chemical burns," some requiring doctor visits and prescription creams or medications after using Millie Moon diapers this year. The surge in reporting has resulted in the largest number of reports to the Consumer Product Safety Commission for a single diaper brand since at least 2011, when it launched its online reporting site, SaferProducts.gov.

Parents and health care professionals have reported more than 700 incidents this year (as of data through mid-October) of diaper rash and what they describe as "chemical burns" after using a new package of Millie Moon diapers. Many babies had used the diapers before with no problems before experiencing a new rash. Consumer Reports is calling on Millie Moon to issue a recall of their diapers.

"We think the number of incidents, as well as the severity of the incidents, speak for themselves," said Gabe Knight, a senior policy analyst at Consumer Reports. "And even if [Millie Moon has] yet to identify a cause, that's a meaningful safety signal. Something is not right, and kids are suffering."

Millie Moon, in an email to CBS News, said it has "gone substantially beyond routine regulatory and product safety testing" and worked with seven different independent organizations to test for chemical safety, potential skin irritants and contamination.

"Based on our investigation and extensive independent testing, we have found no product-related cause of the reported reactions. We take every report seriously and continue to monitor and review all feedback closely. Currently, skin-irritation complaints represent fewer than 0.1% of Millie Moon diaper packs sold," the email said.
St. Ward said she feels frustrated that the company is not doing more to address the problems.
"There's legitimate issues that are happening, and this is not just one person, or it's not just this one city … it's not environmental, it's obviously spread so far," she said.
The hundreds of incident reports involving Millie Moon diapers this year dwarf complaints from previous years.

Last year saw the second-highest number of incident reports, with parents, caregivers and health care professionals reporting a total of 95 incidents, 83 of them involving Huggies diapers. And in 2011, the data shows 77 incidents involving Pampers. In fact, the 735 Millie Moon incidents are more than the combined complaints from all manufacturers over more than a decade and a half, according to the data.
Knight said most people don't know about CPSC's SaferProduct.gov website and typically, most incidents don't get reported.

In February 2026, a Reddit user posted in the r/NewParents subreddit asking other users if they'd had any similar experiences with Millie Moon diapers and diaper rash. At the end of April, another user linked directly to the CPSC's incident reporting site. Subsequently, the number of Millie Moon diaper incidents jumped from 16 reported in April to 108 in May.
"I'm truly just grateful that someone on Reddit posted [and said] 'this is where you should report it,'" Knight said.

St. Ward, the mom who said her children experienced rashes after using Millie Moon diapers, reported her experience directly to Millie Moon. A representative emailed her back, asking follow-up questions about the size, manufacturing details and descriptions of the irritation. Since then, St. Ward said she hasn't received any more messages from the company besides a customer service survey.
The CPSC is investigating the incidents, and a spokesman told CBS News in an email that they cannot comment on active investigations.
Hundreds of incidents, zero recalls

Diaper rash is the most common skin condition for infants. Despite the name, studies have found it can reflect other systemic conditions other than irritation caused by a diaper or bodily fluids and can be caused by many factors, making a direct cause hard to pin down.

Between 2011 and 2026, diapers had the highest number of incident reports to the CPSC out of all product categories. Even excluding the 2026 data, largely driven by Millie Moon reports, diapers were the fifth-highest category, with more than 300 reports between 2011 and 2025.
But other diaper brands have also experienced similar problems, though with a lower volume of reports.

CBS News reported in May 2010 that the CPSC was investigating complaints of babies and toddlers suffering severe and persistent diaper rashes and blisters that resembled chemical burns after using Pampers Dry Max diapers, likely the cause of the higher number of reports in 2011 compared with the next few years.

The CPSC found no link between the new diapers and the rashes, and Procter & Gamble, Pampers' parent company, never issued a recall. A group of parents filed a class action lawsuit in 2011. P&G settled, paying $1,000 to each of the 59 parents in the case and paid nearly $3 million in legal fees, Reuters reported. The company also agreed to contribute $400,000 to training programs in pediatric skin health.

Then another jump in reports regarding Huggies diapers came in 2025. A class action lawsuit filed last November alleges that the Kimberly-Clark Corporation, Huggies' parent company, changed the formulation of its hypoallergenic diapers without informing consumers, leading to skin reactions.
Kimberly-Clark said in a statement that its "regular and robust product testing shows our diapers are safe — and have been used safely by millions of caregivers for decades."

The company also said that all its diapers are "made without parabens, elemental chlorine, natural rubber latex, phthalates and fragrance," and encouraged consumers to visit the Center for Baby and Adult Hygiene Products' website for more information about diaper safety and ingredient transparency.

Still, the CPSC has never announced a diaper recall. Knight said most recalls are voluntary, meaning companies agree to recall a product. The CPSC can order recalls without a company agreeing, but the process is "painstaking; sometimes they have to sue," according to Knight.

A slightly easier course of action for the CPSC would be to issue a safety warning, but it doesn't come with any refunds or exchanges. Notably, however, the CPSC has never issued a product safety warning for diapers.

In order to do so, under the Consumer Product Safety Act, the CPSC must establish a "substantial product hazard." This means a product either failed to comply with an existing standard or safety rule or had a defect that would create a "substantial risk of injury to the public."

"While CPSC has conducted prior investigations into diapers, none of those found sufficient justification to rise to the required level of a 'substantial' product hazard. CPSC is constantly testing and investigating potentially violative products," said a CPSC spokesman in an email to CBS News.
Knight said by the time a recall happens, "there's been a failure."
"It means that something unsafe has already made its way into consumers' hands, and unfortunately, a lot of the time, already caused harm," she said.
A push for more transparency

Diapers, unlike cribs, strollers, carriers and nursing pillows, do not have a dedicated standard under the Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act. The CPSC's general infant and toddler product rules apply to diapers, which include identifying the manufacturer, date and batch of a box as well as testing for contaminants like lead. Companies do not, however, have to disclose ingredients or use standardized absorbency tests.

"I think it's a space that we need more regulation," said Sydney Swanson, a senior science analyst at the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit activist group that sponsored state-level diaper labeling transparency legislation.

There is no federal law requiring companies to disclose the ingredients used in their diapers, which experts say makes it hard for parents and pediatricians to identify what might be causing reactions like what parents say is currently happening with Millie Moon diapers.
"It leaves parents and caretakers in the dark about what the products and materials are made of, and what babies are sitting in for a majority of their first years of life," said Swanson.

A CPSC spokesman noted that the commission has jurisdiction over about 15,000 types of products and most do not have specific standards, but that they are "always open to considering new rulemaking initiates."

At the state level, California lawmakers recently passed AB1901, which requires manufacturers of children's diapers sold, distributed, or manufactured in California to fully disclose their ingredients on product packaging and online — including the functions listed alongside the chemical names. New York and Illinois have similar laws.

"This can help parents, researchers and doctors fully identify what's exactly in a product. And then, because brands tend to standardize labels, we're hopeful that California's law can help benefit parents everywhere," Swanson said.
Parents like St. Ward.

"When you're dealing with really sensitive and important parts of people's bodies, like, having no regulations, or little to no regulations, just doesn't make sense. Yes, everybody's body is different. But protecting bodies…that should make our standards a lot higher, not lower," she said.
Experts say if a parent, caregiver or doctor notices a safety problem with diapers or any other product, they should report it to the CPSC at SaferProducts.gov.

title: Woman runs 7 marathons while pregnant this year: "I am very stubborn"
summary: Deirdre Keane, a 38-year-old nurse and management consultant, achieved her goal of completing all seven World Marathon Majors while pregnant with her first child.
story: Deirdre Keane had already run more than 60 marathons when she decided to take on a new challenge of completing the World Marathon Majors. She just didn't expect to be running them while pregnant.

Earlier this month, the 38-year-old nurse practitioner and management consultant ran the New York City Marathon — her hometown race — in her third trimester. It was the seventh marathon she finished while pregnant and the final race she needed to achieve her goal of running all the Majors in the same year.
In addition to New York, the other marathons in the premier series are Berlin, Boston, Chicago, London, Sydney and Tokyo.

Keane completed the New York City Marathon in just over 4 hours, with an average mile pace of 9 minutes, 26 seconds, according to New York Road Runners, the group that organized the race. She had completed the same marathon in just over three hours in 2025, records show.

"I knew how bizarre it was to be running a marathon at 34 weeks, but I also knew how fit I was and self-aware of my body at this point," Keane told The Associated Press. "And while it is very unusual, I wasn't the first woman to have ever done this."

Keane, who has completed 74 marathons and ultramarathons, received clearance from her doctor to compete in the races, as long as she remained vigilant about nutrition, hydration and stopping exercise at the first sign of muscle cramping, the World Running Network reported. That advice worked for Keane because she was already such a highly trained athlete.
"My last hurrah"
After getting married last year, Keane and her husband Brian began talking about starting a family. Expecting pregnancy to take a while, Keane made other plans for herself in the interim.
"In my mind, 2026 was going to be my year of bucket list items," Keane recalled. "I was like, this is going to be my last hurrah before settling down and becoming pregnant, becoming a mother."
She signed up for 11 races: the seven World Marathon Majors, a trail marathon in Ireland, two ultramarathons and an Ironman.

Keane kicked off her quest by running the Tokyo Marathon in March. But when the Boston and London marathons rolled around in April, she noticed she was running a bit slower than usual and wasn't quite feeling like herself. So, she took a pregnancy test.
It was positive, but she wasn't going to let that get in the way of her goals.

She promised her husband she would take the next marathon in Ireland slowly. She also agreed to forgo the Ironman and the second ultramarathon — she had already completed the first before finding out she was pregnant.

"Brian was understandably skeptical and worried at first. Neither of us fully understood the physical limitations of pregnancy and why. The research we found was surprisingly limited and frustrating," Keane said. "So, we decided to take it one marathon at a time, with me not pushing the pace and keeping walking in my back pocket."
Keane was initially nervous to tell her OB-GYN about her marathon plans but was relieved when she got the go-ahead.

"I don't think she thought I would do them towards the end, especially being so pregnant at New York. But I am very stubborn and determined," Keane said. "Plus I got lucky, I was feeling good. So I was able to do it."

Exercise is generally considered safe and beneficial during most healthy pregnancies. Experts recommend that pregnant women who were physically active before pregnancy or regularly engaged in vigorous aerobic exercise can continue those activities with approval from their doctor. There is limited research on intensive exercise beyond the recommended amount.

With the approval of her doctor, Keane flew to Australia in August to compete in the Sydney Marathon at 25 weeks pregnant, followed by Berlin at 29 weeks. She then completed the Chicago Marathon at 31 weeks in just under 4 hours and finished with the New York City Marathon at 34 weeks in 4:06:55.

Keane was more worried about the race in New York "because I was starting to look heavily pregnant and feel it too." But she had friends along the course while her husband appeared at multiple spots with water to keep her hydrated.

"The marathon passed a block away from Weill Cornell at mile 16, where I'm delivering, so there were plenty of jokes about just pulling off there to have the baby or testing the medical volunteers' training on the course with an unusual medical intervention of a delivery," she said.
Keane's determination was modeled for her at an early age by her father, John, an Irish immigrant who ran marathons in the 1980s and 1990s.
He died of cancer when she was 13, but continued to run in his final months, completing his final New York City Marathon one day before undergoing surgery to have a tumor removed, Keane said.
Years later, when Keane went to college, she was inspired to run a marathon in her dad's honor. That's when she caught the bug.

"I loved marathons from the beginning, because it really shows me what the human body is capable of, not only from a physical standpoint, but from a mental standpoint," she said. "I realized how much grit I have and how capable I am to overcome hard things."

Since then, running has become a constant in Keane's life. She says it helped her cope with the emotional toll of working as a nurse practitioner at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York during the COVID-19 pandemic.

During the pandemic, feeling isolated and needing something to look forward to, Keane signed up for the World Marathon Challenge: running seven marathons on seven different continents in just seven days. She completed the challenge in 2023 and was the fastest woman to do so that year.

Now, with the World Majors in her rearview, Keane says she's taking time to reflect on the past eight months. Just as she learned from her father's example, she hopes to pass the lessons running has taught her on to her son.

"I want to teach my son resilience and that he can do hard things," she said. "And that when life inevitably gets tough and throws challenges at him, he will push through them and see the other side of them, whether we elect to do them like a marathon or some things that are way beyond our control."

title: Putin says Russia won't negotiate with Ukraine after bridge strike
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin said Russia will not negotiate any limited ceasefire now with Ukraine, citing a Ukrainian strike on a highly symbolic bridge this week.
story: President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia will not negotiate with Ukraine on a limited ceasefire, citing a Ukrainian strike this week on a major bridge connecting Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Putin made the remarks to reporters in Russian after meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. He said he had discussed the possibility of a ceasefire in certain areas of Ukraine, but would not move forward with negotiations after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian state news agencies.

The 12-mile bridge, which Putin ceremonially opened himself in 2018, is hugely symbolic as it links the Russian mainland with Crimea — territory that Russian forces occupied about four years earlier. The missile strike this week wasn't the first time Ukraine had targeted the piece of infrastructure, but it inflicted severe damage. Russia also struck two major bridges in Kyiv the same day.

Putin played down the bridge's strategic importance on Thursday and said he had heard the calls "from all sides" for a naval ceasefire or a suspension of strikes on energy facilities, but he ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing the attack on the bridge.

"Honestly, I discussed the issue with my colleagues at the Security Council, and I asked them to think about it and go back to the issue, so that we could reach some agreements," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency TASS. "However, we will not make agreements after strikes on the Crimean Bridge. We will respond to these strikes."
Putin vowed that Russia's retaliation for the strike on the bridge would be severe, TASS reported.
While Putin claims frequently to want peace, he denies that Russia started the war with his order for a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine have been relentless.

It's not clear how much Ukraine came up in Mr. Trump's one-on-one meeting with Putin on Wednesday, or in the meeting with both Putin and Xi on Thursday. Last week, the White House said Ukraine wouldn't be a topic of discussion, but before he left for Asia, Mr. Trump said the three leaders would be discussing the war. The White House readout of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was sparse on detail, and did not mention Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff have been in Germany to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders of Germany, France, the U.K. and other European nations — a group known as the Coalition of the Willing — about Ukraine and other topics.
Kushner said they discussed the "latest efforts to achieve a just, lasting and durable peace in Ukraine."

"We are grateful for his leadership, constructive engagement, and close partnership as we work together toward our shared goal of ending this terrible war and building a secure and prosperous future for Ukraine and Europe," Kushner posted to X.
Merz, speaking to reporters after the meeting, called the China summit a photo-op and said the trilateral format "will not bring peace" in Ukraine.
As he went to shake Putin's hand before an earlier meeting Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, Mr. Trump referred to the Russian leader as "my friend."
"Who is he?" the president said, pointing at Putin and smiling. "He's my friend."

title: Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for a rare 3-way meeting in China
summary: Russia says Putin, Trump and China's Xi agreed during a rare meeting to boost gas and oil production, and "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war."
story: President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.

The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.

The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine, which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.

Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.

The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."

They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the "International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
"A great relationship"

The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.

"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Focus on Ukraine
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.

"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."

Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."

Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."

Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons, with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.

Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program, ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year.

China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi, however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence.
Global trade and AI

The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."

Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed, is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.

Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.
Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence.

"We do not want to do anything to destroy the tremendous potential of this technology," he said. "We have to watch it, we have to be careful, we have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements."

Beyond AI, the U.S. and China have sought to stabilize their economic relationship over the last year, following a tit-for-tat trade war that sent tariffs above 100% in 2025. A tariff truce between the two countries is set to expire on Jan. 10 of next year.

Mr. Trump said in his APEC speech the U.S. is committed to "growth and stability" in the Asia-Pacific region, and argued the American economy is "thriving like it has never thrived before." He also said the U.S. is negotiating "numerous trade agreements" and expects to sign some agreements with APEC members in the near future.

During Xi's remarks earlier in the session, the Chinese leader called on countries in the region to "look out for each other" and "expand our shared interests," including on free trade and economic growth.
Foreign conflicts loomed large during the Trump-Putin-Xi talks. Iran is one contentious area, given China's status as one of the largest customers of Iranian oil, and Russia's ties with Iran.

The White House previously said the war in Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said he expected the issue to come up, calling it "my favorite subject."

Taiwan is another frequent discussion topic between the U.S. and China. During the U.S. president's visit to Beijing in the spring, Xi reportedly delivered a stern warning about the island, which he has long vowed to reintegrate with mainland China, floating potential "clashes and even conflicts" if the issue isn't "handled properly."
And Mr. Trump was expected to press Xi to release two detained Americans during his visit to China, CBS News has reported. Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.

title: Law firm that cut deal with Trump has done $11.8M in pro bono work
summary: A lawyer representing the law firm Kirkland & Ellis said it has provided nearly $12 million in free legal services for the Trump administration.
story: Washington — A major law firm that reached an agreement with President Trump to avoid being targeted by an executive order told Congress it has provided nearly $12 million in free legal services for his administration. The firm disclosed the departments receiving the services, as well as the requests it turned down.

Kirkland & Ellis was one of 10 law firms that cut deals with the White House last year after the president signed directives that punished four other firms that either employed his perceived political enemies or represented clients he disfavors.
As part of the agreement, announced by Mr. Trump on Truth Social in April 2025, Kirkland & Ellis pledged to provide $125 million in pro bono legal services to causes supported by the president.

A trio of top Democrats in Congress, Sens. Adam Schiff and Richard Blumenthal, and Rep. Jamie Raskin, launched an investigation into the deals last year, and earlier this month, a lawyer representing Kirkland & Ellis disclosed details of the free legal work the firm has done.

The lawyer, Beth Wilkinson, said in a Nov. 5 letter to the three Democrats that Kirkland & Ellis has provided more than 6,000 hours of pro bono services valued at $11.8 million representing the Commerce Department, U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, U.S. Postal Service and the Defense Department, as well as for a $550 billion investment pledge between the U.S. and Japan.

As of the end of September, Kirkland & Ellis has devoted 15,469 hours of legal services worth more than $18.7 million on non-government pro bono matters related to causes specified by Mr. Trump in his April 2025 Truth Social post, including in support of veterans and other public servants, a fair justice system and combating anti-Semitism, Wilkinson said.

Kirkland & Ellis has also turned down requests to work on projects for the Trump administration, including "Trump Accounts," the census, the renaming of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, and challenges to the Postal Service's handling of mail ballots, according to Wilkinson's letter.

The firm has also declined administration requests for it to represent third parties on a pro bono basis, including a veterans' group backing construction of Mr. Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch and scientists involved in cases regarding the Trump administration's position on climate change.

"Critical to Kirkland's willingness to enter into the Truth Social agreement was that it retain absolute discretion in deciding which matters to take and could decline to take matters suggested by the Administration," Wilkinson wrote. "In practice, Kirkland has exercised that discretion and declined numerous matters. And it has never faced any repercussions or threats from the Administration for turning down work."

A federal judge has blocked the Kennedy Center from closing its doors for two years during proposed renovations and prohibited its board from adding Mr. Trump's name to the building. Judges have also temporarily blocked the Trump administration from starting construction on the arch and prevented the Postal Service from enforcing new regulations for mail voting ahead of this month's midterm elections.

Blumenthal, Raskin and Schiff have also demanded the other nine law firms that cut deals with the White House provide information about their agreements. The 10 firms collectively agreed to provide roughly $1 billion in free legal services in order to avoid being targeted by the president and his administration.

"The Trump Administration also unsuccessfully tried to involve Kirkland & Ellis in work supporting the President's political vanity projects, such as the renaming of the Kennedy Center or supporting the illegal construction of his triumphal arch in Washington, DC — raising serious questions of whether other firms acceded to these demands," they wrote to each of the law firms in letters Wednesday.

Raskin told reporters on Capitol Hill that the arrangements between the White House and law firms raise legal questions. A federal law called the Antideficiency Act prohibits the executive branch from spending outside of congressional appropriations and says federal employees cannot accept free services.

"It's an extremely problematic thing if you've got law firms that have been shaken down for their service to Donald Trump, and they're out there doing millions of dollars of work for the federal government," he said.

Mr. Trump rolled out a series of executive orders last year that sought to impose sweeping punishments on five firms in all: Perkins Coie; Paul, Weiss; Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr LLP; Jenner & Block; and Susman Godfrey. The orders targeted the firms' clients, access to federal buildings and government officials, and security clearances held by their employees.

The president rescinded his directive against Paul, Weiss after the firm pledged $40 million in pro bono legal services. Kirkland & Ellis said in its letter to the Democrats that Paul, Weiss' agreement was "the first of its kind and set forth a precedent for how firms that wished to avoid immediate irreparable harm and protracted, intrusive litigation could resolve potential disputes with the Administration."

The four other firms — Perkins Coie, WilmerHale, Jenner & Block and Susman Godfrey — each filed lawsuits challenging Mr. Trump's executive order. Four different federal judges all sided with the firms and invalidated the measures as unconstitutional. A federal appeals court has been considering since May the Trump administration's bid to restore them.

In addition to providing information about the amount of work Kirkland & Ellis has done for the Trump administration, Wilkinson's letter detailed the firm's efforts to reach a deal with the president. She said Ballard Partners, a consultant for Kirkland & Ellis, spoke to May Mailman, a White House official, in March 2025, "in which she expressed the Administration's openness to achieving resolutions with law firms."

Mr. Trump's former chief of staff, Susie Wiles, worked at Ballard Partners for nearly a decade before leaving in 2019. The firm made more than $88 million in lobbying revenue last year, CBS News found.

Four people were involved in negotiations with Kirkland & Ellis on behalf of the Trump administration, Wilkinson said, including Mailman, two officials from the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and Boris Epshteyn, an outside adviser to the president. Kirkland & Ellis did not communicate with the president about the deal, she said.

title: Meet the 19 new senators set to be sworn in to Congress
summary: From a former wheelchair basketball Paralympian to a Methodist pastor and one senator returning after defeat, the new class hails from different backgrounds and parts of the country.
story: Washington — Nineteen new senators are preparing to take their seats in the 120th Congress in January — the largest class in almost five decades — after Democrats flipped a slew of seats in the midterm elections, and some incumbents chose to retire.

From a former wheelchair basketball Paralympian to a Methodist pastor and one senator returning after defeat, the new class hails from different backgrounds and parts of the country. But mostly, they're much younger: With several freshmen in their 40s and one in his 30s, the Senate's average age is dropping by a couple of years — to 63.
These are the new senators:
Abdul El-Sayed, D-Michigan

Abdul El-Sayed, 42, is a former Michigan health official who defended an open Senate seat in Michigan after Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek reelection. El-Sayed, a Democrat, defeated former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, running on a leftist platform including "Medicare for All." He won a bruising campaign, despite reservations about his appeal to Jewish and Black voters over his opposition to U.S. support for Israel and his progressive platform. At the same time, top Republicans, including President Trump and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz called him a "jihadist" and sought to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood, and even implied that electing him could be deadly to Americans.
With his victory, El-Sayed will become the first Muslim senator in U.S. history.
Adam Hamilton, D-Kansas

Adam Hamilton, 62, is a fifth-generation Kansan and pastor. He defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, flipping the seat for Democrats for the first time in nearly a century. Formerly a Republican, Hamilton ran on an affordability-focused agenda, while appealing to a cross-party coalition to take on Marshall. As a pastor, Hamilton led the U.S.' largest United Methodist church and is a well-known author and speaker.
Andy Barr, R-Kentucky

Republican Andy Barr, 53, has represented Kentucky in the House since 2013, and won the Senate seat after Sen. Mitch McConnell announced he would retire. Barr, an attorney, had the president's endorsement, and billed his Democratic opponent in the race as too extreme for the Bluegrass State. In the House, Barr served as co-chair of the Congressional Horse Caucus and the Congressional Bourbon Caucus, two of Kentucky's defining interests.
Annie Andrews, D-South Carolina

Democrat Annie Andrews, 46, is a pediatrician who defeated Trump-endorsed incumbent GOP Sen. Darline Graham, who had been appointed to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, after his sudden death in July. Andrews campaigned on healthcare access and affordability, along with fighting corruption in Washington. With her victory, she became the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the Senate, and the first Democrat elected to represent the state in the upper chamber since 1998.
Barry Moore, R-Alabama

Republican Barry Moore, 60, has represented Alabama in the House since 2021. A member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, Moore ran as a staunch supporter of Mr. Trump and touted being the first elected official to endorse the president in 2015. He won the seat after Sen. Tommy Tuberville launched a gubernatorial bid, rather than seeking reelection. Moore and the state's other senator, Katie Britt, both hail from Enterprise, Alabama, and attended the same high school.
Chris Pappas, D-New Hampshire

Democrat Chris Pappas, 46, has represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019 and defended an open Senate seat in the Granite State after Sen. Jeanne Shaheen opted not to seek reelection. Along the campaign trail, Pappas billed himself as an independent voice for the state and ran on his record in the lower chamber, where he's a member of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus. With his victory, Pappas is set to become the first openly gay male senator in the chamber's history.
Harriet Hageman, R-Wyoming

Harriet Hageman, 64, a Republican, has represented Wyoming as the state's at-large representative in the House since 2023. Hageman's Senate victory came after GOP Sen. Cynthia Lummis, a first-term senator, announced she would not run for reelection. Hageman grew up on a ranch and attended college on a livestock judging scholarship. A former litigator and staunch supporter of Mr. Trump, Hageman first came to Congress after defeating former GOP Rep. Liz Cheney.
James Talarico, D-Texas

James Talarico, 37, is a Texas state representative, former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who flipped the Senate seat for Democrats in the Lone Star State. Talarico defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who had bested incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the primary. The Texas Democrat calls himself a progressive Christian, and ran on fighting corruption and lowering costs, overcoming widespread GOP criticism that he was too extreme for the state, as they pointed to comments he's previously made on issues like veganism and gender. Derided as "Tofu Talarico" by Republicans, he toasted Democrats' victory on election night with Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa at a Whataburger.
Josh Turek, D-Iowa

Josh Turek, 47, is a state representative and former wheelchair basketball Paralympian. A Democrat, he flipped Iowa's Senate seat after Sen. Joni Ernst opted not to seek reelection, defeating GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson. On the campaign trail, he touted his background in the state legislature representing the most conservative district held by a Democrat in the state, and he pledged to work — including with Mr. Trump — to deliver for Iowans.
Julia Letlow, R-Louisiana

Julia Letlow, 45, has represented Louisiana in the House since 2021, when she became the first Republican woman to represent the state. She won the Senate seat after defeating incumbent Sen. Bill Cassidy in the primary, following Mr. Trump's endorsement. Letlow, who previously worked in education, initially came to Congress after winning a special election for Louisiana's 5th Congressional District following the death of her husband, who died in 2020 from complications related to COVID-19 before he could be sworn into office.
Juliana Stratton, D-Illinois

Juliana Stratton, 61, is a former state representative and Illinois lieutenant governor who launched a Senate bid after Dick Durbin, the No. 2 Senate Democrat, announced his retirement. Stratton, a fellow Democrat who ran on a progressive platform, is the fifth Black woman ever to be elected to the upper chamber, where she and Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland will make history, with three Black women serving simultaneously for the first time.
Kevin Hern, R-Oklahoma

Republican Kevin Hern, 64, has represented Oklahoma in the House since 2018, and joins the Senate's ranks after Sen. Alan Armstrong was appointed as a placeholder following Markwayne Mullin's departure to become Homeland Security secretary earlier this year. Hern, a former aerospace engineer and businessman, who at one time owned 24 McDonald's franchises, chaired the conservative House Republican Policy Committee in the House. He's set to be sworn in later this month, due to Armstrong's temporary appointment to the position.
Kurt Alme, R-Montana

Kurt Alme, 60, a Republican, is a Harvard-trained former U.S. Attorney for the District of Montana, nominated to the position twice by Mr. Trump. Alme comes to the Senate after GOP Sen. Steve Daines opted not to seek reelection, in a move that sparked controversy when Daines made the announcement just before the filing deadline and endorsed Alme, blocking any major challengers. Alme, who has also served as Montana's budget director, said he plans to target government spending, telling supporters on election night, "My first bill will say, if Congress can't balance a budget, Congress doesn't get paid."
Peggy Flanagan, D-Minnesota

Peggy Flanagan, 47, is Minnesota's lieutenant governor and a former state representative. She held on to an open seat for Democrats after Sen. Tina Smith opted not to seek reelection. Flanagan defeated the GOP candidate, former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya, after winning the Democratic primary in August against a more moderate candidate. Flanagan ran on progressive priorities like Medicare for All and secured endorsements from top progressives. With the victory, Flanagan is set to become the first Native American woman in the U.S. Senate.
Mary Peltola, D-Alaska

Mary Peltola, 53, is a former congresswoman who became the first Democrat to represent the state in the House in 50 years in 2022. She ultimately lost her reelection bid for Alaska's sole House seat in 2024, before going on to defeat incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan this cycle. Peltola, who framed herself as an independent voice for the state, is set to become the first Alaska Native to be elected to the Senate. Republicans accused Democrats of foul play after another candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Dan Sullivan, joined the race and advanced to the ranked-choice November election. But as it turned out, Peltola won by more than 12,000 votes, and the second Dan Sullivan won just about 4,800, far less than the margin of victory.
Roy Cooper, D-North Carolina

Roy Cooper, 69, is a popular former two-term North Carolina governor who flipped the Senate seat for Democrats after Sen. Thom Tillis decided not to seek reelection. Cooper faced off against former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley in the race, making an affordability message central to his campaign, like with his "Make Stuff Cost Less" tour throughout the state. Cooper is also the longest-serving state attorney general in North Carolina's history, where he's become known for his love of diet soda. The self-identified "diet soda sommelier" is fond of Diet Sun Drop and said he dreamed of drinking it from the Stanley Cup if the Hurricanes won (they did win).
Scott Colom, D-Mississippi

Democrat Scott Colom, 43, is a district attorney and seventh-generation Mississippian who defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a major upset that few saw coming this cycle. Colom, who will be the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction, campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues, while pledging to deliver for the Magnolia State in places that he argued Hyde-Smith fell short. Colom may have taken the political world by surprise with his victory, but when he arrives at the Capitol, he's sure to be recognized from what may have been the catchiest ad of the midterms cycle — the "Pick Another Senator" spot that seized on Hyde-Smith's response to rising beef prices.
Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio

Sherrod Brown, 74, is a former three-term Democratic senator who lost his reelection to Ohio GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno in 2024. But he's back, after defeating incumbent Sen. Jon Husted in November. Brown's strong working-class brand in the Buckeye State resonated with voters, as issues like affordability and data centers were the dominant concerns. Husted was appointed to fill Vice President JD Vance's Senate seat last year until this past special election. Now, Brown will take his seat and serve out the remainder of Vance's Senate term, which will end in early 2029.
Troy Jackson, D-Maine

Democrat Troy Jackson, 58, is a fifth-generation logger who was previously president of the Maine state Senate. He ousted GOP Sen. Susan Collins, who had survived several challenges to her reelection in her nearly three decades in the upper chamber. Jackson, who became the Democratic nominee after Graham Platner exited the race, billed himself as a champion of the working class on the campaign trail. And though he first ran for office more than two decades ago as a Republican, his politics have since shifted leftward, with backing from prominent progressives like independent Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts.

title: Anthropic's IPO set for blastoff in key test for AI boom
summary: Anthropic's stock is poised to start trading on Nasdaq Thursday in one of the largest IPOs of all time. The AI world is watching.
story: Anthropic's blockbuster initial public offering is set to launch on Thursday, a milestone that will test investor enthusiasm for the company behind the popular Claude chatbot and the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector.

"This is a case where the deal is so large and important, so central to the AI thesis, that it's going to be a turning point for the AI sector," Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at investment bank Renaissance Capital, told CBS News. "Even non-AI companies are going to feel the ripple effects, especially in the IPO market."
Anthropic shares are scheduled to start trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol "ANT" sometime after markets open Thursday at 9:30 a.m. ET.
Anthropic increases stock price amid high demand

In an announcement on Wednesday night, San Francisco-based Anthropic said it will offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 each. The initial public offering raised around $81 billion and valued Anthropic at $1.5 trillion, making it the largest public offering in history. Elon Musk's SpaceX raised $75 billion when it went public in June.
Anthropic is selling 956.3 million shares, although only 7.4% will be available for public trading (up to 9.8% including Class A shares held by nonfounder employees), according to Renaissance.

The company plans to raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, all of which have a stake in the AI race.

Kennedy thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading, an increase that would represent a "solid pop," he said. If the stock rises closer to $140, "that would tell me that AI enthusiasm has come roaring back," he added.
Great expectations
Although many investors appear eager to own a piece of Anthropic, the IPO comes amid growing concerns about whether the torrid spending on AI will deliver the expected productivity and profit boom.

AI-related stocks have fluctuated in recent weeks following subpar earnings and the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance data center construction. Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors, with the chipmaker's stock now down more than 35% from its October all-time high.

"The whole AI sector has sold off from its July peak. Investor enthusiasm was greatest then," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, told CBS News.

Although Anthropic has yet to turn a profit, the company has shown explosive revenue growth over its short time in business. Anthropic raked in nearly $17 billion in the third quarter this year, up 45% from the second quarter, a recent regulatory filing shows. Given that heady rate of expansion, Ritter expects Anthropic to reach profitability quickly.

To justify its projected trillion-dollar valuation, however, the company will need to sustain that momentum while operating under Wall Street's unsparing gaze. Compounding the challenge is how quickly the AI landscape itself is changing. For instance, Anthropic could struggle to maintain its growth rate as consumers shift from pricier AI models like Claude and ChatGPT to cheaper open-source models, Ritter noted.

Anthropic also will have to spend heavily to keep developing its AI models and stay ahead of rivals, from OpenAI, Alphabet and Meta to Chinese platforms. Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is "substantial." Meanwhile, the company has committed to spending nearly a trillion dollars on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045, according to a securities filing.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
"The company is likely to be very successful, but the market is pricing in very lofty expectations," Ritter said. "It could be hard for management to execute."
Wall Street analysts said Anthropic's share offering has broader ramifications for the AI sector, with the IPO's pricing setting a benchmark for other tech companies planning to go public.
Even if Anthropic's stock soars on the first day of trading, it won't necessarily create a swarm of IPO activity, Kennedy said. Still, it could reinvigorate markets, he added.

Meanwhile, by going public, Anthropic is effectively asking investors to discount the threats that Anthropic founder Dario Amodei himself has identified as posed by AI. In September, he called for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after a former Anthropic researcher warned of the existential threat AI poses to humanity.

title: Putin says Russia won't negotiate with Ukraine after bridge strike
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin said Russia will not negotiate any limited ceasefire now with Ukraine, citing a Ukrainian strike on a highly symbolic bridge this week.
story: President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia will not negotiate with Ukraine on a limited ceasefire, citing a Ukrainian strike this week on a major bridge connecting Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Putin made the remarks to reporters in Russian after meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. He said he had discussed the possibility of a ceasefire in certain areas of Ukraine, but would not move forward with negotiations after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian state news agencies.

The 12-mile bridge, which Putin ceremonially opened himself in 2018, is hugely symbolic as it links the Russian mainland with Crimea — territory that Russian forces occupied about four years earlier. The missile strike this week wasn't the first time Ukraine had targeted the piece of infrastructure, but it inflicted severe damage. Russia also struck two major bridges in Kyiv the same day.

Putin played down the bridge's strategic importance on Thursday and said he had heard the calls "from all sides" for a naval ceasefire or a suspension of strikes on energy facilities, but he ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing the attack on the bridge.

"Honestly, I discussed the issue with my colleagues at the Security Council, and I asked them to think about it and go back to the issue, so that we could reach some agreements," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency TASS. "However, we will not make agreements after strikes on the Crimean Bridge. We will respond to these strikes."
Putin vowed that Russia's retaliation for the strike on the bridge would be severe, TASS reported.
While Putin claims frequently to want peace, he denies that Russia started the war with his order for a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine have been relentless.

It's not clear how much Ukraine came up in Mr. Trump's one-on-one meeting with Putin on Wednesday, or in the meeting with both Putin and Xi on Thursday. Last week, the White House said Ukraine wouldn't be a topic of discussion, but before he left for Asia, Mr. Trump said the three leaders would be discussing the war. The White House readout of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was sparse on detail, and did not mention Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff have been in Germany to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders of Germany, France, the U.K. and other European nations — a group known as the Coalition of the Willing — about Ukraine and other topics.
Kushner said they discussed the "latest efforts to achieve a just, lasting and durable peace in Ukraine."

"We are grateful for his leadership, constructive engagement, and close partnership as we work together toward our shared goal of ending this terrible war and building a secure and prosperous future for Ukraine and Europe," Kushner posted to X.
Merz, speaking to reporters after the meeting, called the China summit a photo-op and said the trilateral format "will not bring peace" in Ukraine.
As he went to shake Putin's hand before an earlier meeting Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, Mr. Trump referred to the Russian leader as "my friend."
"Who is he?" the president said, pointing at Putin and smiling. "He's my friend."
