"The good news is that it doesn’t have to be the nominee who makes these commitments. The administration can do it because it has admitted that it can take these actions immediately using its own authority," he argued. "That power is within the administration’s possession. It’s a matter of political will, not legal ability."

"With regard to fixing the study, I think they can make those changes now," Baptist continued. "They don’t need to wait for a confirmation, especially when they’re saying they’re going to finish the study in December of this year. We might not have an FDA commissioner at that point, or even a nominee. So they need to fix it immediately and course-correct the study before it’s fatally flawed and completed next year."
Fox News' Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

title: Senate Republicans break through Washington gridlock with massive American energy, data center overhaul
summary: Senate Republicans advanced a sweeping permitting bill to speed environmental review, expand the electric grid and limit legal challenges on projects.
story: Oklahoma Sen. Alan Armstrong discusses the critical need for permitting reform to boost American energy independence. He explains that despite abundant U.S. oil and gas resources, outdated processes and litigation delay essential infrastructure projects. Armstrong, a former CEO, highlights how legal challenges can halt multi-billion dollar projects, emphasizing the need for robust political action to streamline energy development.
Senate Republicans scored a major win after advancing a massive bill that would overhaul America’s permitting system in a bid to turbocharge infrastructure and energy development in the country.

The Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) on a major bipartisan vote Thursday night. The legislation went through fits and starts over the last few months, until a bipartisan coalition, with buy-in from the White House, formed to tinker with the final product.

At the 30,000-foot level, the sweeping package would accelerate environmental review of projects, limit legal challenges, protect approved projects, expand the electric grid and streamline energy development in all fields — like oil, gas and renewables.
AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING
An Amazon Web Services data center is seen on Aug. 26, 2026 in Stone Ridge, Virginia. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"This is a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects, certainly without giving up any of the strong protections for our environment," Chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., said when the bill was introduced in September.
The bill also tackles an issue that was front and center for voters across the country: data centers.

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the Democratic lead on the legislation, pushed for stronger language in the bill that would shield ratepayers from higher costs that stem from data center development and their usage of electricity.
WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE
That comes after Republicans tried to ram through similar safeguards before the election with a bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, that Democrats argued lacked real enforcement teeth.

"This process will mean that we develop responsibly. It will mean more jobs. It will mean cheaper energy," Heinrich said. "It will mean that we actually require big load centers, whether that's a factory or a data center, to not pass those costs on to the American consumer by statute, not a suggestion, an actual law."

The provision covers data centers with a demand of at least 20 megawatts of power, and would require them to cover the cost of additional power for them to run, financial guarantees covering costs to build or upgrade facilities, to pay the tab if they leave an area for unpaid infrastructure costs, allow states to charge higher rates to reduce other customers’ bills and tack on power supply conditions.
DEMS KILL REPUBLICAN'S CHANCES OF LOWERING AMERICANS' ELECTRICITY BILLS IN KEY ELECTION FLASHPOINT

Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah, Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Meanwhile, whether the legislation makes it through the House is an open question.

Sen. Alan Armstrong, R-Okla., who was appointed to the position earlier this year to replace Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and has made permitting reform his primary policy issue, told Fox News Digital that there were "a lot of good supporters on both sides of the aisle in the House." But he worried about attendance issues in the lower chamber.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"A lot of the language that's in here came right out of a lot of the House’s work," Armstrong said. "So, I think there'll be some support. I just hope we have people, you know, show up in the numbers that we need to vote for it."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Trump’s National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross fired amid widespread tech outages
summary: President Donald Trump backed the firing of National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross over cybersecurity credentials, with Kirsten A. Davies stepping in.
story: The ‘Special Report’ All-Star panel debates the diplomatic implications of the historic summit and evaluates key takeaways regarding the ongoing Ukraine conflict, global energy markets and American foreign policy.
National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is out after President Donald Trump backed his firing over concerns he lacked the cybersecurity credentials for the job, Fox News has confirmed.
Kirsten A. Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, will step into the position in an acting capacity.

Davies, who was Senate-confirmed, will join Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, White House technology advisor Michael Kratsios and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the administration's national security and cyber leadership team.

An administration official separately told Fox News that Cairncross did not want to serve another two years in the role. Cairncross took office Aug. 4, 2025, after Senate confirmation, and the exact date of his departure remains unclear.
TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS
National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired from his job after a series of major tech outages. (Godofredo A. Vasquez/AFP via Getty Images)
Senior administration officials welcomed Davies' appointment on X.
"Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies — look forward to working together to strengthen America’s cybersecurity," Rubio wrote.

Clayton praised her background, writing, "With nearly two decades of leadership experience in the technology space, Kirsten Davies will be a strong asset for the Trump administration in her new position with the Office of the National Cyber Director. It has been my pleasure to work closely with Kirsten on national security matters, and I look forward to now working with her to navigate an increasingly dynamic and fast-moving cyber landscape."

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth wrote, "The Department congratulates Kirsten Davies on her new role as the National Cyber Director. Throughout her tenure at DOW, she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump’s America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape."
US INFRASTRUCTURE CRUMBLES AS ADVERSARIES POWER UP – LEAVING AMERICANS DANGEROUSLY EXPOSED: CYBER EXPERT
Davies thanked Trump, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Hegseth in her own post on X, calling the moment a critical juncture for U.S. technology.

"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future. Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future," Davies wrote. "I am honored to continue to serve."

The leadership shakeup follows a nearly weeklong stretch of technical disruptions that hit air travel, major banks, Microsoft services, Apple, Marriott, the National Weather Service and internal systems at the National Security Agency.

A Nov. 13 Federal Aviation Administration outage triggered a nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop and thousands of flight cancellations after contractor work on air traffic control wiring overloaded the system.

Administration officials have pushed back against speculation that hackers or foreign adversaries were behind the disruptions. Rubio said Tuesday that officials found "zero evidence" tying the incidents together or to malicious actors, while Clayton said the outages appeared linked to routine software patches and system upgrades rather than a coordinated cyberattack.
DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK

Department of War Chief Information Officer Kirsten A. Davies testifies during a Senate Armed Services subcommittee hearing on cybersecurity on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on March 24, 2026. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The Office of the National Cyber Director and Cairncross did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Retired police sergeant issues warning over Mamdani's NYPD shake-up ahead of Thanksgiving parade
summary: New York City's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade could face security gaps after the NYPD's Strategic Response Group disbandment, a retired sergeant warns.
story: National Police Association spokesperson and retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, raises concerns over Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plan to disband the NYPD's Strategic Response Group in an interview with Fox News Digital.

EXCLUSIVE: A retired police sergeant with nearly three decades of law enforcement experience warned that she would not bring her own family to New York City amid Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plans to dismantle a specialized NYPD unit responsible for counterterrorism support and crowd control.
"I wouldn't take my family there right now," retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, a spokesperson for the National Police Association, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.

Smith's warning follows Mamdani's announcement that the NYPD's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a roughly 500-officer specialized unit involved in counterterrorism, major event security and protest response, will be disbanded as part of a broader overhaul of how the nation's largest police department handles demonstrations.
MAMDANI GUTS ELITE NYPD TACTICAL UNIT, BACKS 'CIVILIAN-LED APPROACH' TO RESPONDING TO PROTESTS

Retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, left, a National Police Association spokesperson, speaks during an interview. Smith, right, poses beside a Naperville police cruiser during her law enforcement career in Chicago. (Courtesy of Betsy Brantner Smith/National Police Association)
The democratic socialist mayor has defended the decision as fulfilling a campaign promise to separate counterterrorism operations from the policing of constitutionally protected protests.
Critics, however, argue that dismantling the established unit could undermine the coordination and specialized training needed to respond to emergencies.
Smith, who spent 29 years in Chicago-area law enforcement and has experience supervising crowd control operations, said the consequences could extend beyond protests.

"One of the beauties of this strategic response group is that these are a group of officers who are used to working together," Smith said. "They train together. They have specialized knowledge of how to deal quickly and safely with these types of situations, including an active shooter."
MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani attends a news conference at Athens Square Park Tuesday in New York City. The appearance came a day after Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch announced plans to disband the department's Strategic Response Group. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
Her concerns come as New York City prepares for the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Nov. 26, an event expected to draw enormous crowds of visitors to Manhattan.
Smith warned that breaking up the specialized unit could create vulnerabilities if its responsibilities were redistributed without preserving existing operational relationships.
"First and foremost, I'm concerned that any intelligence may be lost or may be ignored for a large scale event like this," she said.

NYPD Assistant Commissioner Brad Weeks told Fox News Digital the restructuring will not affect security arrangements for this year's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, explaining that the new First Amendment Support Team and Patrol Support Division will not begin operating until February 2027.
FLORIDA EYES POACHING NYPD OFFICERS AFTER MAMDANI DISMANTLES ELITE UNIT
NYPD Counterterrorism officers at the 2018 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. (Noam Galai/FilmMagic via Getty Images, File)

The department also said counterterrorism personnel currently assigned to the Strategic Response Group will be transferred to the NYPD's Counterterrorism Bureau, consolidating those capabilities within the specialized bureau.
In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, Mamdani's office directed the outlet to remarks the mayor delivered during a news conference earlier this week.

"I've long said that counterterrorism and protest response are fundamentally different responsibilities and that New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," Mamdani said.
The overhaul also imposes new restrictions on police tactics during protests, including prohibitions on long guns and tear gas, according to the mayor's office.

Pepper spray will no longer be permitted as a general crowd management tool, while officers assigned to the new Patrol Support Division will receive specialized training and retain arrest powers when necessary.
MAMDANI UNVEILS SWEEPING NYPD USE-OF-FORCE REVIEW, BUT STOPS SHORT OF FULFILLING KEY CAMPAIGN PROMISES

A Change.org petition created by the National Police Association calls on New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to restore the NYPD's Strategic Response Group. The petition displayed 1,938 verified signatures in the supplied screenshot. (Courtesy of National Police Association/Change.org)
Mamdani said the initial changes would take effect in approximately 90 days, with a First Amendment Support Team (FAST) operating within the NYPD's Community Affairs Bureau during the transition.
A separate civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division, housed within the Office of Community Safety, is scheduled to launch in 2028.
The mayor said the division would focus on engaging with protest organizers, mediation and preventing tensions from escalating.
Mamdani rejected suggestions that civilians would be expected to confront violent demonstrators without police support.
"Now, police will always be present in the case of any kind of violence," he said. "So this idea that New Yorkers' safety will be compromised is not true."
FAR-LEFT GROUPS CHEER MAMDANI FOR DISBANDING ELITE NYPD PROTEST TEAM
Protesters and counter-protesters gathered inside Washington Square Park in New York City. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital, File)
Smith, however, questioned whether the new approach could preserve the capabilities of officers accustomed to responding together during major incidents.
"It is a political decision on his part. And it's an incredibly dangerous one," she said.
NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch defended the restructuring, saying the department would maintain the resources necessary to respond to serious threats.

"I would never support changes that diminish the NYPD's ability to protect New Yorkers or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat," Tisch said in the city's announcement.
Mamdani's announcement also drew praise from far-left activist organizations that have long criticized the NYPD's handling of demonstrations.
NYC MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI SAYS HE WON'T FIRE NYPD COMMISSIONER JESSICA TISCH DESPITE SOCIALIST PRESSURE
NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch has defended the restructuring. (Cristina Matuozzi/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect, File)

As Fox News Digital reported Wednesday, the Party for Socialism and Liberation celebrated the decision, declaring in a social media post that "the mass movement has won the disbanding of NYPD’s Strategic Response Group — but the fight continues."
Nerdeen Kiswani, founder of the anti-Israel activist organization Within Our Lifetime, also welcomed the announcement, describing it as "overdue and welcome news."
Self-described Marxist streamer Hasan Piker also praised the move, writing that he was "glad the mayor is moving on this promise to disband."
Fox News Digital's earlier reporting noted that it remained unclear whether those organizations or influencers had influenced the self-described democratic socialist mayor's decision.
MAMDANI'S LUXURY SECOND HOME TAX HITSD $500M MILESTONE DESPITE THOUSANDS OF EXEMPTIONS
NYPD Strategic Response Group officers monitor a crowd outside 26 Federal Plaza in New York City. (Adam Gray/Getty Images, File)

The National Police Association has launched a Change.org petition urging Mamdani to reverse the decision to disband the Strategic Response Group, arguing that its specialized capabilities are essential to public safety.
According to the petition's organizers, nearly 2,000 people signed it within its first two days.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Smith urged the mayor to preserve the NYPD's ability to deploy officers with established training and experience.

"We urge the mayor of New York City to continue to allow the NYPD to do everything in its power to keep the city safe," she said.Fox News Digital's Asra Nomani and Preston Mizell contributed to this reporting.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: House China panel calls for cutting defense contracts over aerospace ties to Beijing's military
summary: A new House report says Airbus and U.S. defense contractors like GE Aerospace and Honeywell should lose taxpayer funds over China aerospace joint ventures.
story: Congressional watchdog leaders Randall Schriver and Mike Kuiken warn China could exploit American chips and AI to strengthen its military.

A new congressional report is urging the U.S. to restrict investments in China’s aerospace sector and withhold taxpayer funding from companies that build military capabilities for U.S. adversaries, warning that Western commercial partnerships transferred technology and expertise to Chinese firms with military ties.

The 65-page report, titled "China's Wingmen: How Western Government Policy Enabled China's Rise in the Skies," follows a year-long investigation by the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, led by Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and Ranking Member Ro Khanna, D-Calif. It examined how legal commercial partnerships transferred advanced technology and manufacturing expertise to Chinese military-linked companies.
China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) is the country's military, which the committee says has benefited from civilian aerospace technology transfers.

"American and European companies transferred technology to China that could be used against our brave men and women in uniform. With the CCP’s military-civil fusion there are no private companies in China," Moolenaar said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.
CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN
China's domestically produced C919 passenger jet sits on display at the Singapore Airshow on Feb. 4, 2026, in Singapore. (VCG/VCG via Getty Images)
"The PLA will exploit civilian technology and use it to advance its military ambitions and that is what happened here."

The report singled out European aerospace giant Airbus, which receives U.S. defense contracts while maintaining manufacturing partnerships in China. Although Airbus sold its stake in an AVIC affiliate in 2025, its commercial partnerships with the Chinese aerospace conglomerate continue, according to the committee.
The bipartisan panel examined at least six U.S.-China joint ventures involving American defense suppliers GE Aerospace, Honeywell Aerospace and RTX subsidiary Collins Aerospace.

Investigators found that GE transferred foundational avionics technology to a joint venture with a subsidiary of AVIC, the Chinese state-owned conglomerate that develops military aircraft, including the J-20 stealth fighter. The committee said GE withheld its original joint venture agreement despite repeated requests.
RUSSIA IS HELPING CHINA CLOSE GAP WITH US FORCES AMID TAIWAN TENSIONS, WARNS LONGTIME MILITARY LEADER

An Airbus aircraft assembly facility in Tianjin, China, on Oct. 25, 2025. The European aerospace manufacturer opened its second A320-family final assembly line in the city that month. (VCG/VCG via Getty Images)

The American companies maintained that their Chinese partnerships supported civilian aircraft and complied with U.S. export controls. The report also cited previous export-control settlements involving all three companies but did not establish that the partnerships under investigation violated U.S. law.

"We appreciate the Committee’s work ensuring the U.S. retains its position as the world’s commercial aviation leader while protecting our most sensitive technologies. We have and will continue to follow relevant U.S. laws and regulations, as the report acknowledges,"a Collins Aerospace spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

"GE Aerospace takes national security, compliance, and the protection of its intellectual property seriously, and we work closely with the U.S. government – including this Committee – to ensure we continue to do so," a GE Aerospace spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

GE also said its joint venture with AVIC involves older avionics technology sold exclusively in China, not jet engines, and that the arrangement includes safeguards intended to protect sensitive information and ensure compliance with U.S. law.
AMERICA'S ENEMIES PREPARE TO TAKE THE NEXT MAJOR WAR INTO OUTER SPACE

A J-20 stealth fighter jet of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force performs at the China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, or Airshow China, in Zhuhai, Guangdong province, China Nov. 9, 2022. (China Daily via Reuters)

Honeywell Aerospace told Fox News Digital that its commercial partnerships were fully licensed and approved by the U.S. government, adding that it cooperated transparently with the committee and continues to comply with U.S. export laws.

The committee urged the Federal Aviation Administration not to certify Chinese-manufactured aircraft, citing state subsidies and Beijing's refusal to release a final report on the 2022 China Eastern Airlines crash.
"The report’s only recommendation directed at the FAA is that they do not certify Chinese-made aircraft, which the agency has not done," an FAA spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

A representative for Airbus did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Hakeem Jeffries wins overwhelming Speaker-designate vote as progressives' revolt falls flat
summary: House Democrats unified behind Hakeem Jeffries with 251 of 262 secret ballots as 11 progressive holdouts demanded votes on ICE, Gaza and Citizens United.
story: House Democrats nominated Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., for speaker after he ran unopposed. 11 Democrats voted against his nomination, including two from his home state of New York, Rep.-elects Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier.
Democrats are fretting that the "Bloc" of progressives will lug House Democrats to the left.
But, there is strength in numbers.
Yours truly wanted to understand just how much sway progressives might have over the House Democratic Caucus. Look no further than Wednesday morning’s vote for speaker.
No one challenged House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to become speaker-designate in the internal caucus vote.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, House Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic candidate Suzan DelBene celebrate at a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee midterm election night watch party in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 3, 2026. (REUTERS)
It’s about the math.

Jeffries marshaled 251 of the 262 secret ballots cast. The recorded vote revealed that despite all of their noise and clamor, extreme progressives really don’t have much juice compared to the rest of the Democratic Caucus. In fact, rank-and-file Democrats crushed their progressive colleagues.

Democrats did not vote by name. But numbers say a lot. While the recorded vote could have revealed potential craters of dissent among Democrats and questions about Jeffries, the tally registered the opposite. It showed just how diminutive the hard left is in the Democratic Caucus.
JEFFRIES BRUSHES OFF OPPOSITION FROM FAR-LEFT DEMS WHO VOTED NO: 'WE’RE GOING TO WORK TOGETHER'

Do they exude an outsized political voice? Yes. But success in Congress is measured in numbers. And at least on Wednesday, the numbers signaled few results for the Bloc and a show of unity among Democrats.
"With the majority as big as it is, it's going to be very hard for anybody to try and hold our group of hostage," forecast Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.).
"We’re going to work together to find the highest common denominator in order to make life better for the American people," said Jeffries.
With more than 260 likely members in the Democratic Caucus, the Bloc wasn’t a factor on the first vote which mattered.
In January, Jeffries becomes the 57th person and the first Black speaker to grip the gavel. Members of the Congressional Black Caucus celebrated the ascendency of their colleague.

"I've been thinking about (the former Rep.) John Lewis (D-Ga.) a lot this week," said former House Majority Whip and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.), invoking the civil rights figure. "This is a very surreal moment for me."
Clyburn spoke on behalf of Jeffries’ candidacy in the caucus, declaring that the path for the New York Democrat to the speakership makes him "feel vindicated."
"As a Black woman from the South, having the next speaker of the House to be a Black man means a lot to me," said Rep. Nikema Williams (D-Ga.).
Rep. Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.) is the son of late Rev. Jesse Jackson. I asked what Jackson’s father would think of Jeffries rising to the speakership.
"He’d be more than happy to see America making progress. This is what the world looks like. This is what America looks like," said Jackson.
WATCH: JEFFRIES FACES UNCERTAINTY FROM INCOMING DEMOCRATS AS HOUSE SPEAKER VOTE APPROACHES
But let’s filet the caucus vote for speaker to understand what unfolded with 11 Democrats who withheld their support from Jeffries.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill in Washington. (J. Scott Applewhite/AP)

Representative-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) is a populist in a district which President Trump won by 10 points in 2024. Leonard defeated Rep. Mike Carey (R-Ohio). The district Leonard flipped in central Ohio is a long way politically from left-leaning districts in New York City and New Jersey where renegade members of the Bloc refused to cast their ballots for Jeffries.

"What we need is a commitment from the speaker to get a 28th Amendment passed in 2028, to end Citizens United, end the corruption and call a vote on U.S. military aid to Israel," said Leonard. "If he does those things, he's got my vote."
Seven of the progressives published a joint statement, demanding commitments from Jeffries to stop ICE and end "genocide in Gaza."
The seven declared they saw "meaningful progress" in their talks with Jeffries. But since those negotiations continue, "our vote in caucus today was no" against Jeffries.
Despite repeated efforts, none of the seven spoke to Fox.

But what’s remarkable is that two of the seven withholding their support hail from Jeffries’ hometown, New York City. One is Representative-elect Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.) — who will represent a wide swath of Brooklyn and Queens. The other is Representative-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.). That district comprises parts of Upper Manhattan and The Bronx.
Your trusty reporter tried to understand what the dissent meant.
"How are their districts different than yours, being next door?" I asked Jeffries.
He deflected.
"The numbers speak for themselves," said Jeffries.
I tried again.
"But those districts — are they that different from what you represent? And yet they weren't willing to vote for you, Mr. speaker-designate?"
No response.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks at a news conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington. Jeffries secured the Democratic nomination for speaker in a closed-door caucus vote on Wednesday, positioning him to become the first Black speaker of the House in January. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
The lack of support for Jeffries from the dissidents annoyed Rep. Marilyn Strickland (D-Wash.).
"This idea that Hakeem Jeffries has not earned this is completely absurd. He has worked hard. He's done everything he needed to do," said Strickland.

Rep. Nydia Velázquez (D-N.Y.) is retiring at the end of this Congress. She opposed Valdez as her successor. She was bewildered that Valdez and Avila Chevalier wouldn’t support their hometown, Big Apple Congressman for speaker.
"My advice to them is take the time to know how this institution runs and what it takes to be successful here," said an agitated Velázquez.
Rep. Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.) served with Jeffries in the state legislature. He argued that Valdez and Avila Chevalier made a mistake.
"They’re going to have to answer to their constituents," said Morelle. "I think they should have been with Hakeem Jeffries who’s led us to this historic majority."
And if you aren’t on the team in politics, the team also isn’t on you.
"It is a small group that marginalized themselves," said Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) about the holdouts.
However, Representative-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) saw it differently.

"They all got elected with very different constituencies. A lot of them have different priorities," said Koh. "There are things that their constituencies have demanded. And they want to make sure have the audience of the leader."
Rep. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) believed there was strategy in the dissent.
"They probably chose to do this because it's a way of lifting up their issues," said Landsman.

And keep in mind, this wasn’t the actual vote for speaker. That comes on the floor in January. It’s a win-win for Jeffries and the holdouts if they forge an accord. He promises them certain votes. And they can then tout what they extracted from the next speaker.
This is politics.
But let’s put the 11 defections into context.

Democrats flipped the House in 2018. In the internal caucus election, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) lost 32 votes. In the vote for speaker in January 2019, 12 Democrats voted for someone else. Three members voted present.
"Nancy Pelosi will be remembered," said Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.). "And the 30 people who voted against her will not be remembered."

title: ASRA Q. NOMANI: Inside the coordinated activist blitz that crashed Anthropic’s historic Nasdaq debut
summary: As Anthropic rang the Nasdaq opening bell in Times Square, NYPD zip-tied four protesters who blocked the doors with linked arms and pre-printed banners.
story: Protesters blocked the door outside the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square on Thursday following the AI giant's IPO. (Credit: FreedomNewsTV)

As Anthropic executives gathered inside the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square on Thursday morning to ring the opening bell for a historic $81 billion initial public offering, a tightly orchestrated coalition of far-left, socialist, environmental, anti-Israel and Democratic grassroots groups executed a staged street action outside, complete with linked-arm sit-ins, pre-printed banners and rapid-fire social media drops timed to hijack the news cycle.
"This IPO has got to go! Hey, hey, ho, ho," the staged protesters chanted to a small cadre of photographers as the audience.
"Shame! Shame!" a protester yelled to a few responding "Shame!" in response.
Protesters against rapid artificial intelligence growth demonstrate outside Anthropic headquarters on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, in San Francisco. (Noah Berger/AP Photo)
A close look at Thursday’s demonstration reveals the coordinated protest infrastructure that lawmakers have long warned is engineered to "sow discord" rather than produce meaningful policy solutions.

According to Fox News Digital's analysis, the protest was no organic, grassroots effort. Rather, 14 groups, several of them part of well-funded organizations with estimated combined annual revenues of $43 million, coordinated the protest with a careful run-of-show and media choreography.

A Fox News Digital tracker of the Anthropic protest organizers reveals a well-orchestrated effort across multiple organizations. They represent a spectrum of views from socialists to far-left environmental groups and anti-Israel activists.
CHAOS INC.: COMMUNISTS, ANTIFA, AGITATORS IN THE RED-GREEN ALLIANCE
A series of socialist, far-left, anti-Israel and radical environmental organizations announce a protest against the Anthropic IPO on Nov. 19, 2026. (Climate Defiance)

Roughly 21 hours before the market opened, around 5:45 p.m. EST on Wednesday, the activist network laid the groundwork online, complete with an "Anthropic IPO Day of Action Toolkit" for actions in New York City and the company's San Francisco headquarters, providing ready-made organizing tips to activists with pre-produced graphics, directions to "comment-storm Anthropic's official pages" and "some ideas for signage."

In a joint Instagram announcement, posted by Climate Defenders Action and amplified by Climate Defiance and other partner accounts, organizers summoned demonstrators to 43rd Street and Broadway in New York City at 9 a.m. "sharp" on Thursday. Last week, activists from Climate Defiance heckled New York Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, calling him a "traitor."

The digital flyer, emblazoned with "STOP AI TECH OLIGARCHS: RALLY AGAINST THE ANTHROPIC IPO," framed the listing as an existential threat to working Americans. Organizers claimed Anthropic was rushing to cash in before an "AI bubble" bursts, arguing that fast-track index inclusion rules would force workers’ 401(k)s and municipal pension funds to buy inflated shares while tech billionaires walk away with billions.
The "Day of Action Toolkit" included sign slogan suggestions like "FREEZE AI," the precise language that landed on one sign in New York City.
INSIDE THE PROTEST PLAYBOOK TO VILIFY ISRAEL ON 'GLOBAL DAY OF ACTION'
People protest as the Anthropic logo is displayed on the Nasdaq MarketSite building as part of the Anthropic IPO in New York, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Andres Kudacki/AP Photo)
The promotional flyer and Instagram collaborator tags reveal a cross-movement coalition spanning socialist, environmentalist, anti-Israel and progressive advocacy groups:

The "Red," socialist, "anti-capitalist" and far-left: New York City Democratic Socialists of America, Democratic Socialists of America's "Tech Action Working Group," New York Communities for Change, "Stop Funding Billionaires," "Empire Must Fall" and "Quit GPT." These groups drove the "anti-oligarch" economic narrative, accusing Wall Street and tech executives of rigging financial markets and risking public pensions .The First "Green," anti-Israel, pro-Palestinian networks: Jewish Voice for Peace NYC and the Europe Palestine Network. Despite the event being a domestic tech IPO, these groups injected foreign-policy grievances directly into the rally, accusing U.S. tech companies of profiteering off "Israel’s genocide in Palestine" and "US war crimes in Iran."

The Second "Green," radical climate activism: Climate Defiance, Climate Defenders, Sunrise Movement NYC, and Planet Over Profit. This wing targeted the massive energy and water demands of AI data centers, warning of an escalating "climate emergency."The "Blue," mainstream progressive and Democratic activism: NY Indivisible – whose Instagram handle pairs the grassroots progressive Indivisible brand with watermelon, Palestinian and Congolese flag emojis — alongside legacy healthcare activist group ACT UP NY, which protested the use of AI in medical screening and healthcare administration.

Police arrest a protester outside the Nasdaq MarketSite in Times Square after the opening bell ceremony marking Anthropic's initial public offering in New York on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Andres Kudacki/AP Photo)
On Thursday morning, activists arrived outside Nasdaq’s glass-walled studio at 9 a.m., positioning themselves directly beneath glowing Times Square billboards bearing the ANTHROPIC logo.

The Visual Setup: Demonstrators unfurled large red, yellow and black banners reading "FREEZE AI: END ICE, END WAR," "STOP TECH OLIGARCHS" and "AI OUT OF OUR HEALTHCARE!" Organizers used megaphones to deliver speeches linking Anthropic's market debut to ICE deportations, police surveillance and overseas military strikes.

The Staged Blockade: As the 9:30 a.m. opening bell rang inside and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei prepared to exit the building, a smaller core of activists moved in front of the Nasdaq entrance doors. Sitting shoulder-to-shoulder on the pavement in front of revolving doors – while NYPD officers and private security looked on – protesters linked arms and held banners across their laps to block access. Their banners didn't include their branding, a strategy that organizers sometimes use to make a protest look more organic.

The Arrests and On-Camera Soundbites: NYPD officers moved in to clear the entrance, placing four demonstrators in zip-tie restraints. Rather than resisting quietly, detainees used the "perp walk" to deliver rehearsed talking points directly into activist cameras. Indivisible's New York chapter shared the "perp walk" videos across its social media followers, with photographers scrambling beside the detainees.

One masked demonstrator — captioned on screen with his speech about "an IPO" — argued to onlookers and social media cameras that corporations were rushing public offerings to "receive assets" at the expense of everyday workers .

From the "Action Toolkit," the organizers wrote their own narrative: "Every newspaper and talk show in the world will cover this IPO," the organizers at "Quit GPT" wrote.

"If we take action publicly, in the streets, on social media and in Anthropic’s own comments, then this will be swept up in the press story. It could be enough to change the headlines from 'Anthropic delivers best IPO in history' to 'Anthropic IPOs amidst safety outcry.'"

title: Trump scores key win over House progressive accused of assaulting ICE agent
summary: New Jersey Rep. LaMonica McIver says she faces 17 years in prison after the 3rd Circuit refused to reconsider her ICE charges at Delaney Hall.
story: Rep. LaMonica McIver confronted DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin during a heated House hearing on Thursday.
The Trump administration scored another win in court Thursday over a House progressive who was accused of assaulting federal immigration agents at a facility in New Jersey in 2025.

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., was denied her request that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit reconsider its August 2026 decision that would have her face at least two of the three charges related to a confrontation between Democrats and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at Delaney Hall in Newark, New Jersey.

McIver previously tried to invoke the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause in order to evade the charges, but the federal court's three-judge panel denied that motion in a 2-1 decision earlier this year. Thursday's order upholds that decision.
EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET
President Donald Trump smiles while meeting with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at the White House on Oct. 7, 2025. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

"Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison," McIver said in a statement. "Now, due to the disappointing decision by the Third Circuit, we are all one step closer to a world in which the President of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for."
McIver called the result "disappointing" and said she and her lawyers "are looking at every possible option for what comes next."
WATCH: AMERICA’S FIRST ‘FORMERLY UNDOCUMENTED’ CONGRESSMAN DELIVERS ULTIMATUM AT BESIEGED ICE FACILITY

An unannounced visit to the Delaney Hall detention center by a group of Democratic officials devolved into chaos in May 2025 that culminated in a physical standoff between federal lawmakers and ICE agents and the arrest of Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. McIver was charged with three counts, including assaulting and impeding federal officers.
McIver initially argued that her actions fell under her constitutionally protected duties as a member of Congress and, therefore, she could not be prosecuted.
Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., exits the grounds at Delaney Hall ICE detention center on May 9, 2025, in Newark, N.J. (Angelina Katsanis/AP)

But a 2-1 decision issued in August 2026 by Biden-appointed Judge Cindy Chung and Trump-appointed Judge Stephanos Bibas stated that McIver's argument of legislative immunity would not stand for two of the three counts, while the third count was sent back to a lower court for further review.

Court documents say McIver allegedly "slammed her forearm" into a federal officer trying to arrest Baraka. On that count, the federal appellate court agreed with a lower court decision that her "alleged intervention into the Mayor’s questionable arrest had no cognizable connection to any legislative function" protected by the Constitution.
NEW JERSEY AGITATORS BITE, KICK AND PUNCH ICE AGENTS AS DELANEY HALL CLASHES CONTINUE; 9 MORE ARRESTED: DHS
The second count alleged that McIver used both of her forearms to "strike [an officer] as she returned inside of the secured area of Delaney Hall."
Newark's Delaney Hall, being used by ICE, has seen a significant amount of controversy over the last two years. (Michael Nigro/Getty Images)
The two judges wrote, "Like the acts charged in Count One, the acts of pushing past and forcibly striking someone are unambiguously non-legislative: they are not integral to the legislative process."
Judge Thomas Ambro wrote in dissent, "When an Executive Branch official prevents a Member from entering a DHS facility, she is denied effective access to an oversight inspection."

The case could make it all the way to the Supreme Court if McIver continues fighting against the charges.

title: $1M-a-day China tech crackdown proposed amid cascade of US cyber disruptions
summary: Rep. Pat Harrigan says his Digital Infrastructure Act of 2026 would bar high-risk carriers from U.S. data centers and cloud services, with $1M daily fines.
story: Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., says Chinese telecom companies that lost federal operating authorizations can still maintain a foothold in American digital infrastructure.

FIRST ON FOX — Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., wants to close a glaring national-security loophole that allows Chinese entities to cohabitate the same data centers where critical American services also run.

The North Carolina lawmaker is proposing the Digital Infrastructure Act of 2026 to address the potential risk with a $1 million-per-day fine for violators. Meanwhile, the U.S. has experienced a series of outages and incidents this week that have put a microscope on the potential for foreign cyber threats and have prompted skepticism regarding U.S. readiness to defend against digital weaknesses.

"Look, the federal government already determined that companies like China Telecom and China Unicom posed a threat to our national security and revoked their licenses to operate here," Harrigan said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"But those companies were still able to maintain connections inside of American data centers. So, if we think about that, we determined that they were too dangerous to operate here, but we left them with a foothold in the very infrastructure that carries Americans' information."
An Amazon Web Services data center in Stone Ridge, Virginia, on July 28, 2024. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE

Despite the cascade of outages — including in U.S. air traffic control systems, Microsoft and banking services —Harrigan did not directly draw a line between Chinese companies and the disrupted services. There is also no proof that any of the incidents were the result of cyberattacks.
Harrigan, instead, argued that preventing cyber vulnerabilities in the future requires lawmakers to eliminate what they know to be weaknesses now.
"What we're talking about is the infrastructure that supports our banks, our hospitals, our businesses and our communication systems," Harrigan said.

He declined to elaborate on whether the existing loophole has already led to cyberattacks or stolen data but noted that he was made aware of the liability when American businesses approached him with concerns.

His bill would prohibit high-risk carriers from owning or operating a data center in the U.S. or offering cloud services to Americans. The measure would be enforced by a $1 million fine for every day of a continuing violation — a penalty that would extend to affiliates and even American venture partners doing business with Chinese entities.
The bill also includes a time-limited exception for companies approved by American communications officials.
CHINA’S GREAT AI CHIP LOOPHOLE: HOW AMERICAN ESPIONAGE STOPPED CHINA — THIS TIME

An airport departures board, left, displaying multiple flights marked as canceled pictured alongside Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., right. (Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images; Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"We talked to a lot of companies, frontier labs and data center owners, as well as operators that are concerned about this," Harrigan said. "And it's also part of folks from our national security apparatus within government."

As part of its mission, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) reviews foreign communication companies and green-lights their operation in the U.S. When identifying a security risk, the FCC issues a denial of application, a power granted to it under Section 214 of the Communications Act of 1934.
In China’s case, companies like China Telecom Corporation, China Unicom Operations Limited and Pacific Networks Corp. have all failed to secure FCC authorization for security reasons.

"The Commission finds that due to several factors related to China Mobile USA’s ownership and control by the Chinese government, grant of the application would raise substantial and serious national security and law enforcement risks," the FCC wrote in its evaluation of China Mobile USA, a Delaware-based company.
Even so, the FCC order does not address what the company needs to do with its hardware.
"A Section 214 order is a license to sell regulated telecom service, not a physical eviction order," Harrigan’s office noted.

Asked if he believes Republicans will be able to address the legislation before the end of the 119th Congress, Harrigan said he believes the issue will likely have to be left to the next session, which begins in January.
FOREIGN ADVERSARIES RUNNING 'PSYOP' TO FUEL ANTI-AI AND ANTI-DATA CENTER MOVEMENT, WAR OFFICIAL SAYS
The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., is seen on Nov. 5, 2025. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
He voiced optimism that the incoming Democratic majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate might recognize his bill as part of a larger interest in AI security.

"This is a bipartisan problem. And there's a lot of work that I have done with my Democratic colleagues over this last year on artificial intelligence and the next generation of technology in our market economy and how that intertwines with our nation's defense," Harrigan said.
