title: Trump's historic summit with Xi, Putin marks diplomatic milestone, but breakthroughs remain elusive
summary: Donald Trump declares the U.S., China and Russia are "really making history" as nuclear arms reduction and an end to the Ukraine war anchor the summit.
story: The leaders of the United States, Russia and China gathered in Shenzhen for historic three-way talks, emphasizing the importance of continued diplomacy and maintaining open dialogue despite longstanding differences.

President Donald Trump joined the leaders of China and Russia Thursday for an unprecedented three-way summit, marking a historic moment in global diplomacy as the three powers discussed nuclear arms reductions, the war in Ukraine and global security without announcing a major breakthrough.

The unprecedented three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin underscored the leaders' commitment to continued diplomacy, with Trump emphasizing the importance of maintaining dialogue among rival nuclear powers.

Trump left the trilateral meeting, which lasted more than an hour, around 5 a.m. ET and headed to the airport. He is not expected to deliver public remarks before flying back to Washington, Fox News reported.
"We are really making history," Trump declared during the meeting in Shenzhen, China, as he sought to cast the gathering itself as a diplomatic achievement.
CHINA WATCHDOG WARNS TRUMP FACES ‘2-ON-1’ SHOWDOWN WITH XI, PUTIN AS TAIWAN RISKS MOUNT
The three leaders are meeting on the sidelines of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by China from November 18–19. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
The three leaders sat down at a roundtable just after 3 a.m. ET, roughly two hours behind schedule.
Trump argued that bringing the three leaders together offered an opportunity to address issues that had long divided their countries.
"Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," Trump said. "But no problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them."
"Together we are choosing a different course," he added.
Ahead of the summit, Trump told Fox News' Jacqui Heinrich that he wanted to meet with Xi and Putin together "because they work together, they have a relationship."
Trump argued that previous U.S. policies had helped bring Moscow and Beijing closer together, despite their historically strained relationship.
"They were natural enemies, but because of Obama, not Biden, it was Obama before he drove them together because of energy," Trump said.

Russia and China had a fractured relationship for decades following their split in the 1960s, but energy ties deepened through a major 2014 gas deal signed during Obama's presidency after roughly a decade of negotiations.

President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin attend a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on November 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Xi, who hosted the gathering, called the meeting a "groundbreaking move" and stressed the responsibility of the three powers to maintain global stability. However, no substantial breakthroughs were immediately announced.
"Our positive interaction is not optional, but a must," Xi said through a translator, arguing that the countries must work together to confront global challenges and preserve international peace.

Putin similarly emphasized the countries' shared responsibility for international security, pointing to their status as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council before turning to one of the summit's most pressing issues: the war in Ukraine.
KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including, obviously, the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said through a translator.
The Russian president confirmed that Ukraine had been a focus of his earlier bilateral meeting with Trump, saying the discussion took place at the American president's initiative.
UKRAINE STRIKES 'ONE OF THE LARGEST OIL REFINERIES' IN SOUTHERN RUSSIA AHEAD OF PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING IN CHINA

Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin take part in a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026. (Mandel NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)
Trump also addressed the conflict directly, saying he believed both sides wanted to bring the fighting to an end.
"I think things are happening," Trump said. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war."
The historic summit followed separate meetings between Trump and the two leaders. Trump met with Putin for approximately 40 minutes before holding a meeting with Xi that lasted more than an hour.
The president also raised the possibility of broader nuclear arms reductions while acknowledging the difficulty of persuading nuclear-armed nations to surrender their weapons.
"It's a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them," Trump said.
KIM JONG UN'S NUCLEAR BUILDUP SPARKS 'SERIOUS CONCERN' AHEAD OF TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT
President Xi Jinping listens as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation. (Andres Martinez Casares - Pool/Getty Images)

Trump said ahead of the trilateral meeting that the leaders would discuss nuclear proliferation, including Iran, and indicated he would propose ways to protect national sovereignty from international organizations, singling out the International Criminal Court.

Trump held separate bilateral meetings with Putin and Xi earlier in the day, first meeting with the Russian leader at the APEC summit site before traveling to Kylin Villa, a government-owned lakeside resort, for talks with the Chinese president.
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SANCTIONS SITTING PRESIDENT OF THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT FOR 'ABUSES OF POWER'

Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump shake hands as leaders take a group photo during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen. (Sergei BOBYLYOV/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Trump said his meeting with Putin helped "set the stage" for the trilateral talks and expressed hope that cooperation with China could help end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

"The dialogue between President Putin and President Trump, which the entire world is watching closely, is crucial both to resolving the conflict in Ukraine and to advancing relations between Russia and the United States, including economic cooperation," Special Envoy to the Russian President Kirill Dmitriev told Fox News Digital.

"Both presidents are committed to finding a peaceful solution to the Ukraine conflict. There are, of course, forces in Europe and elsewhere seeking to derail this process, but the importance of this dialogue cannot be overstated," Dmitriev added.

Prior to his meeting with Xi, Trump identified Iran as an area of potential cooperation with Beijing, emphasizing the importance of keeping energy flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and preventing Tehran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL

Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump ride an escalator ahead of the plenary session during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen. (Vyacheslav PROKOFYEV/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

"Both the United States and China have an interest in ensuring that energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, and that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon," Trump said. "We both feel that very strongly on both points."
TRUMP KICKS OFF HIGH-STAKES ASIA TRIP WITH XI, PUTIN MEETINGS LOOMING ON WORLD STAGE
World leaders pose for a "family photo" during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Qilai Shen/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Speaking on China's own turf amid a fierce technological rivalry between Washington and Beijing, Trump asserted American dominance in artificial intelligence, declaring the U.S. the world leader in "superintelligence" and claiming Americans invented the technology.
"Americans invented. We just invented [superintelligence], and it is unleashing extraordinary prosperity and growth for people all around the globe," Trump said.

Trump described superintelligence as the greatest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution, acknowledging that the technology has "some bad elements" that must be carefully managed while rejecting international efforts to regulate it.
TRUMP CANNOT DETER XI AND PUTIN’S NUCLEAR GOALS WITH A STRATEGY DESIGNED FOR JUST ONE

President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump shake hands during a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen. (Photo by Vyacheslav PROKOFYEV/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

The competition over advanced technology also surfaced in a tense moment involving the press, when a Bloomberg reporter was barred from the trilateral meeting after questioning Trump about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during an earlier bilateral session.

The reporter had asked Trump, "President Trump, has Jensen Huang been disloyal to the United States?" Chinese officials blocked her access to the trilateral talks despite efforts by White House officials to have her reinstated, according to a White House pool report.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Supreme Court urged to defang ‘criminal trap’ that has sent Trump officials to prison
summary: Peter Navarro asks the Supreme Court to overturn his contempt of Congress convictions, arguing willfulness could make such prosecutions harder to prove.
story: Abhi Kambli, Navarro's attorney, says a ruling in his favor could curb the 'weaponization' of congressional subpoenas by making contempt convictions harder to secure.

A Trump administration official who served four months in federal prison for defying a congressional subpoena is asking the Supreme Court to overturn his convictions in a case that could raise the bar for criminally prosecuting others who refuse to comply with Congress’s demands.

Peter Navarro, who was a senior trade advisor to President Donald Trump during his first administration, filed a petition with the Supreme Court last month. Navarro currently serves in the Trump administration as senior counselor for trade and manufacturing. He was convicted in 2023 on two counts of contempt of Congress stemming from his refusal to provide testimony and documents to the Democratic-led House Jan. 6 committee on the grounds that he believed he was barred by executive privilege.
If the justices take the case, they could make it harder to convict someone for defying a congressional subpoena by requiring proof that the person knew they were breaking the law.
JUDGE TOSSES CASE AGAINST EX-FBI OFFICIALS ACCUSED OF LYING TO CONGRESS ABOUT HUNTER BIDEN INVESTIGATION

Peter Navarro, White House senior counselor for trade and manufacturing, during a television interview at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Monday, July 7, 2025. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Before Navarro’s trial, U. S. District Judge Amit Mehta ruled in August 2023 that he had failed to establish that Trump invoked executive privilege for the subpoena, barring him from relying on that claim as a defense. After serving his sentence, Navarro appealed his conviction to the U. S. Court of Appeals for the D. C. Circuit, which ruled that a person violates federal law by refusing to comply with a subpoena "even if he subjectively and mistakenly believed his default was lawful. "
The three-judge panel ruled that only the president can invoke executive privilege under Article II, and Trump never granted Navarro protection.

"Dr. Navarro claimed executive privilege before even seeing the subpoena and refused to turn over documents, appear for his deposition, or engage with the Select Committee’s efforts to accommodate his privilege claim," the court wrote.
"A court, in other words, cannot simply take a defendant at his word that the President invoked privilege because doing so would impermissibly tangle separation-of-powers lines."

But Abhishek Kambli, counsel for Navarro, argued the D.C. Circuit misinterpreted the statute, pointing to United States v. Murdock. In that 1933 ruling, the Supreme Court held that the presence of the word "willfully" in one part of a statute, but not another, required them to be interpreted differently — allowing a taxpayer's sincere, mistaken belief about his Constitutional rights to serve as a valid defense against acting "willfully."

"We absolutely believe that we are correct on the law on this, because Congress chose to use the word willful when it put this statute together, and there's no reason to believe that willful applies any differently in this context than it has in just about every other one, but it would have the added effect of toning down lawfare and weaponization if we were to succeed," Kambli told Fox News Digital.

The House voted to hold Navarro in contempt for failing to comply with a subpoena, but Kambli argued the Jan. 6 committee bypassed the negotiations traditionally used to resolve disputes involving executive branch officials.
WHITE HOUSE LAWYER'S HARDBALL WARNING TO DEMS HAS LEGAL EXPERTS ON BOTH SIDES QUESTIONING ONE KEY THREAT

U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., gives remarks to media outside the House Democratic Caucus meeting in the Longworth House Office Building on Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

"When it comes to executive branch officials, there was an accommodation process where they would negotiate terms of the appearance of the witness that's an executive branch official, and then determined whether executive privilege applies or not," Kambli told Fox News Digital. "What happened with the J-6 committee is that they short-circuited a lot of that and sent people straight to getting prosecuted and indicted."
Kambli said a Supreme Court ruling in Navarro's favor could help "tone down the weaponization that could potentially occur" once Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.

"What would happen is that if we were to win and the correct mental state is required to prove someone violated this law and get convicted and sent to jail, you would have fewer prosecutions for contempt of Congress because they're going to be much harder to prove," Kambli told Fox News Digital. "And what will happen is that there's less of an opportunity to wield a congressional subpoena in a weaponized manner rather than just through a legitimate legislative purpose, which Congress is limited to traditionally."

Navarro’s lawyers filed the petition a week before Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., called for an investigation of alleged Trump administration corruption, saying cases targeting those who "enabled" the president could send a "deterrence message" to young people considering administration jobs.

Following Democrats’ wins in the 2026 midterm elections, lawmakers took to social media to vow investigations into Trump officials, with House Oversight Committee ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., posting on X, "LAWYER UP." However, Republicans still control both chambers of Congress until Democrats take control in January 2027.

"We can't keep this up where people are utilizing lawfare and other weaponization tactics to harm their political opponents, so we think that this petition would protect everyone in the long term and allow our politics to be better, because we're not constantly trying to utilize congressional subpoenas as a way to indict people," Kambli told Fox News Digital.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Steve Bannon speaks at the National Conservatism Conference in Washington D.C., Sept. 3, 2025. (Photo by Dominic Gwinn / Middle East Images via AFP)

Mike Davis, a conservative lawyer and founder and president of the Article III Project, which filed an amicus brief supporting the petition, said the Supreme Court must take this case up to end "lawfare."

"Democrats weaponized Congress to throw Peter Navarro in prison for standing up for President Trump’s executive privilege in good faith," Davis said. "The D.C. Circuit then ruled that good faith is no defense to contempt of Congress, and that turns every congressional subpoena into a criminal trap. It tears up more than two centuries of negotiation between the co-equal branches."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The petition from Navarro comes after the Supreme Court vacated the ruling against Steve Bannon. The former Trump White House strategist served four months in federal prison in 2024 after being convicted of two counts of contempt of Congress for defying a subpoena from the House Jan. 6 committee. In April 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the D.C. Circuit’s decision in his case and sent it back for further proceedings following the Justice Department's motion to dismiss his indictment.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Trump's China trip: Historic Xi-Putin talks, 'superintelligence' boast and other top moments
summary: President Donald Trump declared the U.S. the world leader in "superintelligence" at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, staking a tech claim amid the AI rivalry.
story: President Donald Trump meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of trilateral talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

President Donald Trump's visit to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit featured an elaborate welcome, warm exchanges with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and a declaration of American technological dominance on Chinese soil.

The gathering in Shenzhen culminated in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia, with nuclear arms reductions and the war in Ukraine among the issues on the table.
Here are some of the standout moments from Trump's visit.
XI BREAKS PROTOCOL TO PERSONALLY WELCOME TRUMP AHEAD OF HISTORIC TRILATERAL SUMMIT AND MORE TOP HEADLINES
Trump touts US 'superintelligence' on China's turf
Trump declared the United States the world leader in "superintelligence" during remarks at the summit Thursday, making the assertion in one of China's major technology hubs.
"The United States is also proud to be the world leader in superintelligence, the greatest technological transformation since the Industrial Revolution," Trump told APEC leaders.
The remarks came as Washington and Beijing compete for leadership in artificial intelligence and advanced semiconductors.
Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic three-way talks

Trump joined Xi and Putin for the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia just after 3 a.m. ET, calling the gathering an opportunity to reduce nuclear weapons and address global conflicts.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth," Trump said.
The president also said he had held extensive discussions with Putin about ending the war in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China November 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
"I think things are happening," Trump said. "I think that he and I hope the other side would like to see an end to that war."

Trump also raised preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons and said he would propose ways for the three countries to protect their sovereignty from the International Criminal Court, which he accused of exceeding its jurisdiction.

A Bloomberg reporter was barred from the trilateral meeting after asking Trump during his bilateral with Xi whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had been "disloyal to the United States," according to White House pool reports. Chinese officials warned that shouting questions was considered extremely rude and that reporters could be removed for doing so, despite White House efforts to secure the Bloomberg reporter's access.
Xi rolls out red carpet for Trump
Xi personally greeted Trump upon his arrival in Shenzhen Wednesday, meeting the president at the foot of the aircraft stairs in an elaborate welcome.
The two exchanged greetings before standing together for the American and Chinese national anthems. A military flyover followed, with five jets leaving trails of colored smoke overhead.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
Trump later praised the reception as a display of "great respect."

U.S. President Donald Trump (L) is greeted by President of the People's Republic of China Xi Jinping at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on November 18, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. Trump is visiting China to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping November 18–19. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)

Chinese President Xi Jinping, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin greet each other before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center on November 18, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. (Photo by Iori Sagisawa-China Pool/Getty Images)
Trump strikes warm tone with Xi, Putin
Trump offered warm words for both Xi and Putin during the summit, praising his personal relationship with the Chinese leader and referring to the Russian president as a "friend."
"President Xi and I have formed an outstanding personal relationship," Trump said during their bilateral meeting. "Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it."

U.S. President Donald Trump is greeted by China's President Xi Jinping as he arrives at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 18, 2026. (Mandel NGAN / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
Trump also told Xi, "You're my friend, and we have a very special relationship."

"Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it," he went on, telling the Chinese leader: "And I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we'll never have a problem."
During a separate encounter with Putin, Trump was heard saying, "Who is he? It's my friend. Nice to see you," according to video shared by Clash Report.

The friendly exchanges came despite ongoing tensions between Washington and Beijing over trade and technology and Trump's efforts to negotiate an end to Russia's war in Ukraine.

title: Data broker opt-out steps retirees need before the holidays
summary: A single data broker opt-out may not be enough. Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified can still expose your address and family details to scammers.
story: Artificial intelligence is rapidly accelerating elder fraud schemes across the U.S., targeting older Americans who hold a significant share of household wealth. ScamSkeptic founder Matt Sanner joins 'America's Newsroom' to highlight how fraudsters utilize AI to mimic voices and create deepfakes. Sanner provides key strategies for families to identify these scams and protect their vulnerable loved ones.

Many retirees think they're protecting their privacy by staying off social media, removing their information from one people-search site or paying for credit monitoring. But a single data broker opt-out request may leave your home address, phone number and family details exposed elsewhere. With the holidays approaching, now is a good time to find out what's available about you online and take steps to remove it.

People-search sites like Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified can make personal details available to strangers. Some information is free to view, while more detailed reports may require payment. And here's where it gets concerning. A scammer who knows your grandson's name or where your daughter lives could use those details to make a fake emergency call sound convincing. Here's where that information comes from, how to remove it and what you can do to help protect your family before the holidays.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Submitting opt-out requests and checking for new listings regularly can help reduce your personal information online. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Where your personal information comes from

You don't need a social media account to have your information collected. Data brokers gather information from public records, including property deeds, voter registration records where accessible and court filings. They may also obtain details from commercial databases, online activity and companies that collect personal information. Over time, those details can become part of a profile showing where you live, previous addresses, phone numbers and possible family connections.

According to the Federal Trade Commission, opting out of one people-search site doesn't remove your information from others. Your details may also reappear when public records change or websites collect updated information. For older adults, the financial risks can be especially serious. An FTC report released in October 2026 found that adults ages 60 and older reported approximately $3 billion in fraud losses during 2025. Although older adults reported losing money to fraud less frequently than younger adults overall, their reported individual losses tended to be higher.

You can use a free exposure scanner at CyberGuy.com to check whether your personal information appears on publicly searchable websites. Keep in mind that a free scan cannot uncover every private data broker database. The results might surprise you.
The data broker opt-out steps to take now
You can start removing your personal information yourself without paying for a service.

Search for your information. Look up your name on major people-search sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified, Intelius and TruthFinder. Try searching your phone number and home address, too.Find each site's opt-out page. Look for links labeled "Opt Out," "Remove My Information" or "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information." You can usually find these in the website's footer or privacy policy.Submit removal requests. Follow each site's instructions. Some may require email confirmation or other verification. Share only the personal information necessary to complete the request, and make sure you're using the legitimate website.Keep a record of your requests. Save the website addresses and dates when you submitted them. This makes it easier to follow up if your information remains visible.Check again regularly. Return after about a month to see whether your information has been removed. Then check every few months because new listings may appear.Freeze your credit. Contact Experian, Equifax and TransUnion to request a free credit freeze. This can help prevent identity thieves from opening new credit accounts in your name.
Search for your information. Look up your name on major people-search sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified, Intelius and TruthFinder. Try searching your phone number and home address, too.

Find each site's opt-out page. Look for links labeled "Opt Out," "Remove My Information" or "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information." You can usually find these in the website's footer or privacy policy.

Submit removal requests. Follow each site's instructions. Some may require email confirmation or other verification. Share only the personal information necessary to complete the request, and make sure you're using the legitimate website.
Keep a record of your requests. Save the website addresses and dates when you submitted them. This makes it easier to follow up if your information remains visible.
Check again regularly. Return after about a month to see whether your information has been removed. Then check every few months because new listings may appear.
Freeze your credit. Contact Experian, Equifax and TransUnion to request a free credit freeze. This can help prevent identity thieves from opening new credit accounts in your name.

A credit freeze won't remove your information from data brokers, and credit monitoring generally alerts you to possible problems rather than preventing your details from appearing online. These tools serve different purposes.

One thing to remember: Removing your information from people-search sites doesn't erase public records. Your details may still appear in property records, court documents or even listings connected to family members. That's why it's important to check more than your own name. Doing this yourself can take hours, especially when you're dealing with multiple websites. And because data brokers continue collecting information, the work may need to be repeated.
DATA BROKER OPT-OUT: HOW RETIREES CAN PROTECT THEIR DATA
Searching for your personal information online is the first step toward identifying data broker listings you may want removed. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Free tools that can help remove your information
Before paying for a data removal service, there are two other options worth knowing about.

Google offers a free tool called Results about you that can help you find personal information appearing in Google Search. Depending on eligibility, you may be able to request the removal of results containing your home address, phone number or email address.
Here's how to get started:

Open the Google app and tap your profile picture, then select Results about you. You can also access the tool through Google's website.Select Get started or Settings.Enter your name and the personal contact information you want Google to check.Review any matching results and request removal of eligible listings.Check the tool for updates on your requests.
Open the Google app and tap your profile picture, then select Results about you. You can also access the tool through Google's website.
Select Get started or Settings.
Enter your name and the personal contact information you want Google to check.
Review any matching results and request removal of eligible listings.
Check the tool for updates on your requests.
Keep in mind that removing a Google search result doesn't delete the information from the original website. You may still need to contact the site directly.

If you live in California, you have another option. The state's free Delete Request and Opt-out Platform, called DROP, launched in January 2026. It allows eligible California residents to submit a single deletion request covering more than 600 registered data brokers.

Beginning Aug. 1, 2026, covered data brokers were required to start processing requests through the system. Removal can take time, and some information may be exempt under the law. You can submit a request and check its status at California's official DROP website at privacy.ca.gov/drop/. Other states also have privacy laws that may give residents additional rights to request deletion of their information.
WHY REMOVING YOUR DATA ONLINE MAY STILL LEAVE YOUR FAMILY EXPOSED
Retirees can unknowingly have their home addresses, phone numbers and family details listed on people-search websites. (iStock)
How a personal data removal service can help
If you don't want to spend hours contacting websites and tracking removal requests, a personal data removal service can help.
These services contact data brokers on your behalf and submit requests to remove your personal information. Depending on the provider and plan, features may include:

Automated removal requests sent to participating data brokers and people-search websites.Recurring removal requests to help address personal information that reappears online.Progress tracking so you can monitor the status of removal requests.Family protection options that allow you to include additional family members.Custom removal requests for websites that may not be covered by standard automated services.
Automated removal requests sent to participating data brokers and people-search websites.
Recurring removal requests to help address personal information that reappears online.
Progress tracking so you can monitor the status of removal requests.
Family protection options that allow you to include additional family members.
Custom removal requests for websites that may not be covered by standard automated services.

Some services offer ongoing monitoring and follow-up requests, which can save time compared with handling each website yourself. It's important to understand that no service can guarantee every piece of personal information will disappear from the internet. Public records may remain accessible, and some websites may fall outside the service's coverage. Still, reducing the number of places where your information appears can make your personal details harder to find.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Bring this conversation to the Thanksgiving table

Thanksgiving brings families together, making it a great opportunity to talk about protecting everyone's personal information. You don't need to make it a lengthy discussion. A few simple checks can help everyone understand what scammers may already know about them.

After dinner, sit down with a family member and search your names on a few people-search sites. Look for home addresses, phone numbers and family connections. If you find something you don't want publicly available, discuss how to request its removal. Check your parents' information, too, with their permission. Even if you've removed your own details, your name or address may still appear in a relative's profile.

Choose a private phrase that family members can use if someone calls claiming there's an emergency. Avoid birthdays, pet names or other details someone could easily discover online. Agree on the phrase privately rather than sharing it in a group chat. A code word adds another layer of protection, but it shouldn't be your only way to verify someone's identity.

If someone claims to be a grandchild or another relative who urgently needs money, don't send anything until you've checked the story. Hang up and call your loved one directly using a phone number you already know. If you can't reach them, contact another trusted family member. Scammers can now use AI voice cloning to sound like someone you love. That means even a familiar voice may not be enough to prove who's calling. Learn more about how AI voice scams can clone your family's voice and what you can do to protect yourself. And be especially suspicious if someone demands payment through gift cards, cryptocurrency or wire transfers.

Agree that nobody will send emergency money based solely on an unexpected phone call or text. If something sounds suspicious, contact another family member before taking action. Scammers often pressure people to respond immediately or keep the situation secret. The more your family talks about these tactics ahead of time, the easier it becomes to recognize a suspicious request. Scammers may already know more about your family than you realize. A private code word adds protection, but always confirm an unexpected emergency by contacting your loved one directly before sending money.
Kurt's key takeaways

Here's what concerns me. You can be careful about what you share online and still have your home address, phone number and family details available on people-search sites. Removing that information once is a good start, but it can show up again. That's why I recommend checking these sites regularly or using a trusted data removal service to help handle the work. And with Thanksgiving bringing families together, this is a great time to talk about scams and make sure everyone knows what to do if a suspicious call comes in. A few simple steps now could help keep your family's personal information out of the wrong hands.

title: Apple Photos AI watermark can tag your real pictures
summary: Apple Photos now embeds an invisible SynthID watermark in images edited with Apple Intelligence tools like Clean Up, Extend and Reframe in iOS 27.2.
story: Apple's Clean Up, Extend and Reframe tools let you change photos using AI, with certain edits now receiving an invisible SynthID watermark. (Apple)

You take a great family photo, but there's one problem. Someone you don't know walked into the background. So you open Apple Photos, use Clean Up to remove the person and save your picture. Problem solved, right? Well, there's something new happening behind the scenes.

With iOS 27.2, Apple Photos can now add an invisible AI watermark to pictures you edit using certain Apple Intelligence tools. You won't see it on your screen. And if you share the photo, the person receiving it probably won't notice anything different either. But the watermark could still be there.

Apple introduced the feature in its Oct. 26 update. It uses Google's SynthID technology to identify images created or modified with artificial intelligence. Even a photo you took yourself can receive this hidden marker after certain AI edits. So how does it work, and what does it mean for the photos you share?
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
STOP LOSING PHOTO QUALITY WHEN YOU SHARE PICTURES
Why Apple Photos is adding invisible AI watermarks

AI photo editing has come a long way. What once required complicated software can now take a few taps on your phone. That's convenient when you want to improve a picture. However, it also makes it harder to tell what's real. Someone can remove an important detail from a photo without leaving an obvious trace. AI can even generate parts of a scene that the camera never captured.

Apple's new watermarking feature gives people a way to tell when AI has been used to create or change an image. According to Apple's official support documentation, certain Apple Intelligence tools now add a hidden SynthID watermark when you create or edit images.

SynthID is technology developed by Google. It embeds a digital signal into an image that compatible detection tools can recognize. The watermark doesn't visibly change your photo. There's no stamp across the bottom or warning in the corner. Instead, the marker remains hidden unless someone checks the image with a SynthID detector.
Which Apple Photos tools add an AI watermark?
Apple says the feature applies to certain Apple Intelligence tools starting with iOS 27.2. Here's where you might encounter it.

Clean Up lets you erase distractions from your pictures. Maybe someone wandered into your vacation photo. Or perhaps there's an object in the background you wish you could remove. You can use Clean Up to erase that distraction while AI fills in the missing area. With iOS 27.2, some photos edited this way can receive a SynthID watermark. However, Apple doesn't say that every small edit will trigger one. The watermark can depend on the changes made to the image.

Have you ever taken a picture and realized you were standing too close? Apple's Extend tool can help by generating additional scenery beyond the original edges of your photo. For example, you might have cropped out part of a building. Extend can generate additional background to make the composition look better. The result may look like you captured a wider shot in the first place. However, because AI creates part of the finished image, the photo can receive a hidden SynthID watermark. We've previously explained how Extend works in our article on fixing badly framed photos after you take them.

Apple also includes Spatial Reframing, called Reframe in Photos, among the tools covered by SynthID. Reframe lets you change the apparent perspective of a picture after you've taken it. You can adjust the angle or shift the composition while Apple Intelligence generates the necessary visual information. That can make a photo look quite different from what your camera originally captured. And because AI helps create that result, the edited image may carry a watermark.

Apple's watermarking feature also covers images generated using Image Playground and Image Wand. Image Playground lets you create images with AI using descriptions or other visual inputs. Image Wand can turn a rough sketch into a more developed image. Since these tools generate visual content, their inclusion makes sense. But Apple's decision to mark certain edits to genuine photos raises a more interesting question. Should a real photo receive an AI marker because you removed one distracting object?
NEW YORK MAKES HISTORY WITH FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND LAW REGULATING AI-POWERED COMMERCIALS
Apple Photos uses Google’s SynthID technology to mark certain AI-edited images, but detecting a watermark does not necessarily mean a picture is fake. (iStock)
How to check whether a photo has Apple's AI watermark

You might be wondering whether there's an easy way to see if a photo contains one of these hidden markers. There is, although you'll need to use an online detector. Apple recommends Google's SynthID Detector, which can analyze an uploaded image for the watermark.

Open a web browser on your iPhone, iPad, Mac or computer.Visit synthid.com.Upload the picture you want to check.Follow the on-screen instructions.Review the result to see whether the detector identifies a SynthID watermark.
Open a web browser on your iPhone, iPad, Mac or computer.
Visit synthid.com.
Upload the picture you want to check.
Follow the on-screen instructions.
Review the result to see whether the detector identifies a SynthID watermark.

One thing to understand: finding a watermark doesn't automatically mean a photo is fake. It simply indicates that AI was involved in creating or modifying the image. And the reverse is also true. If no watermark appears, that doesn't prove the picture is genuine. Other AI image generators may not use SynthID. Detection can also have limitations. I would also be careful about uploading private family pictures or sensitive images to any online service. Review how the service handles uploaded files before submitting them.
Will Apple add watermarks to your older photos?

Apple says photos created or edited before the 27.2 update won't automatically receive a new SynthID watermark from Apple. So you don't have to worry about the update going through your entire photo library and adding markers to everything.

However, that changes if you open an older picture and edit it using one of the supported AI tools. For example, you could take a photo from five years ago and use Extend to improve the framing today. The newly edited version may then receive the invisible watermark.

Apple has also expanded this feature beyond iPhones. According to the company, SynthID support begins with these software versions: iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 and visionOS 27.2. Keep in mind that the software update and Apple Intelligence have different device requirements.
OPENAI CHILD SAFETY TOOLS TARGET AI-GENERATED ABUSE

Apple’s Photos app can add invisible AI watermarks to real pictures edited with certain Apple Intelligence tools, including Clean Up, Extend and Reframe. (Photo by Katharina Kausche/Picture Alliance via Getty Images)
Which iPhones support Apple's AI photo tools?

You'll need an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone to use the editing features that trigger these watermarks. Apple Intelligence works on the iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max, along with iPhone 16 models and newer compatible iPhones. The standard iPhone 15 can install iOS 27.2, but it doesn't support these Apple Intelligence editing features. Availability may also depend on your region and language.
To check for the latest software update:
Open Settings on your iPhone.Tap General.Select Software Update.Install an available update if your device supports it.
Open Settings on your iPhone.
Tap General.
Select Software Update.
Install an available update if your device supports it.
Can invisible watermarks help you spot fake photos?

I like the idea of giving people another way to question what they're seeing online. But there's an important limitation. Let's say you use Clean Up to remove someone standing behind your family in a vacation photo. Now compare that with an AI-generated picture showing an event that never happened. Both images could carry SynthID watermarks, even though the circumstances are very different.

The detector may identify AI involvement. However, it won't necessarily explain what was changed or how significant those changes were. That's a pretty big limitation when you're trying to decide whether to trust an image.

There's also the issue of AI-generated pictures that have no detectable watermark. So, while SynthID can provide a useful clue, it shouldn't be your only way of evaluating a suspicious photo. If a picture online seems questionable, look for the original source. You can also use a reverse image search to see where a photo originally appeared and whether earlier versions exist.
Kurt's key takeaways

I can see why Apple is doing this. AI has gotten so good at changing photos that it's becoming harder to know what you're actually looking at. And I think that's a real concern. At the same time, I like having tools that can fix a great picture when someone walks into the background. Why should that photo get the same kind of watermark as a picture created entirely by AI? That's where I think Apple could do better. I'd love to see a way to check a photo and find out exactly what AI changed. Was it something minor, or did someone completely alter what happened? That's what I'd want to know before deciding whether to trust what I'm seeing.

Should Apple put a hidden AI watermark on your personal photos simply because you removed something from the background? Or should these markers be reserved for images that AI creates entirely? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fake vacation rental sites use live chat to steal your data
summary: Fortra researchers say fake vacation rental sites use live customer support chats to trick travelers into handing over credit card details this holiday.
story: Travel expert and advisor Bobby Laurie explains when Europe's ETIAS travel authorization system is expected to launch, how the application process will work and what travelers should know about potential scams taking place right now.

You're booking a vacation rental for the holidays when a message appears saying there's a problem with your reservation. Before you can figure out what's wrong, a customer support chat opens and offers to help. You're told your credit card won't be charged, but you'll need to enter the number to complete a security check. Sounds helpful, right? That's exactly what scammers want you to think.

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered fake vacation rental sites that look remarkably similar to legitimate booking platforms. Some even include live customer support chats designed to convince travelers to hand over their credit card information. With Thanksgiving travel approaching, it's worth knowing how these scams work before you book your next trip.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS
Scammers copy legitimate vacation rental listings, complete with property photos, prices and reviews, to convince travelers to hand over their credit card information. (Yuliya Taba/Getty Images)
Fake vacation rental sites are getting harder to spot

Researchers with Fortra's Intelligence and Research Experts (FIRE) team recently identified fraudulent travel-booking websites that impersonate popular vacation rental platforms. The scammers copy legitimate property listings and surround them with details you'd expect to see on a real booking site. You might recognize the familiar layout or see reviews that make a property seem trustworthy. The photos may even come from an actual vacation rental.

One example uncovered by researchers showed listings for an apartment and a house. Both appeared to be legitimate properties available for booking. Someone searching for a holiday rental could easily spend more time comparing the accommodations than questioning the website itself. That's the problem. A professional-looking listing tells you very little about who's actually running the website. Fortra says its researchers identified and remediated examples of these phishing sites. The company did not report how many travelers may have fallen for the scams or whether money was stolen.
Fake booking messages make travelers think something went wrong

The scammers also know that travel plans can be stressful, especially around the holidays. If you've already arranged transportation and suddenly see a warning about your accommodations, you're probably going to want answers.
Researchers found fraudulent booking pages displaying messages such as:
"Your reservation is unconfirmed.""Complete verification to continue.""Your payment has not been processed.""Your booking will be canceled.""Special pricing is available for a limited time."
"Your reservation is unconfirmed."
"Complete verification to continue."
"Your payment has not been processed."
"Your booking will be canceled."
"Special pricing is available for a limited time."

In one case, a fake booking page told visitors their reservation was still unconfirmed. To finish the process, they needed to complete what the website called a mandatory verification step. The page reassured them that there would be no additional charge. But the next screen asked for personal information, including contact details that scammers could potentially use for future phishing attacks. Researchers also identified a separate website impersonating a major lodging platform. Its login page used recognizable branding and familiar sign-in options to encourage visitors to submit account information. That creates another risk. If you use the same password for multiple services, giving it to a fake booking website could put those other accounts in danger.
Fake customer support chats make the scam more convincing

The live chat feature is what makes this scam particularly concerning. In a separate case, Fortra's researchers discovered a fraudulent travel-booking page with a credit card payment form and a live support chat. When visitors expressed concerns, the chat responded and described the card request as a routine security check. It even reassured visitors that their cards wouldn't be charged. Now consider how often you've used an online customer support chat to straighten out a billing problem. You explain what's happening, someone responds and you follow their instructions. Most of the time, that experience is perfectly legitimate.

Scammers are borrowing that familiar interaction to make their websites seem more trustworthy. The chat's reassurance was designed to encourage visitors to submit payment details. The researchers did not say whether a real person or an automated system operated the chat. Either way, the conversation was part of the fraudulent booking process. And that's an important reminder. Just because someone responds to your questions in real time doesn't mean you're dealing with the company you think you're dealing with.
FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL

A fake customer support chat reassures travelers that their credit cards won't be charged while directing them to enter payment information for a supposed reservation verification. (Fortra Intelligence and Research Experts)
Tips to protect yourself from fake vacation rental sites

Before you enter your credit card information or book a place to stay, take a moment to make sure you're dealing with a legitimate website. A little extra checking now could save you from losing money or having your personal information stolen.

If you're using Airbnb, Vrbo or another rental platform, open its official app or enter the website address yourself. Don't rely on links in unexpected emails or text messages, even when they mention a reservation you recognize. Be cautious with sponsored search results as well. Scammers sometimes pay for advertisements that lead to fraudulent websites. If you're unsure about a booking message, go back to your account through the official platform and look for it there.

A fake website may use a familiar company logo while hiding behind a completely unrelated web address. Scammers also add extra words to brand names to make fraudulent domains appear legitimate. Check the address before signing in or entering your credit card number. Remember that a padlock symbol doesn't guarantee a website is safe. It only indicates that the connection is encrypted.

Found a rental you really like? Search for the address separately and see whether the property appears on another reputable booking website. Compare the details and pay attention to prices that seem unusually low. You can also reverse-search the listing photos to see where else they're being used. However, finding matching photos doesn't automatically prove the listing is legitimate. Scammers often steal pictures from real properties. Take a few minutes to read reviews from previous guests. If something about the listing doesn't add up, contact the booking platform directly.

If a message claims your reservation will be canceled unless you act immediately, check your booking through the official website or app. A legitimate reservation problem may require attention, but that doesn't mean you should trust a link that arrived unexpectedly. If the warning doesn't appear in your account, contact customer support using the information published on the company's official website.

Be especially careful if a host asks you to visit another website to complete payment. The same goes for unexpected requests to move the conversation to WhatsApp or another messaging service. Airbnb warns that paying outside its platform can leave guests without AirCover protection. Vrbo also requires bookings and payments to follow its authorized process. Some legitimate properties may collect certain disclosed charges separately. If that happens, confirm the payment instructions through the official booking platform before sending money.

Strong antivirus software that includes malicious website and phishing protection can help warn you about known fraudulent booking pages. Some security programs can also detect suspicious links before you enter sensitive information. Keep your browser updated as well, since updates often include important security fixes. Of course, newly created scam websites may escape detection. Security software helps, but you still need to check where you're entering your information. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Credit cards generally offer stronger protections for disputing fraudulent charges than many other payment methods. That's especially useful when you're paying for an expensive vacation rental. Be suspicious if someone insists on a wire transfer or wants payment through cryptocurrency. Gift card requests are another major warning sign. Once money is sent using these methods, recovering it can be difficult. Even when paying by credit card, make sure you're using the actual booking platform.
32 TRAVEL ESSENTIALS THAT HELP PROTECT YOU AND YOUR BELONGINGS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON

Fraudulent vacation rental booking pages tell travelers their reservation remains unconfirmed and ask them to provide personal information to complete a mandatory verification process. (Halfpoint/iStock/Getty Images)

Some legitimate vacation rentals require identification. However, that doesn't mean you should upload your driver's license or other sensitive documents to an unfamiliar website. If you're asked to complete an unexpected verification process, confirm it through your official reservation. Also, never share a one-time security code with someone contacting you through a support chat or message. That code could give a scammer access to your account.

A password manager can help you recognize a suspicious login page. If the website address doesn't match the saved address for your account, the password manager generally won't autofill your credentials. That doesn't automatically prove the site is fraudulent, but it's a good reason to check the address more carefully. Use unique passwords for your booking accounts and enable two-factor authentication. Passkeys are another good option when a service supports them.
What to do if you've entered information on a fake rental website
If you think you've shared personal or financial information with a scammer, act quickly. Here's what to do based on the information you provided.

Contact your credit card company. If you entered your card details, call the number on the back of your card or contact your issuer through its official app. Explain what happened and ask whether your card should be replaced. Review recent transactions and dispute any unauthorized charges. Don't wait for a fraudulent charge to appear before reporting your card information as compromised.Change your passwords. If you entered login credentials, go directly to the legitimate booking website and change your password. Update any other accounts where you used the same password. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) if you haven't already and check for unfamiliar account activity.Monitor your identity and financial accounts. Watch your bank statements and credit card transactions for suspicious activity. If you shared sensitive identity information, visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance. If your Social Security number was exposed, consider placing a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion to help prevent someone from opening new credit accounts in your name.Report the fraudulent website. Notify the legitimate rental company being impersonated. You can also report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/ or the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. Save screenshots of suspicious messages and payment confirmations in case you need them for a fraud investigation or dispute.Make sure you have a real reservation. If you've been dealing with a fraudulent booking website, you may not have an actual reservation. Sign in to the legitimate booking platform to verify your stay. If you can't find your reservation, contact customer support directly. You don't want to arrive at your destination and discover you have nowhere to stay.

Contact your credit card company. If you entered your card details, call the number on the back of your card or contact your issuer through its official app. Explain what happened and ask whether your card should be replaced. Review recent transactions and dispute any unauthorized charges. Don't wait for a fraudulent charge to appear before reporting your card information as compromised.

Change your passwords. If you entered login credentials, go directly to the legitimate booking website and change your password. Update any other accounts where you used the same password. Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) if you haven't already and check for unfamiliar account activity.

Monitor your identity and financial accounts. Watch your bank statements and credit card transactions for suspicious activity. If you shared sensitive identity information, visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance. If your Social Security number was exposed, consider placing a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion to help prevent someone from opening new credit accounts in your name.

Report the fraudulent website. Notify the legitimate rental company being impersonated. You can also report the scam to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/ or the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. Save screenshots of suspicious messages and payment confirmations in case you need them for a fraud investigation or dispute.

Make sure you have a real reservation. If you've been dealing with a fraudulent booking website, you may not have an actual reservation. Sign in to the legitimate booking platform to verify your stay. If you can't find your reservation, contact customer support directly. You don't want to arrive at your destination and discover you have nowhere to stay.
Kurt's key takeaways

I think the live chat feature makes this scam especially troubling. We're so used to turning to customer support when something goes wrong that we tend to trust the person offering to help. And that's exactly the reaction these scammers are hoping for. I wouldn't assume a booking website is legitimate simply because someone in a chat window tells me everything is fine. My advice? If you're asked to enter your credit card information to fix an unexpected reservation problem, stop and check with the booking company directly. I know that's frustrating when you're trying to get your holiday plans settled. But I'd rather spend a few extra minutes verifying a reservation than find out later that a scammer has my credit card number.

Have you ever had a vacation rental reservation suddenly require additional payment or verification? Did you trust the request, or did something make you suspicious? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: AI data centers could consume more water than Americans drink in a year by 2030, says CEO working on solution
summary: Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck says AI data centers could drink as much water as Americans by 2030 unless direct chip cooling and water recycling catch on.
story: Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck says that under current trends, data centers in the U.S. could consume as much water as the American public drinks yearly by 2030. Beck’s company is developing more sustainable cooling solutions for data center chips.

Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck, whose company is working on sustainable solutions to ecological problems like AI data centers’ robust water consumption, said that without reform, AI data centers could wind up consuming more water than Americans drink every year.

"Ninety-five percent of the data centers today use a lot of water," he told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. "We estimate that by 2030, with the old technologies in the U.S., we will use as much water to cool data centers as Americans are using for drinking needs."
DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS
Beck argued that this phenomenon is "not sustainable," and laid out the technologies his company is working on in an effort to reduce data centers’ water consumption.
Ecolab CEO Christophe Beck (Fox News)

"Behind AI there's water in every step of the process. You need water to produce the chips, to power the chips and to cool the chips. And for the last four or five years, the chips generation that we were using were just cooled with air," he told Fox News Digital.
However, with the increasing complexity of chips to match an ever-building demand for computer power, air conditioning alone is no longer sufficient to cool chips in data centers, Beck explained.

"You need something that's way stronger. Water is 30 times better at extracting heat than air from the chips. So that's why many of those new data centers are moving toward direct chip water cooling, which ultimately is bringing cold water on top of the chip," he said.

Direct water cooling, he explained, has the dual benefits of increasing efficiency and sustainability, because the water used to cool the chips can be recycled and used on every chip in a given data center.
Racks of graphics processing units (GPUs) with a closed-loop liquid cooling system are seen inside an operational Microsoft data center. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images)

"So you end up in a place where you have a data center that is much more powerful [than] using no water, using less power, and ultimately not having an impact on natural resources and in communities around us, which is one of the unlocks that people are pushing back so much against right now," he said.
ONE INDUSTRY FACES MULTI-TRILLION-DOLLAR RECKONING AFTER HISTORIC MIDTERM ELECTION RESHUFFLE
On Nov. 4, voters across the U.S. elected lawmakers and executives who ran on campaigns to limit the number of data centers.

In Texas, Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa upset incumbent Republican Greg Abbott. Voters who ticked the box for Hinojosa did so after she campaigned heavily on instituting a data center moratorium, a fact that Beck took note of.
THE POWERFUL WAY AMERICAN COMMUNITIES CAN BENEFIT FROM THE NEW TECH BOOM REVEALED BY DATA CENTER CEO
Gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa speaks during a campaign event in Austin, Texas, on Nov. 2, 2026. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Most of the data centers that were installed in Texas or anywhere else in the country or in the world, for that matter, were using a lot of water, a lot of power. And that's created a lot of backlash from the communities, which is rightfully so," Beck told Fox News Digital.
Beck noted that while Texas is one of the most economically strong states in the union, it is also one of the most water-stressed.

"It's a bad combination," he said. "Obviously, high growth, great news; no water, less good news. So we've looked at those technological solutions on how do you bring higher growth, more data processing while using much less water."
Beck added that the technologies Ecolab is developing will exclusively be used in new-build data centers, while the political pushback is surrounding the existing, more resource-demanding projects.
Direct cooling allows for what is known as a closed loop system, a method that is far more sustainable and requires less water than previous iterations of water-cooling methods.
Ecolab, Beck explained, has found a way to recycle water not only in the chip cooling process, but in chip fabrication as well, a process that necessitates extremely pure water.
An employee works in the cleanroom at X-FAB, a chip manufacturer in Erfurt, Germany, on June 23, 2026. (Martin Schutt/picture alliance via Getty Images)
"The so-called fabs, they use huge amounts of water, which is very specialized water because it needs to be ultra pure," Beck explained.

"And that, to be recycled, is even way harder than in a data center. But even there, at Ecolab we found solutions to not only get the highest purity of water to get the most advanced chips, but we can reuse that water as well in ways that are water neutral," he said.
Beck also put in context just how pure the water for chip fabrication needs to be.
"The purity is a million times more pure than what you would inject in your blood if it's a drug. So super high quality, super high purity of water at the end," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"So the way we do it, in short, is ultimately at every step of the process we try to extract the water from that process step. We treat, we purify that water, we bring it back to an ultra-pure water level, and we bring back to the process. And the very special thing that we have at Ecolab, within that water you have some trace materials that we call connected water," he said.

"So we understand the quality of the water throughout the process within the fab or the data center, for that matter, that we know exactly the quality of that water to make sure that the chips are perfectly produced. And we know what we need to do in order to re-treat that water so that it can be reused afterwards. And you end up with better chips, lower cost, and most importantly, water neutral," Beck said.

title: What to know about Ring Drone Cam, which can patrol your home for $250
summary: Ring's Drone Cam flies room to room with AI navigation, 2K video and a $249.99 price, but it still awaits FCC authorization before it can ship in the U.S.
story: Ring's $250 Drone Cam uses AI to fly through your home, investigate security alerts and stream live video. Kurt "Cyberguy" Knutsson breaks down what to expect from the new technology.

Ever leave the house and suddenly wonder whether you closed the back door? You pull up your security camera, but it only shows the driveway. Not much help when you want to see what's happening inside. Well, Ring thinks it has an answer. And this one actually flies. Amazon-owned Ring has unveiled the Ring Drone Cam, a tiny $249.99 indoor security camera that flies from room to room. It can investigate security alerts, check specific areas of your home and send live video directly to your phone.

Earlier this month, the company announced the new drone as part of its new Ring Robotics lineup. And thanks to artificial intelligence, it can navigate your home without someone steering it around. We also talked in depth about this new technology on "The CyberGuy Report Podcast," including what a flying camera could mean for home security. But before you get too excited about having your own miniature security patrol, there are some things worth knowing.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
