title: A Complicated Friendship Inspired Lucy Tan’s ‘Tiger’s Mouth,’ the Latest Book From Jenna Bush Hager’s Imprint
summary: “Tiger’s Mouth,” the latest book out from Jenna Bush Hager’s Thousand Voices x Random House Publishing Group, is the story of a charged friendship.
story: “Tiger’s Mouth,” the latest book out from Jenna Bush Hager’s Thousand Voices x Random House Publishing Group, is the story of a charged friendship.
Jack Chen and Jack Owens meet at an internship and nearly immediately recognize each wants what the other has.

“In every relationship, whether it’s romantic or platonic, or professional, there’s a power balance. You hope it’s somewhat equal but often it’s not, and if it’s not, what then?” author Lucy Tan tells TODAY.com.

Tan’s first novel, “What We Were Promised,” was a family epic set in Shanghai. Her sophomore novel opens on the two Jacks crossing path one summer during a New York internship. Jack Owens may be the son of the company’s billionaire founder, but he lacks his father’s ambition, and also struggles with depression.

Jack Chen, on the other hand, comes from a family of caterers. Growing up, he studied rich kids and learned to act more like them to build a life like theirs. When he finesses his way into a prestigious internship meant for Columbia graduate students, Chen is ready to fake his way through everything.
“The characters we meet have entirely different lives but they both make each other feel seen,” Jenna says.
Tan, a Seattle bookseller, was inspired by a past personal friendship that had a complicated power dynamic. The questions that it raised drew her to write about privilege and interpersonal dynamics.

These tensions play out in the the two Jacks’ friendship. Chen longs for access to the resources and opportunities that Owens had growing up, while Owens longs for the love and care that Chen experienced.
Betrayal ends up driving the men apart, but their careers keep them in the same circle, where they compete like opponents in their favorite board game, Go.
Tan brings these men on a journey through platonic love and resentment, traversing the finite and abstract aspects of the world.
“Together they will decide: What is a life worth? And are some worth more than others?” Tan says.

title: McDonald’s Launches ‘Home Alone’ Meal Inspired by Kevin’s Cravings
summary: McDonald’s is lauching a “Home Alone” Meal, with a special McFlurry, fries and dipping sauce, 36 years after the Macaulay Culkin film premiered.
story: This yuletide season, McDonald’s is offering the gift of nostalgia.

Thirty-six years after the debut of the classic holiday movie, the burger behemoth announced the “Home Alone” Meal, with limited-time menu items and collectible socks, as well as in-person and virtual experiences. The Disney partnership meal will be available at participating restaurants nationwide starting Dec. 1, while supplies last.
McDonald’s has turned some of Kevin McCallister’s (Macaulay Culkin) most memorable movie moments into a trio of menu items, encased in a box designed to look like his family’s home:

Medium Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries are inspired by the rambunctious kid’s go-to pizza (plain cheese), with McShaker seasoning (notes of tomato, garlic, Italian herbs and cheese) that you can add with a McShaker bag.

Medium Little Nero’s Pizza McShaker Fries are inspired by the rambunctious kid’s go-to pizza (plain cheese), with McShaker seasoning (notes of tomato, garlic, Italian herbs and cheese) that you can add with a McShaker bag.

Lovely Cheese Pizza Dipping Sauce, also inspired by McCallister’s preferred pizza, combines tomato flavor, Parmesan cheese, garden herbs and a hint of garlic. You get this sauce with the choice of Chicken McNuggets or McCrispy Strips, or you can just order it a la carte.

Lovely Cheese Pizza Dipping Sauce, also inspired by McCallister’s preferred pizza, combines tomato flavor, Parmesan cheese, garden herbs and a hint of garlic. You get this sauce with the choice of Chicken McNuggets or McCrispy Strips, or you can just order it a la carte.
Everything Sundae McFlurry features vanilla soft-serve swirled with hot fudge, Oreo cookie pieces and M&M’s, channeling Kevin’s room-service feast in “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.”
Everything Sundae McFlurry features vanilla soft-serve swirled with hot fudge, Oreo cookie pieces and M&M’s, channeling Kevin’s room-service feast in “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.”

Customers can collect one of four sock designs with their meal, including one inspired by the film’s most culturally enduring moment: Kevin’s scream. The other three socks feature Grimace, Birdy and the Hamburglar, who might’ve joined the Wet Bandits if they only stole Big Macs.
“Home Alone” came out 36 years ago, on Nov. 10, 1990. Culkin, who may have a reboot in the works, is starring an ad campaign for the partnership in which he enjoys time alone in an empty McDonald’s.

“What I love about this collaboration is that the Home Alone Meal captures something bigger than just one character, it’s about the playful spirit that resonates with people across generations,”  Culkin said in a press release. “Bringing this to life with McDonald’s and getting to reexperience these moments with my own kids, reminds me why fans keep coming back to Kevin’s story. That’s the magic we’re celebrating here.”

On Dec. 4 through Dec. 5 from 5 — 10 p.m. PT, the McDonald’s Home Alone Challenge, an immersive pop-up experience in Los Angeles, California, will let fans complete a series of challenges in themed, interactive rooms, like sliding into a ball pit or testing out your slingshot skills, for a free “Home Alone” Meal.
You can register for the experience here.

In the McDonald’s app, customers can redeem $5 off a $20 McDelivery order or use MyMcDonald’s Rewards points to redeem a 14-day free trial of the Disney+Hulu bundle, where they can access the “Home Alone” collection.
Customers also have the ability to round up their order cost to help Ronald McDonald House families stay together during a child’s medical journey.
Last year, McDonald’s partnered with another iconic Christmas movie, “The Grinch,” to launch a meal featuring Dill Pickle “Grinch Salt” McShaker Fries.

title: 25 Years Later, Watch Daniel Radcliffe Talk to TODAY in 2001 About Landing Harry Potter Role
summary: Daniel Radcliffe spoke with TODAY in 2001 before “Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone” was released on Nov. 16.
story: Welcome to the “TODAY Archives,” where we revisit memories from our show when celebrities and newsmakers started discourse, made us laugh or shaped our culture. This latest installment features an interview with Daniel Radcliffe on Nov. 12, 2001, shortly before the “Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone,” the first film in the “Harry Potter” series, was released.

“Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone” brought the adventures of the young wizard from the page to the big screen. The film — the first of eight to be adapted from J.K. Rowling’s series of beloved books — opened Nov. 16, 2001.

On Nov. 12 of that year, newcomer Daniel Radcliffe, who landed the title role, sat down with TODAY’s Katie Couric to talk about the highly anticipated movie. This was the first of many appearances from the franchise’s stars on TODAY.
Radcliffe, who was 12 at the time of the interview, had recently attended the New York and London premieres of the film.
“It was pretty scary, but it was really good fun,” Radcliffe said. “And everybody there, like (director) Chris Columbus, he was there, and he just makes you feel really at ease.”
Were the premieres exciting after all the hard work that went into making the movie?
“It was fun, but I was quite nervous. But it was very cool,” he said.
How Did Daniel Radcliffe Land the Role of Harry Potter?

Radcliffe beat out thousands of hopefuls to snag the plum role — a part that would eventually set him up for a thriving career in Hollywood. He didn’t have any keen insight into just why he got the coveted lead role.
“I have no idea,” he told Couric.
“I really don’t know why they chose me, but I’m glad they did,” he continued.
How Did Daniel Radcliffe’s Parents Guide Him?

Radcliffe’s parents were somewhat worried when he was up for the part. He was not a household name yet at the point — his credits prior to the “Harry Potter” franchise included the British miniseries “David Copperfield” and the Pierce Brosnan movie “The Tailor of Panama.”
His parents knew it was no slam dunk he’d get the role.

“They only had one concern, and that was because I’ve been up for ‘David Copperfield’ and I’ve been up for ‘Tailor of Panama,’ and on both of those, I kind of had a tendency to get my hopes up,” he said. “And they knew that there were thousands of boys going up for the part, so they didn’t want me to get my hopes up and then be disappointed.”
Adding, “So they were just protecting me.”
Did Daniel Radcliffe Read the ‘Harry Potter’ Books?
Radcliffe didn’t read the books until after he was cast, but he was quickly enchanted by the world of Hogwarts. At the time, only four books in the seven-book series had been published.
However, after diving into the world, the actor said he was one of many people who could see themselves in Harry.

“It was the fact that, I think not only myself, but I think everybody can relate to Harry in some way ... it’s the idea of magic,” he said. “When magic kind of comes to life, there’s so much opportunity for absolutely anything to happen ... I kind of like to read about what would happen if magic really came to life.”

title: Beanie Feldstein Says Ariana Grande Saved Ben Stiller’s Life on Set of ‘Focker-In-Law’
summary: Beanie Feldstein reveals behind-the-scenes moments during the filming of “Focker-In-Law,” including how Ariana Grande saved Ben Stiller’s life.
story: When the camera cuts, the interview isn’t over. With “Commercial Break,” TODAY.com catches up with guests between takes in Studio 1A for unfiltered moments and more questions.
Beanie Feldstein walks into the TODAY Lounge and instantly lights up the room with her smile and infectious personality.

The star of stage and hit films, including “Ladybird” and “Booksmart,” is visiting Studio 1A to talk about her latest project, “Focker-In-Law.” The fourth installment in the the “Meet the Parents” franchise, “Focker-In-Law” picks up 16 years after the last sequel (“Little Fockers”) left off, with Greg Focker’s (Ben Stiller) young twins all grown up and in relationships of their own.
Feldstein plays Stiller’s daughter, Samantha, and Skyler Gisondo is Henry, Stiller’s over-parented son who’s planning to propose to his girlfriend, Olivia (Ariana Grande).

The new movie, which hits theaters Nov. 25, reunites the original cast including Stiller, Robert De Niro, Blythe Danner, Teri Polo, Owen Wilson and Mr. Jinx (well, sort of), along with adding Feldstein, Gisondo, Grande and Eduardo Franco to the mix.

As expected, there are high jinks, mishaps, injuries and a whole lot of uncomfortable moments that make for pure comedy gold. Among them is Stiller doing a vocal performance that’s guaranteed to live on in YouTube infamy and a dinner table choking scene that became all too real, as Feldstein reveals when we sit down to talk.

Read on to find out how Grande stepped in to assist, how Feldstein felt about the Grammy-winner’s singing on set, as well as what it was like reuniting with her “Booksmart” co-stars and how they “got deep” during the filming of “Focker-In-Law.”
This interview has been lightly edited for clarity.
I truly think it was like one of the most singularly joyful experiences I’ve ever had working on anything.

I think because Samantha’s so along for the ride and it was so fun to be like, “This is the support system,” but also the one calling everything out a little bit. I think because (Samantha) is so close to her dad, she’s able to like call him out in a way that feels like deeply loving and not mean.
And I got to be Ben Stiller’s daughter. Like, it was unbelievable.

John Hamburg, who’s our writer director, he co-wrote the first movie when he was 29. So, he’s grown up with these movies, working on them. And he said that Greg Focker is like a little bit of his own persona coming out.
He’s much less insane than Greg Focker, but he is a hovercraft dad in like the sweetest way.

I think that both Eduardo and I in real life, but also as Samantha and the character Eduardo — which obviously was written for him — we’re very earnest people, both of us. And I think we bring an earnestness to Samantha and Eduardo.
Even though they’re a little bit more artsy and a little bit less straitlaced than Henry (Gisondo), I think we bring like a little bit of the heartbeat, like the grounding force.

And Eduardo, the character, and Eduardo the person, are just so pure. He’s one of the most pure people I’ve ever known. And I think he brings this like genuineness and purity to the character, which is so unexpected and so fun.

Ari just sings all the time, like under her breath, when she’s like walking between sets and stuff. And obviously everyone’s like stopping and listening because it’s the Ariana Grande just like, you know, bebopping around.

We talked a lot of musical theater, but I don’t think we officially sang anything together. But Ari’s kind of just vocalizing all the time and everyone’s just like staring because it’s the most beautiful sound you’ve ever heard.
That moment was 100, and we filmed that for two full days. When I tell you, every single take, I laughed. Like there was not one time where I didn’t find it out-loud funny, even on the 60th take.

That was definitely the moment where it was this out-of-body experience of like, “I’m in ‘Meet the Parents’ and I’m watching ‘Meet the Parents.’ Like what is happening right now? This is one of the best days of my life.”
But those dinner table scenes I think are also so fun because we’re all together. The first one with Blythe (Danner) and it’s this real family togetherness. But, also, they’re so uncomfortable.

The other moment that was crazy was, I swear to God, I think Ben actually turned purple. Like he wasn’t acting. He was so committed to the choking on the steak that he literally turned purple and Ariana Grande saved his life. I swear to God.
He was so purple. He was like, “I was seeing stars. I couldn’t see for a second.” I was like, “Ben, you’ve taken it too far.”
Heaven. I love those boys. I would do anything for those boys.
Skyler and I have been joking, because we play lovers in “Booksmart,” and then he’s my brother (in “Focker-In-Law”). Now I need to play his mother next, in a flashback or something.
But, yeah, Skyler and I got to do a lot on “Booksmart,” so I feel like I came in like really knowing what to expect.

Eduardo and I don’t have as much to do together in “Booksmart,” we have like that big opening scene in the bathroom, but otherwise we’re kind of in separate worlds, which is kind of the setup of the movie.
So it was just heaven to get to be like literally right next to him for three months filming this movie. We had so much fun together.
I feel like we went so deep. We would ride together to work every day and we just got so deep, like deep heart-to-hearts.
And, yeah, “Samuardo Forever.” That was our little couple name. Samurado Forever. I think they’re a really funny, unexpected couple and it really works.

title: When J. Lo Joked About Her 4 Divorces, a Fan’s Witty Response Left Her Cackling: ‘Funniest Thing I Ever Heard’
summary: Jennifer Lopez laughed when a fan made a joke about her four divorces. Hear the line that cracked her up.
story: When it comes to the highs and lows of her very public love life, Jennifer Lopez has a sense of humor.
Over the weekend, the  “Ain’t It Funny” singer spoke to fans at a screening of her new TV special, “The JLO Show: Live in Las Vegas,” at the 92nd Street Y in New York.
She said her four divorces are a “big part of my story.” The singer then said, “Four times,” and held up four fingers.
When a fan in the audience shouted, “You have six more fingers!” Lopez couldn’t help but laugh, per a video captured at the event.
“Yes I do!” she said as she excitedly tapped her feet on the floor and pointed into the crowd.
Lopez was clearly impressed with the witty comment and said, “Oh my God, that is the funniest thing I’ve ever heard in my life.”
Someone on the stage also acknowledged that the clever phrase has potential.
“That’s a T-shirt,” they said, prompting Lopez to agree.
In a video clip of the moment, the crowd erupted in laughter over the comedic exchange. Social media users also got a good giggle.
“You know its funny when you laugh and stomp at the same time,” one commented.
“Collect those rings,” another wrote.
One Instagram user said, “I’d buy that tshirt too!!!” and another embraced Lopez’s honesty, writing, “Right! Live your life.”
Marina Prut, the content creator who captured the video, called Lopez an “inspiration.”
“If she can work this hard, reaching new heights, fall and rise again — so can we,” she tells TODAY.com.

Lopez has been married four times. First to Ojani Noa for a year from 1997 to 1998, then Cris Judd from 2001 to 2003. She has twins with her third husband, Marc Anthony, to whom she was married from 2004 to 2014.
She and Ben Affleck, who were previously engaged, married in 2022 and split in 2024.
She was also engaged to Alex Rodriguez; the couple was together from 2017 to 2021.
Lopez poked fun at her weddings in her 2024 music video “Can’t Get Enough.”
During a 2025 interview on the “Howard Stern Show,” she said she felt that she has never been truly loved, but she has loved.

“It’s not that I’m not lovable. It’s that they’re not capable,” she said. “They don’t have it in them. And they gave me what they had, they gave me all of it every time. All the rings, all the things I could ever want. The houses, the rings, the marriage, all of it. But they didn’t love me and I didn’t love myself.”
She said her last divorce was the “best thing that happened to (her).”

title: Robert Pattinson Announced as the New James Bond
summary: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond, Amazon MGM Studios announced.
story: Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond.

Pattinson will take on the role of film’s most famous British secret agent in the 26th installment of the long-running Bond franchise. The upcoming movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, the mastermind behind the “Dune” trilogy.

Pattinson starred in “The Drama,” “The Odyssey,” “Primetime” and “Dune: Part Three” this year alone. He follows in the footsteps of Daniel Craig, Pierce Brosnan, Timothy Dalton, Roger Moore, Sean Connery and George Lazenby, who all played Bond on the big screen.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement. “... To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”
The announcement comes five years after Craig played the suave spy, whose code name is 007, in the last Bond film, 2021’s “No Time to Die.”
Casting rumors about the new Bond have been making headlines for months.

In October, Deadline reported that several A-list British actors were performing screen tests for the coveted role. Insiders told the publication that top contenders at that time were “One Night Only” star Callum Turner, “Slow Horses” and “White Lotus” actor Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor of “The Crown” and “Challengers.”
Weeks later, Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were suddenly in the running, according to Variety.
Pop star Harry Styles also engaged in “discussions” about the part, Variety reported.
The Bond character was created in 1952 by British author Ian Fleming, who wrote about the secret agent across 12 novels and two short story collections.
Brosnan, who played Bond from 1995 until 2002, told Vanity Fair he would be pleased to see Turner, his co-star in 2017’s “The Only Living Boy in New York,” take on the role.

“All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire. Callum Turner is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong. They all have a voice and a physique, and a presence on film. They all have longevity as actors, all of these young men,” Brosnan said.
“Whoever plays the role, I wish him the very best of life and strength and courage,” Brosnan added.

title: The Most Important Line in ‘The Good Daughter,’ According to Karin Slaughter, Is ‘Not a Message Women Get Often’
summary: Warning: This story contains spoilers for “The Good Daughter.”
story: Warning: This story contains spoilers for “The Good Daughter.”

From the moment two masked men with guns step into the home of teenage sisters Samantha and Charlotte Quinn, it’s clear that crime drama “The Good Daughter” is a story about survival — what happens after violence changes the trajectory of your life, and the pain of piecing together your past.
It’s just one of several traumatic plot points in the six-episode series, based on the book of the same name by bestselling author Karin Slaughter, out Nov. 12 on Peacock.
While sexual violence is a theme in much of Slaughter’s work, extra care was given to how this story was brought to the small screen, Slaughter tells TODAY.com.

“One of the things I’m most proud of in this show is I set these rules that we were only going to tell the story from the perspective of Sam or Charlie,” she says. “If it’s young Charlie, (director Steph Green) would lower the camera angle, and the focus is always on the girls and not on the bad men doing bad things.”

“I’m very mindful that when you see a woman’s body, you think about how you feel, and when you see a man’s body, you think about how the man feels. So I wanted to really make sure that we weren’t being exploitative and we were showing this perspective.”

“The Good Daughter” revolves around the sisters Charlotte “Charlie” and Samantha “Sam,” played by Meghann Fahy and Rose Byrne respectively, who are estranged as adults but reunite after one of them becomes unintentionally linked to a murder case. Together, the siblings must contend with the past in order to reconcile and embrace their futures.
Both Byrne and Fahy tell TODAY.com that they were drawn to the project because of the show’s focus on the strength of the characters, rather than on the abuse and suffering that they had endured.

“The show is about hope, and it’s about perseverance, and it’s about confronting the things that scare you, relieving yourself of unnecessary shame, and claiming the life that you really want to have for yourself and the people that you love,” Fahy says.

Byrne adds: “We wanted to celebrate the resilience of all situations like that and all people who survived these horrific events. ... A huge part of the conversation around when I signed on (was) how will this be dealt with? How will this be depicted?”

Both actors were tasked with embodying survivorship in different ways. For Byrne, Sam’s disability from a bullet wound to the head meant two months working on her gait with a physical therapist who rehabilitates similar patients in real life.
Fahy’s character Charlie, meanwhile, has kept a secret about the attack from everyone except her father, Rusty. Asked how she was able to bring that to life, Fahy points to the “responsibly run set.”

“There was a mental health specialist on set every day that was available to all of the actors and all of the crew if anybody needed support,” Fahy says, adding that Green “took very good care of everybody, so that created a super safe space.”
Slaughter hopes the show helps viewers, particularly those who have gone through trauma of their own, feel supported and safe.

“The most important line in the entire series and in the book is when Rusty says, ‘Whatever you did to survive is exactly what you should do,’” Slaughter explains. “That’s not a message women get often. We aren’t usually told, ‘You did the right thing.’ We’re told, ‘Why didn’t you do this? Why didn’t you do that?’”

On its face, “The Good Daughter” may seem like a quintessential thriller about women solving a crime in a small-town. But, according to Slaughter, it relies just as heavily on other warmer storytelling elements, like comedy and family dynamics.

“It’s so important to me to balance the light and dark,” the author says. “There are laugh-out-loud funny moments ... and that was so important for me to carry from the book into the show because, particularly being from the South ... there is that sensibility of even the worst situation you can find humor in.”
Slaughter adds that connection between the two sisters “propels you through the show as much as the whodunit.”
“At its heart, it’s about a family and this universal sense of dislocation and separation that we all feel as we grow up,” she says.
In fact, the least surprising but perhaps most satisfying aspect of the ending is that Sam and Charlie finally accept how much they need each other.

“The thing about writing about complicated, interesting women and not sentimentalizing them is that you have to know, as a viewer, that you trust the writer (is) going to leave you in a good place, and all my books end on a place of hope, and definitely the show ends on that hope too,” Slaughter says.

title: Palestinians flee as Israeli tanks cross Gaza ceasefire’s ‘yellow line’
summary: Israel’s ground operation across the yellow ceasefire line in Gaza, which forced Palestinians to flee their makeshift shelters, marks a fresh escalation in the conflict and risks undermining an already floundering truce with Hamas, analysts said Thursday.
story: Israel’s ground operation across the yellow ceasefire line in Gaza, which forced Palestinians to flee their makeshift shelters, marks a fresh escalation in the conflict and risks undermining an already floundering truce with Hamas, analysts said Thursday.

As tanks rolled into central Gaza on Wednesday, residents could be seen carrying blankets and other belongings away from their tents in pictures and video taken shortly after the Israeli military began what it said was an operation targeting a “terror tunnel.”

Others could be seen rolling away mattresses on carts and pushing loved ones in wheelchairs away from the scene near the Nuseirat camp in central Gaza. At least one person was reported to have been killed in an Israeli airstrike near the raid, Palestinian medics said, according to Reuters.

“Bullets were fired at us,” Amna al-Gasar, 49, told NBC News after she fled the scene with her young children, her baby in a pink fluffy sweater strapped to her chest. She said her family had received “evacuation orders” from the Israeli military and that tanks had advanced on the area.

“This is the 14th time that we’re getting displaced,” al-Gasar said, who added that she is from Gaza City in the north of the enclave which is now on the side of the “yellow line” occupied by Israeli forces. “Where should we go? We are exhausted. This is not a life,” she said.

Muna Abu Shehadeh, 37, said in a separate interview that along with some of her relatives, she left “with nothing but our children — no bedding, no food, and no water.” She added that she had a daughter who was ill, as well as a baby, and that they had to leave behind what few supplies they had.

The Israeli military told NBC News the ground operation was the first to be executed beyond the yellow line — the boundary marking the roughly 60% of Gaza that remains occupied by Israeli forces — since the U.S.-brokered ceasefire with Hamas came into effect in October 2025.

Separately, in a joint statement with the Israel Security Agency, or Shin Bet, the Israel Defense Forces said the operation was a “targeted” assault aimed at dismantling a tunnel that “posed an immediate and direct threat” to troops.

title: Highlights from Pope Leo’s historic, 12-day tour of South America
summary: They turned out in their millions to greet Pope Leo as he made his way around Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on a gruelling 12-day tour of the South America.
story: LIMA, Peru — They turned out in the millions to greet Pope Leo as he made his way around Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on a grueling 12-day tour of the South American nations, weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.
Pope keeps energetic pace in trip to South America after surgery

For some — particularly those in Argentina, which had not received a papal visit since Pope John Paul II in 1987 — it was the first time they would get to see a pontiff in person. A record 2.5 million people flooded onto the streets of Buenos Aires last week to try and catch a glimpse of Leo.

The Vatican dubbed it a “homecoming” tour for the 71-year-old, as the Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, spent the final six days in the country where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.
NBC News takes a look at some of the highlights from his trip.
Montevideo, Uruguay

After a 17-hour flight from Rome, Leo and his entourage touched down in Uruguay’s capital, Montevideo. Praising the Lord and thanking his wonderful medical assistants, Leo said that while some had questioned whether he would be able to make the trip because of his recent surgery, he “had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward.”

title: Trump urges nuclear arms control in historic meeting with Putin and Xi
summary: What these three men might decide has the potential to reverberate across the globe.
story: SHENZHEN, China — It’s unclear what decisions may come from this historic meeting.
But the spectacle of President Donald Trump’s meeting with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping may be what delivers the defining image.

On Thursday, Trump, Putin and Xi met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen. Sitting around a huge, doughnut-shaped table at the Kylin Villa resort were leaders of three of the world’s most powerful nations: the U.S. with its largest economy, Russia with its biggest nuclear arsenal, and China its largest standing army and manufacturing sector.
“We are really making history,” Trump said.

The sight of Trump expressing such warmth toward two authoritarian strongmen will have left many American allies outside the room dismayed. After Trump called Putin his “friend,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted to X, “God, protect us from such friends.” Russia has invaded Ukraine and waged a yearslong campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and misinformation against the West.
Others were concerned about the prospect of a “Yalta 2.0,” a reprise of the 1945 Yalta Conference in which the U.S., Britain and the then-Soviet Union met to carve up the postwar world.
After Thursday’s meeting finished, Russia and China issued a brief statement that was light on detail or major announcements. The U.S. did not immediately release a version.

The “China-Russia-U.S. Declaration on Peace” agreed to “reform” the United Nations “so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges.” (Russia and China have long sought to shift the body away from Western human rights concerns, while Trump has been a strident critic of the world body.) The declaration agreed to boost the production and supply of petroleum products, which have been disrupted by the Ukraine and Iran wars, and it rebuked the International Criminal Court not to abuse its power. (The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Putin.)
The final point was that the leaders vowed to take steps to avoid nuclear war, although no specifics were mentioned.

The last remaining treaty between Washington and Moscow, New START, lapsed in February, but China, which has a far smaller nuclear arsenal than the other two, has resisted calls to be included in a new agreement.

“As the world’s three largest nuclear powers, by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used,” Trump said in the public section of the meeting.
“Once you have the nuclear weapons, it’s very hard to not have them, it’s very hard to give them up,” he added. “That’s the way life works.”

title: Trump pushes for three-way nuclear deal as Russia and China show little interest
summary: President Donald Trump has repeatedly placed nonproliferation near the top of the agenda for his unprecedented trilateral meeting Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, but his counterparts have expressed little interest in committing to new limitations on their nuclear arsenals.
story: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has repeatedly placed nonproliferation near the top of the agenda for his trilateral meeting Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, although his counterparts have expressed little interest in committing to new limitations on their nuclear arsenals.

Trump has been pushing for China to join the U.S. and Russia in a new nuclear arms control agreement since his first term in office. Still, he has sought to limit expectations for any major progress in Shenzhen, China, where the world’s top three nuclear powers are meeting on the sidelines of a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders.

Russia suspended its participation in New START, its last remaining nuclear arms pact with the U.S., when it invaded Ukraine in 2022, denying inspections of its nuclear sites. Ahead of the treaty’s expiration this past February, Russia said it would keep to the deal’s limitations on its arsenal for another year, but Trump insisted a new agreement must include China and possibly other nuclear powers.

China has said an arms control agreement should remain between the U.S. and Russia, which together hold nearly 90% of the world’s nuclear arsenal, with more than 5,000 warheads each. China has about 600, according to Pentagon estimates, though by 2030 it could have up to 1,000 if its arsenal continues to expand at the current rate.

“China is building up its nuclear arsenal to a very significant degree, and it will continue to do so, and wants to continue to do so,” David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told reporters Wednesday.

The Chinese foreign ministry has declined to say whether nuclear arms control will be discussed at the trilateral meeting on Thursday, with spokesperson Mao Ning saying earlier this week that the three leaders “will have an in-depth exchange of views on important issues bearing on global peace.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

In a call last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearization,” according to a U.S. readout of the call. The Chinese readout made no reference to such a discussion.
Trump has admitted that it will be difficult to get Russia and China to consider reducing their nuclear arsenals.

“So we’re going to talk about denuclearization. Tough subject because it’s very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes, right? But especially since you do have other countries,” he said Monday. “But we’re going to be talking about denuclearization.”

Even in the hours leading up to this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, the world’s top two nuclear powers were making shows of force. On Tuesday, the U.S. launched an unarmed intercontinental ballistic missile in a previously unannounced test at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Hours later, Russia landed two strategic bombers in Vietnam to coincide with Putin’s arrival in China.

While one meeting is not likely to produce dramatic breakthroughs, it could kick-start a process that leads to sustained, formal bilateral or multilateral negotiations on nuclear risk reduction, arms control and disarmament, said Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Washington-based Arms Control Association.

“A top priority for all three leaders should be to head off a costly, escalatory nuclear arms race involving the further buildup of nuclear forces and the resumption of nuclear testing by any state,” he said.

Da Wei, director of the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, said nuclear arms control was not a “proper topic” for the trilateral meeting given the complexity of the issue and how little time Trump, Putin and Xi will have together.
But if the three leaders “can say something about nuclear stability, like a nuclear war is not winnable and should not be fought, I think that will be helpful,” he said in an interview Wednesday.
Rubio has acknowledged that a new agreement could take some time.

“Past agreements, including New START, took years to negotiate and were built upon decades of precedent. They were also between two powers, not three or more,” he wrote on Substack in February. “However, just because something is hard does not mean we should not pursue it or settle for less.”

title: Xi greets Trump as he arrives in China, a rare move ahead of Putin talks
summary: In a rare and surprising move, Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump as he arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of historic three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
story: SHENZHEN, China — In a rare and surprising move, Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump as he arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of historic three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
It is believed to be the first time that Xi, in power for more than a decade, has been on hand to greet any foreign leader arriving in China.

He was reciprocating the personal greeting he had received from Trump in September, when the American leader met him at the plane upon his arrival for a White House state visit. Lawmakers from both parties had criticized Trump over the move, which is also rare for U.S. presidents.

A report by Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency, said that during Trump’s arrival in the city of Shenzhen on Wednesday, Xi noted the special trip the American president and first lady Melania Trump had made to welcome him at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.
“China is a nation that values courtesy and has a tradition of returning goodwill with goodwill,” the Xinhua report said.

After Trump descended from Air Force One, a handshake between the two leaders turned into a quick hug as rows of military regiments and performers wearing bright pink and turquoise outfits stood at attention. A martial band played the American and Chinese national anthems as dancers waved flowers, pompoms and Chinese and American flags.

title: Meghan Markle’s father faces new child sex abuse complaints in the Philippines
summary: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was charged with the possession of child abuse material, police in the Philippines said.
story: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, has had criminal complaints filed against him over alleged online child sexual abuse offences, police in the Philippines said Wednesday.

The complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, police told Reuters. They added that the complaints were filed before the prosecutor’s office in Cebu on Monday, following an investigation last month into the alleged distribution and possession of child sexual abuse materials.
Markle had lived in Cebu for a period before returning to the United States.

Prosecutors the evaluating the charges filed by police before they decide whether to issue a subpoena against Markle whose legal team would have 10 days to respond with a counter-affidavit. Prosecutors would then decide whether to proceed with a court case.
Prince Harry and Meghan’s spokesperson declined to comment when NBC News asked about the latest charges.

The announcement came less than two weeks after the 82-year-old was arrested in Florida and charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to a criminal complaint filed by the Justice Department.

The FBI seized around 78 items from two storage units rented by Markle in Los Angeles, that contained “suspected child pornography,” according to court documents. Items seized include film negatives featuring an adult man with naked “pre-pubescent” girls, the complaint said, which added that a witness “positively identified the adult man as Markle.”
Based on background in one photo, the FBI determined the images found in California were taken in a hotel in the Philippines, according to the court document.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Markle was taken into custody in Tampa, Florida, and was later released under house arrest.
But after he cut off his ankle monitor, a federal judge ordered last week that Markle remain in custody for violating the conditions of his release.

Markle had been living in a senior care facility in Lakeland, Florida after he was forced to return to the U.S. from the Philippines when he suffered a stroke and a leg was amputated, according to The Associated Press.
The retired television lighting and photography director denied the allegations last month, calling them “sick lies.”

Meghan Markle asaid in a statement last month that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations against her father. Their relationship has been limited and fraught in recent years, with her father not attending her wedding to Harry in 2018 amid widespread media scrutiny.

Her statement said that she was previously informed of “disturbing allegations” against him, with British police subsequently confirming she was passed a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.”

London’s Metropolitan Police said it had not informed other law enforcement agencies about the allegations in the letter at the time, referring itself to Britain’s policing watchdog over the handling of the allegations.

“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, who said she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
Meghan Markle and her husband, Prince Harry, stepped back as working royals in 2020 amid widespread reports of a royal rift and moved to, leaving Britain for California.

Harry, the second son of King Charles III and the late Princess Diana, leveled harsh criticism at Buckingham Palace and other senior royals across a series of media interviews and a tell-all memoir, “Spare.”
The couple returned to Britain two months ago, with their two children moving to schools in the country.

title: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
summary: European leaders have long feared being frozen out of U.S.-Russia peace talks about Ukraine. Now  Trump’s team negotiating the continent’s security structure.
story: LONDON — When European nations said they wanted greater involvement in Ukraine peace talks, this was almost certainly not what they had in mind.

Europe has long demanded more say in negotiations to end Russia’s war, fearful of being frozen out by Washington and Moscow. They dread a deal favorable to President Vladimir Putin — who will meet President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a historic three-way meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.

The good news for them is that the United States says it is now pushing to include Europe in the next rounds of diplomacy. The bad news, say governments, officials and foreign policy analysts, is the alarming new suggestion from Trump’s team: that the entire future of European security should be up for discussion too  — the same demand that Putin has pushed for years.

To the Russian leader, redrawing Europe’s security map means scaling back NATO’s presence, righting what he perceives as the injustices imposed on Moscow after the Soviet Union’s collapse. A succession of senior European officials have lambasted the idea, warning that Washington risks “walking into Moscow’s trap,” as Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, put it.
“This is all rather bizarre,” former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves said, summing up this sentiment in an interview with NBC News on Monday.

It’s not clear how or why the U.S. came to float a maximalist demand that Putin first made in 2021, one that was widely rejected by Western governments months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But in recent days, as Washington ups its pressure for a breakthrough in peace talks, Russia and the U.S. have both revived the idea.
Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and envoy, wrote Friday that talks should tackle the “broader postwar European security arrangements.”

Earlier this month, he lamented “decades of mistrust” and “competing security concerns” between Russia and Europe, vowing to address these by building an “enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” Kushner has also stressed that NATO would remain central to European defense and that no country should have a veto over another’s alliances.

Trump himself has also hinted that he seeks a final deal encompassing the entire continent. “It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” he told reporters in the Oval Office earlier this month. “I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.”
Instead, the idea has been met with unease and dismay, viewed by many in Europe as echoing Putin’s hard-line war goals.

Whereas Kushner described Europe and Russia as neighbors unable to resolve their differences, the historical record shows the aggression has chiefly been directed one way. Russia seized Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula in 2014, then launching a full-scale invasion in 2022, while waging sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation against the West.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Kushner’s suggestion also touches on a central European fear: that Washington will pursue a deal at almost any cost, even if  that emboldens Putin to expand his aggression.
“Why are two real estate agents pushing this idea?” Ilves  said referring to Kushner and Steve Witkoff, another Trump envoy, both of whom made their fortunes in real estate before entering diplomacy.

“These people aren’t even diplomats,” said Ilves, who led his former Soviet republic from 2006 to 2016. “I’m not sure they have much of an idea of the long history of the development of security architecture in Europe relating to Russia.”

Asked about the criticisms, assistant White House press secretary Olivia Wales said the U.S. proposal sought to “strengthen existing European security arrangements, with NATO at their core, while developing practical mechanisms to prevent future conflict.”

Security guarantees for  Ukraine “cannot be designed without understanding the broader security framework in which they will operate,” she said in an email, adding that any final agreement must respect Europe and Ukraine’s sovereignty “and be agreed by the relevant parties.”
European officials are nonetheless unnerved by Kushner’s remarks.

Kallas, the E.U. foreign policy chief, described Russia’s maximalist war demands as “really absurd,” while German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pointed out that “Europe has a security architecture — we don’t need a new one.”

Elsewhere, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the rules were not the issue: “The problem is that Russia is breaking them.” And even Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was adamant that the “security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe and NATO, not by Russia.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the idea as “dangerous,” saying that European security “should not be the main agenda.”
Ukraine’s view is that Russia is in no place to make such demands, given that it’s spent more than four years failing to win the war.

“At this stage, the most Putin can negotiate is a fair ceasefire along the current line of contact,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said. And “frankly, Europe does not need a new security order; it already exists, and Russia is constantly violating it.”
Kyiv and its European backers also argue that a ceasefire must come before any peace talks, accusing Russia of stalling so it can keep bombing civilian infrastructure ahead of the frigid winter.

If Europe accepts Russia’s demands about wider continental security before there is a ceasefire, Moscow “will try to create the impression that it’s our fault that the war continues, because we don’t want to accept all their demands,” according to Sven Biscop, a director at the Egmont Institute, a Belgian think tank.

He said he believed dialogue with Russia is a good thing, a view echoed by influential Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who in an interview with the Financial Times published Tuesday said that it had been “irresponsible” to outsource talks with Putin to the U.S., which he said could be leaning toward carving up Europe into spheres of influence.
Back in Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., urged Trump’s team to refuse Putin’s demands.

The Russian leader not only wanted control of Ukraine but “he wants to redesign NATO to accommodate his revisionist ambitions,” Shaheen said, adding that any discussions about European security infrastructure should be a “nonstarter,” for the U.S. which “has benefited from the Alliance.”
Amid all of this, any substantial progress toward ending the war remains elusive.

The latest round of talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week produced no major breakthrough. Kushner said Washington was working toward what could be the largest prisoner swap of the war, while reporting that Russia had agreed to give Europe a seat at the table during the next round.

Russia hasn’t quite confirmed that, instead saying that it needs “to understand from the Europeans themselves” what they can “contribute to the peace process” before allowing them to join, as Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday.

There has been some internal wrangling among the European nations about who might represent them. Leaders have agreed on a team comprising the United Kingdom (which left the E.U. in 2020), France, Germany, Italy and Poland, alongside representatives of the European Commission and European Council. Kallas herself was left off the team.
“I don’t know who among the current leaders could be a sane dialogue partner,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the state-run news agency Tass on Monday.

He likened the chosen group of European countries to “the Quartet,” a satirical poem by Russian author Ivan Krylov. In it, a monkey, a donkey, a goat and a bear blame their failure to form a string quartet on the seating arrangement rather than their lack of musical ability.
That, at least, involved agreeing to a seating arrangement.

title: Vladimir Putin’s prized bridge is partially destroyed in Ukrainian strike
summary: A key bridge connecting the occupied Crimean Peninsula with mainland Russia suffered significant damage Tuesday, a landmark blow to President Vladimir Putin.
story: A key bridge connecting the occupied Crimean Peninsula with mainland Russia suffered significant damage Tuesday, a landmark blow to President Vladimir Putin.

Videos and photos geolocated by NBC News show the partial destruction of the strategically important Kerch Bridge, with one section collapsed into the water. Russian authorities confirmed that the structure had been damaged shutting down traffic and that an emergency government meeting had been called after back-to-back attacks starting Monday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack “an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure.” He shared video in a post on X that appears to show a missile approaching the section of the bridge that was later seen damaged.

The SBU, Ukraine’s Security Service, said in a separate statement that one of the bridge’s metal arches and the road span beneath it were completely destroyed, and the railway section was also damaged, using a “wide range of Ukrainian-made weapons.”
Dealing critical damage to the bridge is a significant coup for Kyiv, as it reels from deadly Russian attacks on its own vital infrastructure, including two bridges in the capital.

The damage to his signature achievement is likely to sour Putin’s mood ahead of the extraordinary meeting this week with President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Putin made the construction of the bridge his flagship project, meant to solidify Russian dominance over Crimea, the peninsula he illegally annexed in 2014.
Beyond its symbolic value, the road and rail bridge has served as a vital supply route for the Russian military.

Asked how Putin reacted to the attacks, his spokesman Dmitry Peskov said a plan will be drawn up to restore the bridge. “There is, in fact, no doubt that the bridge will be restored. And it will be even better than before,” Peskov said.

The Russian Transport Ministry said Tuesday all train and vehicular traffic on the bridge had been suspended after the second attack overnight. The first attack was reported early Monday. “Experts are assessing the damage,” the ministry said.

Russia’s Investigative Committee said Tuesday it had opened a criminal case into what it called “a terrorist act” in connection with the bridge attacks, confirming there was “damage to the structure.”

Zelenskyy said the bridge attack was the seventh stage of an operation that lasted several weeks. He said his forces destroyed air defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment and other targets “on the way to the final objective.”

title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented  meeting on the sidelines of APEC, officials say
summary: President Donald Trump will meet with the leaders of China and Russia on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzen, China’s tech hub, next week, an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world’s biggest nuclear powers.
story: President Donald Trump will meet with the leaders of China and Russia on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzen, China’s tech hub, next week, an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world’s biggest nuclear powers.

“President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People’s Republic of China and the president of the Russian Federation,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, said in a call with reporters Friday night. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous.”

It is not anticipated that any sort of agreement will come from the trilateral meeting, according to a senior U.S. official, who described the session as an “entry point” and “the first conversation,” pointing to the reduction of nuclear arsenals as a key topic.

“We do think it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the senior U.S. official said about the issue of nuclear weapons.

Beijing’s arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China.
The three-way summit with Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin comes at a complicated moment in relations for the three countries.

Trump intends to discuss the Iran war with the two leaders, but not the war in Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official, who noted that discussions about the war in Ukraine are a separate “track” that China is not part of so it would not be “appropriate.”

Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world’s foremost economic powers.

Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.
There is no bilateral with Putin scheduled, but the two leaders will appear at events and the trilateral meeting together, according to a senior U.S. official.
There are no plans for Trump to engage with North Korea during the trip, according to a senior U.S. official.

Separately, Elon Musk will be the only business leader who is part of the president’s delegation, according to a senior U.S. official, who noted that other U.S. business leaders will attend the summit in their own capacity but there is no official U.S. business delegation.
Musk will not be part of any official meetings, according to a senior U.S. official.

Two senior U.S. officials said that they don’t think Trump will raise the espionage investigation focused on Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese intelligence agent who allegedly had a romantic relationship with Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, with China.

“The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip. In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls,” a senior U.S. official said. “These are national security matters that we develop in the administration and interagency process, and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there.”
Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit
By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China’s growing clout and prestige.
For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.
For Subscribers

“I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like,” said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
For Subscribers

The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.

More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China’s argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia’s war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.

The trilateral meeting could undercut China’s push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.
“You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism,” he said.
The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years
Putin and Xi are no strangers. They’ve fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.”

Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.
Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.

As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia’s energy resources and became Moscow’s principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.

In the lead-up to Russia’s war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship.” China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv’s Western allies played a part in provoking Russia’s military action in Ukraine.
Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing’s policy on issues related to Taiwan.

Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back.

Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can’t be enforced on others.

“It’s clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant,” Peskov said. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect.”
